title: Delean-Botkin resigns from Talbot Board of Education
content:
Susan Delean-Botkin resigned from the Talbot County Board of Education effective immediately to focus on her new role as an Oxford commissioner. She was appointed to the seat in June 2023 and previously served on the school board from January 2017 to 2022, including a term as president from 2020 to 2022.

Delean-Botkin cited personal reasons for leaving the school board, but praised her experience working with "top quality people" and expressed hope that the board would continue to maintain high graduation rates and low dropout rates. She also emphasized the importance of expanding Career and Technical Education courses and implementing the Blueprint for Maryland's Future plan.

Talbot County Public Schools Executive Assistant Charlene Gould announced that the governor's office will appoint a new board member to fill Delean-Botkin's seat until elections in November 2024. Delean-Botkin had previously lost an election to Commissioner Katrina Greer, who took her place on the board.

In her new role as Oxford commissioner, Delean-Botkin faces challenges due to the town's limited growth and desire to maintain its quality of life. She stated that Oxford has "limits on growth" and that many residents want to preserve the town's integrity.

Notable quotes from Delean-Botkin include: "School board was a fabulous experience...I think what we have to look at is, Oxford a town of about 600 folks...Three sides are surrounded by water, so we have limits on growth. People tend to want to move to Oxford because of the quality of life."

title: Kent 4-H alumna Jill Bramble to lead National Council
content: Jill Bramble, a Kent County 4-H alumna, has been named president and CEO of the National 4-H Council, succeeding Jennifer Sirangelo after 10 years. Bramble's appointment followed an 18-month search process. She began her tenure as a grant writer with the organization in 2005 and rose through ranks to executive vice president and chief growth officer. Her first day is Aug. 18. Bramble credits 4-H for shaping her leadership style, which she aims to give back to the organization that supported her. She has spent nearly 20 years with National 4-H Council and led teams in fundraising, brand management, communications, and legal services. Bramble's grandparents, Edwin C. "Pop" Fry and Lorraine Fry, were early supporters of the program in Montgomery County. Her appointment was widely praised by local leaders, including Pat Hill, Beth Hill, and John Hall, who cited her passion for 4-H and dedication to empowering youth.

title: Community invited to celebrate completion of KI Branch Library renovation
content:
Queen Anne's County Library is hosting a Grand Opening and Dedication celebration for its Kent Island Branch on Aug. 8, marking the completion of a renovation and expansion project led by the State of Maryland, Maryland State Library Agency, Queen Anne's County Commissioners, and community advocates.

Janet Salazar, Queen Anne's County Library director, stated that the expanded spaces aim to foster connections, broaden intellectual horizons, and facilitate sharing of ideas. The new facilities include innovative community meeting rooms with modern audio-visual technology, a welcoming lobby area, and a state-of-the-art Makerspace featuring 3D printers, laser engravers, and other equipment designed for innovation and creativity.

The ribbon-cutting ceremony on Aug. 8 will officially open the spaces to the public, with library staff providing tours and demonstrations of the Makerspace's features. The community is warmly welcomed to join in celebrating this important milestone.

Date: Aug. 8
Location: Kent Island Branch, Queen Anne's County Library
People: Janet Salazar (Queen Anne's County Library director)
Organizations: Queen Anne's County Library, State of Maryland, Maryland State Library Agency, Queen Anne's County Commissioners

title: New director hired at Chesapeake College in Cambridge
content: Lorelly Solano has been hired as director of the Chesapeake College Cambridge Center in Cambridge, MD. Born in Costa Rica, Solano joined Chesapeake College as an English as a Second Language instructor and later became an academic and career adviser before moving to the center. She earned her bachelor's degree in Costa Rica, master's degree in natural resources science from University of Maryland, and Ph.D. in public policy and urban affairs from University of Delaware. Solano will lead staff in providing services to Cambridge-based students, including credit classes, workforce training, personal enrichment opportunities, and the American Job Center. She aims to bring a student perspective to her new role and engage with the community through outreach efforts, stating that the center is a resource for everyone in Dorchester County, playing a critical role in the economic and social health of the downtown area.

title: Chrome City Ride raises $105K for Benedictine School
content:
Chrome City Ride raised $105K for Benedictine School in Ridgely, MD on July 28, 2023. The 18th annual event drew 2,100 participants and classic cars, motorcycles from six rally points across Maryland and Delaware. It supports over 200 children and adults with disabilities served by the school.

The event raised over $2 million since its inception in 2001 and has grown into one of the state's largest rides. Benedictine School serves students from MD, DE, WV, PA, and VA.

Spud Blake, volunteer chair, said the event honors the community's support for children with disabilities. Generous sponsors, community partners, and volunteers made it a success. The event featured a auctioned-off Paul Reed Smith guitar and Kid's Choice Awards.

Benedictine School earned 2-year accreditation from NCASES in 2018 and named Lorraine Slama Educator of the Year. Notable attendees include Jay Leno and celebrity donors.

Chrome City Ride has become a way for the community to learn about Benedictine's mission, which is to help children achieve their greatest potential.

title: Fair offers lots of fun, much more
content:

Skylar Blunt, 17, was crowned queen after 10 years of involvement in 4-H, showcasing her animal husbandry skills. As reigning queen, she plans to promote 4-H in her community. Macrina Zbobysz, 14, won the princess pageant with impressive archery skills, while Lily Hutchison took home first place in the working weather goat show.

Fair Queen Rebecca Brault enjoyed her reign and praised 4-H for its growth opportunities, including improving public speaking skills and learning practical skills like sewing and photography. Her mother, Christina Brault, highlighted the fair's role in giving a platform to 4-H's good qualities and promoting bonding experiences among participants.

Other events included a mechanical bull competition, where Tucker Riddleberger from Marydel tried to hold on for 8 seconds, and an annual cake auction that saw Ally Geib's ocean-themed cake go for $1,000. The fair offers more than just entertainment, providing valuable life lessons and opportunities for local youth.

title: School district saves thousands in energy costs - Program focuses on use and use reduction
content:
Caroline County Public Schools implemented a year-long energy conservation program managed by Cenergistic in July 2022, resulting in almost $260,000 in savings. The program focused on use and reduction of energy sources, with significant reductions in electricity usage due to increased solar use and thermostat adjustments.

Cenergistic's Energy Specialist Josh Rein performed over 1,516 building audits, avoiding 1,451 metric tons of CO2 emissions equivalent to 3.5 million miles driven by an average car or powering 175 homes for a year. The district decreased energy use intensity (EUI) from 50 to 32 EUI, a significant improvement.

Superintendent Dr. Derek Simmons and Cenergistic Client Manager Scott Muir credited the successful start of the program to Josh Rein's early involvement. The five-year contract with Cenergistic aims to improve efficient use of taxpayer dollars.

title: School board adopts new AP Physics textbook
content:
The Caroline County Board of Education adopted a new AP Physics textbook, "2018 Fundamentals of Physics," extended 12th edition, at its Aug. 1 meeting. The 40-textbook purchase costs $3,375, including online resources, and aligns with the College Board AP Physics course audit outline. Authors D. Halliday, R. Resnick, and J. Walker published by John Wiley & Sons.

Committee members included Amy Towers, Chad Shelly, Nikki VonDen-Bosch, Nikki Welzel, John Moyer, Matt Spiker, and Daniell Darling. The board aims to support teachers and students in the high school advanced placement course, affecting a small pool of approximately 10 students currently enrolled at North Caroline High School.

The textbook is expected to be critical in supporting both teachers and students as they build the AP Physics course, which Colonel Richardson High School hopes to establish as well.

title: 'Love In Action' displayed by Black Excellence fund
content:
The Black Excellence Community Fund (BECF) of the Eastern Shore Giving Circle awarded grants to three Lower Shore nonprofits during an August 5 event celebrating Black Philanthropy Month. The recipients received $500 each for their work in:

* Young Elites of the Eastern Shore West to East Coast Aviation Network (Y.E.E.S. W.E. C.A.N.), promoting aviation and aerospace technology among young leaders.
* SchooLARS 4 STEM, a grassroots mentoring program supporting K-12 students with strong STEM aptitude.
* Faith Over Fear Economic Empowerment Inc., building stronger communities through resources and professional development for black-owned businesses.

The event highlighted recent proclamations from Wicomico County designating August as Black Philanthropy Month, along with a citation from the Maryland General Assembly honoring BECF. BECF was created in 2022 at the Community Foundation to preserve cultural awareness and pride while promoting education, health, and welfare in the Black community.

Grantee representatives included Nicole Turner (SchooLARS 4 STEM), Angela Morton (Faith Over Fear Economic Empowerment Inc.), Cheryl Walker (Y.E.E.S. W.E. C.A.N.), Sharon Morris, Lori Carter, and Sonya Whited (BECF founding members).

title: New director takes the helm at Chesapeake's Cambridge Center
content:
Dr. Lorelly Solano is the new director of the Chesapeake College Cambridge Center, located on Race Street in Cambridge, MD. She will lead staff in providing services to Cambridge-based students, including credit classes, workforce training, and personal enrichment opportunities. The center also houses the American Job Center.

Solano previously worked as an English as a Second Language instructor and academic advisor at Chesapeake College. A native of Costa Rica, she earned her bachelor's degree from the University of Costa Rica and later completed a master's degree in natural resources science at the University of Maryland. She went on to earn a Ph.D. in public policy and urban affairs at the University of Delaware.

Solano's interests in education and public policy align with her new role, where she aims to bring a student perspective to community outreach efforts. The Cambridge Center plays a critical role in Dorchester County's economic and social health. Solano's background as a rural-urban bridge between her Costa Rican roots and US experiences informs her approach to building sustainable communities through policy and education.

Solano began her new role on August 16, 2023, with plans to engage with the community through outreach efforts.

title: Governor visits Benedictine
content:
Governor Wes Moore visited Benedictine Programs and Services on August 17, 2023, during his Eastern Shore tour for the Maryland Association of Counties summer conference. He was joined by Secretary Carol Beatty, who believes Benedictine is a critical organization for individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities in Maryland. The campus offers a year-round educational residential program for students aged 5-21, as well as an expansion supported by a $1.5 million capital grant.

Moore met with staff, including Director Scott Evans and Educational Director Julie Hickey, who praised the governor's enthusiasm for the students he met. He high-fived students and gave a "peace out" gesture to teachers. Benedictine has 148 referrals and takes in 12 students per year, serving over 200 children and adults with developmental disabilities.

The organization offers employment and vocational services for transitional youth and adults, ages 22-70, and is one of only four residential facilities for the developmentally disabled and autistic that can accept students with moderate to severe challenges. Benedictine has a non-sectarian, non-religious mission and serves students from 16 counties and several states, including Maryland, Delaware, and West Virginia.

Moore visited a classroom where two students were learning about pirates, and he gave high-fives for correct answers. He also met with Peggy, whose son Jake was enrolled at Benedictine for the first time, and consoled her as she cried tears of both sadness and gratitude.

title: School lunches - yesterday and today
content:
In 1940s and 1950s Bishopville School:

* Meals were packed in round tin pails or brown bags.
* Lunches consisted of biscuits with meat or cornbread leftovers, water, apples, and occasional snacks.
* Late Mrs. Lynch was the cook; she served brownies, gingerbread, sheet cake with frosting, and Jello for dessert.
* Popular sandwiches included meatloaf, tuna fish, peanut butter and jelly, bologna and cheese.

In 1970s-1980s:

* School cafeterias changed with jukeboxes, long tables, and a variety of food options (spaghetti with meatballs, garlic bread, salad).
* Lunches were often purchased on "pizza days" or "taco days," with fewer sandwiches.
* Introduced new foods like beef jerky, cheese sticks, hot chips, and pop-top cans.

In 2000-2023:

* Most schools now offer two or three lunch choices, including a la carte menu options.
* Changes in school food led to increased variety and decreased reliance on traditional school lunches.

Notable figures include Marie Savage's family members who attended Bishopville School; her mother was known for feeding neighbors and sharing food during economic hard times.

title: Uncommon classes: How pop culture imagines Jesus, from cartoons to musicals - Images of Jesus have always been complex and contradictory
content:
Here is a highly condensed version of the article:

The "Jesus in the Modern Imagination" course explores the relationship between religion and media, focusing on ancient depictions of Jesus and comparing them to modern films, comics, and music. The course designer's background in religious studies was shaped by pop culture, including musicals like "Jesus Christ Superstar." 

The course examines gaps in biblical narratives, such as Jesus' childhood, using apocryphal sources like the Infancy Gospel of Thomas. Students discuss these texts alongside novels like Christopher Moore's "Lamb" and engage in conversations about interpretations of Jesus.

The course is relevant now because Jesus is a contested figure with different meanings for various cultures and societies. It does not attempt to answer who Jesus was but examines how humanity has grappled with this question.

Through the course, students learn to analyze how interpretations of religious figures are shaped by their communities. They also create their own Jesus movies as part of the semester's project.

title: Students paying less for college than 15 years ago
content:
Washington - Students are paying less for college than they did 15 years ago. Former Education Department senior adviser Dan Currell's essay dispels "The Truth about College Costs" and reveals that colleges discovered in the late 1980s and early 1990s that high tuition was good for marketing, leading to a 96% of students paying around $15,000 per year in tuition.

Currell states that most elite schools could fill their annual enrollments several times over with affluent students who would pay higher advertised tuition. However, these institutions have large endowments that enable generous tuition assistance for less affluent students. The rest of colleges use "sleight of hand" to keep discounts hidden.

The Economist validates Currell's thesis, stating that average tuition at home-state public colleges is around $10,000 and private colleges discount tuition by more than 50% on average. However, schools have an incentive to seem extortionate due to the association between higher prices and higher quality.

Currell notes that institutions award institutional scholarships with no money behind them, often exceeding 50% discounts. This has led to "fundamental dishonesty" in college pricing, making it appear as though colleges are running out of money despite collecting their full sticker price. The actual reality is that colleges would be struggling to manage the extra funds.

The social cost of this deception is a mountain of college debt, with many families believing there is a $200,000 tollbooth on the road to the American dream. Academia's moral tutelage has led to criticism of deceptive capitalism practices, but Currell's essay reveals that even institutions appointed as moral authorities have questionable practices.

Sources: National Affairs, The Economist, and Dan Currell

title: Caroline schools serve free meals to all students - Cafeterias will still charge for extra items
content:
Caroline County Public Schools now offer free breakfasts and lunches to all students through the Community Eligibility Provision program of the US Department of Agriculture's Food and Nutrition Service. The program allows schools in low-income areas to serve meals at no cost to all enrolled students without collecting household applications.

Caroline County School District Supervisor of Food Services, Beth Brewster, stated that this program will benefit over 3,000 students who already qualify for free meals due to their income level being only $50 above the threshold. The district has had a high rate of free and reduced lunch participation, with 66% last year.

CCPS will still charge for extra items like snacks, but families are encouraged to register with MySchoolBucks to pay for these items. Brewster emphasized that this program makes it an even playing field for students to access nutritious meals, allowing them to develop their gray matter and come to school ready to learn.

The district supports local farmers and businesses by using locally sourced produce in its food services. This approach is also environmentally friendly and more nutritious for students.

title: It's back to school at Easton Elementary
content:
Easton Elementary School welcomed students back for the new school year on August 28, with smiles and warm welcomes from staff members. Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi and Board of Education member Amy Dodson were present to welcome students. 

First grader Jackson Follett arrived excitedly for his first day, accompanied by his mom Danielle, who is starting a new job as an instructional assistant at the school. The Folletts recently moved to Easton from another location.

Talbot County Public Schools staff ensured safe transit and greeted students upon arrival. Teachers connected with students, some of whom were familiar faces, while others had wide-eyed looks of curiosity. 

Staff members performed their duties, and crossing guards welcomed pedestrians. "First day!" was an oft-repeated phrase as teachers and administrators interacted with students. Pepukayi described the scene as "energizing" and a "new beginning."

title: Holt Scholarship Fund awards $560,000
content:
The Roberta B. Holt Scholarship Fund at Mid-Shore Community Foundation awarded $560,000 in scholarships to deserving Caroline County students as part of its 10th anniversary celebration. Over the past decade, the fund has awarded $2.8 million.

Roberta "Bobbie" Baxter Holt was a native of Federalsburg who graduated from Federalsburg High School and received degrees from the University of Delaware, University of Minnesota, and Catholic University of America. She had a successful career as a psychotherapist and research associate at the National Institutes of Mental Health.

Haines Holt, Bobbie's brother, established the scholarship program to fulfill her commitment to education. Education was something Bobbie valued, and she wanted to use her success and estate to encourage others to do the same.

The Mid-Shore Community Foundation awards scholarships to high school seniors in Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's, and Talbot Counties. In FY23, MSCF awarded 221 scholarships totaling $1.7 million. The Roberta B. Holt Scholarship is one of the majority of scholarships awarded through a Pooled Scholarship Application.

Bobbie was exposed to the needs of the Caroline County community while working with the Caroline County Department of Social Services before her death. Her legacy lives on through the scholarship fund, which will open its 2023/24 Pooled Scholarship Application on December 1, 2023.

title: 'ArtScene the Podcast' features QA Teacher of the Year Andrea Schulte
content:
Andrea Schulte, 2023 QACPS Teacher of the Year, is featured on "ArtScene the Podcast". Born to study art therapy in college, she became a nationally renowned art educator with a student-centered approach and passion for helping students with developmental disabilities.

Schulte led Kent Island High School's National Art Honor Society to record-breaking scholarship offers ($1 million), and her advanced art students earned a 100% pass rate on AP 2-D Art and Design portfolios for the fifth straight year.

Principal Dan Harding praises Schulte, saying she dedicates herself to the school community through clubs, activities, and student groups. Her 2-D Studio Art program flourished, earning state, regional, and national awards.

Students, including Alyssa Scalia (Congressional honors), have blossomed into award-winning artists under Schulte's care. Every KIHS art student has had their piece showcased at the district-wide ArtScene exhibition.

Schulte was also recognized by the Maryland Art Education Association as 2023 MAEA Secondary Art Educator of the Year and will be featured on "ArtScene the Podcast" in a two-part interview.

title: University of Maryland Eastern Shore increases enrollment once again
content:
The University of Maryland Eastern Shore (UMES) has increased new student enrollment for the third consecutive year, with 825 students enrolled in the fall of 2022, surpassing the largest class since 2015. The growth is part of a national trend at Historically Black Colleges and Universities, driven by President Heidi M. Anderson's initiative to increase enrollment and retention efforts.

President Anderson challenged the university to grow enrollment while enhancing retention rates, which have seen a 10% uptick. Darryl Isom, director of admissions and recruitment, attributes the gains to the university's brand definition and marketing efforts, including a regional ad campaign and partnerships with consulting firms.

The university is also focusing on registering transfer students, expected to bring approximately 200 new students to campus. Latoya Jenkins, vice president of enrollment management and student experience, notes that transfer students from institutions like Wor-Wic Community College have seen improved success rates at UMES.

Long-term goals include returning enrollment numbers back to pre-pandemic levels, potentially reaching around 4,000 students, but this will require continued progress and time.

title: Caroline schools get off to smooth start
content:

School Principal Stephanie Brohawn greeted students as they arrived, while Simmons observed that elementaries typically start with smiles and hugs. At Colonel Richardson High School, Principal Jared Sherman issued a warning about cell phones, stating that they should be turned off during classes.

Biology teacher Bobbi Bee expressed enthusiasm for the new school year, saying she loves her job. The first day saw no tears among students.

title: Caroline County schools welcome new teachers
content:
Caroline County Public Schools welcomed 55 new teachers for the 2023-2024 school year. The orientation began on August 15 with a breakfast and trainings in instruction, technology, safety, communication, and data systems. 

Superintendent Dr. Derek Simmons led the tour of schools, including Marydel to Federalsburg and its 10 schools. New teachers also visited the Support Services Center and Caroline County Culinary Center. The orientation concluded on August 24 at Colonel Richardson High School with presentations by Simmons and professional development sessions.

Sponsored meals were provided by various organizations, including the Caroline County Educators Association, Educational System Federal Credit Union, WIN Transport, Lions Clubs of Caroline County, Pep-Up/Tri-Gas & Oil, and Summit Bank. 

New teachers were welcomed at each school, with administrators, supervisors, and mentors in attendance.

title: Constitution Day includes Douglass reenactment
content: The Mid-Shore Constitution Alliance will host its second annual Constitution Day celebration on September 16, featuring a reenactment of Frederick Douglass performed by Darius Wallace from noon-2 p.m. at Talbot County Courthouse lawn. Speakers will discuss the Constitution's promise of freedom, local music and activities will be available, and an honor guard ceremony will take place. The event marks part of the alliance's educational programming to increase Constitutional IQ for students; a scholarship program awards $1,000 annually to Mid-Shore students interested in constitutional careers. The alliance partners with Washington College Institute for Religion, Politics & Culture and Operation Frederick Douglass on the Hill to promote civic engagement.

title: Bullying lawsuit in Dorchester County Court
content:
A jury trial is underway in a lawsuit alleging negligence from Dorchester County Public Schools administrators and teachers in handling bullying and harassment of former Mace's Lane Middle School student Sierra Gambrill.
The lawsuit, filed in 2018, claims negligence by the school board, James Bell, Cynitha Woolford, Michael Collins, and two unnamed substitute teachers who allegedly covered up and participated in the behavior.
Gambrill experienced bullying and assault from multiple students over six months in 2016-2017, including hair pulling, name calling, hitting, and physical attacks.
Two violent incidents occurred: October 2016, when Gambrill was attacked by two male classmates; December 14, 2016, when she was flipped backward by another male student.
Plaintiffs alleged that defendants failed to address the family's concerns for Gambrill's safety, failed to supervise and train substitute teachers, and "exacted unjustified discipline" on Gambrill through suspensions.
The case has undergone several court rulings, including a 2019 summary judgment in favor of defendants, which was later reversed by the Maryland Appellate Court of Appeals in 2021.

title: Capital News Service compiled these stories, data
content: "Contracted Out", a massive effort by four faculty members and dozens of students at University of Maryland's Philip Merrill College of Journalism, aimed to process data from 295 vendor payments in each of Maryland's 24 school districts. Faculty members Derek Willis, Jerry Zremski, Adam Marton, and editors Marty Kaiser and Josh Land oversaw the project. Students involved included those from lecturer Derek Willis' news applications class, who worked with data journalist Derek Willis, and multimedia reporting students, including Charles Bachmann, Benicio Balignot, Joseph Barke, and others. Destiny Herbers designed the project's data page, while Kara Thompson and Joel Lev-Tov contributed to the project. The effort was led by Local News Network at University of Maryland and Capital News Service Digital Bureau, with a web application displaying summaries of vendor payments developed by Destiny Herbers.

title: 'Contracted Out' - An unprecedented look at Maryland public school spending
content:
The Local News Network at the University of Maryland's Philip Merrill College of Journalism has published an easily searchable database, "Contracted Out," which provides a comprehensive itemization of public school district vendor payments in Maryland over the past four years. The database includes information from all 24 public school districts, with individual districts able to be broken out. It contains data on every vendor paid over $25,000 between the 2018-2019 and 2021-2022 school years, covering items such as health insurance, buses, computers, and meals.

The database was compiled by students and faculty at UMD's Philip Merrill College of Journalism, with input from experts like Marguerite Roza, director of Georgetown University's Edunomics Lab. The data was obtained through the state's Open Data Portal but lacks detail due to limitations in reporting requirements.

School districts have differing policies regarding vendor payments, and some list state and federal taxes as vendor payments while others exclude them. The Office of Legislative Audits sees the database as a transparency and accountability tool, while the Office of the State Inspector General for Education encourages public contact if suspicious activity is seen.

Key findings include:

- The vast majority (80% to 90%) of school spending goes to teacher and staff salaries.
- Vendor payments account for only a small portion of total spending.
- Some districts have missing data due to non-compliance with reporting requirements.
- A recent audit in Montgomery County Public Schools found evidence of irregularities in the transportation department.

The project's findings will be included in accompanying stories, while local journalists and citizens are encouraged to review the database for potential questionable vendor payments.

title: Audits show trouble lurking in school contracts
content:
Audits show trouble lurking in school contracts:

- Maryland's inspector general for education acknowledges flaws in the system allowing officials to misuse it.
- State audits in recent years raised questions about contract spending in other Maryland public school districts, including:
  • Montgomery County: Two district transportation department officials pleaded guilty to theft and misconduct, with one receiving $352,568.68 from an "off-the-books" account.
  • Baltimore City, Howard County, Charles County, and Calvert County: Auditors found issues such as unauthorized transactions, insufficient documentation, and failure to complete proper procurement processes.

Key findings:
- Nearly every school district failed to complete proper documentation for approval of intergovernmental purchasing agreements.
- Employees made purchases without documenting why they were necessary and beneficial to the district.
- The Office of Legislative Audits released an audit in January finding 171 repeated findings that local school systems had yet to address from previous audits.
- Calvert County Public Schools paid $642,000 in transportation costs with vague invoices or mismatched pricing.
- Montgomery County School District officials confirmed all findings and planned procedures to correct problems.

Important dates:
- May: Charles Ewald pleaded guilty to felony theft and misconduct in office.
- June: Todd Watkins pleaded guilty to misconduct in office.
- January 2022: The Office of Legislative Audits reported on Calvert County Public Schools' spending issues.
- January: The audit of the Maryland State Department of Education was released.

Important people:
- Richard P. Henry, Maryland's inspector general for education
- Matthew Streett, assistant director of the Compliance and Performance Audit Division in the Office of Legislative Audits
- Charles Ewald, former assistant transportation director of Montgomery County Public Schools
- Todd Watkins, former director of the transportation department in Montgomery County Public Schools

title: Teach your kids about giving
content: Mary Hunt, founder of EverydayCheapskate.com and author of "Debt-Proof Living," advises parents to teach their kids about giving as a way to prevent greed and prepare them for success. Money is about values, relationships, choices, and self-worth, and living what you teach is crucial. The antidote to greed is giving away time, talent, and treasure ( possessions). Everyone possesses these three T's: 24 hours/day, various talents, and possessions. Giving helps develop gratitude, joy, contentment, and stops feelings of misery.

title: Backpack giveaway draws big crowd in Goldsboro
content:
CASA of Caroline and Caroline Pride partnered for the third year to host a Backpack Giveaway in Goldsboro on August 30, distributing 110 backpacks with supplies to students and families. Town of Goldsboro representatives participated, donating money and crafts. Jeannette DeLude, town manager, praised the event's success.

Amy Horne, executive director at CASA of Caroline, said their goal is to advocate for kids in multiple systems, ensuring they have necessary supplies for success in the classroom. Angel Perez, CEO of Caroline Pride, emphasized the importance of feeling included and having what's needed to thrive.

The event is part of a community effort led by numerous businesses and individuals who donated items and money. This is CASA and Caroline Pride's third annual Backpack Giveaway, targeting vulnerable populations targeted by bullies.

title: Counties ponder money for college building - Financial commitment worries many of the county officials
content:
On September 20, 2023, counties from Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Talbot, and Queen Anne's came together virtually to discuss a $79 million project to build a new Technical Center at Chesapeake College. The state has agreed to pay for 75% of the capital project, with each county agreeing to provide local funds for the remaining 25%. The facility will be over 90,000 square feet and currently set for construction in 2026.

Chesapeake College President Cliff Coppersmith stated that the new facility is needed due to space constraints in existing buildings. Kent County Commission President Ron Fithian expressed concerns about financial aspects of the project, while Caroline County Commission Vice President Larry Porter sought more information on the cost.

Queen Anne's County Commissioner Jack Wilson Jr. acknowledged the price as a concern but felt confident in receiving additional state funding. Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said they would not be able to send a letter of intent due to fiscal responsibilities, but would send a letter of support without a binding commitment.

Talbot County Council member Keasha Haythe announced her intention to vote in favor of submitting a letter of intent, citing the need for forward-thinking and accommodating future labor force needs. The counties will decide individually on whether to submit letters of intent by September 28.

title: Commission president: 'I'm on the fence with this' - Breeding balks at Caroline's share of $94M building replacement
content:
Commission President Travis Breeding expressed hesitation over funding Chesapeake College's $79 million request to build a new technology center in Caroline County. The project has been submitted to the Maryland State Department of Budget and Management for consideration on September 28. 

Breeding is concerned about future unknown costs associated with the 2021 Blueprint for Maryland's Future and the county's ability to take on debt. He wants to know how much the local Career and Technology Education Program will utilize the facility during the day.

Talbot and Queen Anne's counties have agreed to help finance the project, but Dorchester County declined. Kent County has not announced its decision. Caroline County can join a bond with Queen Anne's County, increasing the final cost to over $6 million.

Commissioner Larry Porter supports funding the project, citing its need for young adults and potential to increase county revenue. However, he is cautious about Blueprint credit for the project.

Commissioners agree that the building is necessary, but Breeding wants more information before making a decision. The commission will make a final decision at their September 26 meeting.

title: Tyranny Of The Loud At Washington College
content:
Here is a highly condensed version of the article:

Washington College professor Robert George was attacked and intimidated by protesters during his presentation on September 21, 2023, at the college in Chestertown, MD. Despite having expressed conservative views in the past, George has also frequently debated progressive thinker Cornel West, indicating that the issue is not about his ideology but rather about free speech and civil dialogue.

George, a renowned legal theorist and director of the James Madison Program, has faced death threats for his views on abortion. The protesters disrupted his presentation, waving flags, signs, whistles, music, and dancing, preventing George from speaking.

Campus security allowed the protesters to enter the room, allowing the disruption to occur. When questioned about the incident, a college spokesperson implied that Washington College agrees with the protesters' interpretation of some statements made by George in the past.

The protest was particularly egregious given Washington College's core values, which include integrity, determination, curiosity, civility, leadership, and moral courage. The college's response to the incident is unclear, but questions remain about whether the institution will uphold its student honor code and commit to free speech and civil discourse.

Notable individuals with ties to George or his ideas include:

* Cornel West, progressive professor and political activist
* Elena Kagan, Supreme Court Justice who praised George for his "sheer brilliance" and "profound and enduring integrity"

Places mentioned:

* Washington College in Chestertown, MD
* Hynson Lounge (location of the presentation)
* Berkeley, Yale, Harvard (universities visited by George)

Important dates:

* September 21, 2023 (date of the incident)

title: 'Fantastic job this summer' - Summer school program to expand next year
content:
Caroline County Public Schools aims to expand its summer education program next year, teaching 400 more students after a successful 2023 program that saw 916 students participate. The program, which ran from June 23 to July 27, was led by director of College and Career Readiness Lindsey McCormick and received "huge shout-outs" from Superintendent Dr. Derek Simmons.

The program included elementary, middle, and high school students, with special programs for students with disabilities and multilingual learners. McCormick praised the success of her team, including certified teachers, instructional assistants, and site coordinators who worked together to provide summer lessons and activities.

Highlights of the 2023 program included:

* Elementary students attended sessions at four elementary schools, with an average attendance of 14 days out of 19.
* Secondary students attended only morning sessions, with a goal to "boost our middle school program" that was met, with 40 students participating.
* Middle school students attended a tri-county career enrichment day in Dorchester County and had access to CTE mini-sessions.
* High school students participated in credit recovery courses, with 131 students passing the courses.

The program received funding from the American Rescue Plan Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief (ARP ESSER) Fund, food services, and in-kind use of buildings. McCormick expects next year's program to be the same duration and is planning to increase summer programming by 400 students. A 21st Century Grant is pending to help fund the program.

Key statistics:

* 916 students participated in the 2023 program.
* 747 elementary students attended sessions at four elementary schools.
* 70 multilingual learners participated, with 49 attending Greensboro Elementary School.
* 127 students with disabilities participated, increasing by 30 from last year.
* 131 high school students passed credit recovery courses.

Dates:

* June 23 - July 27: Duration of the summer program
* Sept. 5: Board of Education meeting where results were presented

title: Raskin leads recognition of Banned Books Week
content:
Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Maryland) and Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) introduced a bill to recognize Banned Books Week (Oct 1-7) and condemn book banning in schools and libraries. The bill has 40 House co-sponsors and 15 Senate co-sponsors, echoing previous bills that did not pass. PEN America reported a 33% increase in book banning instances from 2021-22 to 2022-23, with Florida accounting for 40% of bans. Three witnesses failed to provide solutions at the Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on book bans, citing a lack of tangible federal policy. The first state to pass a law making libraries ineligible for grants if they ban books is Illinois, which passed the legislation on June 12.

The bill recommends protecting students' rights to learn and educators' ability to teach, but does not include a unified national protocol for dealing with book bans. Raskin said, "You know, the proper response to hating a book in a free society is you don't read the book."

title: Counties sue social media over mental health in schools - Talbot among 10 counties claiming classroom distraction
content:
Counties in Maryland, including Charles County, have joined a lawsuit against social media giants Google, Meta, ByteDance, and Snap Inc., accusing them of targeting and manipulating youth to stay engaged for excessive amounts of time.

Ten counties, including Charles County, Anne Arundel, Baltimore City, Carroll, Cecil, Harford, Howard, Montgomery, Prince George's, and Talbot, have filed the lawsuit. The lawsuit claims social media platforms prioritize profit over children's mental health.

Educators in Charles County report classroom distractions, self-control issues, and increased anger and aggression among students. Teachers have implemented policies to limit device use during class, but self-regulation is a significant challenge.

School officials and researchers argue that social media usage during pivotal developmental ages can interrupt growth and exacerbate insecurities. The Centers for Disease Control reported suicide as the second leading cause of death for people aged 10-14 in 2021.

The lawsuit aims to pressure companies to create products geared towards children, with potential compensation expanding resources for behavioral health. Educators emphasize parents' responsibility in monitoring device usage and controlling access to apps.

Key individuals include Maria Navarro (Charles County Public Schools superintendent), Cheryl Davis (Henry E. Lackey High School principal), Brian Street (father of two Piccowaxen middle schoolers), and Tammika Little (St. Charles High School principal).

The lawsuit serves as a message that social media companies, educators, parents, and students must be aware of the harm caused by excessive social media use among young people.

Dates mentioned: October 5, 2023, 2021, and an unspecified year for Facebook research.

Numbers mentioned: Ten counties (including Charles County) have joined the lawsuit; one in three girls feel worse about their bodies due to Instagram according to Facebook research; 10-14 years old age group.

title: Dorchester schools gain proficiency on tests
content:
Dorchester County Public Schools saw significant increases in English language arts scores on the spring 2023 Maryland Comprehensive Assessment Program (MCAP) assessments, with Dorchester County growing 4.1 percentage points and ranking 11th state-wide. Proficient learner percentages increased for grades three through six: 

- Third graders (31% vs 26.4%)
- Fourth graders (32% vs 27.6%)
- Fifth graders (33% vs 26.8%)
- Sixth graders (33% vs 22.2%), a 10.8% increase
- Seventh and eighth graders showed decreases, with percentages dropping from 24.1% to 20% for seventh graders and 29.2% to 27% for eighth graders.

The district's average growth outpaced the state average of 2.9 percentage points. Director of Curriculum, Instruction, and Assessment Jodi Colman attributed the growth to diagnostic testing, training in the science of reading, and targeted instruction. In math, significant increases were seen in grade seven and Algebra I proficiency, while decreases were noted for other grades.

MCAP data showed: 

- Seventh graders increased from less than 5% to 11%
- Algebra I students increased from less than 5% to 10%
- Grade six saw a decrease from 10% to less than 5%

Board Member Chris Wheedleton emphasized the importance of recognizing and improving the data, calling for action to address areas of improvement.

title: Carey Wright appointed interim state superintendent
content:
The Maryland State Board of Education unanimously appointed Carey Wright as Interim State Superintendent of Schools for the remainder of the current term through June 30, 2024. Wright will begin her service on October 23, 2023. She previously served as state superintendent in Mississippi for nine years, improving the Quality Counts grade from an F to a C and increasing literacy rates.

Wright is a Maryland educator with decades of experience, having worked in Prince George's, Howard, and Montgomery County Public Schools. She implemented the first publicly funded Early Learning Collaborative program in Mississippi and earned recognition from the National Institute for Early Education Research.

Wright obtained her bachelor's, master's, and doctoral degrees from the University of Maryland, College Park. Governor Wes Moore welcomed Wright to the position, praising her expertise and commitment to transparency, accountability, and partnership.

Wright will receive an annual salary of $350,000, prorated for the time she serves. The State Board and MSDE Transition Team will support her during onboarding, with a national search for a permanent state superintendent set to continue in the coming months.

title: 'My purpose was fulfilled' - Caregiver awarded scholarship
content:
Casey Hart, a Worton resident and professional caregiver for Griswold Home Care, was awarded $3,000 in scholarship funds for the 2023 National Caregiver Scholarship Program. Hart developed sepsis after surgery in 2020 and required around-the-clock care, thanks to her two aunts who provided her with daily care. The experience gave her insight into the vulnerability of caregivers' clients. Hart began caregiving at an early age and feels fortunate to be part of Griswold Home Care's team.

Hart was nominated for the scholarship due to her exceptional caregiving in Kent County's Worton area. She plans to use the funds towards pursuing a RN nursing degree. Hart finds joy in learning the stories of her clients, including veterans and those with disabilities. The Jean Griswold Foundation Board of Directors supports caregivers financially through scholarships, believing that education elevates the care profession.

CEO Michael Slupecki stated that money often hinders motivated caregivers from obtaining education or certification, which benefits not only Griswold but also the country as a whole. Hart was quoted saying "My purpose was fulfilled," expressing her gratitude for Griswold's support and her desire to continue serving clients.

title: 'We will celebrate some of the books that have been challenged' - Library director 'shocked' by efforts nationwide to remove controversial books
content:
Arnessa Dowell, Executive Director of Kent County Library, discussed her biggest challenges as she adapted to the pandemic and shifted focus to upgrading technology and improving program offerings. She emphasized the importance of inclusivity, citing examples such as the county's free laptop program and e-library expansions.

Dowell's commitment to supporting rural residents is evident in her work, which includes expanding summer reading programs and partnering with Maryland Humanities for the "One Maryland One Book" program featuring author Tommy Orange's "There There."

In response to efforts nationwide to remove controversial books, Dowell stated she was shocked by the movement. Kent County Library will participate in American Libraries Association's Banned Books Week, celebrating challenged books still on their shelves.

Born in Mississippi and raised in Germany, Dowell became a librarian after her mother's illness, citing supportive colleagues as a catalyst for her career. She attributed her greatest success to this year's summer reading program, which saw over 900,000 minutes read.

Upcoming events include a presentation with Chief Donna Wolf Mother Abbott about the Nause-Waiwash Band of Indians, and Dowell expressed excitement about the "One Maryland One Book" program featuring Orange's work. Her favorite book is Dr. Seuss' "Oh, the Places You'll Go," reflecting the library's purpose.

title: 'You are a 10!' - Speaker motivates, inspires at Talbot schools
content:
International motivational performer Alex Boyé visited Talbot County Public Schools October 11-13 to inspire students in healthy thinking and interactions with others. ParentGuidance.org partnered with TCPS to bring Boyé to speak with students in fifth through 12th grade. TCPS Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi described Boyé as "phenomenal" and thanked him for sharing his wisdom.

Boyé, a father of eight, shared his experiences growing up as the son of a single Nigerian immigrant mother in the UK, overcoming challenges to succeed as an international performer and author. He performs hit songs and delivers a message of hope, optimism, and self-worth. His book and video "You Are a 10!" were released with success, garnering positive reviews from school districts and students nationwide.

Boyé is known for his African-infused music and competed on "America's Got Talent" in 2015. He was named Rising Artist of the Year and grand prize winner in a Pepsi & Hard Rock Café music contest in 2017. The "You Are a 10!" tour, funded by the MD Aware II grant, provides support to teachers, parents, and students through ParentGuidance.org's Cook Center for Human Connection.

title: Talbot Mentors celebrates recent college graduates
content:
Talbot Mentors celebrated recent college graduates Tabius J. Wilson, Jr., Randei Collins, and Taylan Brooks, who graduated from Hampton University, Washington College, and Morgan State University respectively in 2022-2023. 

Wilson graduated Cum Laude with a liberal studies degree, minored in leadership studies, and served as president of the Student Government Association and vice president of Eastern Regional Alpha Phi Alpha fraternity. He received full-ride scholarships to George Mason University's Antonin Scalia Law School and won several awards, including the First Annual Gamma Lota Darrell K. Williams Leadership Award.

Collins, who joined Talbot Mentors in 2013, graduated with a communications degree, minors in writing and marketing, and was accepted into the Washington Scholars Program at Washington College. She served in multiple campus organizations and received honors for her academic achievements.

Brooks, who joined Talbot Mentors in 2016, earned a Summa Cum Laude degree in information systems from Morgan State University and was titled Fall 2022 class salutatorian with a GPA of 3.94. He secured a full-time position at Textron Systems and has been accepted into the graduate program at the University of Maryland Global Campus.

Talbot Mentors praised Wilson, Collins, and Brooks for their achievements, acknowledging the impact of mentorship on both mentees and mentors.

title: VALDÉS-BRADNER WINS ANOTHER TEACHER OF THE YEAR AWARD
content: Mirta Valdés-Bradner, a Spanish teacher at North Caroline High School in Ridgely, Maryland, was named the 2023 Maryland Foreign Language Teacher of the Year by the Maryland Foreign Language Association. She previously won the 2022-23 Caroline Teacher of the Year award. title: Making history - Students work towards National History Day competition
content:
Thomas Hayman and Andy Anders, history teachers at Centreville Middle School, have recruited students for National History Day, a competition that encourages research, analysis, and presentation skills. The 2024 NHD theme is "Turning Points in History" and features five project types: documentaries, exhibits, performances, websites, and papers.

Hayman and Anders partnered with public libraries in Queen Anne's, Kent, Talbot, and Cecil counties to provide students with resources and assistance during the fall season. Students learn valuable skills like analyzing information, evaluating sources, and forming their own opinion.

The contest is held on March 23, 2024, at Chesapeake College, with judges from the Upper-Shore community participating. Winners will participate in state finals on May 4 at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County.

Since partnering with the libraries, Hayman and Anders have seen an increase in participation, moving Queen Anne's County to second place in the state for Junior Division participants, surpassing only Baltimore County. The program has helped make history more engaging and real for students, often discovering their true passion for the subject.

title: Cruise benefits St. Michaels library expansion
content:

Over 50 guests were treated to a sunset view over Leeds Creek and entertained by AMPERSAND's musical performance. The event raised over $6,000, which will be used to purchase new books when the library completes its expansion in 2025. This was the second year of the popular Friends Patriot Sunset Cruise.

The Friends of the Talbot County Free Library will hold several events this year, including a Fall Book Sale on October 27 and a pre-sale opportunity on October 26 for FOL members. title: Washington College receives $54.7 Million from Hodson Trust - Guarantees $30k+ scholarships for students with a 3.3+ GPA
content:
Washington College received a $54.7 million gift from The Hodson Trust, increasing its scholarship endowment to approximately $170 million and overall endowment to $325 million. The gift guarantees a minimum scholarship of $30,000 per year for incoming students with at least a 3.3 GPA who apply by Dec. 1.

President Mike Sosulski stated that the gift is transformative, expanding access to education for underprivileged students. Vice President Johnnie Johnson said it will help grow the diversity of campus community and enhance intellectual environment.

The gift is part of The Hodson Trust's dissolution, established in 1920 by Colonel Clarence Hodson. The Trust has donated over $150 million since 1935, supporting scholarships, research, faculty chairs, and academic centers.

title: Chapel District Elementary renovation design plans move to state for review
content:
The Talbot County Board of Education approved design development submission for Chapel District Elementary School renovation and addition at a meeting on October 18. Director of Operations Kevin Shafer stated that the plan needs to be submitted to the state by November 1. 

Project manager Adam McDonald from Hord Coplan Macht presented plans, which include a full building renovation and 16,600 square feet of additions. The additions will provide additional learning space and enhance the overall design. Changes were made to improve construction with existing utilities.

Design plans for outside include an extension to the parking lot and adjustments to traffic patterns. Inside, the media center will move to the front, and the art classroom will take over its current space.

Construction is expected to begin in June 2024 and last two years, with estimated costs of $25.18 million from FY2025-2026 budgets. Additional expenditures may increase the final cost to $29.97 million.

Board members asked questions, including about the school's roof drainage system, which Director Shafer assured would be properly sized and addressed by the architect.

title: It's in the family - Anna Howie speaks on joining Board of Education
content:
Anna Howie, newest member of Talbot County Board of Education, is sworn in after being appointed by Gov. Wes Moore to fill the District 5 seat. Her grandfather and mother taught in the district, and she wanted to be an engineer but ended up pursuing education instead. She became involved with The Algebra Project while in college and worked as a teaching assistant at a middle school. Howie is curriculum supervisor of career and technical education for Dorchester County Public Schools and interim principal at Mace's Lane Middle School.

She expressed her commitment to supporting students' social and emotional and mental health, particularly after COVID-19, stating that schools are safe places but lack resources. She prioritized teacher retention and increasing academic achievement, citing the importance of retaining teachers due to onboarding processes. Howie is continuing her mother's legacy in Talbot County Public Schools.

Howie has two meetings under her belt and appreciates the organization of the meetings. She is considering running for the position next year but hasn't made a decision yet. Her swearing-in was attended by her husband, who switched flights to watch the ceremony, and her late mother's former students and teachers, who praised her family's legacy in the district.

title: Black and Hispanic faculty underrepresented in universities
content:
Black and Hispanic communities are underrepresented among university faculty at Maryland's six largest public universities, according to 2021 IPEDS data. The analysis excludes HBCUs and shows less than 6% of total faculty are Black and less than 5% are Hispanic.

Data from the U.S. Census projects that 32% of Maryland's population are Black and 12% are Hispanic. Across universities, faculty demographics vary widely, with Towson University having 7% Black faculty and Frostburg State University having 4%.

Prior to 2022, individual universities implemented their own plans for cultural diversity, but a new code required public universities to ensure faculty demographics reflect the state's diverse population. Between 2016 and 2021, Black and Hispanic faculty percentages increased by just under a percentage point.

Faculty of color often take on "invisible labor" without recognition, says Laura Perna. The definition of merit is narrow, with publications and course evaluations weighted more heavily than service and mentorship roles. As student body diversity has increased, the gap between representation among students and faculty has widened.

In 2021, the ratio of Black students to Black faculty members was 60:1, while the ratio of white students to white faculty members was 15:1. Tenured professors were predominantly white (71%), with 5% Black and 4% Hispanic.

To combat underrepresentation, intentional mentoring policies are being developed, and best practices for increasing diversity include diversifying the faculty at every stage of the process. Katharina Maisel suggests using rubrics to evaluate candidates and actively seeking out diverse candidates.

As of fall 2021, Black students made up 17% and Hispanic students made up 8% of the student body, with increases since 2016. The gap between representation among students and faculty strains faculty of color.

title: Detecting problems with old plumbing and pipes
content:
EASTON, MD - November 10, 2023

Mid Shore Board of Realtors

* Indoor plumbing systems have been constructed for 150 years using various materials.
* Polybutylene piping (1970s-1990s): flexible, cheap, and easy to install; prone to leaks and deterioration, considered obsolete. Look for exposed gray piping under sinks in homes built in the 80s or 90s.
* Galvanized steel piping (1940s): zinc coating can wash away over time, leading to corrosion and contamination of water. Identify by dull, grayish/silver appearance; test by running multiple water fixtures for two minutes.

Leaky plumbing can cause structural damage if not addressed quickly. Technology such as small water alarms, whole house leak detection meters, and installed water heaters with leak detectors are available to detect leaks.

Certified master inspector Daniel Morris recommends inspecting plumbing systems, especially polybutylene piping and galvanized steel pipes, which have common issues.

For assistance, contact Blackwater Home Inspectors (443-528-1633) or the Mid-Shore Board of Realtors (midshoreboardofrealtors.com).

title: Elks provide Veterans Day assembly for Easton Elementary
content:
Local Elk organization coordinates Veterans Day assembly for Easton Elementary students, featuring veterans from all branches of the military. The event took place on November 8, 2023, at Easton Elementary school. The Elk's Michael Feehley coordinated the event and explained that Veteran's Day is celebrated on November 11, which marks the end of World War I.

Veterans including Mike Detmer, a former Marine, shared their experiences and perspectives with fifth-grade students. Detmer advised considering military service to gain new skills and grow close to others. He also emphasized serving something bigger than oneself.

Fifth-grade students asked veterans for advice on entering the military, and one student inquired about the most positive aspect of their experience. The assembly concluded with students presenting cards to the visiting veterans, which will be delivered to patients at a Maryland VA hospital during the holidays.

Students in Talbot County participate in a service-learning project by writing letters to veterans as part of their fifth-grade education. Easton Elementary students presented these letters to the veteran guests at the end of the assembly.

title: Board of Education to create Special Education Committee
content: The Talbot County Board of Education unanimously voted to create a new Special Education Committee, with Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi leading the charge. The committee will conduct a holistic review of TCPS' special education practices and propose modernization and funding strategies. This move is in response to the state's Blueprint for Maryland's Future plan, which changes budget allocation methods, including eliminating specific line items for special education. Board President Emily Jackson believes the rapidly growing special education population requires this committee to modernize district practices, gather information, and submit a proposal by next year before budget season, estimating costs and funding options.

title: Girl Scouts care for furry friends
content:
Four sixth-grade Girl Scouts from Troop 899 in Centreville, Maryland, Claire Anderson-Schultz, Amelia Beach, Clara Gerber, and Ayesha Tapia, earned their Bronze Award by completing 20 hours of service for a local animal shelter in Chestertown. They aimed to support the Kent County Animal Care Shelter (ACSKC) with handmade supplies and needed items.

The girls researched the ACSKC's needs, including a new cat tree, pet food, toys, storage benches, and cleaning items. After creating a plan using easy-to-clean PVC pipes, they built a new cat tree that was thoughtfully designed. They also made Velcro patches from reused clothing and sewed catnip toys, snuffle mats, and collected donations.

The shelter has 109 dogs and cats, with 32 in need of homes. Shelter worker Paige Tucker praised the girls' efforts, while Allison Otadan, Shelter Media Coordinator, expressed gratitude for the new cat trees and benches. The shelter is also in need of kitten food, cat food, dog food, and cat/dog treats.

The girls worked independently and as a team from June to September, touring the facility and learning about its needs before completing their project. Their effort was recognized by the ACSKC, which has a complete Wish List on its website for those who want to help: https://acskc.org/.

title: High school students become college scientists
content:
Queen Anne's County High School students partnered with Washington College to work alongside college chemistry students on a lab assignment changing copper into various forms. The partnership was developed by Michael Geoffroy, who reached out to Leslie Sherman, W. Alton Jones Professor of Chemistry and Environmental Science at Washington College.

Geoffroy wanted his students to experience using up-to-date technology and learn lab procedures like independent work and safety. Students were grouped with college students, including Betsy Moyer-Taylor's daughter Lucy Taylor, to complete the assignment. Frank Keegan, Professor Emeritus of Chemistry, visited the high school students, noting there were three generations of chemists present.

High school students praised the equipment, stating it was more advanced than their own classrooms. Raven Fairbanks said she felt comfortable with the process, while Terrance Vincent enjoyed working with younger students, saying it kept him honest. The partnership included a Q&A session, tour of facilities, and discussions about college workload, internships, jobs after college, and personal connections with professors.

The group also participated in liquid nitrogen demos, making ice cream and experimenting with slime recipes. After the trip, Geoffroy stated that the collaboration helped students see the bridge between their studies and potential careers. The partnership ended with free t-shirts and lunch in Washington College's dining hall.

title: Education foundation established in Caroline - Four local leaders spearhead funding financial literacy opportunities for students
content:
The Caroline County Education Foundation was established in October 2023 by four local leaders: Tolbert Rowe, Robert Willey, Dr. James Orr Jr., and Wayne Cole. The foundation aims to provide financial literacy opportunities for students through partnerships with organizations like Junior Achievement. The new foundation is a subfund of the Mid-Shore Community Foundation and will focus on financial literacy initially.

The group was inspired by a previous education foundation established in 1987, which operated until the mid-1990s due to lack of funding. Rowe and Willey oversee the former foundation's $8,000 remaining balance. The new foundation's purpose is to enhance, inspire, and support educational opportunities in financial literacy for all students attending Caroline County public schools.

CCPS Superintendent Dr. Derek Simmons expressed enthusiasm for the new foundation, citing the importance of financial literacy in today's economy. He noted that CCPS was the first to sign a memorandum of understanding with Junior Achievement regarding providing students opportunities at their facility. The foundation will help with costs associated with transportation for students attending the facility, which is crucial given the county's distance and poverty levels.

The group is currently working on bylaws and plans to expand its mission if more funding becomes available. They aim to recruit additional members and hold meetings to discuss future decisions.

title: Opening Doors (Again) For Literacy
content:
Here is a highly condensed version of the article:

Ashley Singer and Julie Blyman, co-founders of Open Doors Partners in Education, lost their office to a fire on September 2023, causing an estimated $40,000 loss. Despite the setback, they received widespread community support and secured a new location at Emmanuel Episcopal Church. The organization, founded in 2020 as a response to COVID-19's learning loss, focuses on literacy training using the Orton-Gillingham method for students aged 5-16.

Open Doors has assisted over 100 students with their literacy skills, providing free services to Kent County families through grant funding from Kit Cares, Inc. The organization aims to reach students who might fall through the cracks and is working on a five-year strategic plan with a nonprofit consultant.

title: Apprenticeships explored at local high schools

title: MCAP results show signs of recovery from pandemic learning loss - Science scores still show decline
content:
The Maryland Comprehensive Assessment Program (MCAP) results show signs of recovery from pandemic learning loss, with English proficiency surpassing pre-pandemic levels and improving across all counties except Somerset. However, math scores remain below pre-pandemic levels, with a 24% average passing rate in 2023, indicating that the format of math questions may be contributing to the slower improvement. Historically underserved students continue to lag behind in both English and math.

Grade 8 science proficiency has hit a five-year low, with a decline of 10% or more in most counties, including Baltimore, Kent, Somerset, and Talbot. The decline is attributed to grade 6 and 7 disruptions during the pandemic. Despite this, educators remain optimistic that scores will improve as curriculum continues to change.

Important dates:

* 2021: MCAP results showed a significant decline in English proficiency.
* 2022: Proficiency increased significantly, with an average passing rate of 47% for English.
* 2023: Math scores improved slightly, but remained below pre-pandemic levels. Science scores continued to lag.

Important people:

* Tiara Booker-Dwyer, Baltimore County Public Schools Board of Education Member at Large, emphasized the importance of building cultural competency among educators and encouraging historically underserved students to take honors and AP classes.
* Aya Hussein, Capital News Service author, reported on the MCAP results.

Important places:

* Maryland
* Baltimore County
* Somerset County

Important organizations:

* Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE)
* Baltimore County Public Schools
* Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia)

Key statistics:

* English proficiency: 47% average passing rate in 2023, up from 31% in 2021.
* Math proficiency: 24% average passing rate in 2023, still below pre-pandemic levels.
* Grade 8 science proficiency: hit a five-year low in 2023, with most counties experiencing a decline of 10% or more.

title: School principals prepare for the Blueprint For Maryland's Future
content:
Maryland is implementing the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, a 2021 landmark education reform law aimed at addressing challenges in the state's education system. The plan was established by the Kirwan Commission, formed in 2016 to analyze and establish a baseline for education reform.

The commission's findings showed that half of teachers leave within five years, only two out of five kindergarteners arrive ready to learn, and just a third of students are "college and career ready" in English and math by high school. The Maryland General Assembly passed the Blueprint, allocating $3.8 billion over 10 years.

The plan includes socioeconomically integrated pre-K, publicly funded but provided by both public schools and private providers, and aims to make students ready to learn in kindergarten and succeed by graduation. High schools will focus on college and career readiness by 10th grade through curriculum changes, apprenticeships, and technical education programs.

School administrators must implement the Blueprint at their schools, with a goal of raising teacher salaries to $60,000 by 2026 and providing incentives for National Board Certification. The Accountability and Implementation Board expects updated plans from districts in March 2024 and has offered $100,000 grants to hire strategic planning experts.

State officials and school principals reviewed the Blueprint at an annual conference, with some expressing hope that reforms will address their schools' priorities. Teachers are struggling with low salaries, while others have expressed excitement about pre-K expansion and trepidation about capacity issues.

Key dates:

* 2016: Kirwan Commission formed
* 2019: Commission's findings on Maryland's education system released
* February 2021: Blueprint for Maryland's Future passed by the General Assembly
* March 2023: Every school district submitted a detailed plan to implement the Blueprint
* November 2-4, 2023: Annual School Leaders Conference in Ocean City

* William E. Kirwan: Chairman of the Kirwan Commission

title: Superintendent Outlines Budget Priorities, Timeline
content:
December 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

Derek Simmons, Superintendent of Caroline County Public Schools, outlines budget priorities and timeline for fiscal year 2025 due to uncertain Blueprint demands and decreased pandemic-related grant funding.

Key issues include:

* Funding dual enrollment for high school students at $1,000 per semester
* Meeting the mandated starting teacher salary of $60,000 by fiscal year 2027
* Decreased American Rescue Plan and Maryland Leads grant funding (sunset in September 2024)

Budget breakdown:
- 80% of budget allocated to personnel costs
- 14% comes from county government, with the rest from state and federal funds

Complexity added by Blueprint requirements, including financing at the school level, requiring full-time accounting positions.

Challenges include:

* Inflation rate over 3.5%
* Multiyear contracts increasing above inflation rate in 2024
* Global issues impacting cost of goods

Relief from budget pressure comes from "concentration of poverty" grant funding, available for individual schools, allowing some flexibility in district-level funding decisions.

Priorities for fiscal year 2025 CCPS budget:

- Competitive salaries and benefits for all employees
- Maintaining reasonable staffing levels across the district
- Implementing Blueprint requirements

title: Problems persist in juvenile services schooling
content:
The Victor Cullen Center in rural northern Frederick County is facing challenges in educating incarcerated juveniles. The center's principal, Todd Rasher, praised a 17-year-old graduate who earned his GED with minimal footwork, but noted that other students struggled to attend classes due to lack of residential staff and teacher vacancies.

Teacher vacancy rates are 30% across Juvenile Services schools, leading to reliance on streaming instruction. Director David Domenici stated that streaming is not ideal for most students but better than packet-based activities. The problem persists despite efforts by the state General Assembly to improve education in juvenile facilities.

In 2021, a statewide education board was established within Juvenile Services, but laws did not require pay parity or align teaching calendars with local schools. Audits found that residential staff shortages caused students to be late to class 203 times between April and June, while teachers taught classes inside living units 43 times in the same period.

The department is working towards a goal of 90% on-time attendance by shifting onsite adults to escort students to school. The Maryland General Assembly has struggled to find solutions for juvenile education issues since 2016, when bills aimed at improving teacher pay and benefits were repeatedly defeated.

title: 'Diving Deep' with dyslexia: Local special education teacher works to raise awareness
content:
Robin Williams, Jay Leno, Albert Einstein, Alexander Graham Bell, Magic Johnson, Jennifer Aniston, Gwen Stefani, Abraham Lincoln, and Arnold Schwarzenegger all have dyslexia. Lindsey Parte, a mother of two boys and Special Education teacher, has reignited the Decoding Dyslexia Maryland Eastern Shore Chapter. 

Parte's son, Lincoln, struggled with reading at six years old, which led her to research dyslexia. Two years later, he received his formal diagnosis, bringing relief to both Parte and her son. According to the Mayo Clinic, dyslexia is a learning disorder that involves difficulty reading due to problems identifying speech sounds and learning how they relate to letters and words.

Parte says early identification is crucial (as young as five-years-old) and the dyslexic brain requires explicit instruction. Since advocating for her son's diagnosis, Parte has promoted all adults to learn about dyslexia by listening to podcasts, attending free trainings, reading books, and more.

In February 2024, Decoding Dyslexia Maryland Eastern Shore Chapter will host a workshop "Experience Dyslexia: A Dyslexia Simulation" at the Queen Anne's County Library Kent Island Branch location. The event aims to raise dyslexia awareness, empower families to support their children, encourage educational interventions, and influence policy makers to support Maryland students with dyslexia.

Parte believes releasing the stigma around dyslexia is crucial for a child's mental wellbeing. Dyslexic learners have strengths such as problem-solving, creativity, and leadership skills. Parte recommends testing, finding the right intervention specialist, deep diving into research, reading to children, sharing their qualities, and connecting with local support groups.

Decoding Dyslexia Maryland Eastern Shore Chapter is a grassroots movement without funding, run by parents who are working professionals. To support the chapter, contact Lindsey Parte at decodingdyslexiaES@gmail.com or visit their website for more information.

title: DCTC Masonry instructor surprised by coworkers on last day

title: Some thoughts on those New Year's resolutions
content:
David Reel, a consultant, shares his thoughts on New Year's resolutions in an article titled "Some Thoughts on Those New Year's Resolutions." This year, Reel aims to make a more successful resolution by adopting new approaches.

Reel identifies four key strategies:

1. Embracing a sense of urgency, inspired by Professor John Kotter.
2. Setting SMART (Specific, Measurable, Audacious, Realistic, Time-sensitive) goals, influenced by Peter F. Drucker's philosophy that "go big or go home."
3. Developing and executing tactics to achieve SMART goals, as suggested by Professor Gail Matthews' questions:
   - What actions are needed?
   - Who can help?
   - Potential problems and solutions.
4. Tracking progress regularly.

Reel emphasizes the importance of reviewing goal progress weekly, citing a study that shows 76% of participants with written goals achieved their objectives, compared to 33% without written goals.

He concludes by stating that while some resolutions may not be achieved in one year due to VUCA (Volatility, Uncertainty, Complexity, Ambiguity) nature of the world, SMART goals can always be rolled forward into a following year.
