title: Benedictine hosts ribbon-cutting and groundbreaking
content:
Benedictine School in Ridgely held a ribbon-cutting ceremony and groundbreaking for new student residences on May 1, 2024. Executive Director Scott Evans led the event with over $3 million in funding from the US Senate and state legislature. The project was made possible by community development block grants, including those from Caroline County and the Community Development Administration.

The school's 'Transforming Lives' campaign aims to address the needs of its student demographic, which has seen a significant change since existing residential spaces were built. The new facilities will include suites with recreational and sensory areas, an updated dining area, and state-of-the-art infirmary.

Benedictine received $1.8 million in congressional directed funding and $1.25 million in capital from the state legislature, including support from Governor's offices, Sens. Van Hollen and Cardin, Rep. Andy Harris, and local delegates such as Sen. Stephen Hershey, Sen. Johnny Mautz, Del. Jeff Ghrist, Del. Chris Adams, Del. Steven Arentz, and Del. Jay Jacobs.

The school is now set to start building the new facility in a few weeks.

title: Candidates to face off for Talbot Board of Education positions
content:
Talbot County's Board of Education has three positions up for election in Districts 2, 5, and 6, with six candidates running for the seats. The top two vote-getters in District 2 will move on to the general election.

Candace Henry, currently serving on the Board of Education, is running for re-election. She emphasizes the importance of addressing teacher recruitment and retention, as well as the opportunity gap. Henry proposes increasing support for diverse educators, enhancing professional development opportunities, and prioritizing work-life balance.

Cynthia Jurrius, running in District 6, believes that student mastery of essential knowledge and skills, teacher retention, and a positive school climate are the most significant issues facing Talbot County Public Schools. She supports addressing these challenges through innovative solutions, community partnerships, and targeted resources.

Anna Howie, also running for the District 5 seat, prioritizes providing exceptional education opportunities for all students while being fiscally responsible. She proposes utilizing educational grants to provide high-quality instructional materials and has a background of over 20 years in public education.

Other candidates include Kerry Gunshenan (District 6), Karla Wieland-Cherry (District 5), Ann O'Connor (District 2), Connie Loveland (District 2).

title: St. Michaels library looks to expand its footprint
content:
The Talbot County Free Library St. Michaels Branch plans a 3,700-square-foot expansion with renovations expected to begin this fall, pending county funding. The library has raised $5 million and needs an additional $500,000 through a private fundraising campaign.

Project architects Mike Wheedleton and Payton Bridge are working on the project with a total cost of $6.3 million. A grant from the Maryland Capital Grant Program will provide up to 50% match funding, leaving the library committed to funding 50%.

The new library aims to better serve residents with a community hub, increased technology, study rooms, and quiet spaces for reading and teens. The renovation will feature a 40% larger meeting room, children's area, exhibit space, and interactive outdoor spaces.

The library is currently closed and searching for temporary quarters while the build occurs. Friends of the Talbot County Library have raised $50,000, and other naming opportunities are available.

Dana Newman, director of the library, believes there will be excitement and engagement as the community looks forward to the new library's opening in December 2025 or January 2026.

title: HopStart learners making world a better place
content:
On May 5, 2024, David Reel served as a volunteer mentor and judge at the 24th annual HopStart new venture awards program at Johns Hopkins University's Center for Leadership Education. The competition challenges students to develop innovative business plans and pitch them to a panel of diverse judges. This year, there were 50 entries in two categories: general ventures and medical technology/life science ventures.

Judges included Al Silverstein, Clay Mitchell, Marty Lostrom, and Len Foxwell. Presentations showcased innovative ideas, rigorous research, and a commitment to making a difference worldwide. Examples of programs included:

* Leveraging the internet for agriculture expenses
* Electronic access system for medical care evaluation
* Blockchain technology for credential verification

Every entry demonstrated innovation and dedication. Reel learned that participating students are among the best in the world, committed to lifelong learning, and advancing causes larger than themselves. The event's observations align with Eric Hoffer's quote: "In a world of constant change, learners will inherit the future." At Johns Hopkins, HopStart learners aim not only to inherit but also make the world a better place.

* Program categories: General ventures and medical technology/life science ventures
* Number of entries: 50

title: Moms For Liberty fields candidates in elections
content:
Moms For Liberty-backed candidates Ann C. O'Connor, Karla Wieland-Cherry, and Kerry Gunshenan are running for Talbot County Board of Education in the May 14 primary election. The group has raised questions across the US due to its conservative views on education, including opposition to critical race theory and LGBTQ+ issues. Critics argue that their advocacy could undermine public institutions and democratic processes.

Moms For Liberty advocates for "parental rights" in education, which critics say fuels book bans, anti-LGBT efforts, and whitewashing history. The group has been accused of harassing community members and advancing misinformation.

Only two candidates are running in each district, ensuring they will be on the November ballot again. Connie Loveland withdrew from the race too late to have her name removed from the ballot.

Talbot County recently celebrated its thriving business community and economic development efforts. Chris Pilkerton, former acting administrator of the US Small Business Administration, praised the county's support for small businesses.

A Washington Post story reported alarming sea level rise along the Gulf coast and Atlantic seaboard, with some areas seeing a 2.8-inch increase since 2010. Jianjun Yin, a climate scientist, stated that the rate of sea level rise is "irreversible."

title: Maryland’s education ‘Blueprint’ struggles to expand pre-K
content:
Maryland's education "Blueprint" aims to expand pre-K availability to every 3- and 4-year-old in the state, with research showing benefits for children who attend pre-K, including higher college attendance rates (44% vs. 33%). The plan relies on a mix of private providers and public schools but faces challenges, including:

* Private providers not being incentivized due to low reimbursement rates ($150-$13,500)
* Barriers to participation, such as requiring teaching assistants and teachers with specific certifications
* Insufficient physical space in some school buildings to accommodate pre-K classrooms
* Difficulty enlisting private providers, with only Montgomery County Public Schools meeting the 35% requirement

The state projects a 15.7% increase in funding for pre-K programs between fiscal years 2024-2025 and aims to make government-funded pre-K available to all low-income 4-year-olds by 2025-26.

Key dates:

* 2022-23: 30,718 children enrolled in pre-K
* 2026-27: Districts expected to fill half their pre-K slots through private providers

Key people and organizations:

* Rachel Hise, executive director of the Accountability and Implementation Board
* Molly Scherf, Head Start teacher
* William T. Gormley, co-director of Georgetown University's Center for Research on Children in the United States
* Christina Peusch, executive director of the Maryland State Childcare Association
* Kristen Paul, director of early childhood programs at The Parents' Place of Maryland
* Jamie Miller, principal of Broadneck Elementary School
* Shamoyia Gardiner, executive director of Strong Schools Maryland

title: Elkton teacher has green thumb for growing students' knowledge
content:
Brittany Rigdon, a high school agriculture/horticulture teacher in Cecil County Public Schools, is the 2024 Cecil County Teacher of the Year. She teaches her students about horticulture, business, and landscaping skills through practical applications in her 90'-by-30' greenhouse classroom. Her students grow plants, operate tractors, and identify scores of plants, with some even passing a certification exam to become certified professional horticulturalists.

Rigdon's approach is described as "getting on our level," making the subject understandable for every student. She provides hands-on experience, including selling class-grown poinsettias and flowers, teaching business skills, and using real-world examples. Her students praise her kindness, respect, and dedication to their education.

Born in Wilmington, Del., Rigdon grew up in a suburban neighborhood but never worked on a farm as a child. She pursued a career in agriculture after attending Delaware Valley University, graduating with a B.S. degree in secondary education and agriculture in 2008. She now lives on a 20-acre farm in Conowingo with her husband and teaches horticulture to students aged 16-18.

Key statistics include:
- 1,200 poinsettias grown during the fall semester
- Thousands of colorful flowers grown during the spring semester
- 18 students in the two-year horticulture program
- 33% pass rate on the Maryland Nursery Landscape Greenhouse Association test

Awards and recognition include:
- 2024 Cecil County Teacher of the Year
- Certified pesticide application class passed by all seniors

title: Will plan for better pay ease teacher shortage?
content:
Maryland is struggling with a teacher shortage, with 28 subjects listed as areas of certification, up from 17 five years earlier. The state's Blueprint for Maryland's Future aims to address the issue by increasing teacher pay to $60,000 by 2026 and providing better training and recruitment efforts.

However, experts have mixed views on the effectiveness of the plan. Simon Birenbaum, director of grading, assessment and scheduling at Baltimore City Public Schools, believes that money is not enough and that recruiting, training, and retaining high-quality teachers is the primary focus.

The teacher shortage follows national trends, with 86% of US K-12 public schools facing challenges in hiring teachers for the current school year. Prince George's County experienced a significant increase in teacher resignations (1,126) between July 2022 and July 2023, while Dorchester County had the highest attrition rate at 18%.

The Blueprint provides measures to encourage people to become teachers, including a pay bump, but experts like Hansen from the Brookings Institution express skepticism about its impact. The General Assembly passed the Maryland Educator Shortage Reduction Act, which sets recruitment goals for teacher education programs and establishes a $20,000 yearly stipend for eligible student teachers.

Maryland is not alone in facing a teacher shortage; the National Center for Education Statistics reported 86% of US K-12 public schools faced challenges in hiring teachers for the current school year.

title: School officials: Blueprint money is not enough
content:
Maryland school officials and local district leaders expressed concerns that the state's Blueprint for Maryland's Future funding is not enough to implement all the requirements. The $16.6 billion in additional state funds from 2024-2029 may not cover full implementation, with some districts citing increased costs related to staffing, data systems, student support, and transportation.

Fifteen of the state's 24 school districts listed funding or resource allocations among their top three challenges under the Blueprint. County officials, such as Harford County Executive Bob Cassilly, argue that the Blueprint is unaffordable and calls for pauses and revisits to its spending mandates.

The Maryland Association of Counties said the Blueprint's cost estimates do not account for local impact, leading to a $700 million annual increase in costs by 2034. The Blueprint's Accountability and Implementation Board expects more counties to put in additional funds as the plan ramps up.

Examples include Dorchester County's $3 million jump in funding contributions, which devastated its highway maintenance budget; Cecil County's school funding battle, where the county executive refused to meet the district's funding request, leading to a Facebook group with 6,700 members; and Worcester County's $9 million cash shortfall that could force staff reductions.

The Blueprint shifts resources within school districts at the expense of other schools. Some superintendents express concerns about class-size adjustments, citing potential detrimental effects on student learning.

Inflation and changing cost projections may impact local funding requirements in the future, with some experts suggesting possible changes to the plan's funding amounts or mandates.

title: Dr. Toughlove’s Book Club
content:
Dr. Toughlove's Book Club is written by Carol Franks-Randall, a retired educator with a doctorate in education and children's book author, for The Star Democrat (Easton, MD). 

Published on May 10, 2024, the review features Dr. Toughlove's endorsement of Andrea Beaty's and David Roberts' book "Aaron Slater, Illustrator". The book is a New York Times best-seller and part of Beaty's series including "Iggy Peck, Architect", "Rosie Revere, Engineer", "Ada Twist, Scientist", and "Sofia Valdez, Future Prez".

The story follows Aaron, a young boy who struggles to learn to write. However, he discovers his superpower is capturing thoughts with pictures. The book features colorful illustrations by David Roberts.

The review mentions two additional resources: "Aaron Slater's Big Project Book for Astonishing Artists" and Andrea Beaty's website (andreabeaty.com), which offer information on art influences and downloadable coloring sheets.

"Aaron Slater, Illustrator" is recommended for children aged 4-7 and is available at county libraries.

title: It's time to learn from history and speak out
content:
Here is a highly condensed version of the article:

May 12, 2024 | The Star Democrat (Easton, MD)

Author: DAVID REEL

College campuses are witnessing widespread protests reminiscent of 1960s anti-war movements. However, today's protesters are not anti-war activists but rather rabidly antisemitic individuals supporting Hamas' goals.

They reject Israel's right to exist, drive Jews from Gaza, and challenge western society's principles. These actions are defended under the guise of American constitutional rights on freedom of assembly and speech.

However, these rights do not defend verbal harassment, threats, or physical harm towards Jews or supporters of Israel. Colleges should not permit or tolerate antisemitism under the guise of free speech and assembly.

David Reel shares the story of Martin Niemöller, a theologian who was initially supportive of Nazi ideology before speaking out against it during WWII. Niemöller's warnings about the dangers of inaction in the face of hatred are still relevant today:

* "They came for the communists... I did not speak out because I was not a communist."
* "They came for the Jews... I did not speak out because I was not a Jew."
* Then, they came for him.

Niemöller's story serves as a warning that if we do not learn from history, we are condemned to repeat it. The author urges college students, leaders, and elected officials to become aware of antisemitism and heed this lesson to prevent further harm.

title: Maple Elementary School celebrates Teacher Appreciation Week
content:
Maple Elementary School in Cambridge celebrated Teacher Appreciation Week from May 6-10, 2024, with activities and events to boost staff morale. Principal Myyesha Ford aimed to create a collaborative atmosphere by setting up games inspired by the reality show "Survivor." Teachers participated in challenges such as writing anonymous praise messages to fellow teachers.

Haley Wright and Natalie Drake, teachers at Maple Elementary, enjoyed the appreciation they received from staff and students. The event allowed for teacher-staff connections and provided students with excitement about learning. Ford emphasized that events like these refresh educators during a stressful time of year, especially standardized testing.

Ford aims to show appreciation not only from administrators but also from colleagues. She stated, "Teaching is hard. But it's fun, and it's rewarding." The event culminated in teams earning points, with the winning team being announced at the end of the week.

Key people involved: Myyesha Ford (Principal), Haley Wright (Teacher), Natalie Drake (Teacher).

Important dates: May 6-10, 2024.

Places: Maple Elementary School (Cambridge).

Organizations: Star Democrat, Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia).

title: Blatant attack on character
content: Karla Wieland-Cherry is running for Talbot County Board of Education District 5 in Trappe, MD. A local article by Jim Johnson, editor of the Star Democrat, criticized her character after Moms for Liberty endorsed her candidacy on May 5, 2024. In a phone call to Johnson (Wednesday), Wieland-Cherry explained she was busy with college courses, volunteer work, and preparing for surgery before campaigning in June. She invited him to meet and discuss concerns. The Star Democrat attacked her character based on the endorsement of Moms for Liberty without meeting her.

title: Quality child care is a collective responsibility
content:
The US child care crisis is a collective responsibility that requires national-level solutions, as Republican leaders' efforts to address it at the state level are insufficient. The crisis includes:

- Widespread closures of child care centers and shortages of licensed slots, particularly in "child care deserts."
- Many centers remain under-enrolled due to low wages for early childhood educators ($13.71/hour in 2022), making them among the lowest-paid workers.
- High costs for families (10% to 33% of budget) often exceeding other essential expenses like rent and mortgage.

Recent $1.2 trillion funding bill allocated $9 billion for child care and $12 billion for Headstart, but these funds will only serve a small fraction of eligible families.

Republicans have resisted more substantive solutions, labeling them as "socialist" or citing traditional family roles, shifting the burden to individuals and affluent families.

The alternative is a collective responsibility approach, valued by European countries that recognize high-quality care as a human right. The US must consider alternatives like a "caring society" to address the crisis and promote well-being for all individuals and families.

title: Moms For Liberty advocates for school parents
content:
Jim Johnson, Executive Editor of the Easton Star Democrat, wrote an article on May 5, 2024, stating that three candidates for the Talbot County Board of Education are backed by Moms For Liberty, a group that has raised controversy across the country.

Moms For Liberty Talbot, led by Jan Greenhawk, responded that they did not field any candidates and instead sent out a call to people to run in the 2024 elections. The organization emphasizes supporting parental rights, allowing parents to have a seat at decision-making tables for their children's education, medical, and mental health decisions.

Greenhawk criticized Johnson for using biased, disproven allegations from the Associated Press and a liberal professor, portraying Moms For Liberty as controversial without researching local ties with Talbot County officials. She pointed out that the organization has a positive relationship with Superintendent Dr. Pepukayi and school board President Emily Jackson, who attend member meetings to discuss issues.

Greenhawk argued that a candidate answering questions eight months before the election is counterproductive and that the Star Democrat's questionnaire was premature, especially in districts with no real primary. She accused Johnson of using his article to target and prejudice voters against candidates he doesn't know, employing lies, distortions, and omissions.

Jan Greenhawk, chapter chair of Moms For Liberty Talbot, has scheduled a forum for school board candidates to meet voters and answer questions in the fall, and invites all candidates.

title: Demand proficiency at all grades
content:
A Maryland resident and member of Moms for Liberty wrote to express concerns about school board candidates in Talbot County, citing issues with critical race theory, gender fluidity, and book censorship. The group was formed during the COVID-19 pandemic as a response to masking mandates and school closures, later joining the M4L organization. Parents are upset about books teaching children they can be "oppressors" or "oppressed," trans boys competing in girls' sports, and using female bathrooms. The Maryland Board of Education's Blueprint for the Future is another concern due to its influence on school funding.

The writer advocates for a school board that demands proficiency at all grade levels, with a focus on critical thinking and parental involvement. They suggest doing research before publishing OpEds, as they believe this issue warrants attention.

title: Leave our children alone
content: The author, a Talbot County parent of five, expresses trust in local school professionals and advocates for them to be left alone by Moms for Liberty, an extremist organization that has been designated as such by the Southern Poverty Law Center. Moms for Liberty advocates against rights, equality, book bans, and scientifically grounded healthcare policies. They endorse candidates Anne O'Conner, Kerry Gunshenan, and Karla Wieland Cherry in Talbot County, which the author believes perpetuates anti-education and anti-diversity rhetoric.

title: St. Mary's College of Maryland freezes tuition again; President announces retirement
content: St. Mary's College of Maryland froze tuition for the fifth consecutive year while approving a 3.9% increase in room and board rates for the 2024-25 school year. President Tuajuanda Jordan announced her retirement next June, citing the college's long-term tuition strategy and financial stability. The college's peer institutions raised tuition by an average of 3.3%. Outgoing Chair Susan L. Dyer completed her three-year term, while John Bell will replace her as chair, becoming the first alumnus to hold the position. Jordan credited the college with increasing diversity, steady enrollment growth, and curricular innovations under her leadership. The board also approved a new attendance policy, diversity report, state capital budget proposal, and meeting calendar changes.

title: Will Maryland’s Blueprint for education work?
content:
Maryland plans to spend $16.6 billion through 2029 to improve public schools under the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, a transformative education law passed in 2021. The seven-member oversight board aims to boost student performance and quality throughout Maryland schools in five pillars: prekindergarten expansion, teacher hiring and retention, college and career readiness, additional resources, and accountability and governance.

Lawmakers established the Accountability and Implementation Board to monitor the Blueprint's progress, with a requirement to develop plans for full implementation by March 2024. The board oversees funding and initiative implementation while providing guidance to school districts, aiming to improve academic performance in Maryland.

Concerns arise from educators and school leaders about the Blueprint's deadlines, lack of detailed procedural information, and its overall place in the educational system. Implementing a law as comprehensive as the Blueprint is challenging due to financial challenges, limited pre-implementation planning time for districts, and slow regulations and guidance.

The board will oversee the progress of each public school system in implementing Blueprint initiatives, monitoring 92 data measures, determining if changes need to be made, ensuring expert review teams observe schools, releasing about a quarter of Blueprint funds to implementing districts, hiring an independent contractor to evaluate the Blueprint's success, and withholding funding from systems that fail to implement or show significant student progress.

A slow flow of information to school districts challenges communication with employees regarding their work aligning with the Blueprint. Members of the accountability board encourage community feedback, but teachers and principals express concerns about transparency, data collection, and implementation deadlines.

Implementing the Blueprint hasn't gone exactly as planned, with extended deadlines for criteria and plans, funding uncertainties, staffing shortages, and delays in receiving guidance. School officials across the state expressed concerns about workforce issues, arts, athletics, enrichment, after-school programming, transportation, facilities, healthcare, and other crucial parts of the learning experience.

The Blueprint's implementation is expected to continue, with an independent contractor set to perform an evaluation by October, but some advocates hope for a deadline extension to give initiatives more time to lead to change.

title: Community BBQ hosted to show support for DCPS middle schooler
content:
Here is a condensed version of the article:

A community BBQ was held on May 8 to show support for DCPS middle schooler Tori Gibbs, who is Muslim and was bullied after her hijab was pulled off her head in March. The event was organized by mosques in Baltimore and Philadelphia, led by Anwar Wright and Sabur Carter.

The incident occurred outside Gibbs' home on March 26 and involved verbal and physical attacks, with Islamic phrases chanted to taunt her. Her mom, LaToya Gibbs, said the bullying has been hard on both their mental health.

DCPS Interim Superintendent Jymil Thompson met with the family on May 9, saying it was a positive meeting and calling for better communication between parents and schools to prevent similar incidents.

Police began investigating on April 5, and Rian Johnson, one of the involved parents, has been charged with conspiracy and other crimes. The Dorchester County State's Attorney is looking into whether the incident could be considered a hate crime.

The community BBQ resulted in five attendees taking their Shahada (pledging to convert to Islam), including two fathers of girls from the video. Tori Gibbs' great aunt said she wants her niece to be OK and hopes the event ends bullying and harassment.

Gibbs will continue with home hospital schooling due to mental health issues. The incident has sparked a call for education and change, with Carter saying "Everybody should feel safe."

title: Sandy Hill Elementary teacher dies in Hebron crash
content:
Elizabeth "Lizzi" Cockey, 23, a Sandy Hill Elementary School teacher and coach, was killed in a car crash on May 15, 2024, while driving westbound on US Route 50 near Hebron, Maryland. She taught special education to kindergarteners and first graders in her second year of teaching.

Cockey interned at Vienna Elementary School (2021-2022) before joining Sandy Hill. The school community is mourning her loss, with Principal Deborah Gibson calling families of students she taught and holding classroom discussions for students and staff on May 16.

Education psychologists, social workers, counselors from other schools, and external partners like Mid Shore Mediation and Life's Energy Wellness Center are providing support to students and staff. The school will offer these resources to students on Friday and "play it by ear" thereafter.

Goff said teachers received grief resources for use with students, particularly fourth and fifth graders, who have started conversations about memorializing Cockey.

title: School superintendent proposes FY25 budget
content:
Here is a condensed version of the article:

Dr. Karen Couch, Superintendent of Schools, proposed a FY25 budget of $32,175,451, including an increase in county funding of $246,969 (19.9 million). With 85%-88% dedicated to salaries, the budget aims to prioritize increases in salary, health insurance costs, and utilities. The Maryland Blueprint for Education (Kirwan) requires a balanced budget, but the proposed plan relies on using $800,000 from the school district's fund balance.

Board members Frank Rhodes and Joe Goetz debated budget priorities, with Rhodes advocating for using more of the fund balance to reduce pressure on the county. Couch emphasized that the state mandated Blueprint requirements must be met. The Accountability and Implementation Board (AIB) consultant is aware of the allocated line items problem, which prevents fund transfers among categories.

If the proposed budget is not approved, the school system will need to find ways to operate without it. Couch stated that this plan "is what we need to operate our school system."

title: LWVQAC hosts dinner discussion on advancement of AI during election season
content:
The Queen Anne's County League of Women Voters hosted a dinner discussion on the advancement of artificial intelligence during election season at Prospect Bay Country Club on May 7, 2024. Guest speaker John Lewis, headmaster of Gunston School in Centreville, presented "Artificial Intelligence and Disinformation" and its effects on democracy.

Lewis shared his experience as a founding faculty member of an independent school in Ecuador, where he witnessed the collapse of government in the 1990s. He noted that AI has evolved rapidly since then, with machine learning, neural networks, natural language processing, and robotics being key components.

Lewis warned that AI is already being used to suppress votes, strengthen division, create narratives, and generate realistic fake news. He predicted that 2024 will see a record number of voters participating in polls worldwide, and that AI will continue to grow during election periods, spreading false information rapidly.

However, Lewis also emphasized the importance of information literacy, informed citizenry, civic learning, personal virtue, and "moral finger wagging" as crucial pillars for a functioning democracy. He noted that reliable information is often behind a paywall, while bad information is often free, but advocated for researching before sharing information.

Lewis strongly supported the League's efforts to promote voting and civic education, and encouraged the audience to spread the word on the importance of participating in government. The League has 60 members strong and is active in community voter services, including voter registration events and printing voter guides.

Key points:

* John Lewis presented "Artificial Intelligence and Disinformation" at the Queen Anne's County League of Women Voters dinner discussion.
* AI components include machine learning, neural networks, natural language processing, and robotics.
* AI is being used to suppress votes, strengthen division, create narratives, and generate fake news.
* 2024 will see a record number of voters participating in polls worldwide.
* Crucial pillars for democracy include information literacy, informed citizenry, civic learning, personal virtue, and "moral finger wagging".
* Reliable information is often behind a paywall, while bad information is often free.
* The League advocates for researching before sharing information and promoting voting and civic education.

title: Dorchester BOE passes emergency virtual education plan with amendment
content:
Dorchester County Public Schools' Jodi Colman presented a drafted prolonged state of emergency virtual education plan required by Maryland Senate bill to the board, which must be submitted to the Maryland State Department of Education by June 1. The plan includes staffing, personnel, student instruction and assessment, and learning supports for emergencies lasting over 14 consecutive days.

Board member Talibah Chikwendu questioned why content supervisors are invited into Schoology classrooms, citing concerns about teachers being held accountable and potential disruptions to plans. Colman clarified that the intention was to provide support, not mandate access.

The board approved the plan with an amendment to make content supervisor access optional, as a support rather than mandatory. Other topics discussed included camera usage in virtual classrooms, where Chikwendu expressed concerns about bandwidth; and using standard backgrounds for students on camera to avoid showing their homes in virtual settings.

Key dates:
- May 22, 2024: Board meeting
- June 1, 2024: District must submit plan to Maryland State Department of Education

title: Caroline County Public Library celebrates renovation
content:
Caroline County Public Library celebrated a years-long renovation on May 22, 2024. The renovation aimed to modernize the space, making it more open and community-focused. Politicians, law enforcement, children, and librarians attended the event.

Key figures include:
- Nancy Pollen, library associate
- Connie Kumor, architect of the project
- Debbie Bennett, Executive Director (retiring June 2024)
- Irene Padilla, state librarian

Places involved:
- Caroline County Public Library (Denton)

Notable events and details:
- The renovation started in fiscal year 2019
- Funding came from the Maryland State Library Capital Grant, large donations, and community support
- The project included gaming stations, study rooms, puppet programs, and makerspace
- Original footprint of the building remained unchanged
- Hundreds of small donations were received from the "Friends of the Library"
- Debbie Bennett cited John Hargreaves' 1961 library founding as a legacy

title: BOE approves Sysco food services
content:
Queen Anne's County Public Schools approved a contract with Sysco Eastern Maryland, LLC for food delivery services to join the Shore Educational Food Service Consortium. The decision aims to reduce costs and shift from Sodexo, which was set to expire on June 30.

The district will be self-operational starting July 2024, with a vendor contract needed to provide necessary food and items. Sysco's contract renewal includes options for two more years.

Estimated total cost for FY25 is $800,000, utilizing the food service balance account. No hourly positions are being cut, but staff have been notified of the conversion. Board member Richard Smith noted a return to in-house operations, while President Helen Bennet emphasized local vendor partnerships and cost savings.

The district also approved piggybacking on Wicomico County Public Schools' milk contract with Cloverland Dairy for estimated $190,000 in FY25, replacing their current Sodexo contract. The contract is in effect until June 2026 unless terminated early.

title: Student seeks to share Choptank River history
content:
Kennedy Thomason, a 2019 graduate of Ridgely's North Caroline High School, is sharing her love of history through her family's river cruise business, River City Cruise Company. She majored in American studies at Washington College and works as a digital archiving intern at the Starr Center for the American Experience.

Thomason has worked on various projects, including scanning archives of local African American families' collections and planning river tours that highlight the Choptank River's history and heritage. Her goal is to make history accessible to the public, rather than waiting for them to seek it out.

She considers her family a huge inspiration, particularly her parents who supported all five children pursuing different goals. Thomason also values the sense of community and belonging she found at Washington College, where she navigates balancing college, work, and life as a single mother.

Thomason has recently received funding for her Choptank River History project through the Gerda Blumenthal Grant, which will involve publishing blog posts on the Caroline County Historical Society's website. She aims to create a more robust history tour and hold at least one public event.

title: Nearly 300 Chesapeake College students celebrate graduation
content:
May 23, 2024: Nearly 300 Chesapeake College students graduated with diplomas in a ceremony attended by friends and family. President Clifford Coppersmith congratulated graduates on their achievements, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic. 

Coppersmith referenced Dr. David Harper's statement that pursuing education is a sign of hope. Rob Thompson, director of arts, received the 2024-2026 Bounds Distinguished Teaching Chair Award. In his speech, Thompson honored Victoria Woodhull, the first woman to run for president in 1872, and her dedication to women's rights.

Thompson emphasized the importance of shaping homes and communities through perseverance and adaptation after failure. He praised graduates' creative minds and passionate hearts. 

Milton Nagel presented the John T. Harrison Award to Zulema Delacruz Martinez, who demonstrated exceptional academic performance, leadership, and community contributions. Delacruz Martinez recounted her childhood struggles and perseverance, crediting resources and support for her success.

She encouraged graduates to take advantage of opportunities, build meaningful relationships, and persevere. The ceremony honored graduates including Rob Thompson and Zulema Delacruz Martinez as well as recognizing Chesapeake College's achievements.

title: Graduation ceremonies held for local homeschool students
content:
On May 18, 2024, Shore Christian Fellowship Church in Queenstown hosted a graduation ceremony for its homeschool student class of 2024, comprising 10 students: Cody Blunt, Ashlyn Boyles, Alyssa Jastram, Kylee Koss, Makayla Larson, Mason Patterson, and Hayden Winborne. The ceremony was the largest to date, with three additional students choosing not to participate.

Lora Largent, homeschool umbrella coordinator, oversaw the event for over a decade, having graduated five of her own children as homeschoolers. Each graduate spoke at the podium, sharing their plans for the future, including Ashlyn's wedding in June and attending River Bible Institute, while Cody will train to become an electrician. The graduates listed various interests, with Kylee planning to teach competitive dancing and Makayla aiming for a PhD in psychology.

The ceremony was well-received by parents, who spoke at the podium congratulating their children. Pastor Tom Chandler provided a challenge to the graduates, highlighting the importance of sacrifices made by homeschooling parents and prioritizing selfless love. The event marked a significant milestone for Shore Christian Fellowship's homeschool program, which has over 100 families registered.

Makayla, one of the graduates, mentioned that she valued the flexibility of homeschooling, allowing her to socialize with friends while pursuing her interests. Kylee echoed similar sentiments, stating that homeschooling provided more opportunities than traditional school classes. The event concluded with Pastor Chandler's words of encouragement and appreciation for homeschooling parents.

title: Maryland stories: College hosts Memorial Day ceremony and flag planting
content: Cecil College hosted a Memorial Day Commemoration Ceremony on May 20-21, with faculty, staff, students, and local community members gathering to plant flags in memory of a veteran special to them. The ceremony featured the traditional TAPS bugle call at noon, followed by a "Static Flag Display" showcasing military branches' flags surrounding the American flag. The college's Student Veterans Club also hosted a contest asking community members what Memorial Day means to them, with winners Gavin Roger (essay) and Ashley Kifer (drawing) attending the event; Roger and Kifer are students at Bohemia Manor High School.

title: Easton Middle teams win Stock Market Game championships
content:
Easton Middle School teams won state and regional Stock Market Game championships, led by social studies teacher Edward Keeler. The winning teams achieved highest portfolio returns among student teams in their age group, with:

- Fall regional team: Wilmer Rodriguez Argueta, Javir Harrington, Gibson Taylor
- Spring regional team: Jordan Langrell, Cameron Rodrigue
- Fall state team: Caiden Sackett, Braden Streaker, Miles Fink

The Stock Market Game allowed students to develop skills in math, language arts, research, and critical thinking. The competition provides real-world experience in investing, with updates on portfolio statements and rankings.

Easton Middle School won the MD State Stock Market Games sponsored by the Maryland Council on Economic Education, with Mr. Keeler having led more students to victory than any teacher in Maryland.

title: Thank you for your service
content:
Michael Feehley and Tom Carlson, two decorated veterans, are on a mission to educate young people about the sacrifices made by veterans. They replaced flags at the Easton Elks Lodge with dozens of new ones. Feehley's "Teach-in" program takes veterans into schools to teach kids that veterans are all around them, including family members and neighbors.

Feehley says that from the Korean War era, veterans were often overlooked, leading him to share the famous saying "All gave some and some gave all." He aims to impart this message through his sessions, teaching students about the sacrifices made by veterans and their families. Feehley highlights that veterans' experiences differ from those of 9-to-5 workers, as they serve without pay and often face challenges upon returning home.

Feehley's program includes interacting with various military branches and encouraging young people to express gratitude. When asked how students should engage with veterans, he advises a simple "Thank you" when seeing a veteran's service. The sessions are not recruitment efforts but rather a lesson in gratitude, aimed at reminding people of the sacrifices made by veterans.

Feehley teaches that without veterans, many modern conveniences might not exist, and his program has been met with enthusiasm from young students and teachers alike. He hopes to continue the program next year.

title: Embrace uncertainty, Joe Flacco tells University of Delaware graduates
content:
Joe Flacco, University of Delaware football legend, told graduates to embrace uncertainty in a commencement address on May 29, 2024. Flacco shared his personal experience of self-doubt and fear of failure, realizing that he had been searching for the wrong thing all along. He emphasized the importance of learning from failure and embracing uncertainty to find peace and success.

Flacco spoke about his career journey, including struggles in Baltimore, trades to the Broncos and Eagles, and a career resurgence with Cleveland. He encouraged graduates to lean on their family and friends for support, work hard, and accept that success may take time.

Flacco also answered questions from graduates, including one about playing with Ray Lewis, who was "really good men" off the field as well as tough competitors on it. University of Delaware President Dennis Assanis praised the Class of 2024 for their hard work and reminded them to value empathy, compassion, and human understanding in a rapidly changing world.

Key points:

* Joe Flacco's commencement address
* Emphasis on embracing uncertainty and learning from failure
* Career journey and personal growth
* Importance of family support, hard work, and perseverance
* Tribute to Ray Lewis as a role model
* University President Dennis Assanis' message on empathy, compassion, and human connection

title: 'It’s very fulfilling': Local students recognized for accomplishments
content:
Local students were recognized for their academic achievements at Kent Island High School Senior Night 2024 on May 22. The ceremony honored over 100 individual students attending college, scholarship awardees, and top-performing students in each department. Principal Daniel Harding expressed pride in the Class of 2024.

Shelby Faery, a senior who accumulated 60 credits through dual enrollment programs with Chesapeake College and Anne Arundel Community College, received recognition for her Associate's Degree in transfer studies. Shelby completed her AA degree before graduating from Kent Island High School and plans to attend the University of Maryland College Park in the fall.

Kent Island students received record-breaking scholarship amounts, and 6 seniors earned 18 or more college credits through dual enrollment programs. Queen Anne's County High School also recognized its dual enrollment students, scholarship winners, and department recognitions during its annual Senior Awards Night on May 16.

Notable achievements include:

- Shelby Faery: 60 credits, Associate's Degree in transfer studies, University of Maryland College Park acceptance
- Kent Island High School: Record-breaking scholarship amounts, 6 seniors with 18+ college credits through dual enrollment programs
- Queen Anne's County High School: Dual enrollment students recognized, scholarship winners honored, department recognitions

Key dates:

- May 16: Queen Anne's County Senior Awards Night
- May 22: Kent Island High School Senior Night 2024

title: Sending Shelly home
content:
Chestertown-based Kent County Middle School's Terrapin Program, in partnership with Maryland Environmental Service and Ohio University's Willem Roosenburg, sent a diamondback terrapin named Shelly back to her natural habitat on Poplar Island. As part of the research program, Shelly was raised by teachers Samantha Cawthorne and Roberto-Luis Copeland, who traveled from Chestertown to Tilghman Island with sixth-graders, including Shelly in a plastic box. The Terrapin Program, which started in 2013, aims to study terrapins' ecology and physiology while teaching students about environmental conservation.

Shelly was originally from Poplar Island, where the Maryland Environmental Service is rebuilding the island after it eroded due to Chesapeake Bay waters. Scientists collect around 150 eggs annually and give juveniles to schools for a "head start" program, which aims to determine if human involvement in terrapins' early stages of life affects their survival. The field trip was funded by the Kent County Public Schools Education Foundation Fund, part of Mid-Shore Community Foundation.

Cawthorne and Copeland expressed hope that middle school students learned about the impact of human actions on the Bay's ecosystem through Shelly's release. The program provides a unique opportunity for hands-on involvement in conservation efforts, inspiring emotional connections with the Chesapeake Bay.

title: Raising the future at the Talbot County Free Library
content:
The article by Bill Peak for The Star Democrat discusses how adult life may recapitulate childhood experiences and fears. It wonders if psychiatrists are correct that our adult lives merely repeat patterns from our youth. The author suggests that playing, inventing, and being childlike are essential to creating a new reality.

The Talbot County Free Library's 9th annual Chesapeake Children's Book Festival will take place on June 22, featuring 22 children's book authors and illustrators. The festival includes activities such as a Summer Reading Program voucher for a free book from attending authors, author signings, puppet performances by the Maryland State Opera Bears, crafts, and more.

Authors participating in the festival include Andi Diehn, Mirka Hokkanen, and Timothy Young, who designed Muppets for Jim Henson. The event aims to provide a fun day for children, encouraging creativity and playfulness from an early age.

title: Veteran Affairs Committee honors students for USO posters
content:
The Veterans Affairs Committee honored students from Saints Peter and Paul High School in Easton, MD for designing USO posters for a fundraising event. Chairman Michael Freely expressed gratitude for the students' work, drawing parallels between his own military experience and the poster's impact on community engagement. Art teacher Jacqui Gosselin praised the opportunity for her students to conduct research and community service for veterans. Committee members Duane Hilghman thanked the students and their teacher for creating beautiful posters, emphasizing the importance of youth involvement in supporting veteran services.

Key details:
- Date: May 31, 2024
- Location: Easton, MD (Saints Peter and Paul High School)
- Organizations: Veterans Affairs Committee, USO, Easton Elk's 1622
- People: Michael Freely (Veterans Affairs Committee chairman), Jacqui Gosselin (art teacher), Duane Hilghman (Veterans Affairs Committee member)
- Dates: December 7, 2023 (USO-themed benefit dance)

title: St. Michaels High School class of 2024 advised to 'just keep swimming'
content: St. Michaels High School Class of 2024 graduates received diplomas on June 2, 2024. Senior class president Madi White welcomed students and parents with a speech highlighting their journey's hardships and support system. Will Bridges presented the mantel, passing it to Lexi Rockwell as valedictorian Nathan Henckel gave his address, quoting Hannah Montana and thanking teacher Lauren Greer for her encouragement. Talbot County Public Schools Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi congratulated the class, advising them to "just keep swimming" as they enter the future.

title: 287 Easton High students get diplomas
content:
287 Easton High School students received diplomas on June 2, 2024, in a ceremony where NJROTC presented colors and senior Kristian Cherry sang the National Anthem. Principal Sherry Spurry spoke of the class's resilience during COVID-19, earning $14,095,882 in scholarships and completing over 37,291 service learning hours.

TCPS Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi focused on encouraging graduates to be great, make mistakes, and fail forward again. Valedictorian Iven Chen addressed the audience, reminiscing about losing a year due to COVID but finding rhythm as the four years progressed.

Chen emphasized pursuing one's own path and making memories in life. Salutatorian Sabin Long welcomed future communities to accept graduates as they move forward. Senior Class President Colin Smith urged graduates to break patterns and seize opportunities. Board Member Samantha Jessee referenced school spirit and following dreams, quoting Elvis Presley.

Dr. Pepukayi and Emily Jackson handed out 287 diplomas, with each graduate throwing their tassels and caps in the air after receiving their diploma.

title: Class of 2024 NDHS eagles fly the nest
content:
The Class of 2024 at North Dorchester High School (NDHS) graduated on May 29, despite rain preventing a traditional flagpole ceremony in the school's auditorium. NDHS Salutatorian Ta'Tyana Maradiaga and Valedictorian Fatima Kaleem addressed the graduates, expressing pride, hope, and appreciation for their experiences.

Maradiaga spoke about the "lasts" of the class year, including spirit weeks, pep rallies, prom, homecoming, field trips, and morning announcements. She urged her classmates to pursue their dreams with confidence and determination, and thanked them for enduring triumphs and learning.

Kaleem reflected on her own journey, acknowledging that memories have shaped her into the person she is today. She asked her classmates to look back on their experiences with pride and recognition, saying "say thank you to your past self" and embracing their future with a heart free of regrets.

Principal David Stofa reminded the class to carry NDHS values – diversity, empathy, and kindness – as they pursue their dreams. NDHS teacher Phil Albert shared his personal experience of supporting his son through a bone marrow transplant, saying that "service from the heart" is what makes people and organizations great.

title: 'Unparalleled resilience, adaptability and determination:' CSD class of 2024 graduates
content:
Wil and Luke Reinbold, identical twin brothers with matching GPAs, were named co-valedictorians of Cambridge-South Dorchester High School's 2024 class. During their commencement speech, they emphasized the importance of taking risks and perseverance in the face of challenges. The class received $2.8 million in scholarships.

The COVID-19 pandemic was a significant challenge for the class, but Principal Jerome Stover praised their resilience, adaptability, and determination. Teacher Shawn Tucker shared an anecdote about a student who transformed from disengaged to motivated after being inspired by Tucker's teaching.

The ceremony featured performances of "I Lived" by OneRepublic, "Don't Stop Believin'" by Journey, and "The Time of My Life" by Bill Medley and Jennifer Warnes. The graduates' parents and staff were present, marking a milestone after the school had no traditional eighth-grade graduation ceremony four years ago.

title: Class of 2024 displays '24-karat shine'
content:
Principal Kris Hemstetter led the 53rd annual commencement ceremony at Kent County High School on May 31, 2024, with a "24K Magic" theme highlighting the class of 2024's shine. Valedictorian Ben Loller will attend Brown University to study computer science, while salutatorian Madison Messick earned a full ride to the University of Maryland, College Park.

Dr. Karen Couch, superintendent of Kent County Public Schools, praised the graduates' resilience and dedication to excellence. Guest speaker Darius Johnson encouraged the class to find their own paths to success. Messick spoke about perseverance in the face of challenges and urged her classmates to use their unique talents to build a future reflecting compassion, empathy, and equality.

Class members will attend college or trade schools (70%), enter the workforce (26%), or enlist in the military (4%). The Class of 2024 Secretary Jessica Rosanova hosted the ceremony, with Jaeda Hoxter introducing platform guests. The class rang their class rings and turned their tassels to mark graduation.

Key dates: May 31, 2024; Kent County High School's 53rd annual commencement ceremony; Bruno Mars' "24K Magic"

title: Caroline County high schools mark graduations
content: Two Caroline County high schools, Colonel Richardson and North Caroline High Schools, held graduations on May 30 and May 29, respectively. Graduates wore school colors and mortar boards, with some attending military service, colleges, trade schools, or entering the workforce. Princips Jared Sherman (Colonel Richardson) and Matt Spiker (North Caroline) expressed congratulations and appreciation for the successful events.

title: Dorchester County talks Blueprint with MACo
content:
Dorchester County Council discussed Blueprint for Maryland's Future requirements with MACo representatives Johnny Olszewski and Michael Sanderson on June 4. Olszewski stated that large counties like Dorchester are struggling to fund the plan, which aims to improve student outcomes through increasing education funding by $3.8 billion over 10 years.

MACo Executive Director Sanderson highlighted that income taxes and property taxes are the primary revenue sources for county governments, but two-thirds of Marylanders are at the "absolute cap" on income tax. This means property taxes must be relied upon to fund Blueprint requirements, which MACo considers unsustainable.

Council members expressed concerns about funding Blueprint, with Ricky Travers stating that it's forcing the county to strip other services and Rob Kramer noting that 72% of Dorchester County is considered critical area, making it difficult to increase property tax revenues without raising taxes.

William Nichols refused to raise taxes on seniors, citing a large number of seniors in his district. Olszewski acknowledged that counties are struggling to meet Blueprint requirements, which would impact funding for community colleges and roads.

MACo requests include a comprehensive cost analysis of the Blueprint, increased state aid for pre-K facilities, and more time for educator career ladder model development. The organization also warned that if counties don't meet Blueprint requirements, their county income taxes will be sent directly to schools rather than the county.

Johnny Olszewski emphasized the importance of facilitating conversations between MACo and Maryland counties, stating that it's already sounding like Blueprint will be a major issue in the upcoming year.

title: Summer aviation, model rocket events at Easton Airport
content:
The Easton Airport's Aviation Career Education (ACE) Program and the Easton Composite Squadron — Civil Air Patrol (CAP) are hosting a series of summer events for kids and teens aged 12-16. Events include:

* July 16: Airfield Design
* July 17: Paper Airplane/Aircraft Characteristics
* July 23: Model Rocket Construction (Part 1)
* July 24: Model Rocket Launch Day (Time TBD)

Instructors will conduct the sessions at Easton Airport's ACE Hangar, located at 29051 Corkran Road, Easton, MD 21601.

title: Young runners recognized by Board of Education
content: The Caroline County Board of Education recognized members of the school community on June 4, including young runners from Greensboro Elementary School who achieved great strides by running a 5k in Cambridge on May 4. Superintendent Derek Simmons praised their efforts, saying "Keep running, keep running, keep running." The male athletes' fundraiser, which raised $4,287 for Parkinson's awareness, was also recognized and donated to the Rock Steady boxing group in Easton.

title: Done for the children
content: Barbara Lee Jefferson, a therapy dog handler, reported that her canine and handler team was banned from Easton Elementary School due to a "policy change." Despite background checks, handling tests, and 1,000+ visits, they were told their dogs would not be allowed after an anonymous message claimed it was based on policy. Jefferson's teams have been visiting special needs classrooms in Talbot and Queen Anne's counties since 2012 without compensation, using Alliance of Therapy Dogs and Crisis Response Canines resources. The ban affects over 7 classrooms scheduled for September-December sessions, leaving Jefferson hoping to regain access next year.

title: QACPS approves piggybacking bread and paper product contracts
content:
Queens Anne's County Public Schools approved piggybacking contracts with Cecil County Public Schools for bread products ($140,000) and cafeteria paper products ($142,000), both from Schmidt Baking Company and FPC Distribution, respectively. Superintendent Patricia Saelens said contract piggybacking offers better options and buying power to smaller districts like Queen Anne's County.

The BOE also approved purchasing a new or used school bus for the 2024-2025 school year. Bus #2510 has reached its 15-year life cycle, according to Sidney Pinder.

Next BOE meetings: June 19 (work session at 5 p.m.) and July 17 (regular meeting at 6 p.m.).

title: High school teacher guilty of assault on prankster
content: Dylan M. Aiman, a 54-year-old Rising Sun High School teacher, pleaded guilty to second-degree assault for assaulting a 13-year-old boy after being pranked at his residence on May 4. The victim and friend had rung the doorbell and ran away, prompting Aiman to chase them across the street. After catching them, Aiman forced them back to his porch, where he made them wait for police to arrive. He grabbed one of the boys by the sweatshirt, lifted him up, and kneed him in the ribs. The incident occurred on May 4, and charges were filed on May 5. Aiman was released on personal recognizance but later received a suspended six-month sentence and 15 months of supervised probation after pleading guilty to second-degree assault. The Cecil County Public Schools district is reviewing the situation and will follow their human resources processes to address it.

title: Classmate's legacy lives on in Kent Island
content: Kent Island High school held its graduation ceremony on June 11, 2024, at a packed Buccaneer's stadium. Valedictorian Darcy Lynn gave an emotional speech, honoring her classmate Jacob Sloan, who died in their seventh-grade year due to his kindness and generosity. Sloan's impact continues to inspire the class, and Lynn encouraged them to carry on his legacy by making the world a better place through everyday actions. Quoting Taylor Swift, Lynn said, "No matter what happens in life, be good to people." The class wore red heart pins in honor of Sloan, who left a lasting mark on many.

title: It's official: Thompson to lead Dochester schools
content: Jymil Thompson has been selected as the new superintendent of Dorchester County Public Schools after a national search. Thompson, a former assistant superintendent, will take over from interim Superintendent David Bromwell on July 1. Thompson holds a doctorate in educational leadership and a Bachelor's degree from Pennsylvania State University. He plans to improve instructional practices and climate within schools, aiming to boost the district's ranking from 23rd to 15th in the state. The board, led by President Mike Diaz, voted to approve Thompson's contract at its regular meeting on Thursday.

title: Caroline Board of Education recognizes student representatives
content:
Caroline County Board of Education recognized Vanessa Odidika and Kadeen Belle as Student Board Representatives for the 2024-2025 school year. Derek Simmons, superintendent, described them as outstanding students with extensive leadership roles and accomplishments. Odidika is a senior at Colonel Richardson High School, while Belle is a junior at North Caroline High School.

Odidika is treasurer of the Straight Gay Alliance, National Honor Society, Technical Honor Society, LEO Club, orchestra, and chorus; she plans to be a pediatric emergency physician after graduation. Belle is treasurer of her class and Student Government Association; she's also involved with TRIO Upward Bound, Regional Policy Director, and Stanford University's intensive law trial program.

Simmons expressed excitement for the students' leadership and encouraged them to engage with the community, visit schools, and participate in events. The student representatives will begin their responsibilities in September.

title: DCPS approves fiscal year 2025 budget in 3 to 1 vote
content:
DCPS approves fiscal year 2025 budget in 3-1 vote. The $88.5 million balanced budget is a $7.4 million increase from FY 2024 and includes measures to address financial shortfalls due to COVID-19-related funding ending. Media specialists were initially set to be removed, but this decision was reversed after public outcry.

Board members Talibah Chikwendu, Chris Wheedleton, Sheri Hubbard, and Mike Diaz voted in favor of the budget, while board member Susan Morgan voted against it.

Chikwendu expressed concerns about frontline staff cuts. Board President Diaz acknowledged that alternative education contracts, such as with Vision Quest, will be reviewed. Lucas Thorpe criticized the district's reliance on these contracts, which include high monthly payments.

The fiscal year 2025 budget includes an $1386 news article reference, 313k in salary and wage expenditures savings, a 32.3% reduction, 23.7 million county revenue sources, and a 22% increase in fixed charges expenditures.

Dorchester County Public Schools Interim Superintendent Jymil Thompson reassured media specialists that their positions are secure after meeting with them on June 6.

title: Rock Hall Garden Club offers yearly scholarship
content: The Garden Club of Rock Hall awards a $1,000 scholarship to a high school senior promoting a career in agriculture, horticulture, or natural resources. This year's recipient is Kent County High School graduate Bradley Trice Moore II. The club promotes gardening, native tree and plant conservation, and community protection. Their next event is a potluck and flower show in July (gcrh.weebly.com).

title: It's official: Thompson to lead Dochester schools
content:
Jymil Thompson, current interim superintendent of Dorchester County Public Schools, has been selected as the district's new superintendent after a national search. Thompson holds a BA from Pennsylvania State University, MA from Trinity University, certificate from Howard University, and PhD in educational leadership from Indiana Wesleyan University. He served as assistant superintendent before becoming interim superintendent in March 2024.

Thompson aims to improve the district's ranking from 23rd to 15th in the state by enhancing instructional practices and school climate. His official start date is July 1. Board President Mike Diaz stated that Thompson was the best fit, and the board looks forward to working with him to ensure all students reach their full potential.

Thompson expressed his commitment to student success, citing the district's current struggles in preparing students for national and global competitiveness. He plans to implement changes over the next five years to address this issue.

title: Talbot school board passes special education staffing plan
content:
Talbot County Board of Education unanimously approved a special education staffing plan, with projected decreases in elementary students at all five schools except Easton Middle and St. Michaels Middle High. Director of Special Education Kristin Mentges recommended maintaining current staffing levels, citing sufficient support for 116 students per teacher. The board questioned the method used to calculate staffing needs, suggesting an analysis based on hours of need rather than student numbers.

Mentges added a special education supervisor and four instructional assistants, aiming to support young students with significant disabilities. Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi announced a work session next month to analyze data and identify areas for improvement. 

Talbot County Public Schools director of operations Kevin Shafer reported steady enrollment, with no schools at risk of overutilization. However, he noted potential uncertainty due to housing development, demographic shifts, and the state's education plan, Blueprint for Maryland's Future.

The board approved a revised budget for special education staffing, which includes seven current speech therapists. Board members expressed concerns about the need for more frequent discussions on staffing and funding, with President Emily Jackson stating that "the special ed staff has been pretty flat" despite growing student needs.

title: Dorchester school board Vice President Susan Morgan resigns
content:
Here is a highly condensed version of the article:

Susan Morgan, Dorchester County Board of Education Vice President and former president, has resigned following a contentious vote and discussion during Thursday's meeting. She also withdrew from running for reelection on the November ballot.

The resignation came after Morgan voted in favor of keeping the contract with Vision Quest, an alternative education program for district high schoolers, despite criticism from residents since its approval in September. The contract would have cost the district over $3.3 million and was a primary reason other members voted against it.

Morgan's decision to resign also stems from disagreements with appointed board members Chris Wheedleton and Tabilah Chikwendu, who filled vacancies on the board this year. Wheedleton called out the board for not being more collaborative at Thursday's meeting, while Morgan stated that she was shocked by the approval of the proposed fiscal year 2025 budget without her input.

Interim Superintendent Jymil Thompson emphasized the need for collaboration and cooperation among board members. He also talked about increasing the district's ranking from 23rd in the state and using the hashtag #23nomore this year.

Morgan cited rampant misspending with no real controls or oversight as a major factor in her decision to resign. She stated that she was "simply amazed" at what was spent on expenses over the past three fiscal years.

Board President Mike Diaz said he would have a statement about the situation on Wednesday, but Morgan stated that she is no longer running for reelection.

title: Dorchester BOE votes to terminate alternative education contract
content:
The Dorchester County Board of Education voted to terminate its three-year contract with Vision Quest, an alternative education program for district high schoolers, following a tense discussion. The motion was made by board member Chris Wheedleton, who opposed the initial approval in September.

Key points:

- 180 days written notice is required for termination.
- Monthly payment: $93,363 for services including in-school and off-campus programs for up to 26 students at any given time.
- Over three years, this would have cost the district over $3.3 million.
- Wheedleton cited "fiscally irresponsible" reasons and concerns about lack of monthly reports.

Supporting statements:

- Board member Susan Morgan said she had visited Morningstar Youth Academy in Woolford and talked to parents, citing 7 students who graduated this year without support from Vision Quest.
- Talibah Chikwendu believed the contract was not in DCPS' best interest based on information from people familiar with the program.
- Sheri Hubbard voted to terminate due to "numerous complaints" about Vision Quest and a conversation with a former staff member.

Date: June 16, 2024.

title: This Juneteenth, let's prioritize education policy
content:
Today marks Juneteenth, a federal holiday commemorating the end of slavery in the US. Scholars describe it as a celebration of Frederick Douglass' legacy as a Maryland abolitionist who emphasized education's importance in breaking cycles of poverty and oppression. Born into slavery, Douglass secretly learned to read and write, demonstrating that knowledge was vital for freedom.

Douglass advocated for education as a tool against racial injustice and inequality. His mentorship inspired future generations to use education to combat social injustices. However, Maryland politicians have forgotten these principles, with Prince George's County serving as an example. Despite being one of the wealthiest majority African American counties in the US, it ranks last in statewide education rankings.

The county's graduation rate is less than 75%, and its high schools underperformed state education targets, leading to increased income inequality and social injustices. County Executive Angela Alsobrooks claimed "Not my responsibility" when asked about the school system's challenges, which is concerning given her nomination for US Senate. 

Studies show that private school-choice programs tend to have positive effects on student achievement, especially among marginalized students. African Americans and underserved communities support these policies. Douglass' legacy emphasizes the importance of education in building a cycle of success for future generations.

On this Juneteenth, we should recognize and act upon Douglass' vital lesson by re-prioritizing education policy in Maryland's political landscape, honoring his memory and paving the way for a more just and equitable future.
