title: Mothers of Baltimore: Local women try to overcome lack of child care
content:
Baltimore's single mothers face a lack of affordable childcare options, with many centers catering to individual needs rather than providing comprehensive support. Yvonne Turner, owner of Old Mother Hubbard's Child Care Center, prioritizes empathy and flexibility for young families. LaKesha Solomon, owner of Solomon's Family Daycare, credits her 25-year network in the neighborhood for supporting both parents and providers, including covering costs for government-provided childcare vouchers.

In 2024, there are only 669 registered child care providers in Baltimore City, a 15.6% loss since the COVID-19 pandemic. Latoya Turpin's Little Steps Childcare prioritizes curriculum and development, with an app that keeps parents informed about their child's activities.

Single mothers face challenges such as delayed access to childcare vouchers, theft of personal belongings, and stress from navigating urban life. Turner notes some parents turn to substance abuse as a coping mechanism. Neighborhood-run day care centers like Solomon's and Turpin's provide relief for parents seeking quality childcare.

According to the Baltimore Neighborhood Indicators Alliance-Jacob France Institute, 51% of female-headed households in Baltimore have children under 18. Parents praise centers like Little Steps Childcare for their focus on child development, safety, and transparency. Turner says providing one-on-one time with children is essential, while Solomon emphasizes her role in caring for the entire community.

Key statistics:
- 35,285 women-owned day care centers in the United States (2021)
- 793 registered child care providers in Baltimore City (2020)
- 669 registered child care providers in Baltimore City (2024), a 15.6% loss
- 51% of female-headed households in Baltimore have children under 18

title: Summer Speaker Series panel empowers audience to find passion and purpose
content:
The second annual Women to Watch Summer Speaker Series kicked off at Chesapeake College with a panel discussion on finding passion and purpose. The panel featured Shelly Gross-Wade, CEO of Bay Crossing Consulting; Kim Montooth, assistant vice president of M&T Bank; Shawna D. Payne, founder of The BE Academy; Liz Verhelle, financial advisor of Edward Jones; and moderator Carrie-Ann Barrow.

Panelists shared personal and professional stories about career changes, raising families, education, health scares, and finding purpose after facing burnout. Gross-Wade emphasized the importance of quality of life over quantity, while Payne highlighted creating her own schedule to prioritize family time. Montooth used the concept of "ikigai" to identify her passion for helping others.

Verhelle noted sacrificing ego for humility and Payne warned about financial sacrifices but encouraged surrounding oneself with encouragement and building connections. Gross-Wade stressed breaking out of boundaries and reaching fullest potential. The series includes networking, discussion panels, and small group mentoring sessions.

Since 2020, APG Media has recognized women in Mid-Shore communities through the Women to Watch program, with over 350 nominations this year. The Summer Speaker Series continues until August 15 at Wharves at Choptank Visitor Center and Avalon Theatre, with $30 tickets available.

title: Maritime Museum celebrates Education Professionals
content:
The Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum hosted its second annual Education Professionals Gratitude Day on June 23, 2024, attracting over 200 educators from nationwide. The event aimed to recognize educators' hard work and dedication during the COVID-19 pandemic. Vice President of Education and Interpretation Jill Ferris initiated the idea, citing the museum's goal to connect people with the Chesapeake Bay region through interactive exhibits.

The museum provided various activities for educators, including a musical performance by Fresh Squeezed OJ, free shaved ice from Kona Ice, and Harbor Highlights cruises. Educators praised the hands-on experience, saying it elevated their students' learning experience and connected classroom lessons to real-world scenarios. Key attendees included elementary school teachers Mia Alvarez (Pennsylvania) and Michelle McDaniel.

Ferris acknowledged educators' dedication to guiding students throughout the year and helping them grow. She emphasized the museum's role in supporting educators and celebrating their work, noting that it is a delight to collaborate with schools to make learning come alive for students. The event was part of the "Your museum, Your community" initiative, which aims to welcome and recognize local efforts and be a support system for the community.

Key dates and events: 
- June 23, 2024 (Education Professionals Gratitude Day)
- Second annual event

Key people:
- Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado, Author/Byline
- Jill Ferris, Vice President of Education and Interpretation
- Mia Alvarez, Elementary school teacher
- Michelle McDaniel, Elementary school teacher

title: Schools should do better
content:
The article discusses the low ranking of Maryland school districts, particularly in Eastern Shore counties. The rankings were compared from two websites: Schooldigger.com and Niche.com. The results showed:

- Queen Anne's County (3rd), Worcester County (4th)
- Talbot County (13th), Caroline County (16th), Wicomico County (17th), Kent County (19th), Dorchester County (22nd), Somerset County (23rd)

Baltimore City ranked 24th. The author, Gerry Early, suggests that schools should be doing better.

title: Wearing hoods, having cellphones on are not allowed in Calvert schools
content:
Calvert County Public Schools will prohibit students from wearing hoods in school buildings starting August 2024. The decision was made after a majority of school board members voted to ban hooded sweatshirts with hoods on, citing concerns about concealment of earbuds and difficulty in identifying students on surveillance cameras.

The proposal was based on a survey of nearly 1,300 educators, which found strong support for the ban. Board member Lisa Grenis stated that some students wear hoods to ignore classroom instruction or evade recognition by teachers and administrators.

However, not all board members agreed with the ban. Student member Grace Minakowski expressed concerns that banning hoods would not address underlying issues such as vaping and fights. The board ultimately voted unanimously to approve the revised code of conduct, which also includes new policies on cellphone use, including prohibiting personal laptops and requiring phones to be powered off during school.

The revised policy states that students can bring their phones to school but must power them off and keep them in a secure location, with exceptions for high school students. The changes are intended to promote student safety and dignity, while also considering individual needs.

title: FOR THE RECORD
content: A story published in last week's Times Record incorrectly stated Chrissy Bartz was sworn into Caroline County Board of Education on June 18, but her swearing-in was postponed due to scheduling issues.

title: Caroline Commissioners approve CCPS FY25 budget summary
content: The Caroline County Public Schools (CCPS) FY25 budget summary was approved by commissioners on June 26, 2024, with a $94.48 million balanced operating budget, an increase of nearly $4 million from FY24. Superintendent Derek Simmons attributed the increase to rising business costs and state revenue growth ($18.49M, up $2.4M, and $75M, up $1.38M). Expenditures include Blueprint programming ($559,688) and increased health insurance costs (5%). Teacher pension costs continue to rise. The district will fund positions previously funded by COVID-19 grants. Simmons believes the district is on track to reach a $60,000 starting salary for teachers by 2026, with new hires starting on the career ladder scale.

title: County approves budget transfers for Talbot schools
content:
Talbot County Public Schools requested categorical transfers in its FY24 budget to balance FY25, including prepayments and covering anticipated overages. The district asked for approval of $1.425 million transfers: $75,000 to student services, $500,000 to transportation, and $600,000 to fixed charges for other postemployment benefits contributions and health insurance prepayments.

Council Vice President Pete Lesher expressed concerns about the impact on instructional salaries, which were behind by $850,000 due to vacant positions. However, district officials assured him that a director of recruitment and retention and mentorship programs would help fill those gaps.

Lesher acknowledged that successful schools contribute to economic development, benefiting local businesses and job creation. The council approved the request unanimously.

title: KCHS valedictorian codes bus program for families
content: Kent County High School's valedictorian, Ben Loller, has developed a web-based program to track school bus locations for parents. The program was sparked by discussions at a citizen advisory committee meeting and with the encouragement of Kent County Public Schools superintendent Karen Couch. Loller worked on the project with IT supervisor William Poore and incorporated necessary safeguards despite privacy concerns. He presented his progress to the Board of Education, where it received positive feedback. Loller plans to continue working on the program while attending Brown University in Rhode Island this fall. The valedictorian has been coding for several hours a night since completing high school and aims to copyright his work.

title: Diaz resigns from Dorchester Board of Education
content:
Mike Diaz, president of Dorchester County Board of Education, resigned on June 28 due to health and family concerns, citing a liver transplant in February that made him reconsider his role. He stated he wanted to ensure the board was "in good hands" before leaving.

Diaz' resignation comes after Board Vice President Susan Morgan's departure in mid-June, following a board meeting where relationships were strained. The remaining three board members will hold a special meeting to elect new president and vice president.

The Dorchester County Council is responsible for appointing vacant seats. Diaz was running for reelection in District 1; Morgan had withdrawn from the November election. Diaz has not decided if he'll withdraw, citing discussing with his family.

Superintendent Jymil Thompson remains appointed, and board members are focused on preparing for the next school year.

title: Finding childcare in Maryland is hard. Finding good childcare is even harder
content:
Stephanie Jovine searched for child care for her 4-year-old daughter in 2015, finding two options that were deemed bad due to affordability and quality issues. After six months, she found a small before-and-after care service, LiLi's Child Care Center, run by her grandmother. 

Maryland offers a rating system to help parents select the right child care facility, but providers claim it's difficult to navigate. Most parents interviewed never looked at the state rating system. The state also offers a generous scholarship program, but providers often have to wait months for payment.

Doug Lent, communications director for Maryland Family Network, said that when families are on waiting lists, they're more likely to rely on unlicensed care. Linda Garey, a level-3 provider with Maryland EXCELS, has over 20 years of experience but can't go higher than level 3 due to lack of national accreditation.

The EXCELS rating system is based on five categories, and even providers with high ratings like Garey struggle with the process. Javiera King, an administrator at the University of Maryland, had to hire a nanny while searching for a child care facility.

Jovine found another option after 10 months of searching but was only satisfied when her daughter started going there without having to take any days off work. She applied for a scholarship program and received temporary aid covering two months of costs.

In 2022, Maryland expanded its child care scholarship program, making it easier for middle-class families to afford child care. However, providers complain that the system is difficult to navigate due to long wait times and requirements.

Christine Morris, director of Trinity Lutheran Christian School and Early Learning Center, said the state owes her $40,000 in scholarship payments. Shantel Rouzer, who runs Happy Feet Enrichment Childcare Center, turned away students on the scholarship program because she knows the state's reimbursements will come late.

Solving her own problem, Jovine got licensed to start a home daycare to alleviate Maryland's child care shortage. Her fledgling facility, Elite Kidz Clubhouse, opens in August and is already taking over her home.

title: La Plata siblings commemorate D-Day in Normandy
content: Two La Plata high school siblings, Jack and Lauren Compton, represented their Civil Air Patrol squadron at the 80th anniversary of D-Day in Normandy, France. The siblings raised $8,000 to participate in commemoration events, which was only possible through donations from family, friends, and local businesses like the Harry White Wilmer American Legion Post 82 ($4,000). The group visited Brittany American Cemetery and Memorial, where over 44,000 Americans are buried, and participated in a memorial ceremony. Jack and Lauren said standing as a representation for lost lives made a difference, with their mother describing it as "representation" and "honor." During the trip, they met Chris Langlois, author of "How Easy Company Became a Band of Brothers," who informed them that their relative Lynn "Buck" Compton was part of the 101st Airborne Division. The siblings visited the La Cambe German Military Cemetery, where over 21,000 German soldiers are buried, and met people dressed in World War II costumes representing generals, pilots, and code breakers. The nine-day trip cost more than $8,000.

title: Young author presents local bird guide to Horizons students
content:
Xaviana Leis, 13, a homeschool student in Edgewater, MD, presented her self-published book "Maryland Bird Guide" to Horizons students at the Gunston School on June 25, as part of their summer program focused on birds. The program aims to prevent "summer slide" and provide engaging educational opportunities for under-resourced students.

Horizons executive director Emily Murphy highlighted the program's focus on environmental stewardship and wildlife appreciation. Leis shared her experiences as a raptor volunteer at Owl Moon Raptor Center, where she developed a passion for local birds.

Leis' book features over 50 Maryland bird species with vibrant watercolor illustrations and includes information on habitats, diet, size, and fun facts. She emphasized the importance of responsible feeding practices, litter removal, and supporting wildlife conservation efforts.

The book is available on Amazon, with proceeds going to Owl Moon Raptor Center. Leis has raised over $10,000 through her self-published project. Horizons students received free copies of the book and were encouraged to use it throughout the summer program to identify local birds in the area.

title: Dorchester County Council president, VP thank Board of Education leadership after resignations
content: Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer and Vice President Mike Detmer thanked Dorchester County Board of Education leaders Mike Diaz and Susan Morgan for their service at a June 28 council meeting. Diaz resigned due to family and health concerns after undergoing a liver transplant in February. Morgan resigned on June 14, citing the contentious vote to terminate Vision Quest's contract with the school district as a contributing factor. In an interview, Pfeffer expressed appreciation for Diaz and Morgan's dedication to the community.

title: Local district hikes school lunch, milk prices
content:
Queen Anne's County Public Schools (QACPS) approved a 15-cent per meal price increase and 5-cent per milk carton price increase for the 2024-2025 school year on June 26, citing cost increases. The new prices are: $1.75 for breakfast, $2.75 for elementary school lunch, $3 for middle school and high school lunches, and $4.25 for staff lunch. Milk cartons now cost 55 cents each.

Historically, meal prices increase every two years by 10 cents, but the current increases were based on the Maryland Department of Education Paid Lunch Equity Tool and minimum wage increases to $15 an hour. The Consumer Price Index for Food Away From Home has also increased by four percent over the past 12 months.

Board President Helen Bennett noted the irony of the state's unfunded Blueprint For Maryland's Future, which led to a need for meal price increases despite minimum wage hikes. Meal prices do not impact eligibility for free or reduced meals.

QACPS approved a contract with Hershey Creamery Company for ice cream products and freezers, piggybacking off an Anne Arundel County Public Schools contract set to expire in March 2025. The fiscal impact is $50,000, funding from the food service fund balance account.

title: 'It didn't die with her:' New Beginnings continues to grow after death of executive director
content:
Theresa Stafford, executive director of New Beginnings Youth and Family Services, died in December after battling cancer. The organization has continued to grow under Executive Director Goldie Cooper. Phil Feldman, a friend and classmate of Stafford's, donated $25,000 to the center on July 2 in her honor. Plans are to rename the center "Dr. Theresa Stafford's New Beginnings Learning Academy." A dedication event is planned for later this summer. The center has received additional funding through grants, including a $10,000 grant from the John and Janice Wyatt Foundation, bringing the total grant awards to over $72,000.

Stafford grew the center, expanding its budget from $43,000 to over $185,000 per year. She aimed to provide children with the best education in the best environment, especially those without ideal home situations. Current staff member Myche Smith mentioned a new STEM program and a recent donation of golf clubs for kids to practice their swings. Stafford's sister Norby Lee said her sister made significant contributions to the center, including writing over $180,000 in grants.

Stafford served as executive director for eight years, leaving behind a legacy that continues to grow through donations and grant awards. A dedication event is planned to honor Stafford's memory.

title: Dorchester County Council makes appointments to vacant Board of Education seats
content:
Dorchester County Council appointed Brandy Dawson Cumberland and Christine LaMonica to fill Board of Education vacancies created by resigning members Mike Diaz and Susan Morgan.

* Cumberland, a psychiatric mental health nurse practitioner, was appointed to District 1 vacancy.
* Cumberland prioritizes improving the district's ranking (23rd in state), safe learning environments, and addressing student mental health concerns.
* LaMonica, a deputy first class with the Dorchester County Sheriff's Office pursuing a master's degree in social work, was appointed to District 3 vacancy.
* LaMonica emphasizes school safety, transparency, academic excellence, and community involvement in school decisions.
* Diaz resigned June 28 due to family and health concerns after undergoing a liver transplant.
* Morgan resigned June 14, following a contentious vote to terminate the district's contract with Vision Quest.

title: Commissioners keep Master Gardeners rooted in the Kent
content:
Kent County Commissioners awarded $20,353 to keep the Master Gardeners program operational through a part-time Coordinator and Horticulture Educator. The program, established in 2007, provides free educational programming and services, including pollinator topics, native plants, and organic gardening.

23 certified Master Gardeners volunteered 877 hours in 2023, providing $29,369 in services. President Ron Fithian, Albert Nickerson, and John Price voted unanimously to approve the funding. Commissioners acknowledged the program's importance, particularly for educating younger generations on horticulture.

Nancy Robson, Kent County Master Gardeners' representative, emphasized the program's role as a bridge between the University of Maryland and the public. The Master Gardeners aim to promote community health through free projects and education, connecting agriculture with land stewardship.

Without funding, the program would be discontinued due to insufficient office funding, leaving a horticulture position in jeopardy. Commissioner Paul Rickert acknowledged the request and expressed appreciation for the commissioners' consideration.

title: Stronger defense, improved education
content:
In the November election, American top concerns are inflation, illegal migration, and crime. However, issues of national defense and youth education should be higher on the worry list due to relative public indifference. 

The proposed national defense budget mandates spending less on military readiness in real terms than several years ago, with interest payments on federal debt soon exceeding it. This poses a threat to long-term security amidst a growing number of adversaries, including China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea.

Diplomacy has proven unreliable compared to military superiority. Political pressure must be applied to both parties to prioritize enhanced military readiness. 

In youth education, public funding for schools has increased, but test results show no improvement in academic return on investment. This is concerning due to a competitive global work environment, growing need for domestic innovation, and historical correlation between income potential and educational achievement.

The preeminent standing of the US will be at jeopardy if national defense and educational outcomes are not prioritized.

title: Girl Scouts build gaga ball pit at Ridgely park
content:
Girl Scouts from Troop 896 and Troop 899 in Queen Anne's County built a Gaga Ball Pit at Martin Sutton Park in Ridgely as part of their Bronze Award service project. The girls spent nine months planning and advocating for the project, which aimed to create a fun outdoor space for families and children. They presented their plan to the Town Council last fall and received permission to build the pit.

The construction process was led by the girls, with the help of their dads, and taught them basic construction skills such as drawing up plans and taking measurements. The Gaga Ball Pit combines physical activity, outdoor play, and social interaction, making it a popular sport for children.

On June 2, the project was completed, with the Gaga Ball Pit being installed at the park. The Girl Scouts also have Gaga Ball Pits nearby at Camp Todd and Camp Grove Point, promoting physical activity and fun for those who visit.

Key details:

* Project duration: 9 months
* Date of construction: June 2
* Location: Martin Sutton Park in Ridgely
* Troop numbers: 896 and 899
* Bronze Award level: Junior (4th and 5th graders)
* Number of girls involved: Not specified

title: Dorchester BOE elects board leadership, approves alternative education contract
content: The Dorchester County Board of Education unanimously elected Sheri Hubbard as president and Talibah Chikwendu as vice president until December 2024. The board welcomed new members Brandy Dawson Cumberland and Christine LaMonica, who will be sworn in on July 18. The board approved a one-year contract with Transforming Lives for an alternative education program for elementary and middle school students, costing $950,000. Superintendent Jymil Thompson said the district views this program as part of a student's education journey to remedy behavior and improve academics. The district previously terminated its three-year contract with Vision Quest in June after criticism from residents. Hubbard stated that the Vision Quest program will be available to district high school students for the first half of the 2024-2025 school year, with plans to train teachers through Transforming Lives and potentially self-fund the program in the future.

title: 2 new Dorchester Board of Education members sworn in
content: Dorchester Board of Education members Brandy Dawson Cumberland and Christine LaMonica were sworn in on July 21, 2024, to fill vacant seats following resignations of Mike Diaz and Susan Morgan. New Vice President Talibah Chikwendu expressed excitement for a full board, noting increased perspectives would benefit students and staff. DCPS Superintendent Jymil Thompson welcomed the new members, hoping they could improve the district's ranking from 23rd in Maryland to 15th, with a focus on making "big things happen" for Dorchester County Public Schools.

title: Rotary Club of Cambridge visits Ruark Boat Works
content:
The Rotary Club of Cambridge visited the Richardson Maritime Museum and Ruark Boat Works on July 23, 2024. Rotarian Dave Williams gave a tour, discussing the Educational Program with the club members. The program partners with the YMCA to bring in students aged 6-10, teaching skills like reading, measuring, and tool use. Students create toolboxes as part of the program.

Williams also showed guests projects taking place at Ruark Boat Works, explaining construction techniques and highlighting the need for younger volunteers to sustain the craft. The Rotary Club of Cambridge toured the facilities, learning about ongoing plans and goals for the organization.

title: Men For Change recognizes volunteers' service
content:
Men For Change recognized six people for their service at a banquet in Federalsburg, MD on July 20, 2024. The honorees included:

- Brandy James, District One Councilman
- Stephanie Brohawn, Principal of Federalsburg Elementary School
- William Eric Smith, coach and volunteer
- Cynthia Fletcher, community activist
- Cederick Turner, Haitian community liaison
- Roberta Butler, NAACP member

The event's keynote speaker was Vaughn Evans Sr., a former principal at North Dorchester Middle School. Men For Change's theme was "Let's Get Busy," emphasizing the importance of community service and giving back.

State Sen. Johnny Mautz cited all honorees via pre-recorded message due to absence, while Betty Jarman, media spokesperson for Men For Change, expressed gratitude for recognition and highlighted an upcoming partnership with the Federalsburg Activity Center.

The organization is seeking donations to support the construction of a new after-school mentoring program at the center, which is expected to open by September.

title: Talbot County pledges support for Chesapeake College project
content:
Talbot County Council approved a letter of intent to fund a $56 million Chesapeake College facility project, with Talbot's share estimated at $3 million (21.8%). The project will support various trade programs, including agricultural, electrical, welding, HVAC, advanced manufacturing, carpentry, and masonry. David Harper, vice president for workforce and academic programs, hopes the project inspires students to value local careers.

Chesapeake College had originally requested over $4 million from Talbot County, but scope was reduced due to the exclusion of marine technology program. The facility will be built at the Wye Mills campus.

The college also presented to Caroline County Commissioners, who are discussing the request with their finance team. Dorchester County did not provide a letter of support due to financial constraints caused by "The Blueprint for Maryland's Future" public education program.

Queen Anne's County pledged 28.9% of the remaining funding ($3.1 million), while Talbot County is second at 21.8%. The project's construction will span fiscal years 2026, 2027, and 2028.

Council President Chuck Callahan expressed support for the project, stating it will "make a difference in 10 years" and "lack trades."

title: Talbot Mentors calling for more volunteers
content:
Talbot Mentors, a 25-year-old organization in Easton, MD, has seen a 34% decrease in mentor volunteers since the pandemic, from 71 to 50-60 mentors. Executive Director Kentavius Jones said COVID shut down face-to-face interactions and is now ramping up recruitment while focusing on meaningful connections. The organization has piloted a peer-to-peer program, pairing high schoolers with elementary students, which has shown positive results in reducing substance use, improving academic performance, and increasing positive decision-making skills.

The Scholars program, a collaborative effort with Building African American Minds and Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center, aims to help first-generation and marginalized students achieve their academic goals through tutoring, college admissions assistance, and scholarship research. College Success Manager Jennifer Kott said the program provides premier life skills and hope for students from Easton community.

Mentor Joan Evans encouraged anyone interested in volunteering to "take the leap" and said being a mentor requires providing time and attention, not particular skills. She praised Talbot Mentors as a wonderful community resource for connecting children with positive role models.

Key dates: July 25, 2024
Places: Easton, MD; Talbot County; Texas
Organizations: Talbot Mentors; Building African American Minds; Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center; Scholars Program
People: Kentavius Jones (Executive Director); Jennifer Kott (College Success Manager); Joan Evans (Mentor)

title: ‘Stretched very thin’: Child care providers in Talbot County seeing long waitlists
content:
Child care providers in Talbot County face long waitlists due to limited space and staffing issues. Critchlow Adkins Children's Centers' director Melissa Johnson reports a 3-year-old waitlist, including some under a year old, for their Cordova site. Executive Director Christy Morrell plans to double the number of before- and after-school children served from 30 to 60.

Renovation plans at Chapel District Elementary School will allow Critchlow to build a new preschool room and expand its program. Barbra Diaz, director of the Talbot County Center for Children and Families, faces staffing challenges in her Early Head Start program due to state-mandated staff-child ratios.

The Lab Child Care Center owner John Givens has a rolling waitlist for children under two, citing rising costs and new state scholarship program issues. The program aims to help families afford high-quality child care but faces implementation challenges.

State budget cuts have reduced funding for the Rural Maryland Council, affecting Critchlow's grant opportunities. Governor Wes Moore's approval of $148.3 million in state budget cuts for child care and Medicaid has raised concerns about rural county funding. Givens calls the scholarship program "fantastic in theory" but notes implementation issues causing late payments.

Critchlow's Cordova expansion, totaling $1.82 million, aims to provide a better learning environment with dedicated classrooms. The Lab Child Care Center received a $300,000 boost from Talbot County Council funding for American Rescue Plan initiatives.

Maryland EXCELS accredits Critchlow's Cordova site and has maintained a Level 5 rating, the highest rank. Givens advocates for child care to be considered "critical infrastructure," prioritizing its importance for supporting families and children.

title: QACPS celebrates record-breaking success in scholastic art & writing awards
content:
Queen Anne's County Public Schools (QACPS) achieved a record-breaking success in the 2024 Scholastic Art & Writing Awards, with students from Kent Island High School and Queen Anne's County High School earning:

* 24 Gold Keys
* 17 Silver Keys
* 47 Honorable Mentions

Notable winners include:
- Jackson Powell (National Gold Medalist) and Casey Johnson (National Silver Medalist)
- First-ever National Silver Medalist and New York Life Award recipient, Casey Johnson
QACPS continues to foster artistic and literary talents with a video of award-winning artists available on the QACPS YouTube channel.

title: Maryland READS presents to State Board of Education
content:
Maryland READS, a nonprofit founded in 2021, presented updates and addressed drafted literacy policy with the Maryland State Department of Education on July 23. Executive Director Trish Brennan-Gac emphasized the organization's mission to improve reading instruction using research data and evidence-based approaches.

Maryland READS focuses on three main systems of support: improving instruction through the science of reading, building thriving reading ecosystems, and addressing barriers to reading proficiency. The organization has launched a report on the state of reading in Maryland and conducted summer series convenings to build networks and establish planning networks across the state.

The convenings, which included stakeholders from various sectors, provided ideas for establishing strong reading ecosystems rooted in the science of reading. Maryland READS will compile data from these meetings for implementing feedback and continuous improvement.

The organization is actively recruiting new board members and accepting recommendations for its Expert Advisory Committee. Maryland READS has compiled a complete report on the state literacy crisis, which can be found at https://marylandreads.org.

Key dates include:

* 2021: Maryland READS was founded
* November 2021: Public launch of Maryland READS
* Spring 2024: Report on the state of reading in Maryland launched
* July 23, 2024: Presentation to the Maryland State Department of Education
* Fall 2024: Additional READ Strong Network meetings planned

title: Chrome City fundraiser revs up Benedictine's Ridgely campus
content:
Benedictine School held its 22nd annual Chrome City Fundraiser on July 27, 2024, attracting hundreds of car and motorcycle enthusiasts. The event raised over $100,000 for the non-sectarian service provider supporting individuals with developmental disabilities and autism.

Key figures include Megan Efland, director of supply chain for Paul Reed Smith (PRS), who supported the school due to their COO's son being a student; Scott Evans, Benedictine's executive director; Mark Tremonti of Creed signed a guitar for raffle; Jack and William Higginbottom judged the car and motorcycle show.

Winners included Bill and Debra Bugaj with their 1949 Vindian Replica Chief prototype and Craig and Diane Postlewait with their 1938 Packard Model Eight. Sponsors supported the event, including PRS Guitars, Queenstown Bank, Red Knights Motorcycle Club, and others.

The event featured live music by "Stoneflies," food trucks serving lobster, shaved ice, barbecue, and a Chrome City t-shirt for each registered person. The success of the event grew, attracting new attendees who learned about Benedictine's mission, allowing them to interact with students and see the care provided for individuals with developmental disabilities and autism.

title: Carefully vet candidates
content: Sharon Harrington, a social worker and therapist, is concerned about Moms For Liberty (MFL) organization's mission to defend parents' rights at all levels of government. MFL's co-founder Bridget Zielgler was involved in an investigation, leading to further research on the group. The author notes that children can be harmed within families more than by reading a banned book. Harrington identifies Talbot County candidates running for positions affecting schoolchildren and plans to vet them carefully. She finds irony in Zielgler's promotion of family values while being involved in a scandal, and MFL's manifesto lacking child rights.

title: Reading League presents to state board
content:
The Reading League of Maryland presented to the Maryland State Board of Education on July 23, led by vice president Susan White. The organization aims to advance evidence-based literacy instruction and practices, with a focus on professional learning for teachers, administrators, and parents. As part of its mission, the league provides resources such as:

- Science of Reading: Defining Guide
- Reading League Compass
- National Center on Improving Literacy

The league's latest series is a summer book study on the National Reading Panel Report, inviting literacy experts to provide overviews and new findings. The board thanked the reading league for their dedication to education.

Key details:

- Maryland chapter of the National Reading League formed in 2021
- State has 33 chapters nationwide
- The state board meeting took place on July 23
- The summer book study series ran concurrently with the presentation
- Additional literacy resources are available online at md.thereadingleague.org.

title: Maryland Corps, Service Year Option graduates reflect on their experiences
content:
In August 2024, Maryland Corps and Service Year Option graduated their first class of approximately 235 individuals. The state-run programs provided hands-on experience, valuable connections, and a chance to give back to communities. 

Brad Krantz, a St. Michaels graduate, described the program as life-changing, leading him to secure a full-time position at Talisman Therapeutic Riding after working on certification. Krantz credited Maryland Corps for setting him up for success.

Emma Bush, a Salisbury Service Year Option graduate, built skills that aided her future career, including time management and financial trainings. She secured a role as a school liaison at the Epoch Dream Center, a free after-school program serving under-resourced children.

The programs were launched last year, with partnerships between Maryland Historically Black Colleges and Universities, community colleges, skilled trades, and apprenticeship programs. The Maryland Corps was rolled out alongside the Service Year Option, targeted at recent high school graduates.

title: MSDE presents draft literacy policy
content:
Maryland State Department of Education presents draft literacy policy on July 23, aligning with the science of reading and addressing economic issues. The policy aims to clarify state statutes' requirements, improve early warning systems, assessment data, intervention, and accountability. Key components include teacher support, assessment and parent notification, instruction and intervention, and retention and intervention.

Deann Collins, deputy state superintendent, emphasized the importance of addressing literacy at a young age and closing achievement gaps across demographics. Tenette Smith, executive director of literacy programs, noted that research suggests "reading is an economic issue as well." According to 2022 National Assessment of Educational Progress data, 69% of Maryland students did not reach proficiency in reading.

The draft policy highlights the need for a unified approach to ensure all students develop strong reading skills early on. Research from the Annie E. Casey Foundation shows that 88% of students who failed to earn a diploma were struggling readers in third grade.

Four major components of the comprehensive literacy policy spotlight teacher support, assessment and parent notification, instruction and intervention, and retention and intervention. The department welcomes feedback and input from stakeholders and partner collaboration. Over 900 responses have been collected so far, and public comment is expected.

title: St. Mary's board announces new school cellphone infractions
content:
St. Mary's public schools superintendent Scott Smith introduced a new cellphone policy on July 17, banning devices during school hours except for lunchtime. High school students can use phones during lunch, while middle and elementary school students cannot use theirs at any time.

Consequences include:

- First offense in high school: Phone confiscated until end of day
- Second offense: Phone confiscated until end of day, only parent/guardian can pick up after written warning
- Three or more offenses: Phone confiscated with additional discipline codes

Middle school and elementary school students will have their phones confiscated for the entire day.

Staff members are prohibited from using cellphones during instructional time, except for emergencies. Cellphones will be returned to middle and high school students on the first three days of school only, starting August 21.

Exceptions will not be made unless a student needs a device due to technical issues, with priority given to providing a working laptop instead.

The policy will be communicated through home phone calls, emails, morning announcements, video, and posters.

title: Strawberry named to Talbot Board of Education
content: Dyshekia Strawberry, a healthcare professional with over 15 years of experience, was appointed by Gov. Wes Moore to fill a vacancy on Talbot County's Board of Education, succeeding Jymil Thompson who resigned as interim superintendent of Dorchester County Public Schools in June. Strawberry, who resides in Easton and has two children in the school district, expressed her commitment to focusing on student safety, adequate staffing, and community preparation for students' education. She holds a Bachelor's and Master's degree in nursing from Hampton University and Wesley College, as well as a post-masters certificate in nurse leadership. Strawberry is an adjunct professor and mentor, entrepreneur, and member of the American and Maryland Nurses Associations, serving until 2026 when a successor will be elected during the next congressional election.

title: One-way conversation on schools
content: Mary Yancey, a writer for The Star Democrat, criticized an unknown sender who distributed a glossy mailing disparaging county schools in Easton, MD. The mailer claimed 17.2% math proficiency is "abysmal," citing a state average of 25%. Yancey defended the local rate, leaving interpretation to readers. She also noted the lack of transparency from those engaging in public discourse about schools, wishing they would identify themselves.

title: Delaware school boards increasingly see controversy
content:
Delaware's school boards have seen an increase in controversy over the past year, particularly around hiring and working with superintendents. The Christina School District Board of Education has been at the center of this controversy, with a nearly eight-hour-long meeting last month that sparked tension between board members and community members.

Rep. Madinah Wilson-Anton (D-Newark) criticized the board's labeling of attendees as "guests," saying it was dis respects to the public's right to comment. The audience applauded her statement, and she compared the board to elected officials who should be more accountable to their constituents.

The National School Boards Association notes that most boards are doing good work, but issues like budgets, boundary changes, and closing schools are more typical sources of controversy. Schools' governing authority is a local school board's role in overseeing the district, hiring a superintendent, and approving budgets and curriculum priorities.

Delaware law requires school board members to be Delaware residents and U.S. citizens, with no term limits. They must attend state training sessions within their first year and have access to resources like the Center for School Board Excellence in Governance.

The Christina School District has faced FOIA violations complaints, including one from five state legislators who filed a complaint against the board after they selected an interim superintendent without adequate notice. The Department of Justice has mandated that an attorney attend all meetings for the next year.

Other school districts, such as Brandywine and Capital, have also faced similar controversies, including allegations of FOIA violations. Brandywine's former superintendent cited a hostile work environment in her resignation letter, while Christina's Board President apologized for the board's dysfunction and acknowledged the need for stricter structures on meetings.

DelawareCAN and First State Educate are working to promote transparency and provide resources for school board members. The organization has announced its Center for School Board Excellence in Governance and plans to recruit more people to develop a school board consultant role.

title: Summer Youth Program Graduation at EVFC
content:
On July 14, 2024, 46 students completed a six-week work program at the Easton Volunteer Fire Department, administered by the Upper Shore Workforce Investment Board. The program, aimed at youth with learning disabilities and handicaps, provided paid work experience across five counties, including Aaron's Place, Dorchester Parks and Recreation, and Kent County Animal Shelter.

Executive director Dan Schneckenburger praised the program, saying it gave students a stepping stone into employment, often leading to job retention. Case manager Elizabeth Chiocca noted that local youth face difficulties finding jobs, while Youth coordinator Deborah Boulden emphasized her organization's commitment to inclusivity and supporting students with disabilities.

Graduates included Mason Callis (Mamma Mia's), Savannah Quinn (Chesapeake College), and Connor Swann (Dogwood Acres Pet Retreat), who credited the program for helping him secure jobs in animal care. The event was attended by proud parents, who received photos with their child's diploma, amidst a celebratory atmosphere.

Upper Shore Workforce Investment Board partners with employers, including Division of Rehabilitation Services within The Maryland Department of Education, to provide job coaching and support. This year's graduation marked the culmination of students' first paid work experience, often facilitated by the organization.

title: DCPS to offer new service for middle and high schoolers who can't attend in person
content:
Dorchester County Public Schools approved a contract with Edmentum for virtual synchronous instruction for middle and high school students who require home and hospital services due to health reasons or other limitations. The service will provide instruction from real teachers throughout the week, including support like office hours. Students in need of this service will be enrolled in Edmentum courses on an as-need basis, with a cost of $200 per student per course.

The district will receive funding for the service through various means, including budgeted line items and Title IV or Title V funds. The total estimated cost is around $100,000, which may vary depending on the number of students enrolling.

Key dates include:

* September 3: First day of school for first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and ninth graders
* September 4: First day of school for seventh, eighth, 10th, 11th, and 12th graders
* September 5: First day of school for pre-K and kindergarteners

Key people include:

* Jodi Colman, assistant superintendent of academics and student services
* Talibah Chikwendu, board Vice President
* Sheri Hubbard, board President
* Jymil Thompson, superintendent

title: Talbot County Free Library hosts youth STEAM Camp
content:
Talbot County Free Library hosted a two-week-long STEAM Camp for elementary and middle school students, designed by high school students Vivi Morris, Van Tran, and Mia Mazzeo, with funding from the Council of Friends of the Library. The program aimed to integrate science, technology, engineering, arts, and mathematics to foster creativity and critical thinking.

STEAM Camps were offered free of charge, including snacks and refreshments, to 40 students aged 6-12. Volunteer leaders adapted a traditional STEAM approach to suit each group's needs. Activities included tie-dyeing shirts, print-making tote bags, pass-and-paint, fruit art, making slime, and "cooking through chemistry" exercises.

The program encouraged collaboration, teamwork, and creative problem-solving. Library staff assistant Alanna Peerman praised the effectiveness of the program, saying it broke campers into small groups to learn interaction skills while applying individual skills.

Parents and students praised the program, with parents noting its structure, organization, and engagement for their children. The Council of Friends will fund next year's STEAM Camp based on its success, with FOL President Emilie Knud-Hansen stating her confidence in funding future events.

title: TCPS superintendent addresses mailers questioning district spending
content: Talbot County Public Schools Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi addressed concerns about district spending rates per student after receiving mailers from Pay Attention America Inc., a newly formed group with unknown contact information. The mailers featured a screenshot of the district's finances and questioned math proficiency rates, which were inaccurate according to Pepukayi. She stated there is work to be done in this area and plans to present recent state testing data at a Board of Education work session in September. The state average math proficiency rate for the 2022-23 school year was around 25%. Pay Attention America's registered agent, The Corporation Trust Company, has not filed an annual tax report, making it difficult to contact the group directly. Residents Hilary Spence and Shari Wilcoxon responded to the mailers with differing opinions on their impact, with Spence criticizing the anonymity of the sender and Wilcoxon appreciating the truth-telling. The mailers were sent from Wilmington, Delaware.

title: Annual Back to School Resource Fair: Preparing students for success
content:

Beth Anne Dorman, president and CEO of For All Seasons, stated that the fair aims to provide resources for students' mental health and well-being beyond just academic needs. Marilou Russ, assistant director at Appleseed Books, emphasized the importance of providing access to books as a way to promote children's literacy and self-expression.

Attendee Mayra Casillas praised the event's inclusivity and variety of activities, including games, arts, and craft stations, as well as free Rita's Italian Ice. The fair has grown significantly since its origin six years ago, with For All Seasons expanding the venue for next year due to overcrowding.

title: Family holding out hope for turf field project at Easton High
content:
Easton High School's artificial turf field project faces uncertainty due to uncertain school district allocation. Jen Hawley, Elgin's mother, who had aneurysm on the field in 2021 and wished for a turf field through Make-A-Wish Mid-Atlantic, is disappointed after being told the Board of Education will not partner with Make-A-Wish.

Talbot County Public Schools received $1.5 million allocated towards outstanding capital projects, including the turf field with an estimated price of $1.8 million. Hawley hopes to see the project take shape before her daughter leaves for college this summer. 

Make-A-Wish Mid-Atlantic granted Elgin's wish in 2023 and contributed approximately $10,000 towards the project. However, President Emily Jackson expressed concerns about investing in turf versus grass, citing potential injuries.

County Council Member Dave Stepp supports the efforts of "Elgin's Army" and believes the district can make up the difference between the allocated funds and the estimated cost. Lesli Creedon, president and CEO of Make-A-Wish Mid-Atlantic, expressed disappointment but hopes for future support from the county and citizens.

The Board of Education has not made an official decision on allocating the $1.5 million towards the turf field project.

content:

title: Courage needed by Blueprint Accountability Board
content:
The Blueprint Accountability and Implementation Board has done a commendable job in holding state and local educators accountable for implementing the Blueprint for Maryland's Future. However, the board is not holding the governor and General Assembly accountable for inadequate funding.

Funding shortfalls have been evident since 2021, with a lack of funding for classroom essentials, interventions for struggling learners, and career education. The governor and legislators have ignored these issues, despite the board's recommendations to "recommend legislative changes" to address the funding gap.

The Blueprint requires the AIB to determine whether state and local government funds are sufficient to implement the plan, but its 2022 and 2023 reports failed to mention this. The board has established benchmarks to measure progress, but it is too late to address the issue.

In recent meetings, state Superintendent Carey Wright acknowledged that interventions in all grades are necessary, but argued that funding for kindergarten to 12th grade education was required. However, the Blueprint only includes limited funding for early-grade interventions and no funding at all for interventions in middle school.

The disconnect between the Blueprint's ambitions and resources is due to Annapolis' reluctance to raise taxes to fund adequacy. The state has projected budget deficits, but raising revenue is necessary to fulfill its constitutional mandate.

To address this issue, the AIB must sound the alarm about the lack of resources, particularly timely interventions for struggling learners. Educators must also demonstrate that Blueprint funding will be well-spent through better management. The AIB must take a leading role in addressing these issues and convincing Annapolis to raise taxes to support the Blueprint.

title: Chapel District Elementary breaks ground on renovation project
content:
Chapel District Elementary School broke ground on a $26.9 million renovation project on August 24, 2024. The Whiting-Turner Contracting Company is leading construction, which started on August 5. A ceremony featured Talbot County Public Schools Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi, Principal Kari Clow, and others, highlighting the project's benefits and safety priorities.

The school was built in 1952 and last renovated in 1994. The renovation includes a full rebuild of the existing building and 16,000 square feet of additions. The project also involves moving the media center to the center of the building, renovating the playground, and adding additional learning space at the Critchlow Adkins Children's Centers site.

The Talbot County Council allocated funding for the project, which will span across fiscal years 2025 and 2026. State funding was also approved in April, with an estimated $3.8 million allocation. Construction is expected to take two years to complete.

title: Students head back to school in Talbot County
content: Easton Elementary School in Talbot County welcomed students back on August 26, 2024, with principal Lisa Devaric and superintendent Sharon Pepukayi leading the effort. Pepukayi emphasized the theme of "transforming and performing together" and highlighted professional development efforts, including training for multilingual learners. Easton Elementary saw colorful backpacks and beaming smiles from students, with Amy Dodson praising the school's readiness for her children, who began their year without incident.

title: Plans to address test scores, cell phones shared by district staff at Moms for Liberty meeting
content:
Talbot County's Moms for Liberty chapter held a meeting with superintendent Sharon Pepukayi and district staff on August 28, 2024. Concerns about low math scores, student cell phone use, and English proficiency were shared. Jan Greenhawk, chapter chair, expressed gratitude for the attendance of district representatives.

Pepukayi discussed the implementation of research-based math and English language arts curriculums, including the addition of math coaches to support teachers. The changes aim to be rolled out slowly to avoid overwhelming staff.

An anonymous countywide postcard criticized Talbot County Public Schools' finances and stated that students' math proficiency is 17.2% below the state average. Shari Wilcoxon expressed concern over future postcards addressing English proficiency, stating 59% of third- through eighth-grade students are not proficient in English.

The district's policy on cell phone usage during school hours was discussed. Pepukayi shared the district is piloting a new program called YONDER to limit cell phone use in classrooms, where students will lock their phones in pouches that can be accessed after pressing a magnet.

Math teacher Robert Jurrius emphasized the need for parents to break their addiction to texting students during school hours. Superintendent Pepukayi stressed the importance of partnering with community groups and hearing concerns, aligning with the district's "transforming and performing together" theme.

title: Leonard Hall Junior Naval Academy prepares for move after a century
content:
Leonard Hall Junior Naval Academy is preparing to leave its long-time home in St. Mary's County, MD after 115 years due to a lease renewal issue. The academy has been on a month-to-month lease since January and currently has 15 students. Board of Trustees President Amie Milan said they are working closely with commissioners to find a new location and aim to move by this fall. A move would require significant logistics, but Milan aims to get enrollment up to 100.

In January, the county commissioners voted to terminate the academy's lease as of June 30, citing concerns about the school's effectiveness. However, after temporary closure, they agreed to a month-to-month lease. Leonard Hall graduate and historian Anita Drury expressed sadness about leaving its historic location, but emphasized that the school's mission and values would remain unchanged.

The academy has seen significant success in transforming students' lives, with examples including Israel Camlin, whose son attended the school after failing summer school and now has a 4.0 GPA, and Rex Bothwell, whose grades improved after transferring to Leonard Hall. The nonprofit relies on tuition, donations, and funding from the county.

Commissioner Eric Colvin (R) acknowledged the school's impact, stating that there is "no ill will" towards it. Milan aims to focus on providing a positive environment for current students and communicating its mission and achievements despite the uncertainty surrounding its future location.

title: "ArtScene | the Podcast" kicks off new season, new school year
content:
"ArtScene | The Podcast," featuring Centreville Middle School art teacher Jackie Jablecki, launches a new episode on Sept. 1 to kick off the 2024-2025 school year. Jablecki shares her journey from personal loss to professional triumph, highlighting her passion for art and education. She began teaching at Kent Island Elementary before transitioning to middle school and inherits her love of art from her father, a skilled glass artist.

Jablecki discusses the transformative power of art education in TAB classrooms, empowering students to explore their creativity and develop confidence. She shares a story about a seventh-grade student who overcame struggles with a self-portrait assignment, demonstrating perseverance and support's impact on the classroom. Jablecki is involved with Art of Education University, where she completed her Master's degree and is documenting "A Year in the Life of an Art Teacher" as a YouTube Vlog series.

Jablecki's enthusiasm for visual journaling and choice-based art education has made her classroom a haven for creativity. She shares stories of her travels, including a recent trip through France and Spain, which connected her students with the wider world through art. "ArtScene | The Podcast" explores the personal lives of teachers, providing a glimpse into their world and inspiring communities.

Jablecki's career has been marked by significant challenges, including the loss of her father at a young age and life-altering surgeries due to a rare genetic mutation. Despite these hurdles, she has driven her passion for art and education, inspiring students and making her classroom a transformative environment.

title: Time to reframe conversation about literacy
content:
The Maryland State Department of Education's draft literacy policy aims to create a robust support system for students and teachers, focusing on preparing and empowering children to become fluent readers. The policy seeks to tackle the reading crisis by addressing far more than retention, including:

* Leveraging the Ready to Read Act with early screening and assessment
* Providing professional learning and coaching for teachers
* Outlining a plan for ongoing professional development to support students at every stage

The draft policy also introduces a Student Reading Improvement Plan, a collaborative effort between teachers and parents, and a toolkit to communicate effectively with parents.

While the conversation has been dominated by retention, the policy is as much about prevention as intervention. Retention should be strategically designed as a last-resort intervention after other support measures have been exhausted.

The policy represents a comprehensive statewide approach to improving literacy, focusing on assessments, professional development, and coaching for teachers and parents.

Key figures include:

* Lisa Blottenberger, founder of Boundless Expectations Inc., Maryland READS board member, and co-founder of Decoding Dyslexia Maryland
* Trish Brennan-Gac, executive director of Maryland READS

title: Aiming to fly: Civil Air Patrol holds open house for young, aspiring pilots
content:
Ainsley Taylor, a 14-year-old from Lexington Park, joined the Civil Air Patrol two years ago and is now pursuing her dream of becoming an F-35 pilot. The organization held an open house on Aug. 28 at the St. Mary's County Regional Airport to welcome young potential members.

Civil Air Patrol cadet program director David Trick emphasized the program's career exploration in military aviation, flying, search and rescue, community service, and other activities. Cadets typically join from ages 12-17 but can remain until age 21.

Parents Charles and Emma David attended with their 11-year-old daughter Amelia, who was drawn to the program's values, structure, and opportunities for adventure. Amelia liked learning about flying, emergency rescue, and wilderness survival.

Current member Evelyn Roulhand shared her positive experience despite initially thinking the military aspect wasn't for her. She found it appealing due to its variety of branches and activities. 

The Civil Air Patrol has squadrons in Calvert, St. Mary's, and Charles counties. The program's core values are integrity, excellence, volunteer service, and respect.

Ainsley Taylor's brother Eric joined the program before her and initially wasn't interested but discovered he could fly and get his pilot's license, changing his mind.

content:
Alden Swanson, a rising junior at Kent County High School, was sworn in as the newest student member of the Kent County Board of Education on August 12, 2024. She was elected by her peers and will serve a one-year term. During her meeting, she expressed excitement to be part of the board and contribute to upcoming events. Board President Joseph Goetz thanked Swanson for running for student board member and encouraged her participation in conversations. title: School lunches through the years
content:
School lunches have changed over the years but remain essential for students' daily success. In the 1950s, author Marie Savage was an elementary student who packed homemade soup and Kool-Aid in her lunch box. Today's students enjoy a variety of lunch options.

BBQ Chicken Cups: Mix cooked chicken with barbecue sauce, shred, and serve on biscuits.

PB&J Apples: Spread peanut butter on jelly-coated apple slices.

PB&J Sushi: Roll flat bread with peanut butter and jelly, then cut into pieces.

Pickle Roll-Ups: Layer meat, cheese, and a pickle wedge, then roll tight.

Turkey Club Roll-Ups: Roll deli turkey, lettuce, tomato, avocado, and bacon in a large tortilla.

Grilled Cheese Roll-Ups: Flatten bread slices, fill with cheese, and fry until golden brown.

Nutella Banana Sushi: Slather Nutella on a wrap, place banana inside, roll, and slice.

Ham, Mac N Cheese Muffins: Mix cooked macaroni and cheese with ham and breadcrumbs, then bake in muffin cups.

Rice Krispie Peanut Butter Bananas: Roll peanut butter-coated bananas in cereal.

Pepperoni Pizza Sticks: Roll pizza dough around pepperoni slices, mozzarella cheese sticks, and marinara sauce.

title: County agrees to audit of school system financial records
content:
Queen Anne's County Commissioners unanimously approved hiring an independent auditing firm to conduct a performance audit of the Queen Anne's County Public School Board of Education's financial records and budgetary development procedures. The county does not suspect any fraudulent activity but aims for transparency. Commissioner Jim Moran stated that the board faces significant turnover, operational funding requests exceeding maintenance of effort requirements, and increasing budgetary demands despite flat student enrollment numbers.

The commissioners provided an additional $6.2 million in funding, exceeding the required MOE, resulting in a total operating budget of $118,400,000 for FY 25. However, the board operates with a projected budgetary deficit six weeks into FY 25. The audit is not a witch hunt but aims to support the Board of Education by identifying resources and best practices.

Commissioners Chris Corchiarino, Jack Wilson, and Phil Dumenil emphasized the need for transparency and cooperation from Superintendent Patrica Saelens, the Board of Education, and leadership. The audit is capped at $100,000, with work underway to select firms and expedite the auditing process.

title: Caroline County pilots cell phone pouches in schools, other districts to follow
content:
Caroline County Public Schools piloted a cell phone restriction policy where middle school students put their phones in locked pouches designed by Yondr to prevent usage during class. The program aims to improve student focus and achievement, attendance, and discipline. Superintendents Derek Simmons of Caroline County, Valerie Goff of Dorchester County, and Sharon Pepukayi of Talbot County are testing the technology.
