title: First Friday ice cream social welcomes new Washington College students to town
content: Chestertown, MD hosted a First Friday ice cream social for Washington College students on Sept 6, 2024. The event, partnered with the United Way, featured music by Quinn Arnold, free ice cream from vendors, and volunteer organizations passing out brochures and supplies. Mayor David Foster welcomed students to town, highlighting Chestertown's landmarks and history. He mentioned Hebe, a mythological wine-bearer honored on Aug 15, marking her 125th anniversary of installation. Washington College President Mike Sosulski congratulated his largest incoming class (293) and announced the college had broken Guinness World Record for electric boat travel distance (6 hours ahead of English record holders in 2001).

title: Birding and boating the Harriet Tubman Byway
content:
A group of 25 bird species were spotted by a tour group along the Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad Scenic Byway on September 14, 2024. The "Birding & Boating" event was hosted by Alex Green and Jim Rapp, who guided participants through sites central to Harriet Tubman's life and work as an abolitionist and social activist.

The tour began at the Leverton House, a dairy farm owned by Quakers Jacob and Hannah Leverton, supporters of the Underground Railroad. The group then visited the Webb Cabin in Preston, where James Webb hid escaping slaves using a "potato hole" trap door beneath his house.

Guides Green and Rapp also stopped at the Caroline County Courthouse, where slaves were sold, and Linchester Mill. At the courthouse, they highlighted the impact of land on the slave trade and commerce along the Choptank River.

The tour included several participants who had never stopped at the Underground Railroad signs before, and a former history teacher who wrote her senior thesis on abolitionists. The group also spotted hummingbirds, red-tailed hawks, and turkey vultures during the tour.

After concluding the driving tour, the group boarded a 33-foot tritoon named Ellen B. and continued north to Philadelphia along the Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad Scenic Byway.

title: Easton High teacher named finalist for Maryland Teacher of the Year
content:
Jeremy Hillyard, a Spanish and English as a second language math teacher at Easton High School, was named one of seven finalists for Maryland Teacher of the Year by the state's Board of Education on September 14, 2024. Hillyard, who is also Talbot County Public Schools' 2024-25 Teacher of the Year, uses the "Yes, and" philosophy in his classroom to encourage students to listen to each other's ideas. He was a finalist from 24 district teachers of the year through a rigorous application and evaluation process.

Hillyard has taught at Easton High School since 2010 and stepped in to teach an ESOL math course when needed. He uses his math and Spanish skills to support students with varying English abilities, starting with basic math in English before moving to more advanced arithmetic.

The finalists will attend a reception in Baltimore on October 4 to be announced as the Maryland Teacher of the Year. Hillyard was named Talbot County Public Schools' teacher of the year in April 2024 and expressed gratitude for the recognition, saying it's "very humbling" and acknowledges his efforts to go above and beyond.

Hillyard aims to create a safe and supportive learning environment for all students, regardless of their background or language proficiency. He is excited about the opportunity to explore the state and collaborate with colleagues throughout the upcoming months, including stops at Deep Creek Lake in Garrett County and the statehouse in Annapolis.

title: Rotary club members learn about All4Love
content:
The Rotary Club of Cambridge learned about All4Love on September 16, 2024. Lucas Thorpe, co-founder and executive director of All4Love, spoke about the organization's mission to improve the lives of adolescents and young adults in Dorchester County through transformative programs.

All4Love was formed 10 years ago by Thorpe and Khail Johnson, who began mentoring middle and high school students. The organization has created several programs, including a high school mentoring program, flag football league, breakfast club, and after-school music program, to help achieve its goals.

Thorpe, born and raised in Dorchester County, graduated from North Dorchester High School, attended Chesapeake College, and the University of Maryland Eastern Shore. He oversees All4Love's development and operations, emphasizing the power of consistent and collaborative efforts to create lasting change.

All4Love serves an increasing number of youth and aims to change the narrative for Cambridge's community, which has faced tumultuous times politically, economically, and socially. The organization believes every day brings new opportunities to make a better tomorrow.

title: For Dorchester superintendent, it's all about teaching and learning
content:
Dorchester County Public Schools Superintendent Jymil Thompson visits schools weekly to promote a comfortable teaching and learning environment, offering guidance when needed. As superintendent since June, Thompson aims to improve student success by focusing on instructional leadership, with administration having the most impact on student achievement. Thompson prioritizes this approach to lift the district's ranking from 23rd to 15th in four years.

Thompson considers instructional leadership a top priority, citing its focus on teaching and learning as crucial for student success. Assistant Superintendent Jodi Colman emphasizes that the district must focus on instructional leadership within the school system to change its state ranking. The board of education approved a purchasing agreement for coaching and professional development support in March, including regular meetings on how administrators should give feedback to teachers.

Thompson believes consistent development of instructional leadership is essential, involving regular meetings with principals and conversations about their progress towards goals. He also emphasizes the importance of accountability without firing people, but rather providing supports to help them improve their craft.

title: Talbot school board sees test scores, improvement initiatives
content:
State test scores for Talbot County Public Schools showed a slight increase in math and English proficiency levels at both district and state levels. In English, 47.3% of students tested proficient, up 2.8% from 44.5% in 2022-2023, while in math, 18.3% were proficient, up 1.1% from 17.2%. The district ranks 14th and 18th among state's 24 districts in English and math proficiency.

Assistant Superintendent Helga Einhorn emphasized that the district internally tracks student learning levels and noted that more than 47% of students are mastering grade level standards, but not showing it across the state on this particular assessment. Positive trends include third-grade English proficiency and growth for certain cohorts and subgroups.

The district has initiatives to increase math proficiency, including increasing elementary math coaches from three to six and adding a middle school coach, as well as implementing an adaptive testing program. However, Hispanic and Latino students showed less of an increase in math proficiency, with fewer than 5% proficient, along with Black students and multilingual learners.

State reviewers will visit three Talbot County elementary schools this year: Chapel District Elementary, St. Michaels Elementary, and White Marsh Elementary, to review literacy instruction, practices for multilingual learners, and success in state testing. The district plans to take lessons learned from these schools to its largest elementary school, Easton Elementary, by committing similar resources on a larger scale.

Talbot County Council's commitment to funding education was praised, with Board President Emily Jackson thanking the council for supporting math coaches and acknowledging intentional decisions that have a big impact on learning.

title: Easton flying event gets women up in the air
content:
Here is a highly condensed version of the article:

The Maryland Chapter of the Ninety-Nines, an international nonprofit organization, hosted its first "Let's Fly Now" event at Easton Airport on September 14, 2024, giving 21 women the chance to learn about planes and sit in the passenger seat as pilots took flight. Maria Esparraguera, a member and pilot of the group, piloted two flights and said both women were enthusiastic about flying. Organizer Cheryl Mohrmann aimed to encourage more women to take up aviation, noting that despite low advertising, the event filled up quickly with participants from across Maryland, including one woman who drove from Brooklyn, NY.

The event included an hour-long ground school session on planes, followed by flight time with licensed pilots. Attendees aged 15-99 were invited to participate, with four under 18 years old. Pilots observed attendees' strong engagement and interest in pursuing flying careers. Mohrmann said there are plans for future events, with attendees expressing excitement. Esparraguera likened the event to a Women in Aviation conference, where she saw women enthusiastically participating without being pushed aside.

title: Constitution Alliance hosts Liberty and Freedom event in Easton for 3rd year
content:
The Mid-Shore Constitution Alliance hosted its third annual "Our Journey to Liberty and Freedom" event on September 17, 2024, at the Academy Art Museum in Easton, Maryland. The gathering featured performances by Darius Wallace as Frederick Douglass and Kurt Smith as Thomas Jefferson, who discussed the importance of reading history, liberty, and freedom. State Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) delivered a welcome address.

The event drew a large crowd, including students from Saints Peter and Paul High School and North Dorchester High School, who were honored as new U.S. citizens in Talbot County. Organizers also distributed free Constitution giveaways and sweet treats.

Event supporters included The Institute for Religion, Politics and Culture at Washington College, Operation Frederick Douglass on the Hill, and local sponsors. The event was part of the Constitution Alliance's efforts to increase Constitutional literacy among students through educational programming and annual $1,000 higher education scholarships.

title: St. Michaels reading specialist receives Fulbright award
content:
Kelly Coutts, a reading specialist at St. Michaels Elementary School, received a Fulbright Teacher Exchange award for the 2024-2025 cycle from the U.S. Department of State and the Fulbright Foreign Scholarship Board. The Talbot County Board of Education recognized her achievements with a certificate of recognition. As part of the program, Coutts will participate in an online course for 10 weeks before being sent to study abroad.

Coutts is one of over 800 U.S. citizens selected to teach, study or conduct research abroad through the Fulbright Program annually. The program provides opportunities for exchange and collaboration between institutions, often leading to future partnerships. Coutts' experiences will be published in a global education publication.

The Fulbright Program has provided over 400,000 participants from 160 countries since its inception in 1946. Notable alumni include 62 Nobel Prize laureates, 89 Pulitzer Prize recipients, and 78 MacArthur Fellows. The program is funded through annual U.S. Congress appropriations to the U.S. Department of State's Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs.

The Fulbright Program supports more than 800 U.S. participants annually, with approximately 400 master teachers and administrators participating in the Teacher Exchanges each year. Coutts will join a network of thousands of esteemed scholars upon returning from her abroad trip.

title: Kaitlyn Wright named state Teacher of the Year finalist
content: Kaitlyn Wright, a Kent County Middle School English and drama teacher, is one of seven finalists for Maryland Teacher of the Year. She was previously named Kent County Public Schools' Teacher of the Year and has been competing for state honors with a cohort of teachers since last spring. Mary Boswell-McComas, superintendent of Kent County Public Schools, expressed pride in Wright's selection as a finalist. A panel of state judges will interview Wright this month, with the next Maryland Teacher of the Year to be announced in October; Wright was previously named state Teacher of the Year finalist for 2024.

title: Talbot school board discusses concerns over athletic fields
content:
The Talbot County Board of Education discussed concerns over athletic fields at a September 20, 2024 meeting. Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi and board members emphasized the need for more information on maintaining an artificial turf field at Easton High School due to estimated costs of $1.8 million. The district received $1.5 million from the county for capital projects, including auditorium lights, a basketball court, stadium lights, and a new playground. Board President Emily Jackson said choosing between these projects was unfair and asked exploring funding options beyond the allocated budget.

Board members noted injury tendencies on turf fields, with research indicating certain sports teams have fewer injuries than others. Student board members Brynn Lizewski and Gabriella Streaker shared their experiences as athletes, citing issues with practice field conditions. Board members asked district staff to begin immediate inspections of practice fields.

Pepukayi said she and her team will present a plan on athletic field improvements in October, including a potential phased approach. Jackson emphasized the need to address past underfunding of athletics programs and suggested exploring multi-year funding projects.

title: Dorchester MCAP data shows some progress, some areas of concern
content:
Dorchester County Public Schools' Spring 2024 MCAP data shows year-to-year increases in English and math proficiency rates. The district ranks 22nd for English (33.7% proficiency) and 21st for math (12.3% proficiency). Assistant Superintendent Jodi Colman reported:

- 8 grade levels with increased state rankings in math
- 6 grade levels with increased state rankings in English
- Fifth-grade science proficiency increased from 22nd to 20th in the state
- Tenth-grade English scores remain lowest in the state (30.6% proficient)
- Elementary English scores decrease as students progress in grade level
- Discussions about revising instructional programs and adopting new literacy plans

The district is working on improving tier-one instruction, formative assessment data, and teaching strategies. Superintendent Jymil Thompson views score increases as progress, stating that continued improvement will add up over time.

title: Dorchester schools to create strategic plan for coming years
content:
Dorchester County Public Schools is developing a strategic plan with Integrated Impact Group to guide work from 2025-2028. Consultant Connie Casson led the meeting on September 19, explaining that the purpose of the plan is to prepare students, recruit and retain teachers, provide career exploration opportunities, and utilize available resources.

The planning process will involve:

* Reviewing district data (September-October)
* Conducting student, parent, and staff surveys
* Researching other districts' initiatives (October-June)
* Prioritizing strengths and new initiatives
* Creating plans and budgets
* Communicating district priorities to local partners

Integrated Impact Group will provide monthly updates to the board. The district will hold three community meetings:

* October 14: Hurlock United Methodist Church
* October 15: St. Luke Methodist Church
* October 16: South Dorchester School, starting at 6 p.m.

Email planning@dcpsmd.org can be used for inquiries.

title: Multicultural Resource Center awards scholarships to 14 students
content: The Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center awarded $35,000 in scholarships to 14 students from the Eastern Shore for the upcoming fall term. Established about four years ago, the scholarship aims to support first-generation college students and those with financial needs. Victoria Gomez Lozano, director of the center, stated that there is no set criteria for applicants but emphasized the importance of being a college first-generational student. The funds have been used for laptop purchases, books, and dorm fees. Awardees include Morgan Lewis, who plans to pursue a master's and possible doctorate in psychology. Gomez Lozano encourages others to apply, believing that access to education is crucial for achieving one's dreams.

title: Washington College Electric Boat Team visits Radcliffe Creek School
content:
Washington College Electric Boat Team visited Radcliffe Creek School on Sept. 20, where team members shared their story of overcoming design failures to win first place in multiple races against top engineering programs. President Douglas Hewes and advisors Mac Sansbury, Tiyaba Jamil, and Brian Palmer spoke about strategies used to improve boat designs, including battery technology, electric motors, solar panels, and hull designs.

The team broke the Guinness World Record for the greatest distance by an electric boat on a single charge without solar (21 miles) on Sept. 2, surpassing the previous record. Students watched video footage of the record-breaking success, saw the winning boat in person, and asked questions about its design and future plans.

Head of School Peter Thayer praised the team's visit, stating that the students' experience was inspiring and valuable, teaching them that failure is a part of the learning process.

title: Child care priority needed
content:
Here is a condensed version of the article:

As the US approaches the election, candidates must prioritize child care to address the crisis. The average cost of infant care in Maryland ($15,335/year) is higher than rent in all 50 states, affecting 40% of families with young children. Talbot County, known as a "child care desert," struggles with affordable options.

Maryland ranks 7th in most expensive infant care. Single mothers face financial burdens, including mortgage payments and college loans. Voters (89%) demand policy solutions for working parents.

The writer urges candidates to commit to prioritizing child care in their first 100 days if elected: Angela Alsobrooks, Larry Hogan, Blane Miller, and Andy Harris are targeted. Families, businesses, and children's futures depend on affordable, accessible, and quality childcare.

title: Two student representatives appointed to Talbot Board of Education
content:
Two student representatives were appointed to the Talbot County Board of Education: Gabriella Streaker, senior at Easton High School, and Brynn Lizewski, senior at St. Michaels Middle High School. They were sworn in on September 18, 2024, as part of the board's monthly meeting.

Streaker is president of Easton National Honor Society, class treasurer, and a member of soccer and swim teams. She plans to attend college for health sciences and become a pediatrician or surgeon. Lizewski is president of the Student Government Association and a member of tennis and field hockey teams. She plans to study political science and women's studies before attending law school.

Board members welcomed Streaker and Lizewski, encouraging them to provide feedback and opinions throughout the year. Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi said, "We are excited to have these student leaders represent their schools this year."

Key dates: September 18, 2024; 2024-2025 school year

title: Baltimore fire cuts internet in Talbot schools, libraries
content: A fire in Baltimore's manhole damaged fiber optic cable, impacting internet service for Talbot County Public Schools and libraries. The outage, caused by a problem with Sailor internet service provider, affected all schools, with phone service only available at some buildings. The Talbot County Free Library used hotspots to run laptops. Director Dana Newman stated the Baltimore hub is crucial for libraries and rural school districts, and repairs are uncertain. Patrons could check out books but not use the internet until the service was restored, which occurred on Tuesday at 3:30 p.m.

title: Washington College Electric Boat Team visits Radcliffe Creek School
content:
The Washington College Electric Boat Team visited Radcliffe Creek School on September 20, 2024. The team members shared their story of overcoming design failures to win first place in multiple races against top engineering programs like Princeton University. President Douglas Hewes, Mac Sansbury, Tiyaba Jamil, and Brian Palmer presented the strategies that led to their success, including improved battery technology, electric motors, solar panels, and hydrodynamic hull designs.

The team broke the Guinness World Record for the greatest distance by an electric boat on a single charge without solar on September 2, 2024, with a 21-mile increase from the previous record. The students watched video footage of the record-breaking success and saw the winning boat in person, learning about the design process and future plans.

Head of School Peter Thayer expressed gratitude for the team's visit, stating that it was important for students to hear that failure is a part of the learning process.

title: Four years after her murder, Madison Sparrow's legacy lives on
content:
Madison Sparrow, a 17-year-old Newark Charter School junior, was murdered by her ex-boyfriend and friend in Delaware on October 2, 2020. Four years later, her legacy lives on through five scholarship recipients pursuing careers in education, funded by the Madison Sparrow Scholarship established by her mother, Heather Murphy.

Murphy, a victim of the crime, forgave the perpetrators during sentencing due to her daughter's message of "love wins." She has since participated in a victim-offender dialog program with Annika Stalczynski, who lured Madison into the woods where she was killed. The meeting helped Murphy process her grief and find closure.

The annual Love Wins 5K fundraiser, now in its fourth year, draws over 200 participants to Glasgow Park, raising money for the scholarship and keeping Madison's memory alive. Last year, two seniors received scholarships, and this year, five recipients were awarded funding.

The scholarship is awarded each year to a Newark Charter senior pursuing education, with recipients able to reapply for funding annually. Murphy continues to raise money through the Love Wins 5K and seeks sponsors for next year's event.

Madison was known as a gentle soul who loved children, friends, and her community. Her mother describes her as an amazing daughter who impacted their community significantly. The Madison Sparrow Scholarship Fund can be donated at runsignup.com/Race/DE/Newark/LoveWins5KDE.

title: How Maryland schools are cracking down on cell phones this fall
content:
Maryland public schools are cracking down on cell phones this fall, with at least a third of schools tightening rules to keep them off and out of sight. A Capital News Service survey found that 387 schools have implemented new policies.

In Caroline County, a pilot program requires middle school students to place their phones in locked pouches until the end of the day. In St. Mary's County, Superintendent Scott Smith released a video describing the district's plan to limit phone distractions, including confiscating around 30 cell phones per day.

Superintendent Derek L. Simmons in Caroline County stated that constant distraction caused by cell phones affects school culture and learning. Superintendents are using creative approaches to persuade students to follow new rules, such as Smith's video, which shows him texting during a presentation and highlighting the importance of being present in class.

Key statistics:

* At least 1/3 of Maryland public schools have tightened up phone policies this fall
* 387 schools were surveyed by Capital News Service
* 30 cell phones are confiscated per day in St. Mary's County

title: Talbot Board of Education candidates speak at town hall forum
content:
Here is a condensed version of the article:

Talbot County Board of Education candidates held a town hall forum on October 4, 2024, discussing issues such as standardized test scores, student engagement, and teacher retention. Three seats are up for election in November.

Incumbents Candace Henry (District 2) and Anna Howie (District 5) were joined by newcomers Karla Wieland-Cherry (District 5) and Kerry Gunshenan (District 6). Mary Wheeler's seat is open, with Cynthia Jurrius as the sole challenger.

Test scores showed slight improvements in math and English proficiency rates. Candidates agreed that test scores must improve, but differed on methods, including benchmark testing and summer reading.

Student engagement was also a topic, with candidates discussing reducing cell phone use and distractions. Howie mentioned Caroline County's successful pilot program for cell phone pouches, while O'Connor advocated for an increased focus on books.

Teacher retention was another key issue, with candidates emphasizing the need for effective recruitment and retention strategies. Henry suggested dedicated attention to the district's "Grow Your Own Teachers" scholarship program, while Howie emphasized retaining teachers and staff.

Candidates also addressed the recent flyers questioning test scores and district spending. Jurrius stated she didn't believe educators were indoctrinating students, while O'Connor attributed the problem to the system being broken.

Residents in Districts 2, 5, and 6 will vote on November 5 for their school board candidates. The three elected will serve four-year terms.

title: Forum notable for absent candidates
content: On October 5, 2024, a Community Town Hall event was held in Easton, MD, featuring four candidates running for Board of Education positions: Candace Henry, Ann O'Connor, Anna Howie, and Cynthia Jurrius. Four candidates did not attend, sparking concern about their level of investment in the community's children. The event provided a platform for the remaining candidates to answer questions from the audience and moderator-led discussions.

title: QACPS joins insulin litigation class action lawsuit
content: Queen Anne's County Public Schools Board of Education joined a lawsuit against companies for price gouging on insulin, with the school district allegedly paying inflated costs due to $35 fair price vials being charged upwards of $1,000. Superintendent Patricia Saelens stated there is no risk or cost to QACPS but noted they may receive monies in a settlement. The board also expressed frustration with state funding received until June and a performance audit of their financial records is underway.

title: Learn beekeeping basics
content: The Cecil County Public Library is offering a free beekeeping class on October 16 from 6:30-8:30 p.m. at the Rising Sun branch. The class, "The Basics of Beekeeping," will provide information on how bees pollinate and help the food chain, as well as tips for starting a beekeeping project. Registration is required and can be done online at https://www.cecilcountylibrary.org/event/buzzing-knowledge-discover-basics-beekeeping-63433.

title: Chess for kids, teens at Talbot library
content: The Talbot County Free Library is hosting a chess event for kids and teens ages 8 to 16 on October 23 from 4:30 p.m. to 5:30 p.m. at its downtown Easton branch. Registration is required online at https://talbot.librarycalendar.com/event/afternoon-chess-170.

title: Focus remains clear
content: Ann O'Connor, a candidate for Talbot County Board of Education, clarifies that she has not received endorsements from Mom's For Liberty. Despite attending meetings with the local M4L Chapter, O'Connor maintains her focus on supporting children, teachers, and parental involvement. Her platform is built around Advancing Academics, Boosting Accountability, and Cultivating Character. A three-legged stool approach to collaboration among educators, parents, and community groups is essential for improving schools. If elected, O'Connor will prioritize listening to all voices and making informed decisions.

title: Candidates have varying views
content:
The 2024 Talbot County School Board election will feature six candidates from three conservative and three progressive backgrounds. Ann O'Connor, Karla Wieland-Cherry, Kerry Gunshenan, represent conservatism, while Cynthia Jurrius, Anna Howie, Candace Henry, represent progressivism.

A debate for the school board candidates was hosted by Moms for Liberty on September 23 at the Easton firehouse, attended by four candidates: Cynthia Jurrius and three conservatives. The event received positive feedback from parents and grandparents.

However, a second debate held at the Avalon Theater on October 2, was criticized for excluding conservative candidates, while the Talbot County Democratic Forum's event at the Academy Art Museum only invited progressive candidates. Moms for Liberty has denied partisan involvement despite being accused of such by local media outlets.

title: Karla Wieland-Cherry
content:
Karla Wieland-Cherry, a 55-year-old resident of Trappe, is running for the District 5 seat on the Talbot County Board of Education. A registered nurse and associate real estate broker, she volunteers with local organizations. 

Wieland-Cherry aims to improve the local school system by enticing more qualified teachers, raising education benchmark standards, increasing CTE programs, improving student discipline rules, enhancing school safety measures, and increasing open communication transparency.

As a future board member, her priorities include rebuilding trust with teachers, addressing the lack of student discipline and teacher safety concerns, and creating a secure learning environment. 

She believes the main issue facing Talbot County Public Schools is the lack of teachers and staff. Wieland-Cherry wants to address this by listening to teacher concerns and improving communication between schools, teachers, parents, and the community.

Regarding postcards criticizing education in the county, she advises residents to investigate local school data from reliable sources, as open communication channels are essential. 

Wieland-Cherry expressed concerns about the Blueprint For Maryland's Future, stating that teachers find it vague with unclear guidelines for implementation and prioritizes equity learning based on poverty levels and individuality.

title: Anna Howie
content:
Anna Howie, 49, is a Talbot County resident and assistant principal at Federalsburg Elementary School, who was appointed to the District 5 seat of the Talbot County Board of Education by Gov. Wes Moore in October 2023. She is married with three children.

Howie aims to represent students, families, and stakeholders, focusing on increasing student achievement in math and reading, and recruiting quality teachers. Her priorities align with the board's goals, particularly improving student outcomes while being fiscally responsible.

The most pressing issue facing Talbot County Public Schools is providing exceptional education opportunities while maintaining fiscal responsibility. The board has adopted high-quality resources through educational grants, which Howie supports as a responsible way to provide students with excellent instructional materials.

Howie responds to postcards criticizing the county's education system by pointing to improved student test scores and the district's efforts to address literacy and mathematics instruction. She also supports the Blueprint For Maryland's Future, believing it addresses key areas of need for Maryland schools, including early childhood education, teacher quality, college readiness, and resources.

Key dates include October 2023, when Howie was appointed, and an unspecified date for the visitation of expert review teams from the Governance and Accountability pillar of the Blueprint.

title: Cynthia Marrah Jurrius
content:
Cynthia Marrah Jurris, 65, is a mediator and conflict resolution director running for District 6 seat on Talbot County Public Schools Board of Education. She's married with three sons from Talbot County Public Schools.

Jurris wants to move schools forward through collaborative problem-solving, fostering academic excellence, supporting educators, and creating a thriving school environment. Priorities include:

- Academic excellence
- Recruiting, retaining, and supporting outstanding teachers
- Providing a positive, safe, effective, and inclusive school climate

She believes advancing academic proficiency is key, supported by innovative community partnerships, technology, targeted resource allocation, and engaging families.

Jurris criticizes postcards criticizing education in the county, calling for honest dialogue. She welcomes open conversation about the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, which includes five pillars: Early Childhood Education; High Quality Teachers and Leaders; College and Career Readiness; More Resources for Student Success; and Governance and Accountability.

She supports continued efforts to address funding formulas applied to Talbot County Public Schools.

Key dates and information:

- Running for District 6 seat on Talbot County Public Schools Board of Education
- Married with three sons from Talbot County Public Schools
- Background in mediation law and conflict resolution

title: Ann O'Connor
content:
Ann O'Connor, a 55-year-old Easton resident and former teacher of six children, is running for the District 2 seat on the Talbot County Board of Education. She aims to make meaningful changes due to observed declines in academic rigor, expectations, and accountability.

Priorities include advancing academics, boosting accountability, and cultivating character, focusing on the whole child. Academic discipline is crucial to good character, and addressing disruptive behavior promptly is essential.

The most pressing issue facing Talbot County Public Schools is the decline of academic rigor, requiring early intervention in elementary schools and emphasizing traditional learning methods, such as cursive writing and critical thinking skills.

O'Connor criticizes postcards criticizing education in the county, viewing them as a wake-up call to address the problem. She advocates for focusing on reading, writing, and math, eliminating distractions, and getting back to basics with her "ABCs of education."

Regarding the Blueprint For Maryland's Future, O'Connor is skeptical, citing concerns about top-down programs removing control from locally elected school boards and unelected officials.

title: Candace Henry
content:
Candace Henry, 43, is a Talbot County Board of Education member and director of the Disability Resource Center at Salisbury University. She's running for reelection to ensure every student has equal access to quality education.

Henry's priorities include:

* Addressing opportunity gaps in reading and math proficiency
* Recruiting and retaining high-quality educators through professional development
* Enhancing special education services, summer school offerings, and college preparatory programs

She addresses concerns about postcards criticizing Talbot County Public Schools by emphasizing the need for open discussion, fact-based information, and celebrating educators' efforts.

Henry supports the Blueprint For Maryland's Future, prioritizing equity, early childhood education, and career readiness. Her concern is ensuring funding remains sustainable and implementation is equitable, particularly in rural areas like Talbot County.

Key facts:

* Henry lives with her family of four in Easton
* She serves District 2 on the Board of Education
* The Board operates as a collective, not driven by individual agendas

title: Kerry Gunshenan
content:
Kerry Gunshenan is a regional sales director for Evoke Pharma and lives in Easton, Maryland. She has served as chairman of the Talbot County Public Schools Advisory Council and president of the St. Michaels YMCA Advisory Board. Gunshenan is married to 22 years with five children (14-20 years old) and is running for the District 6 seat on the Board of Education.

Gunshenan's priorities include ensuring all students are college or career ready, developing critical thinking and problem-solving skills, and promoting personal responsibility, financial literacy, strong communication, and respect. She believes addressing the decline in student performance on standardized tests through transparency will help solve the issue.

Gunshenan criticizes postcards criticizing education in Talbot County, stating they bring attention to the issue without placing blame. She supports local decision-making authority for the school system to address community needs effectively, citing concerns with the Blueprint For Maryland's Future mandates.

Key information: Kerry Gunshenan, Easton, MD, Evoke Pharma, District 6 Board of Education, Talbot County Public Schools Advisory Council, St. Michaels YMCA Advisory Board, marriage and family, education priorities, standardized test decline, transparency, local decision-making authority, Blueprint For Maryland's Future.

title: Easton Middle to pilot cell phone pouches in December
content:
Easton Middle School to pilot cell phone pouches starting December 2 as part of Talbot County Public Schools' effort to restrict student cell phone use during school hours. The program is a result of research and surveys that showed 94% of parents/guardians and 96% of staff supported restrictions on cell phone use during the school day.

Talbot County has partnered with company Yondr to provide pouches, which will be assigned to each student. Students will place their phones in the pouches upon entering school, use a magnetic device to lock them, and unlock them at dismissal. The district has purchased 975 pouches for $27,000.

Surveys found that cell phone use can be a distraction during emergencies, with national experts stating it poses greater safety risks than listening to instructions. The program aims to minimize distractions and ensure student safety.

The pilot program will begin on December 2, with Easton Middle School serving as the first location. Families will receive more details later this week, and a presentation will be given to students on Friday. If successful, the program may extend to other schools in the district next year.

title: Talbot Board of Ed approves funding for capital projects, discusses turf field status
content:
Talbot County Public Schools approved $1.5 million in fiscal year 2025 funding for capital projects, including field improvements. The decision follows a lengthy discussion on athletic fields' conditions. Potential projects total $3.36 million and include Easton High School stadium lights, basketball court at Easton Elementary, St. Michaels Elementary playground replacement, auditorium light replacements, and an artificial turf field.

Grants have funded the first three projects: auditorium lights ($817,321), LED lights at St. Michaels Middle-High School ($566,000), and HVAC unit replacements at Easton High ($1,100,000). Director of Operations Kevin Shafer said the district needs better equipment for maintenance to increase field quality.

Board members unanimously approved $566,000 for LED lights at St. Michaels and $117,000 for athletic field projects in general. The remaining funds will be allocated once capital-enabling legislation is approved by the Talbot County Council.

The board discussed funding an artificial turf field at Easton High, with some suggesting using extra funds to save toward the project's $1.8 million price tag. Director Shafer questioned whether allocating funds for one sport would be a good investment in moving forward. Board President Emily Jackson prioritized safety and equal opportunity for athletes.

title: Safe havens of knowledge
content:
Thomas Jefferson believed that an informed citizenry was essential to democracy's success and best defense against tyranny. In November, citizens should heed his words as they head to the polls.

The American Library Association released preliminary data on attempts to censor books in public, school, and academic libraries from January 1 to August 31, 2024. ALA tracked 414 attempts, with 1,128 unique titles challenged, including 47% targeting people of color and LGBTQ+ voices.

Book bans are "deliberate, coordinated, and dangerous." Public and school libraries should be safe havens for knowledge and information, offering diverse viewpoints to empower informed citizens.

Unite Against Book Bans, a organization dedicated to protecting the First Amendment, designated October 19 as the Freedom to Read Day of Action. Concerned citizens can:

* Learn about book bans
* Read banned books
* Participate in activities on uniteagainstbookbans.org
* Take the pledge to support freedom to read and vote

Key dates: January 1 to August 31, 2024

title: Thoughts on smart phone restrictions in schools
content:
A recent Pew Research Center survey found that 95% of American teenagers have a smartphone and spend nearly all their time online. In response, many school districts in the US, including Talbot County in Maryland, have implemented restrictions on student smartphones during school hours. The Talbot County school district will require students to lock their phones in secure pouches starting December 2.

Jonathan Stephen Haidt's book "The Anxious Generation" explores the surge in anxiety, depression, and suicidal thoughts among American youth, attributing it to three factors: 

1. Decline of play-based childhood due to reduced unsupervised free play time.
2. Rise of phone-based childhood with smartphones loaded with social media platforms.
3. Over-reliance on technology eliminating unstructured face-to-face interactions.

Haidt suggests that parents and guardians should delay giving teenagers smartphones until high school, give them basic phones instead of smartphones, and limit access to social media platforms until high school begins.

Despite the increasing number of schools adopting new or more restrictive rules on smartphone access, Haidt's suggestions remain necessary as only 20% of students' time is controlled by schools, while parents and guardians have control over the other 80%. Parents and guardians need to make unpopular but necessary decisions to ensure their children's well-being.

Dates:
- October 19, 2024: Article publication date
- December 2, 2024: Easton Middle School starts requiring students to lock their phones in secure pouches

People:
- David Reel: Author of the article
- Jonathan Stephen Haidt: Social psychologist and author of "The Anxious Generation"

Places:
- Easton, MD: Location of Talbot County school district
- Maryland: State where Talbot County is located

Organizations:
- Pew Research Center
- Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia)
- Star Democrat
- Talbot County school district

Numbers:
- 95%: Percentage of American teenagers with a smartphone
- 45%: Percentage of teenagers saying they are online nearly all the time
- 20%: Percentage of students' time controlled by schools
- 80%: Percentage of students' time not controlled by schools

title: Dorchester ends alternative education contract in middle, elementary schools
content:
Dorchester County Board of Education unanimously voted to terminate its one-year contract with Transforming Lives for alternative education program for elementary and middle school students due to convenience. The service provided up to 48 students at a time, costing $79,000 per month.

The program, Positive Change Academy-Dorchester, began this summer and was set to end June 30, 2025. The district superintendent approved the contract in July, citing it as a one-stop education journey for students to remedy behavior and improve academics before returning to regular schools.

This decision follows the termination of a three-year contract with Vision Quest, an alternative education program for high schoolers, also due to convenience, which cost $93,363 per month. Former Dorchester County Board of Education Vice President Susan Morgan resigned in June over this decision.

The termination was made after board member Chris Wheedleton's motion to terminate the contract was unanimously approved by the board without comment from Wheedleton.

title: Group promotes extremist agenda
content:
Here is a highly condensed version of the article:

Moms for Liberty (M4L), a nationwide extremist group, has an active chapter in Talbot County, Maryland. M4L was included as an extremist group by the Southern Poverty Law Center, promoting an anti-student inclusion agenda.

Founded in Florida, M4L advocates for "parental rights" and calls to ban books in schools. Three members are part of the Department of Education workgroup overseeing school libraries. M4L's definition of liberty is that individuals have freedom to believe as they do, contradicting deeply held values.

In a local election, three candidates (Ann O'Connor, Karla Wieland-Cherry, and Kerry Gunshenan) supported by M4L are vying for the Board of Education majority. Candidate research reveals that either these candidates did not understand M4L's agenda or agreed with it.

Local educators prioritize children's education over extremist ideologies. Residents in districts with school board races should vote for Candace Henry, Anna Howie, or Cynthia Marrah Jurrius instead, as they are qualified to make decisions about education.

M4L's hateful rhetoric and anti-inclusive agenda do not belong in schools.

title: Should Maryland schools ban cellphones?
content:
Maryland's school board candidates overwhelmingly support stricter cellphone policies in schools, with 64 out of 74 candidates favoring strict restrictions and 10 expressing reservations. Reasons for limiting cellphone use include disciplinary issues, cyberbullying, phone addiction, mental health concerns, and social media distractions.

The trend of implementing stricter cellphone policies has already begun in Maryland schools, with at least a third of districts tightening their regulations this school year. Policies vary, with some banning devices throughout the day, while others allow limited use during non-instructional times.

Candidates cited concerns about the impact of cellphones on students' mental health, social skills, and academic performance. Experts like Annette Anderson from the Johns Hopkins Center for Safe and Healthy Schools warn that excessive cellphone use can lead to internet addiction, suicidal behavior, and reduced interpersonal connections.

Some candidates proposed nuanced approaches, such as allowing limited use during non-instructional times or enforcing a contract for cellphone use between parents and students. Others supported full bans on cellphones in elementary and middle schools, with emergency access only in high schools.

Notable candidates include Rita Montoya from Montgomery County, who advocates for "away all day" policy; Robin Merchant Spickler from Washington County, who supports the current policy; and Maisie T. Howard from Anne Arundel County, who voiced concerns about banning cellphones due to potential harm to special needs students.

A survey found that 72% of high school teachers cite cellphone distractions as a major problem, while another study reported a doubling of suicidal ideation among children and adolescents between 2008 and 2015.

title: Maryland school board candidates push for officers, mental health services
content:
Maryland school board candidates prioritize school safety by advocating for more law enforcement officers and mental health services. Diaz proposes returning school resource officers to Montgomery County schools, while others support increasing SROs across districts. However, concerns about disproportionate discipline of students of color led to the removal of police in Montgomery County.

The state's 2022-2023 statistics show a rise in anonymously reported bullying and cyberbullying incidents, assaults, threats to cause harm, and critical life-threatening incidents. In 2023-2024, violent incidents increased 49% nationwide.

Candidates support school resource officers but also emphasize the importance of mental health services, social-emotional learning, and emergency preparedness. Some suggest a focus on building healthy school atmospheres beginning in early grades to prevent bullying.

Forty-eight out of 74 candidates expressed dissatisfaction with school safety, citing the need for more law enforcement presence and mental health support. Candidates from different districts offer varying solutions, including increased counseling services, improved school discipline measures, and strengthening proactive approaches to preventing problems.

title: Is Maryland’s ‘Blueprint’ the path to better schools?
content:
Maryland's "Blueprint" is a $30 billion 10-year plan aiming to improve public schools by increasing teacher salaries, expanding pre-kindergarten, and rewriting curriculum. The blueprint has sparked debate among school board candidates, with some expressing concerns about costs and mandates. 

Forty-two of the 109 candidates surveyed expressed concerns about the Blueprint's costs and mandates. Candidates from suburban and rural districts said the plan was "transformative" but lacked financial support.

The blueprint is built on five pillars: increasing teacher salaries to $60,000 by 2026, expanding pre-kindergarten, adjusting curriculum, implementing a ninth-grade tracker system, and boosting funding. However, many candidates expressed concerns about implementing the plan without adequate financial support.

State projections show long-term deficits of nearly $2.93 billion in fiscal 2029 due to increased education costs. Governor Wes Moore acknowledged that the plan may need adjustments.

School district candidates said the Blueprint is putting pressure on local school budgets and imposing expensive mandates, leading to unintended consequences such as budget shortfalls and staff cuts.

Key dates: 2021 (BluePrint passed by General Assembly), 2025 (fiscal year when deficit appears), 2029 (year when Blueprint costs state $4 billion).

title: Author empowering young voices
content:
Jessieca Montgomery, an educator with experience in teaching public speaking and communication skills, created a series of coloring and activity books focused on public speaking for kids in grades kindergarten through 5. The series combines creativity with essential communication skills to build confidence and express themselves effectively.

The series consists of several titles: "Speak and Shine: A Coloring Adventure in Public Speaking," "Confidence in Every Word: Activity Book for Young Speakers," and "The Little Speaker's Toolkit: Coloring and Crafting Your Speech." Each book provides interactive lessons, puzzles, games, and scenarios to encourage kids to practice speaking skills.

Montgomery's books feature diverse characters and relatable scenarios, allowing children from various backgrounds to see themselves in the material. The series highlights the significance of public speaking from a young age, equipping children with tools to articulate their thoughts, advocate for themselves, and participate actively in discussions.

Public speaking is a vital skill that lays the foundation for effective communication, critical thinking, and self-confidence. Montgomery's work empowers kids to find their voices, share their stories, and shine in all areas of their lives. Her series is a remarkable contribution to children's literature and education, fostering confidence and inclusivity among young learners.

content:
The Maryland Democratic Party plans to spend "tens of thousands of dollars" on school board elections in at least 18 counties, targeting candidates they deem as supporting a "hateful" and "right-wing agenda." title: Experience, transparency needed
content:
Here is a highly condensed version of the article:

The author, Alison Sanford, will vote for Candace Henry in the upcoming Talbot County school board election. Both candidates are well-liked in the community, but Henry is more qualified due to her knowledge of the state of schools and actions taken by the school board.

Henry pointed out inaccuracies in Ann O'Connor's statements during a candidate forum, including suggesting exit interviews to improve teacher retention, which is already done, and proposing curriculum development involving teachers who are already involved. Sanford notes that Henry's responses were accurate while O'Connor's were not.

Flyers supporting O'Connor have been sent to mailboxes with cherry-picked data on test scores and spending, accompanied by "required reading" in third grade claims. Sanford accuses the group of having a hidden agenda and voting for Henry due to her experience and transparency.

title: Collaborative, open-minded partner
content: Cynthia Jurrius is running for District 6 representative on the Talbot County school board. She's an independent candidate committed to fostering a strong, inclusive, and safe educational environment. Her experience as a mediator will be invaluable in addressing challenges facing the system. Jurrius has a passion for serving the community and participated in public forums to listen to all voices. Margaret Griffin Begor endorses her, describing Cynthia as a collaborative and open-minded partner who will guide Talbot County Schools towards a bright future.

title: Tench Tilghman: A Talbot County-born revolutionary hero
content:
Tench Tilghman was a Revolutionary War hero born in Talbot County, Maryland in 1744 and educated there. He joined George Washington's staff in 1776 and became one of his most trusted men, known as "family" to Washington. Tilghman delivered the news of British surrender following the Battle of Yorktown on October 19, 1781, confirming it to the Continental Congress on October 24.

Tilghman was hardworking and intelligent, providing leadership to patriot soldiers and finding food for them during the war. He refused pay for nearly five years, a great part of which time he served alongside Washington's family. A portrait of Washington commissioned in 1781 features Tilghman and Marquis de Lafayette, painted by Maryland-born Charles Willson Peale.

Tilghman died in 1786 and was initially buried in Baltimore but reinterred in 1971 at the Oxford Cemetery. His spouse spent decades on his father's plantation in Oxford after his death. Today, he is celebrated through the Tench Tilghman Week event by the Maryland Society of the Sons of the American Revolution.

Tilghman played a critical role in the Battle of Brooklyn in 1776 and later wrote that the 1st Maryland Regiment made a gallant resistance under Col. William Smallwood. The Maryland State Archives are working to identify and write biographies on as many Revolutionary War soldiers as possible, including those from the Maryland 400 who saved the Continental Army.

Tench Tilghman Week is an annual event sponsored by the Tench Tilghman Chapter, which aims to educate current and future generations about his life and legacy. The event includes a presentation about the Maryland 400 on October 19-24, followed by a program on how to join the Sons of the American Revolution and Daughters of the American Revolution from 2-4 pm at the Talbot County Free Library.

Key dates:

* 1744: Tench Tilghman was born in Talbot County, Maryland
* 1776: Tilghman joined Washington's staff and participated in the Battle of Brooklyn
* October 19, 1781: British surrender following the Battle of Yorktown
* October 24, 1781: Confirmation of British surrender to the Continental Congress

* Tench Tilghman: Revolutionary War hero and aide-de-camp to George Washington

* Owen Lourie: Project director at the Maryland State Archives

* Talbot County, Maryland: Where Tench Tilghman was born and educated
* Philadelphia: Where Tilghman arrived to confirm British surrender following the Battle of Yorktown
* Baltimore: Initial burial site of Tench Tilghman
* Oxford Cemetery: Final resting place of Tench Tilghman

* Continental Congress: Received news of British surrender following the Battle of Yorktown from Tench Tilghman

title: An open letter on recent education mailers
content:
Talbot County Public Schools Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi and President Emily Jackson wrote an open letter to the community regarding recent mailers that unfairly target their schools, students, and educators. The team acknowledges challenges but emphasizes transparency and direct action. Key initiatives include:

- Investing in rigorous standards-based curricula
- Hiring and retaining qualified teachers and administrators
- Prioritizing math education

The 23-24 Maryland Comprehensive Assessment results showed modest improvement across all districts, with Talbot County's overall margin of progress exceeding the state average. The district had the greatest increase in English/Language Arts students being proficient.

Talbot County Public Schools adhere to Health Education Standards set forth by the Maryland Department of Education and provide opportunities for parental notification and excusal from Family Life unit content. The district supports its staff, teachers, and administrators, emphasizing collaboration and communication to ensure excellence for every child.

The community is invited to participate in monthly public forums during regular Board of Education meetings, which are open to all citizens. The superintendent and president express pride in the district's students and staff, advocating for TCPS students, families, and educators.

title: Ridgely Elementary School students get into the Halloween spirit
content:
Ridgely Elementary School hosted an annual Halloween parade on October 31, 2024, where students, teachers, and staff dressed in costumes and walked down Central Avenue. The event was organized by former Town Hall employee Stephanie Berkey and current Assistant Clerk-Treasurer Melissa Leonard, who started the collaboration with local businesses in 2011.

This year, 18 businesses participated, providing candy for over 291 students. The town's Town Hall office was transformed into a haunted house, where employees dressed up as witches, fortune tellers, and other characters. 

Berkey and Leonard reported that this year's event was the largest since their involvement began. They expressed gratitude for the partnership with local businesses and organizations, including Ridgely Elementary School's Parent Teacher Association.

The event has become a popular tradition in the town of Ridgely, Maryland, with Clerk-Treasurer Berkey stating it is her favorite day to come to work due to the creativity and joy displayed by students.

title: Students learn to build and sell in CBMM's Rising Tide After-School program
content:
The Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum's Rising Tide After-School program, launched in 2017 as a boat building initiative, has expanded to provide middle school students in grades six through nine with seven-week vocational skills training. The program focuses on marketing and project design, allowing students to choose their projects. Students have created wooden ornaments, including Christmas trees, stockings, snowmen, and marine life, which will be sold in the museum's store. All proceeds support the program.

The program's vice president, Jill Ferris, emphasizes accessibility, offering partial to full scholarships and transportation for students who need it. The next session opens in January 2025. Students have enjoyed learning new skills, including hand cutting and decorating ornaments. Proceeds will be reinvested into the program.

- 2017: Rising Tide After-School program launched
- October 31, 2024: Program featured in Star Democrat article

Key people:

- Jill Ferris, Rising Tide's vice president of education and interpretation
- Alyssa Zajan, student and public programs manager
- Harper Black, program student

- St. Michaels, Maryland
- Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum

title: School mailing accusations are false
content:
Talbot County residents received US Postal Service mailings criticizing the quality of teaching in local public schools, falsely attributing low English and math proficiency to "forcing harmful gender ideology." The accusations come from Pay Attention America Inc., a Delaware-based group citing the Daily Citizen's director of communications claiming certain events are "good" or "bad" based on God's principles. 

39% of Talbot County students are economically disadvantaged, 40% are minorities, and 14% study English as second language. The county's public schools earned star ratings of three or higher for all schools out of 24 in Maryland.

In 2023, the district boasted an 91.5% attendance rate and a 95% high school graduation rate, with year-over-year improvement in academic achievement.

Pay Attention America Inc.'s mailings claim radical politicians are pushing "extreme radical agendas" and that public schools engage in "radical indoctrination." The group's methods target the county's public schools, seeking to divide the community instead of promoting fact-based solutions.

Locals can address concerns directly with teachers and administrators through local control.

title: Decline in social capital has reached new lows
content:
Here's a highly condensed version of the article:

Robert Putnam wrote "Bowling Alone" in 2000, analyzing the decline of social capital in America since 1950, which included decreased civic engagement, voter turnout, and distrust in government. Since then, the decline has worsened due to limited social interactions during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Young children's brains are most active in developing communication skills between birth and age 8. An incident at a Talbot County GOP dinner (Oct 25) highlighted the importance of social capital, similar to World War II's struggles against Nazi Germany's threat to civil discourse and democratic governance.

British Prime Minister Winston Churchill rallied the British people during WWII with his understanding of social capital and communication skills, ultimately leading to Britain's victory. America needs a renewed commitment to social capital.

Opportunities for renewal include:

1. Reading Putnam's book at the Talbot County Library
2. Attending the Chesapeake Forum program on Nov 7-21
3. Watching a Baylor University webinar on "Political Desaturation"

Key speakers included Robert B. Talisse, Dr. Curt Thompson, and Elizabeth Oldfield, emphasizing the importance of:

* Getting in the same room as others to find common ground
* Seeking understanding over division
* Rebuilding civic infrastructure away from politics

Working together can change the world, according to Margaret Mead's observation that a small group of thoughtful citizens can make a difference.

title: Relationships key to positive change
content:
Candace Henry is endorsed for Talbot County School Board District 2. She demonstrated preparation and understanding of current issues at a recent forum. Her opponent, Ms. O'Connor, lacks sufficient qualifications to address public school challenges. Henry has:

- Read the Maryland Blueprint for Education and conceptualized its strengths and challenges

title: Talbot Board of Education may see new faces in December
content:
Talbot County Board of Education may see new faces in December 2024. Unofficial results show:

title: Wheedleton wins Dorchester Board of Education seat
content: Chris Wheedleton won the District 5 Dorchester County Board of Education seat with 69.5% of the vote, surpassing all precincts reporting but awaiting mail-in and provisional ballots. As incumbent, Wheedleton was appointed in 2023 as an education and business consultant. His goals remain unchanged: prioritizing students, empowering teachers, and engaging the community. Unopposed winners were Brandy Dawson Cumberland (97.8% in District 1) and Christine LaMonica (97.9% in District 3), both appointed by the Dorchester County Council on July 18 to fill former board members' seats following their resignations.

title: Student vets' stories provide unique insight on service
content:
Veterans from three institutions of higher education in Elizabeth City gathered at College of The Albemarle on November 8, 2024, to share their military experiences and how it affected their lives and career choices. 

Bobby Martin, a MACU student who joined the US Navy in 1977, spoke about his father's influence and his own service, which included traveling to several countries. 

Wendra Costly, a COA student who served in the US Army from 2018-2022, discussed the challenges veterans face when returning to school, citing age and life experience as barriers. However, she found the aviation program at COA to be promising.

Michelle Barnes, an ECSU student who spent eight years working as an aviation electronics technician in the US Navy, talked about her decision to enlist and how it led to meeting her husband. She praised her time in service, saying it was a "best decision" that helped pay for college expenses.

Elizabeth City State University's interim chancellor, Dr. Catherine Edmonds, thanked the veterans who attended and expressed the university's commitment to serving military members, veterans, and their families. 

MACU's vice president of student services, Bane Angles, emphasized the importance of unity learned from his time in the military. COA President Dr. Jack Bagwell urged the veterans to share their feedback on how the college can better serve them.

The event aimed to provide a unique insight into service through the stories of these student veterans and highlighted the role colleges play in helping veterans transition back to civilian life.

title: Athens High School holds Veterans Day event for students
content:
Athens High School held a Veterans Day event for its students to honor veterans and hear from those who have served. According to the US Census Bureau, 6.2% of adults are veterans, down from 23.4 million in 2005. Melissa Myers, student council advisor and French teacher, emphasizes the importance of hearing veterans' stories to gain a deeper understanding of their experiences.

Chad Springer, associate superintendent and former US Army sergeant, delivered a speech at the event. He shared his family's military history, including his uncles Bob and Howard, who served in World War II and the Korean War respectively. Springer highlighted the personal nature of service, saying it changed his perspective on those he served with.

Springer recounted how serving in the military instilled in him a sense of community and belonging, which he values to this day. The event aimed to help high school students appreciate the importance of service and fighting for a cause greater than oneself.

Key details:

- Date: November 8, 2024
- Location: Athens High School, Athens County
- Event: Veterans Day assembly for students
- Speakers: Melissa Myers, Chad Springer
- Veterans' stories shared by: Chad Springer

title: Midshore Technology Services to work with student apprentice
content:
Kyren Hawkins, a North Caroline High School senior, signed a youth apprenticeship contract with Justin Smith, president of Midshore Technology Services in Denton, on November 12, 2024. The apprenticeship will provide on-the-job training in business and expand on Hawkins' knowledge in cybersecurity. Hawkins is currently enrolled in the Project Lead the Way Computer Science Program of Study.

A signing ceremony was held at Midshore Technology Services with Hawkins, his parents, Coordinator of Career Readiness Eric Cook, and Smith. This marks the second youth apprenticeship agreement between Midshore Technology Services and CCPS, following a partnership with North Caroline High School senior Christopher Ireland in 2021.

Christopher Ireland graduated in June 2023 and will serve as Hawkins' mentor at MTS. Hawkins will work on proactive maintenance, monitoring, and backups, essential to maintaining an efficient IT environment. For more information about the Youth Apprenticeship Program, visit the CCPS Youth Apprenticeship page (cook.eric@ccpsstaff.org).

title: Haven Ministries welcomes opening of Jacob Sloan Center
content:
The Jacob Sloan Center in Queenstown, MD, opened on October 31, 2024, as an extension of Haven Ministries emergency shelter. The center provides a respite for clients to spend time during the day and offers education classes such as resume writing, finances, computer literacy, and life skills.

Haven Ministries executive director Peter Grim stated that food and shelter are essential but educational programs can help lift individuals and families out of poverty. Mary Ella Jourdak, a Haven Ministries volunteer, said kitchen enhancements are next on the agenda to provide dignity for under-resourced individuals.

The center is named after Jacob Sloan, who died in 2018 at age 12 in a car accident. His parents, Mary and Peter Sloan, partnered with Haven Ministries to continue their son's legacy and support community organizations. The Jacob Sloan Foundation provided hundreds of thousands of dollars in funding, while Tim and Linette Miller funded center furnishing and equipment.

The mission of Haven Ministries fits perfectly with Jake's lifelong commitment to kindness. Pastor Tom Chandler offered the space at Shore Christian Fellowship Church, which became a hub for education and respite services. The center features a photo collage of memories and smiles of Jake Sloan, showcasing his life and legacy.

title: It's been a wild ride
content:
CHESTERTOWN — Robbi Behr and Matthew Swanson, a married couple from Chestertown, are on a "Busload of Books Tour" to support Title I schools by delivering their children's novel series and providing face time with authors. The initiative aims to provide better access to books for kids in underfunded schools.

The duo has visited numerous elementary schools across Kent County, winning over kids with their lively presentation that encourages imagination. A team of educational researchers from Washington College compiled data on the impact of the tour.

Behr and Swanson plan to visit 12 schools nationwide, six in-person and six virtually, throughout the 2024-2025 school year. They have been recognized for their authentic communication skills and humor as speakers, including an invitation to the Masters of Scale Conference in San Francisco.

The conference, sponsored by WaitWhat media properties, features a roster of thought-leaders, including Reid Hoffman and former President Bill Clinton. The duo's presentation aimed to age their story from elementary school kids to an adult audience, focusing on their outreach, challenges faced by Title I schools, family life on the road, and partnerships forged.

Their talk captivated an audience of 800 people with stories like that of Jenny, a hippo who overcame obstacles to achieve her dream. The couple summarized their talk by encouraging listeners to create their own "colorful school bus" and drive a path of change for betterment.

title: Maryland conservatives make gains in school board races
content:
Conservative school board candidates in Maryland saw sweeping wins across the state, with 11 endorsed by the 1776 Project PAC winning or narrowly leading their races as of Friday. The PAC, a Republican-aligned organization, backed 19 candidates statewide and outspent the teachers' union $450,000. 

The teachers' union spent $516,999.57 during the 2024 election cycle. Stefano Forte, executive director of the 1776 Project PAC, attributed the wins to voters choosing "common sense" over "far-left culture war." Luca Amayo, spokesperson for the Maryland Democratic Party, described the PAC as a "radical ring-wing group."

The party helped defeat five of its endorsed candidates. Ryan James Girdusky, founder of the 1776 Project PAC, aimed to reform school boards and elect conservative reform-minded candidates. In Calvert County, candidates endorsed by the PAC won all three school board seats, while in Washington County, Democrats' targeted candidates flipped the county's school board into conservative control.

Other counties saw similar trends: Frederick, Carroll, Allegany, and Cecil shifted rightward, with some races remaining too close to call. In Howard County, Andrea Chamblee trailed Trent Kittleman by 3.5 points as of Friday morning.

title: St. Michaels temporary library opens at Village Shopping Center
content:
The Talbot County Free Library's St. Michaels Branch has opened a temporary location at Village Shopping Center in St. Michaels, MD, due to construction on the Fremont Street branch, expected to take 1-2 years to complete. The temporary library offers full services, including children's area and audio books, but lacks meeting rooms and an external book drop. Shauna Beulah, branch manager, emphasized accessibility and availability of resources.

Diana Hastings, youth services librarian, will provide fall bags with crafts for families and offer hands-on activities to encourage creativity and literacy. The temporary library offers extensive youth books, including bilingual children's books, and can order books from other libraries if needed.

The grand opening celebration included free coffee, craft bags, and donuts for visitors. Construction on the Fremont Street branch includes an eating area, social computer rooms, a quiet reading section, and a multi-purpose space.

title: Mother can't provide holiday celebration while in school
content:
A mother of three who has been unemployed for nearly four years due to mental health struggles and homelessness is attending school to obtain her nursing certification and hopes to start a career. Despite financial constraints, she fears not being able to provide a holiday celebration for her children.

She will receive assistance from the Brighter Christmas Fund, a nonprofit organization helping families in need on the Mid-Shore. The fund's total donations for 2024 stand at $27,643.75 and are tax-deductible.

Donations can be made to The Star Democrat or online via credit card or PayPal (brighterchristmasfund.org). Organizations supporting the fund include Bill & Diane Aberg, Sidewinder Charitable Foundation, J & L Grabenstein Foundation, Hillsboro Queen Anne United Methodist Men, and Fox Trucking, Inc., among others.

The mother's children have upcoming birthdays during Christmas.

title: Local seniors inducted into hall of fame
content: Phil Cicconi and Ted Clark were inducted into the Maryland Senior Citizens Hall of Fame for 2024, recognizing their outstanding contributions as volunteers to improve lives in Kent County, Maryland. Cicconi, a dedicated community leader and president of The Friends of Eastern Neck since 1998, co-founded the Kent County Learning Center in 2012 and played a crucial role in administering COVID-19 vaccinations to seniors. Clark, a resident of Heron Point, emphasized the benefits of volunteering, stating "Volunteering one's time and skills to others is a win-win situation." The Maryland Senior Citizens Hall of Fame, Inc., a private organization since 1987, honors senior citizens ages 65+ who have performed outstanding service in their communities.

title: Newcomers win Talbot County Board of Education seats
content:
Talbot County Public Schools is undergoing a change in leadership as three newcomers won seats on the Board of Education: Ann O'Connor, Karla Wieland-Cherry, and Cynthia Marrah Jurrius. They took office starting December 1 for four-year terms.

The election results showed:

- District 2: O'Connor (52.7%) defeated Candace Henry
- District 5: Wieland-Cherry (54.6%) defeated Anna Howie
- District 6: Jurrius (51.9%) defeated Kerry Gunshenan

Winners' priorities include:
