title: Student-parents need support from colleges
content:
Mike Munoz, president of Long Beach City College, writes about the need for colleges to support student-parents. As a first-generation student and single father, he faced obstacles like housing insecurity, food scarcity, and lack of affordable child care. Many student-parents feel hopeless and isolated on campus.

One in five college students are parents, with the majority being mothers of color who face financial disadvantages. Single mothers deal with unique stigma. Munoz believes all student-parents face challenges, but single mothers experience more.

Munoz implemented changes at Long Beach Community College, including removing "No children allowed" signs and providing resources like a Child Development Center and cost-free after-school care. The college partners with Raise The Barr to offer affordable child care and housing.

A recent survey found that over half of student-parents are unaware of available resources. Munoz's team is creating a one-stop shop for services and launching an outreach campaign to inform students about available support.

Munoz hopes to nurture student-parents through degree completion or transfer to a four-year university, modeling hard work and commitment for their children. His daughter is now a community college professor, and he's proud of her achievement. Supporting student-parents benefits the entire community, making it essential to dedicate resources to their success.

Date: November 16, 2024
Location: Long Beach City College, California

title: Maryland schools get new rules for shooter drills
content:
Maryland's new state guidelines for active shooter drills in schools aim to limit the impact on students' mental health. The guidelines, released by the Maryland Center for School Safety this fall, ban trauma-inducing elements like imitation of gunfire and explosions, require notification of parents before drills, and encourage a diverse planning team.

The new guidelines will be put into effect at the beginning of the 2025 academic year. Del. Jared Solomon sponsored the measure in response to concerns about the impact of active shooter drills on students' mental health, citing the need for "trauma-informed and age-appropriate" approaches.

Solomon's district experienced an incident where families received texts from their kids during a drill, raising concerns about lack of foresight and notification. The bill also includes a requirement for schools to distribute surveys to gather feedback from staff, parents, and students on the effectiveness and mental impact of drills.

The guidelines emphasize that active shooter drills should be adjusted to fit age groups, with a focus on creating an open dialogue between staff, students, and families. A mechanism will be established to pause or stop drills when necessary, and schools will notify parents before and after drills to increase trust and communication.

Key figures include:

* Del. Jared Solomon (sponsor of the bill)
* Sen. Cheryl Kagan (co-sponsor of the bill)
* President Joe Biden (executive order signed)

Notable dates:

* October: Guidelines released by the Maryland Center for School Safety
* April: Maryland bill passed

Key statistics and numbers:

* 2025: Academic year when new guidelines will be put into effect
* 1999: Year of the Columbine High School shooting

title: Talbot County Education Foundation honors 3 alumni
content:
Keasha Haythe, JoAnn Asparagus Murray, and Ludwig Eglseder III were honored as Talbot County Public Schools' 2024 Distinguished Alumni. A ceremony at the Oxford Community Center raised funds for projects, including a student leadership program, pre-kindergarten language and literacy, and an Easton Middle School band.

Haythe, president of Foundation of Hope, graduated from Easton High in 1991 and remembered supportive teachers who helped her believe in herself. She advocates for self-encouragement to those who doubt themselves.

Eglseder, a physician, graduated from St. Michaels High in 1975 and provided internal medicine services for 38 years. He emphasized the importance of public education and supporting it.

Asparagus Murray, a former family law magistrate, attended Robert Russa Moton High School and later worked as a social worker. She praised the school's camaraderie and faculty, which helped her develop advocacy skills.

The event raised funds for projects requested by teachers, including:

1. Student leadership program
2. Pre-kindergarten language and literacy
3. Easton Middle School band
4. Other six specific requests

TCPS Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi emphasized the importance of innovative ideas and funding for public education initiatives.

title: Character Counts celebrates 24th anniversary
content:
Character Counts celebrated its 24th anniversary on November 12, marking 25 years since its inception in 1999 as a response to the Columbine tragedy. The initiative, launched by Committee Co-Chair Wayne Humphries, aims to increase character education through resources, training, and information on six pillars: trustworthiness, respect, responsibility, fairness, caring, and citizenship.

Character Counts has reached approximately 70,000-100,000 students, with over 4,200 students receiving character education experiences this year. The organization has 10 county pre-k classrooms, all Queen Anne's County middle and elementary schools, and over 1,600 volunteers who have dedicated their time as Character Counts Coaches.

The initiative credits Queen Anne's County Public Schools and its Advisory Board for collaborative support. Over 100 community volunteers make up the organization, with a dozen Kent Island High School Honor Society student coaches serving as role models to younger students.

Coordinators report that these volunteers have put in over 1,000 hours, totaling $30,000 value to the county. Character Counts Coaches visit classrooms to share Pillar of the Month lessons, promoting positive behavior choices and character development.

title: Talbot Board of Ed bids farewell to 3 outgoing board members
content:
The Talbot County Board of Education bid farewell to three board members: Candace Henry, Anna Howie, and Mary Wheeler. Three new members will be sworn in next month. 

Board President Emily Jackson praised the outgoing members for their service, citing improvements in education as a result of their work. Henry, who is stepping down as vice president, thanked colleagues and expressed her commitment to holding people accountable from another role. Wheeler served on the board for 7.5 years and expressed confidence that her successor, Cynthia Jurrius, will continue her efforts. Howie, an assistant principal, will be succeeded by Karla Wieland-Cherry in District 5. 

The three outgoing members have been replaced by Ann O'Connor (District 2), Kerry Gunshenan's defeated opponent in the election.

title: Ravens flock; Local kids honored at NFL game
content:
Here is a highly condensed version of the article:

The Kent Island High School Interact Club was honored by the Baltimore Ravens with the National Football League's Honor Rows distinction for their community service and leadership development on October 13, 2024. Nearly 50 students attended the game against Washington Commanders, celebrating their contributions.

Principal Dan Harding praised the club's efforts under teacher Lacey Phelps, Katie McGrath, and partnership with the Giving the Edge Foundation (GTEF), led by Bobby Woolley and Colleen Williams. GTEF was a winning recipient of the Honor Rows Program, recognizing youth groups providing outstanding community service.

The Leadership Cohort at Kent Island High School started in 2021, allowing student leaders to understand their "WHY" through personalized discussions and personality tests. Last year, an Interact portion was launched with the Rotary of Kent Island; this school year, over 70 students are ready to serve.

At the game, GTEF received a Governor's Citation for Maryland and its logo was recognized on the jumbotron during the second quarter. Students received a t-shirt, ticket, VIP access, and pictures with players during warm-ups. The program supports student leadership development; learn more at https://www.theedge360.net/gtef

title: DCPS not moving forward with new alternative education programming
content: Dorchester County Public Schools (DCPS) will not pursue alternative education contracts due to budgetary restraints. In November 2024, DCPS Superintendent Jymil Thompson recommended terminating proposals from alternative companies. The district will instead focus on staffing its Positive Change Academy at Glasgow Street, which provides alternative education for students. Four months earlier, DCPS terminated a $3.3 million contract with an alternative program for high schoolers, citing criticism from residents since its approval in September 2023.

title: DCPS to examine oldest elementary school buildings as teachers demand change
content:
DCPS to examine oldest elementary school buildings as teachers demand change:

* Sandy Hill Elementary School in Cambridge has experienced plumbing issues, room temperature problems, and mold growth due to its old age.
* Teachers have expressed concerns about teaching and learning in open concept classrooms with critters and bugs getting into the building.
* Architecture firm Hord Coplan Macht will conduct an ed specifications and feasibility study for the district's oldest elementary schools, including Sandy Hill.
* The study is funded by Maryland's Interagency Commission on School Construction (IAC) and allocated $2.75 million for Dorchester County in fiscal year 2026.
* IAC's Built To Learn Program has $3.9 million budgeted for Dorchester County, which needs to be spent by 2031.
* Assistant Superintendent Michael Collins says the district must complete the study within a year to bid out capital improvement projects.
* The process will take six months, and a committee will work with the community to determine ideal school designs.
* Board member Talibah Chikwendu apologizes for the long timeframe, saying "it's going to take so long" to build a new school.

title: 'Share and make merry': International students get a taste of American holidays
content:
On November 27, 2024, the University of Delaware's Center for Global Programs & Services hosted a Thanksgiving dinner for approximately 500 international students and their family members, marking the 11th annual event. The celebration aimed to introduce American students to the tradition, build community among international students, and create belonging.

Vina Titaley, associate director, stated that the event allows students who have never experienced a Thanksgiving holiday to participate in one. Ravi Ammigan, associate provost, recalled his first American Thanksgiving nearly three decades ago when he felt a sense of belonging at a professor's dinner invitation.

The Center for Global Programs & Services started hosting the dinner 11 years ago with around 40 attendees, and it has since grown into a signature event. International students such as Angelica Maisuh (Ghana), Neha Sindhu (India), and Faith Wanjiku (Kenya) attended, expressing gratitude for the experience and feeling included in American culture.

The university welcomes nearly 4,000 international students from over 100 countries each year. During Thanksgiving week, many stay on campus, while others return home due to distance. The annual dinner provides an opportunity for those students to celebrate the holiday and feel part of the community.

title: Caroline Commissioners hear update on potential for new middle school
content:
Caroline County Commissioners received an update on potential plans for a new middle school in November 2024. Bill Mengel, director of operations at Caroline County Public Schools, presented a revised fiscal year 2026 capital improvement plan that includes priority funding for a potential new middle school building.

The commission approved the revised plan, which requests $500,000 for HVAC work and $5.5 million for early planning and design costs over two years. The district has requested $76 million in state funding for a new build, which is approximately 89% of the total estimated cost of $86 million.

The Maryland Interagency Commission on School Construction is reviewing an approximate capacity of 126,000 square feet for the potential new build. Mengel noted that costs have risen sharply year-to-year and that the district's main point of negotiation is increasing square footage.

Commissioner Travis Breeding requested updates from the school district on the early planning and feasibility study results, citing a desire to be involved in discussions about the project's scope, including whether it would be a renovation, addition, or new location.

title: St. Michaels residents donate hygiene supplies for student success
content:
Four St. Michaels residents, Kevin and Marybeth Sullivan, and Commissioners Jay Hudson and Katrina Whittington, donated hygiene supplies to St. Michaels Middle/High School in September 2024, after being told the church's back-to-school event already had the needed supplies. The group, in collaboration with the school, aimed to ensure students could focus on their studies without worrying about basic needs. They provided dental floss, toothbrushes, toothpaste, mouthwash, deodorant, feminine hygiene products, and soap.

St. Michaels Commissioner Jay Hudson emphasized the connection between a child's self-esteem and academic achievement, stating that access to basic hygiene items removes barriers to student success. Assistant Principal Rebecca Mielke-Mann agreed, saying donations create a more inclusive and positive learning environment.

According to Mielke-Mann, particularly accessible hygiene products for girls are critical in ensuring they can attend school confidently. The Sullivans and Hudson plan to continue replenishing supplies if funds run low. Whittington has also expressed willingness to provide additional funding.

title: Four Eleven Kitchen aims to feed minds and bellies through food access program
content:
Amanda Kidd founded Four Eleven Kitchen in Cambridge, MD in 2016 to address community food access issues. The nonprofit's Feed The People program aims to feed both minds and bellies through cooking skills education, farm-to-table education, and urban farming initiatives.

Kidd partnered with the City of Cambridge and Habitat for Humanity to develop an urban "learning" farm on two parcels in Cambridge. The program targets "a starvation of knowledge and education" by providing access to resources and opportunities.

Feed The People focuses on addressing hunger through nutrition and accessibility, aiming to normalize giving people resources without hoops. Four Eleven Kitchen's community supper events were revived after falling off due to the pandemic; the next revival is planned for 2025.

Kidd emphasized that everyone deserves access to food when hungry, regardless of income level. Omeaka Jackson, a board member, praised Kidd's tenacity and vision. The nonprofit offers support through "Foodie Friends" programs, including library access and corporate donations.

title: Gala at Kennard honors former educators
content:
Queen Anne's County Commissioners pledged $50,000 annually for three years to Kennard African American Cultural Heritage Center and Museum (KAACHC), totaling $150,000. The pledge was part of a $140,000 grant from the National Trust for Historic Preservation's African American Cultural Heritage Action Fund.

The county assisted KAACHC in applying for the grant, supporting their mission to preserve and celebrate African American heritage in Queen Anne's County. The center offers programs such as after-school mentoring, exercise classes, and summer camps for youth with special needs.

Former high school building dedicated in 2019, originally serving as Queen Anne's County's only all-Black segregated high school from 1966 to 1967. Restoration efforts led by Kennard Alumni Association President Clayton Washington began over 15 years ago, with donations and grants obtained to complete the renovation process.

Washington recognized and honored three former Kennard High School educators: Dr. Velma Kennedy Speight, Madelyn Matthews Hollis, and Alveta Smith Jones, for their extensive careers in education. The center plans to expand its offerings to include adult literacy, STEM education, cultural arts, and more with the hiring of a dedicated executive director.

KAACHC has become one of 30 sites nationwide to receive funding from the African American Cultural Heritage Action Fund, awarding $3 million to historic sites representing Black cultural heritage. The center is open to the public for rental purposes and aims to foster connections within the community, preserving African American heritage for future generations.

title: New Beginnings Youth and Family Services honors Theresa Stafford with name change
content:
New Beginnings Youth and Family Services renamed to Dr. Theresa Stafford's New Beginnings Learning Academy in honor of late executive director Theresa Stafford, who died in December 2023 after years of battling cancer. The new name aims to capture both past and future of the program, which Stafford led until her death.

Theresa Stafford served as executive director from unknown start date to her death, during which time she helped residents with financial difficulties, organized field trips for children, and addressed local issues such as drugs and gang violence.

Her daughter Ashley Stafford said the name change "embodies" her mother's legacy at the learning center on Greenwood Avenue. Cooper, who took over as executive director after Stafford's death, stated that they wanted to incorporate Stafford into the program's name to honor her work for the community.

Goldie Cooper described Stafford as "our second Moses," comparing her to Harriet Tubman due to her fighting spirit and dedication to helping others. Cooper also mentioned Phil Feldman's $25,000 donation in July, which helped facilitate the name change.

A ribbon cutting and dedication ceremony will be held on November 30 at noon, coinciding with what would have been Theresa Stafford's 71st birthday. The event will feature speakers, tours of the center, and unveiling of the new sign.

Key dates include:
- December 2023: Theresa Stafford passed away after years of battling cancer
- July 2024: Phil Feldman donated $25,000 to the center
- November 29, 2024: Announcement made about renaming the facility

title: Governor puts $1.8 million toward making Maryland a 'cyber capital'
content: Gov. Wes Moore announced a $1.8 million award to Maryland's 16 community colleges to boost cybersecurity training and career opportunities through the Accelerating Cyber Careers grant by the Maryland Department of Labor. The funding supports BCR Cyber's interactive computer platform, which simulates real-world cyber-attacks for experiential learning. Maryland Association of Community Colleges (MACC) executive director Brad Phillips stated that this investment solidifies MACC as a national leader on cyber and workforce development. Gov. Moore aims to make Maryland a "cyber capital" with the goal of connecting all Marylanders with the training needed to compete for jobs in cybersecurity.

title: More than half of Talbot County students receive free and reduced lunches
content:
Talbot County Public Schools: 58.41% of students receive free and reduced lunches, exceeding the national average. 

The Maryland Department of Education reported a significant increase in free and reduced meals between 2022-2023 school years. Talbot Hunger Coalition reports that Easton Middle School (64%) and Easton Elementary School (76%) have the highest rates.

Food insecurity has risen due to increasing costs, wages are not keeping pace with necessities like housing, gas, and utilities. 

CarePacks, a nonprofit founded by Emily Moody, aims to address food insecurity through free meals programs. 
Katie Fox, community school program manager at Easton Elementary School, noted that transportation is a significant factor affecting access to groceries.

Local organizations emphasize it's not an issue of laziness but rather expensive living conditions in Talbot County. 

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore has signed SB 579, requiring the Maryland Department of Education to report costs for universal free school meals.

title: MSDE announces 2024 Maryland School Report Card
content:
The Maryland State Department of Education released the 2024 Maryland School Report Card on Dec. 3, highlighting school performances and releasing state, district, and school-level results for the 2023-2024 academic year. Deputy State Superintendent Geoff Sanderson reported that overall school ratings have increased compared to the previous year.

Key statistics include:
- 41% of schools earned a four- or five-star rating
- 83% earned three stars or more
- 91 schools earned the highest rating of five stars, including 75 elementary schools

The report also shows disparities in performance among student groups, with Black and Hispanic students earning fewer points than white peers. The Maryland School Report Card includes disaggregated data to highlight these differences.

State Superintendent Cary Wright stated that the accountability system is being revised to be more sensitive to granularity growth, with a focus on individualized interventions and gathering high-quality instructional materials. The Department of Education is revising its English language arts, math, social studies, science, and health standards to improve assessment systems.

Important details:

* 100 possible points were awarded based on academic and non-academic indicators
* Schools are held accountable for academic achievement, progress in English language proficiency, school quality, and student success
* Graduation rates and readiness for post-secondary success also contribute to high school ratings
* No schools decreased two stars from prior year to current year
* MSDE is working on revising its accountability system to improve granularity growth

title: Caroline Board of Ed welcomes new members, elects president
content:
Caroline County Board of Education welcomed new members Chrissy Bartz and Stefanie Johnson, who were sworn in on December 6, 2024, alongside returning member Michele Wayman. 

Wayman was unanimously selected as president by a 5-0 vote after serving on the board since 2021. She previously worked at Caroline County Public Schools for 36 years. Bartz nominated Mark Jones to serve as vice president.

Bartz, appointed in June, is director of community-based programs at Choptank Community Health, overseeing school-based health centers and serving as a provider at Greensboro Elementary. She's excited about the district's direction, particularly the state education initiative Blueprint for Maryland's Future, which designates eight of nine schools as community schools.

Johnson, who ran unopposed in District 2, is executive director of the His Hope Ministries shelter in Denton and a board member for the Caroline County Chamber of Commerce. She expressed her desire to "know why" things happen and be part of conversations that can make change.

title: Maintaining parental rights
content:
On November 30, Lena Gill wrote a letter to the editor of The Star Democrat stating that newly elected Talbot County school board members Ann O'Connor and Karla Wieland-Cherry are members of Moms for Liberty, a "conservative national group" advocating for changes in curriculum and policies. However, both O'Connor and Wieland-Cherry denied being members.

Moms for Liberty is actually a support group providing resources for parents, teachers, and citizens to maintain parental rights through grades K-12. Members include Superintendent Dr. Sharon Pepukayi and some of her staff. The organization's agenda includes advocating for better student outcomes in English and mathematics, reducing school violence, and opposing the dispensing of contraceptives to children.

Gill failed to specify which changes in curriculum and policies she was referring to. Trump was criticized by the Left for detention centers built during Obama's presidency; conflating him with Nazis is an insult to the victims of Nazi Germany.

title: Ella Morton, 100, celebrated by her former 3rd grade Trappe Elementary class
content:
Ella Morton, 100, celebrated her milestone birthday with former third-grade students at the Easton Elks Lodge on December 6, 2024. Morton taught at Trappe Elementary School for over 20 years and still lives in Trappe, Maryland. The event was organized by fellow classmates Linda James and Ruth Worm after they discovered Morton's recent 100th birthday.

Morton's former students remembered her as a favorite teacher who was "very sweet" but still commanded respect. She controlled the classroom and left a lasting impression on their lives. Susan Watts recalled Morton's kindness and excellence in teaching, which impacted not only herself but also her own daughter, who had Morton as a kindergarten teacher.

Morton said she loved teaching and wanted to pursue it after college but eventually followed another career path. However, she returned to education and made a significant impact on many students' lives. When asked about her favorite part of teaching, Morton replied that it was all about the students, saying "When you had a group like this, why wouldn't they be good?"

The event brought laughter, smiles, and tears as Morton's former students reminisced about their time in her third-grade classroom in the 1961-1962 school year.

title: DCPS 'encouraged' by 2024 Maryland School Report Card
content:
Here is a condensed version of the article:

DCPS leaders are "encouraged" by the 2024 Maryland School Report Card results. North Dorchester Middle School and Mace's Lane Middle School gained stars due to improved academic achievement (0.2-0.6 points). Elementary schools increased their scores by 0.2 points, while high schools rose by 1.1 points. The district saw improvement in English language arts and math proficiency, as well as graduation and attendance rates.

Superintendent Jymil Thompson stated that the district needs to accelerate progress to reach its goal of moving from 23rd to 15th in academic performance within four years. Since becoming superintendent, Thompson has emphasized the need for consistent instructional leadership and targeted strategies.

Key dates: June (Thompson became superintendent) and September (Thompson discussed the district's goals).

Key figures: Jymil Thompson, Superintendent of Dorchester County Public Schools.

Places: Cambridge, Maryland; Dorchester County.

Numbers: 2024; 23rd-15th rank; 0.2-1.1 points (academic achievement); 20/30 points (elementary/middle/high school scores).

Organizations: Dorchester County Public Schools.

People mentioned: Jymil Thompson.

title: Caroline superintendent projects 'good budget year,' discusses Blueprint
content:
Here is a highly condensed version of the article:

Caroline County Superintendent Derek Simmons projects a 'good budget year' for FY26, citing increased multilingual learner, special education, and overall enrollment in the county. However, funding changes to Blueprint, Maryland's Future initiative, could drastically impact the district.

Simmons notes that 60% of unrestricted funds are spent on salaries and wages, with around 66% coming from state revenue. Contracted services account for under 7%, while audits through outside companies cost an unknown amount.

The district expects no major changes in federal money or county allocations heading into FY26. Simmons is optimistic but warns that drastic funding changes to Blueprint could have "absolute detrimental impacts" on Caroline County Public Schools, which lack extra wealth to fill gaps.

State legislators may discuss Blueprint funding this winter, with a predicted budget deficit of $2.7 million for FY26. Simmons reports progress in increasing starting teacher salaries to meet the minimum $60,000 by FY27, with only $5,000 left to reach that goal.

title: BAAM plans ceremony for new academic center
content: Building African American Minds Inc. announced a ribbon-cutting ceremony for its new academic center on Dec 12, 2024. The event will take place on Saturday, Dec 14, at 10 am at the BAAM Athletic Center. Dina Gomes Daly, executive director and co-founder, described the center as "a space where learning, growth, and community come alive." The ceremony features remarks from organizational leaders and community partners. The new Academic Center will serve as the home of Polaris Village Academy and offer after-school and summer enrichment programs for youth and families.

title: Easton Middle School drops a star in Maryland School Report Card
content: Easton Middle School in Maryland dropped from three stars to two stars and a 48th percentile rank in the 2024 Maryland School Report Card, scoring 44 points compared to 46.1 in 2023. Academic achievement (7.7/30) and academic progress (16.7/35) scores remained steady, while English proficiency increased slightly (2.6/10) and school quality and student success decreased (17.1/35). The district's director of communications, Debbie Gardner, stated that findings and recommendations will be presented to the Talbot County Board of Education on December 18. Other schools in the district saw improvements, including St. Michaels Elementary rising to four stars and White Marsh Elementary increasing its percentile rank from 69th to 82nd. Easton Middle ranks below fellow middle schools Mace's Lane Middle (two stars, 6th percentile) and Lockerman Middle (two stars, 30th percentile), but above North Dorchester Middle (three stars, 56th percentile). By student group, only Asian students in math proficiency improved from 2023.

title: Noam Chomsky at 96: The linguist, educator, philosopher and public thinker has had a massive intellectual and moral influence
content:
Noam Chomsky turned 96 years old on December 7, 2024, and is a renowned linguist, educator, philosopher, and public thinker with a significant intellectual and moral influence. Born Avram Noam Chomsky in Philadelphia on December 7, 1928, he was raised by progressive educators who instilled his interest in teaching and learning.

Chomsky's early days were marked by his love of Hebrew works, close readings, and lively educational experiences at the Oak Lane County Day School. He pursued graduate work while raising a family and eventually developed his groundbreaking theory of innate human abilities, which he outlined in "Syntactic Structures" (1957) and challenged the structuralist paradigm.

Chomsky's research led to significant advances in linguistics, philosophy, psychology, and cognitive sciences, and his political engagement was documented through interviews and books on U.S. imperialism, the Cold War, and human rights. His ideas connected four "problems" related to Plato, Orwell, Descartes, and Humboldt, focusing on human knowledge, development, and language.

Throughout his life, Chomsky continued to publish and speak out on contemporary issues into his mid-90s, earning him recognition as one of the most cited intellectuals in history. He is widely regarded as a voice for the downtrodden and oppressed, advocating for intellectual self-defense against structures of power and subjugation.

title: MACo's Blueprint panelists stress importance of local context at session in Cambridge
content:
State education officials and Blueprint coordinators from Maryland counties called for a readjustment of the Blueprint with more local focus during a MACo session in Cambridge. Panelists, including Nicole Miller, Christina Miller, Derek Simmons, and Sean Bulson, identified challenges and areas of progress in implementing the plan.

The Blueprint, passed in 2021, aims to improve student outcomes through a $3.8 billion education funding increase over 10 years. However, counties face funding challenges due to record spending and mandated additional funding.

Panelists emphasized the importance of equity, local flexibility, and context. Christina Miller stated that every district needs a "shoe that fits" and recommended an assessment to identify what's working and not working. Derek Simmons agreed that something written three years ago isn't perfect and should be revisited.

The panelists also discussed progress made in implementing the Blueprint, such as increasing teacher starting salaries and improving access to pre-K for children with greatest needs.

Gov. Wes Moore has indicated willingness to make adjustments to the Blueprint. Sen. Mary Beth Carozza advised the counties to stand together with their priorities to make changes.

title: Dorchester BOE votes to keep staffing Positive Change Academy through school year
content:
Dorchester County Public Schools will continue to staff Positive Change Academy through school year with PASS Educators. The program serves pre-K through second graders and was previously under contract with Transforming Lives, which is set to end soon due to the district's decision not to renew its contract in October.

The district voted against pursuing contracts with other alternative education companies but instead worked to continue staffing the Positive Change Academy. A new agreement will allow the current PASS Educators staff to finish out the school year and cost the district $238,000.

Founder Ronnell Page of PASS Educators said his company is committed to supporting the program and improving student outcomes. Principal Dane Harris praised the academy's current staff for their growth and success in the program. The board voted in favor of the agreement, with some members expressing concerns about consistency but emphasizing the importance of serving students first.

Key dates: October (district terminates contract with Transforming Lives), November (board votes against pursuing alternative education contracts), December 14 (board votes to continue staffing Positive Change Academy through school year).

People: Jymil Thompson (Superintendent), Valerie Goff (DCPS Communications and Community Outreach Specialist), Ronnell Page (PASS Educators founder), Dane Harris (Positive Change Academy principal), Brandy Dawson Cumberland (Board member), Christine LaMonica (Board member).

title: Dorchester BOE reelects leadership, new members sworn in
content:
Dorchester County Board of Education held a meeting on December 12, where three new members were sworn in: Chris Wheedleton, Brandy Dawson Cumberland, and Christine LaMonica. Sheri Hubbard was reelected as Board President, and Talibah Chikwendu as Vice President, both for another year. The reelection follows the resignations of former Board President Mike Diaz and Vice President Susan Morgan. Hubbard thanked the board for their vote of confidence, while Wheedleton, Cumberland, and LaMonica congratulated Chikwendu on her reelecton.

Key dates:

* 2023: Chris Wheedleton was appointed to replace Laura Layton.
* June 2024 (mid-month): Susan Morgan resigned from the board after a contentious vote.
* July 2024: Sheri Hubbard and Talibah Chikwendu were elected as Board President and Vice President, respectively.
