title: 'Vision from the beginning': BAAM leaders excited for new academic center
content:
Building African American Minds Inc. will unveil its new academic center in Easton on December 14, 2024, marking a significant expansion of their after-school and summer enrichment programs. The $10 million facility, designed by BAAM's director of instruction James Bell, features eight classrooms, a library, media center, multipurpose dining room, wellness wing, esports, art, and music rooms. Executive Director Dina Daly stated that the organization's sister agency Polaris Village Academy will operate out of the center in 2025.

The center's design prioritizes full-group, small-group, and individual learning spaces, with desks situated for optimal student comfort. Adult workforce programs, GED classes, and English second language courses will be hosted on the third floor, starting in February.

BAAM has been serving under-resourced youth in nearby neighborhoods since 2005, initially as a boys-only nonprofit. The organization's focus has expanded to include adult workforce programs, with community donations, state, and federal funding supporting the new center's construction.

The facility is situated on Jowite Street, next to the BAAM Athletic Center, across from a large residential area. Daly reflected on the 20-year journey, stating that starting small and meeting specific needs was crucial to success. The ribbon-cutting ceremony will take place in January, with BAAM aiming to serve more children through their programs.

title: University of Delaware to pay $700K to settle claims it failed to disclose professor's ties to China
content:
The University of Delaware agreed to pay $700,000 to settle claims it failed to disclose professor Xiao-Hai Yan's ties to China when accepting a NASA grant in 2020. The settlement follows a government investigation into whether UD complied with federal regulations requiring disclosure of foreign affiliations.

Yan, a faculty member at Xiamen University in China since 1990, received funding from the National Science Foundation of China and participated in a program recruiting individuals with knowledge of foreign technology intellectual property. The grant was prohibited by NASA from using funds to collaborate or coordinate with China.

The settlement does not constitute an admission of liability by UD, but it prevents the government from pursuing criminal charges against parties involved. The university claimed it made a strategic decision to settle rather than face costly and distracting litigation.

title: UD to pay $700K to settle claims it failed to disclose professor's ties to China
content:
The University of Delaware agreed to pay $700,000 to settle claims it failed to disclose professor Xiao-Hai Yan's ties to China when accepting a NASA grant in 2020. The settlement was announced by the Department of Justice. Federal law requires universities to make disclosures about foreign affiliations when applying for grants.

Yan, a UD professor since 1990, has ties to Xiamen University in China and received funding from the National Science Foundation of China. He participated in a Chinese government program to recruit individuals with knowledge or access to foreign technology intellectual property. The settlement does not constitute an admission of liability by UD and allows for future criminal charges.

US Attorney David C. Weiss stated that universities must submit complete and truthful applications to federal grant processes. NASA Inspector General Adelle K. Harris vowed to safeguard taxpayer funds intended for federal research development programs.

title: Chopping block or all talk: How much will Trump, GOP Congress cut federal education spending?
content:
President-elect Donald Trump and a new Republican Congress may cut federal education spending, potentially eliminating the US Department of Education (DOE) with a total budget of $241.7 billion. Project 2025's policy recommendations call for shifting Title 1 funding to states and localities, converting other federal education spending into grants, and minimizing the federal role in education.

Trump has distanced himself from Project 2025 but supports eliminating the DOE. Special education advocates, such as Hezekiah Herrera and Stefano Lodola, warn that cutting federal funding could exacerbate allocation inequalities and leave underfunded schools resource-starved.

Conservatives also oppose expansions of free and reduced lunch programs and Head Start, which provide services to over 28 million low-income kids and 800,000 preschoolers, respectively. Some Republicans, like Ben Wallerstein, believe that eliminating the DOE is unlikely due to statutory changes required.

Patrick Riccards notes that some education talk from the right may be just "talk," but sees moves to give states and localities more flexibility in how they spend federal money. Linda McMahon, Trump's pick for education secretary, may champion literacy and vocational education programs and give more education power and flexibility to states and localities.

Conservative lawmakers and policy groups want to promote private and charter school vouchers and tax credits as alternatives to public schools. Advocates worry that right-wing agendas will be emboldened, increasing efforts related to curricula, textbook content, and school library offerings.

title: 3 new Talbot Board of Ed members sworn into roles
content:
Three new members joined the Talbot County Board of Education: Cynthia Jurrius (District 6), Ann O'Connor (District 2) and Karla Wieland-Cherry (District 5). They were sworn in on December 18, 2024, by Clerk of Circuit Court Kathleen Dulin Duvall. Mary Wheeler's District 6 seat was vacant after she did not seek reelection.

The new board members will serve at their first monthly meeting on January 2, 2025. O'Connor won her seat over Candace Henry in November's election, while Wieland-Cherry defeated Anna Howie. Jurrius secured the District 6 seat. Nominations for president and vice president roles will be held during the same meeting.

New members:

* Cynthia Jurrius (District 6)
* Ann O'Connor (District 2)
* Karla Wieland-Cherry (District 5)

Previous members:

* Candace Henry (District 2)
* Anna Howie (District 5)
* Mary Wheeler (District 6)

title: Budget discussions kicked off at Talbot Board of Ed work session
content:
The Talbot Board of Education held a work session to discuss preliminary budget considerations for fiscal year 2026. Chief Financial Officer Sarah Jones outlined priorities focusing on academic equity in math, an engaging environment for students and staff, recruiting and retaining staff members, and special education. Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi confirmed these priorities were established during the board retreat last year.

Jones explained that The Blueprint for Maryland's Future allocates money per student, with a base amount called foundation funding covering basic expenses. Additional funds are allocated based on student classifications, but costs like human resources, finance, and transportation often affect multiple schools. Jones noted that the district needs to "make shifts" in programs like compensatory education and multilingual learners to comply with Blueprint requirements.

Compliance is challenging for smaller schools, which face insufficient foundation funding. Pepukayi expressed concerns about rigid budgeting constraints affecting flexibility. The district submits annual budgets and requested positions, but faces challenges in managing grants due to the complexity of tracking results and data.

The Talbot County Board of Education will meet with the Talbot County Council on January 7, followed by a proposed budget discussion on January 13, first reader on January 15, and public hearing on February 10. A potential board vote is scheduled for February 12.

title: CBMM summer camp registration opens Jan. 2 for members
content:
CBMM summer camp registration opens on Jan. 2, 2025, with a two-week sign-up period exclusively for members, who enjoy a 20% discount on tuition. Registration for open programs will begin on Jan. 16.

The museum offers eight weeks of camps from June 23 to Aug. 15:

* Sea Squirts (ages 4-6): $165/week
* Terrapins (grades 1-3): $375/week
* Summer Workshop (grades 4-6 & 6-9): $375/week
* Museum Masters (grades 4-6): $375/week
* Inspiration Chesapeake (grades 6-9): $375/week

Special pricing applies for the Fourth of July week: $300/week for full-day camps, $130/week for Sea Squirts.

CBMM members can register by visiting cbmm.org/summercamps or contacting Membership Services Coordinator Debbie Ruzicka at 410-745-4991. Scholarships are available for campers with financial need.

Camp themes and weeks include:

* Chesapeake Critters: Land & Sky (June 23-27)
* Red, White, & Bay (June 30-July 3)
* Way Back When (July 7-11)
* Bay Scientists (July 14-18)
* Feathers, Fins, & Furs (July 21-25)
* Inspiration Chesapeake (July 28-Aug. 1)
* Adventure on the Bay (Aug. 4-8)
* Chesapeake Critters: Aquatic Animals (Aug. 11-15)

Summer Workshops will be offered for grades 4-6 and 6-9 during various weeks.

The Museum Masters camp offers a behind-the-scenes pass to CBMM, exploring its collection and exhibitions.

Scholarships are available for financial need; contact registration@cbmm.org for questions or registration support.

title: St. Michaels' Classic Motor Museum donation campaign for new property
content:
The Classic Motor Museum in St. Michaels is seeking $300,000 more for a $1.2 million donation campaign to purchase an extension of its Talbot Street property by January 17. The museum aims to provide hands-on experiences for students in its three-year Automotive Technician Apprenticeship Program, which requires 2,000 hours of on-the-job training and 160 hours of classroom instruction.

Gina Verhalen, administrator, reports the Drive Forward Capital Campaign has gathered $900,000 so far. Nationwide, there is a decline in new automotive technicians, with the TechForce Foundation stating the industry needs 258,000 but only receives 48,000 graduates annually.

Jim McCrea, instructor, previously worked 48 years in the automotive industry and supports developing new property for hands-on learning opportunities. Michael Landolo, director of education, emphasizes investing in the future by providing a pathway for young people to find jobs using their skills.

The proposed renovation plans include renovating a '50s-style gas station while incorporating classroom learning inside the 906 S. Talbot St. property. The extension would allow for more realistic shop experiences for apprentices.

title: 'Rare birds': Apprentices learn the boat building ropes at CBMM
content:
Kaeo Clarke and Carstan Gage graduated from CBMM's state-accredited Shipwright Apprenticeship Program, joining full-time staff as shipwrights. Clarke, a native of Annapolis, completed 4,000 hours of hands-on experience in wooden boat building after working on the Maryland Dove build and refit of Chesapeake Bay buyboat Winnie Estelle. Gage, from Oregon, moved to CBMM in 2022 with a design degree and carpentry experience, focusing on maintaining the floating fleet and revitalizing historic vessel Rosie Parks.

Gage credits the community for his success, saying it's an honor to be part of Dove's story. The program, unique nationally, registered over 4,000 hours of apprenticeship training under CBMM staff. Program supporters included Vessel Conservation Manager Sam Hilgartner, Shipwright Educator Steve Garrand, and Maryland Department of Labor's Director Chris MacLarion.

CBMM will add two more Shipwright Apprentices in the new year.

title: Talbot Board of Ed votes in Jackson as president, Dodson as vice president
content:
The Talbot County Board of Education nominated and elected president Emily Jackson and vice president Amy Dodson during a meeting on December 20, 2024. 

Emily Jackson, re-elected for her second term as board member since 2018, will continue in the role of president. Amy Dodson, representing District 3 and serving since 2022, was nominated by the committee and approved unanimously as vice president, replacing Candace Henry.

Jackson expressed enthusiasm for the new year, stating she enjoys her role and looks forward to working with Dodson: "I'm excited to serve with you Amy. We're going to have a good year."

title: Talbot leaders optimistic about improvements at Easton Middle, across TCPS
content:
Talbot County Board of Education officials expressed optimism about improvements at Easton Middle School, which saw a year-to-year drop in star rating from three to two stars. Assistant Superintendent Helga Einhorn attributed the decrease to factors such as increased academic achievement and progress, despite these gains not being reflected in the Maryland School Report Card results due to truncated values.

Einhorn noted significant increases in points scored for English proficiency but highlighted that the school's score for school quality and student success dropped from 19.5 to 17.1 points, largely due to a rise in chronically absent students. The district is working with teachers, social workers, and administrators to address chronic absenteeism.

Board members expressed support for the efforts being made at Easton Middle School, despite the star rating decrease. Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi emphasized the district's internal assessment of school performance and data, which allows for recognition of growth and improvement, such as seen at Easton Middle.

The Talbot County Board of Education meeting took place on December 20, 2024, with several notable events including:

* St. Michaels Elementary School rising to four stars from three in 2023
* White Marsh Elementary School maintaining a four-star rating while producing significant gains in test scores and percentile ranks

Key dates mentioned include the release of the Maryland School Report Card earlier this month.

title: Talbot Board of Ed voices mixed opinions over 2025-26 calendar draft
content:
The Talbot County Board of Education voiced mixed opinions over a draft calendar for the 2025-26 school year. The draft includes two days off in March 2026 and a five-day spring break from April 2 to April 6, 2026. Assistant Superintendent Helga Einhorn presented the draft, but Board President Emily Jackson expressed confusion, citing a lack of multiple drafts as expected.

Board Members Deborah Bridges liked the March break, citing mental health benefits, while Dyshekia Strawberry raised concerns about chronic absenteeism in April. Vice President Amy Dodson suggested moving an off day to extend spring break. Einhorn is awaiting state guidance on staggered starts for transition grades.

Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi emphasized finding a balance between accommodating student needs and staff requests. Board members agreed that the committee should consider keeping March breaks and extending spring break, potentially by moving the last day of school back. The board will review feedback from Wednesday's meeting before presenting a second draft at their January meeting.

title: Lockerman Middle School celebrates new STEM Center
content:
Lockerman Middle School in Denton, MD celebrated its new STEM Center on December 23, 2024, with a ribbon-cutting ceremony featuring partners from the University of Maryland Medical System. A $500,000 grant from the Cal Ripken, Sr. Foundation funded the center at Lockerman and is part of a larger initiative to provide STEM resources to 10 schools in Maryland.

Caroline County Public Schools Superintendent Derek Simmons praised the foundation's contribution, stating that it would not have been possible without their partnership. Students showcased new tools and gadgets, including a 3D printer, coding robots, and electronic kits.

Gracie Spiering, a sixth grader, demonstrated her knowledge of making backpack security alarms using littleBits Electronic kits. Madison Watson, a seventh grader, used the 3D printers to make holiday ornaments and praised the help of her teachers. Lockerman Middle School Principal Jeannine Necessary encouraged staff to integrate STEM tools into everyday learning.

University of Maryland Shore Regional Health President and CEO Ken Kozel emphasized the importance of STEM education for the healthcare system, citing highly motivated and educated students. Simmons reflected on the grant's significance given the district's financial challenges, stating that 60-65% of students qualify for free and reduced meals.

The Cal Ripken, Sr. Foundation provided a $500,000 grant to fund STEM centers at 10 schools in Maryland, including Lockerman Middle School.

title: Beloved bus driver 'Mrs. Dea' brings holiday cheer to young passengers
content:
Mrs. Dea, a 61-year-old bus driver with Marshall Bus Company, has been driving students in Cecil County, Maryland for 28 years, averaging 61 students per semester. She is known for her caring nature and holiday cheer, making an impact on many lives as a positive female role model. Mrs. Dea greets each student entering and leaving the bus daily and spends extra time getting to know them.

Her route includes Elk Neck Elementary, North East High School, and their Twilight program. Many middle school students who grew up riding her bus look forward to reuniting with her in high school. Parents praise Mrs. Dea for making the children feel special, including decorating the bus for holidays and carrying snacks for diabetic students.

Mrs. Dea started this tradition five years ago when she found out some students didn't have a Christmas tree at home. She decorated the bus to give them an idea of what a Christmas tree would be like. The interior roof of her bus 77 is currently embellished with battery-powered string lights and festive colors for the holidays.

In addition to holiday decorations, Mrs. Dea puts on the radio and allows students to sing along when holiday favorites come on. She also gives Halloween and Christmas goodie bags to brighten their day. Parents praise her for being attentive to every child on the bus and for keeping them safe during difficult weather conditions.

Mrs. Dea's retirement is not a decision that's up to her, as parents say she can't retire until their children graduate. She has been told by some students' parents that they wouldn't trust another bus driver due to her care and attention.

In 2024, Mrs. Dea celebrated her love for driving the bus, stating "I don't have to drive a school bus. I choose to drive a school bus." She graduated from Glasgow High School in Delaware, attended college, and became a certified dental assistant before being unable to continue due to rotator cuff surgery.

Mrs. Dea emphasized that she doesn't feel appreciated as a bus driver, but finds joy in her work and would not trade it for anything.

title: Fifth-grader recognized with Hero Award for saving classmate's life
content: On December 11, 2024, fifth-grader James Phillips saved a classmate's life in the cafeteria at Conowingo Elementary School by performing the Heimlich maneuver after another student choked. Cecil County Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Jeffrey Lawson honored Phillips with the Hero Award for his bravery and dedication to helping others.

title: Miles River Yacht Club's Annual Angel Tree event brings holiday joy
content:
Miles River Yacht Club's Annual Angel Tree event is held in St. Michaels on December 25, 2024, to provide holiday gifts and essentials to local children in need. The event is in collaboration with Head Start of Shore Up and has recently partnered with the Benedictine School. Commodore Nick Simpson stated that the club provides gifts to over 30 local children, showcasing the most generous characteristics of their members.

The program identifies children in need, then club members select ornaments representing desired toys and clothing items. Members purchase the listed items and return them to the club for distribution. Head Start of Shore Up volunteer Jackie Tate said the program has been ongoing for over a decade and brings joy to families in need. Parents often remain unaware their child is selected, with Tate recalling a 10-year-old mother's gratitude after receiving gifts for her child due to being laid off from her job.

The event is part of the yacht club's mission to give back to the local community, which also includes donating meals during Thanksgiving and school supplies through the Community Center in St. Michaels. Simpson emphasized that the Angel Tree event is the most anticipated by members, who often race to obtain ornaments.

title: Classical charter school looks to open in Queen Anne's
content:
Queen Anne's Classical Charter School (QACCS) aims to open in fall 2026 as a tuition-free pre-K through eighth grade public charter school serving over 400 students. Founded by local parents, educators, and community leaders, including co-founder Audrey Scott, the school will provide an alternative educational approach to complement the work of other public schools. QACCS will focus on phonics, Western civilization, cursive, Spanish, and Latin in its curriculum.

Scott, a former teacher, believes that hands-on parental involvement can make a significant difference in performance. The board consists entirely of parents, and students will be selected via lottery, with all county students eligible to attend. Queen Anne's County Commissioners have provided a $20,000 grant for an application consultant.

The school is exploring options for facilities, aiming to mirror those of Frederick and Anne Arundel counties' business parks. A public meeting was held on January 25, 2025, at the Kent Island Fire Department, and more information can be found at QueenAnnesCCS.com and its Facebook page.

Key figures: Audrey Scott (co-founder), local parents, educators, and community leaders
Key dates: Fall 2026 opening, March 2025 application submission deadline
Key locations: Queen Anne's County, Kent Island Fire Department
Key organizations: Queen Anne's Classical Charter School, Queen Anne's County Public Schools, Star Democrat

title: State eyes new way to count students in need
content:
Maryland is conducting a study to evaluate poverty in schools, potentially boosting funding for students in need, due to undercounting of poverty. Comptroller Brooke Lierman approved $48,000 monthly funding for "modeling, analysis and providing a presentation on findings" to address the issue. The current method uses proxy measures such as Medicaid and SNAP eligibility, penalizing schools with large immigrant student populations. An accurate count is crucial for resource allocation, especially in Baltimore City where many schools have been shuttered since data from 2013 was used.

The study will examine alternative methods of counting poverty, including those that account for undocumented students and families hesitant to enroll due to citizenship status concerns. The Governor's Office for Children stated that not all low-income families participate in programs like free meals or Medicaid, and that some districts do not collect data on school meal enrollment. A report based on the study will be submitted to the Maryland General Assembly by December 1, 2025.

Key stakeholders include:

* Brooke Lierman: Comptroller of Maryland
* Governor's Office for Children: office overseeing education funding
* Department of General Services: department providing funding for the study

Key dates and locations:

* December 4, 2024: Board of Public Works approved funding for the study
* December 27, 2024: Study launch date (article publication)
* December 1, 2025: Report submission deadline to Maryland General Assembly
* Baltimore City: location where many schools have been shuttered since data from 2013 was used

title: Maryland stories: This reading club is going to the dogs
content:
Southern Maryland-based Pets on Wheels reading club visits Leonardtown Library, where Coordinator Sharon Stapf explains the program's benefits: improving confidence, reading skills, and literacy for children and adults learning a second language. The program, started at Johns Hopkins, uses pets to alleviate loneliness in homebound patients.

People involved include:

- Sharon Stapf (Pets on Wheels Coordinator)
- Brittany Haun (Leonardtown resident)
- Cassondra West (Mechanicsville resident)
- Joshua Crosley (Panera Bread manager, owner of deceased Corgi "Izzy")
- Tracey Quade (Volunteer)

Key locations:

- Leonardtown Library
- Johns Hopkins
- Naval Air Station Patuxent River
- Charlotte Hall Veterans Home
- Chopticon High School

Dates not specified.

Pets involved include dogs and a giant tortoise. The organization's volunteers must have pets meeting specific "canine good citizenship" qualifications, including being calm around other animals and handling wheelchairs.

Key statistics:

- 11-year-old Corgi "Izzy" lost in accident
- New baby in Crosley household

title: Chesapeake College works to become Hispanic-Serving Institution
content:
Chesapeake College aims to become a Hispanic-Serving Institution with an undergraduate enrollment of at least 25% Hispanic students. The college has seen a 64% increase in its Hispanic population over the last decade and expects this growth to continue. Zulema Delacruz Martinez, a 2024 graduate, credits support programs like TRiO for her own success and led the creation of the Hispanic/Latino Student Union, which hosts community nights to assist Latino community members with filling out FAFSA.

Chesapeake College is taking steps to address this growth, including translating documents for Spanish-speaking families and students, increasing the number of Spanish-speaking staff, and collaborating with local schools. Clifford Coppersmith, president, stated that more Hispanic students are transferring to four-year colleges every year, indicating a growing interest in transfer education.

The college has also made efforts to increase diversity among faculty and staff, and Delacruz Martinez was awarded the John T. Harrison Award for her leadership and contributions to the college and community. According to Delacruz Martinez, Hispanic/Latino students are resilient but often face challenges due to lack of opportunities; investing in their education is crucial.

Key statistics:

* 64% increase in Chesapeake College's Hispanic population over the last decade
* Over 90% of attendees at FAFSA Nights applied to Chesapeake College
* More than 43% of Hispanic students make up the college's minority student demographic
* 2023: approximately 600 Hispanic-Serving Institutions in the United States

Organizations:

* Chesapeake College
* TRiO
* U.S. Department of Education
* Hispanic Association of Colleges and Universities
* Biden-Harris Administration

title: Foundation of HOPE moves toward goals in the new year
content:
Foundation of HOPE, a nonprofit based in Easton, Maryland, held its annual gala/luncheon on December 14 to celebrate accomplishments and share upcoming goals. Over 100 people attended, including donors, supporters, past students, and scholarship recipients. Keasha Haythe, founder, said the event provided an opportunity for attendees to see progress and learn about future plans.

The foundation's program, established in 2018, offers after-school classes to sixth-grade girls, focusing on topics such as self-esteem, bullying, workforce development, and economic development. The program aims to empower girls to become viable contributors to the future workforce.

Haythe reported that the program has grown to serve more girls, with a goal of including 30 students, and plans to start construction for a headquarters around quarter two of 2025.

The foundation received $150,000 from the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development in December. Haythe encouraged supporters to donate to the foundation by honoring someone special with a Rose of Hope, a donation made in honor of a woman or girl's name.

Scholarship recipients Kaleigh Hammond (Chesapeake College) and Michaela Gibson (John Hopkins University) shared their experiences with the program and how it helped them achieve their goals. Haythe expressed pride in helping girls blossom into young women who are following their dreams.

title: Schools to remain closed Friday
content: Talbot County Public Schools and Caroline County Public Schools announced all schools would remain closed on Jan 10 due to inclement weather, their fifth inclement weather day. Dorchester County Public Schools will have a virtual instruction day instead. The closure affects approximately 92 students.

title: Biden Hall: UD planning social sciences building named after U.S. president
content:
The University of Delaware is planning to build an interdisciplinary social sciences building named Biden Hall in honor of its most famous alumnus, Joe Biden Jr. The new building will serve as a hub for learning and civic debate, housing the Joseph R. Biden, Jr. School of Public Policy & Administration and the Biden Institute.

The Biden Institute was established in 2017 after Biden left the vice presidency, with Valerie Biden Owens serving as its chair. It hosts events, brings prominent speakers to campus, and focuses on developing domestic public policy.

The new building will be located on the main campus in Newark, but the exact location has not been determined yet. Former Gov. John Carney allocated $20 million in state funding for the project in his 2025 recommended capital budget, which will be debated by the state legislature in June.

University President Dennis Assanis expressed excitement about the project, stating that it will benefit the entire community through productive state investment. The construction process is expected to begin in 2025 calendar year, with fundraising and planning currently underway.

title: Phone pouches improving student focus, discipline in Caroline, district says
content:
Caroline County Public Schools implemented an experimental pilot program using Yondr cellphone pouches in middle schools for its first semester. The program aimed to keep students off their phones during school hours by locking them in individual pouches that can be unlocked with a magnetic device.

Superintendent Derek Simmons reported positive outcomes, including:

- 21% reduction in discipline incidents
- Improved attentiveness and classroom engagement
- Increased pass rates

However, difficulties arose, including:

- Some students attempting to tamper or break into their pouches
- Parents expressing concerns about the lack of direct communication with children
- Need for a system to handle students with health needs checking their phones for medical purposes

The district plans to assess the program's successes and shortcomings before deciding on expansion to ninth graders.

title: Talbot Board of Ed sees initial budget proposal
content:
The Talbot Board of Education reviewed its proposed budget for fiscal year 2026, totaling $85.8 million in unrestricted dollars, an increase of $8.6 million from fiscal year 2025. CFO Sarah Jones presented the draft budget, which includes:

- $2.23 million increase in fixed charges
- $1.7 million increase in instructional salaries
- $1.47 million increase in other instructional costs

Grants are expected to be around $9-10 million, but this is less than last fiscal year's funding. Maryland's education initiative, The Blueprint for Maryland's Future, remains uncertain due to the state's $2.7 billion deficit.

The district prioritized academic equity, engaging environments, recruitment and retention, and meeting Blueprint objectives. Proposed additional positions include:

- 33 new positions
- 6 English for Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL) teacher, assistant, or coach positions
- Athletic trainer at Easton High School and St. Michaels Middle High School

The draft budget will be discussed again on January 22 and a public hearing scheduled for February 10.

title: Talbot Board of Ed adds makeup day for snow; approves 2025-26 calendar
content:
Talbot County Board of Education added a day to the end of this year's school calendar due to snow in January 2025, moving the last student day to Friday, June 13 and the last teacher day to Monday, June 16.

Assistant Superintendent Helga Einhorn recommended the adjustment to comply with Maryland's 180-day requirement. The board also voted on a new calendar for the 2025-26 school year, choosing one that includes:

* Two days off in March
* A five-day spring break
* An eight-day spring break for some schools

The chosen calendar features an amendment allowing two of its inclement weather days to count towards the state's requirement. The board voted unanimously on the revised calendar, except for Board Member Karla Wieland-Cherry, who opposed the inclusion of a longer spring break.

Dates:

* January 17, 2025: Meeting where the calendar was discussed
* December 2024: Previous meeting where a draft calendar was presented
* June 13, 2025: Last student day for this year
* June 16, 2025: Last teacher day for this year

People:

* Helga Einhorn, Assistant Superintendent of School Leadership and Student Success
* Emily Jackson, Board President
* Amy Dodson, Board Vice President
* Karla Wieland-Cherry, Board Member

Places:

* Talbot County Public Schools
* Easton, MD
* Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia)

Organizations:

* Talbot County Board of Education
* Maryland Department of Education

title: Educators need to return to basics
content: Gov. Moore postponed implementing Maryland's Blueprint for Schools due to a $2.7 billion deficit. The Blueprint has been criticized for shifting focus from academic knowledge to social services and promoting 'restorative discipline' with minimal consequences. Talbot County Board of Education plans to implement the Blueprint with an $8.6 million budget increase, despite 60% of students showing lack of proficiency in English language skills and 17.2% in math. The plan promotes "equity in math" by making classes feel inclusive and accessible, but critics argue it lacks academic rigor. Educators are urged to return to basics and stop progressive schemes that prioritize social engineering over academic knowledge.

title: Caroline schools closed, Talbot schools on delay
content: Caroline County Public Schools closed on January 21, 2025, due to icy road conditions. Talbot County Public Schools operate on a two-hour delay the same day. Both districts' offices are open. Dorchester County Public Schools have no closures or delays announced.

title: Local school districts affected by PowerSchool data breach
content:
On December 28, PowerSchool notified its districts it had been breached. The data breach affected Caroline, Dorchester, and Talbot counties in Maryland, impacting schools' student information systems. PowerSchool confirmed that personal information like names, dates of birth, medical info, and social security numbers were accessed by hackers.

Superintendents from each county (Sharon Pepukayi - Talbot County Public Schools, Jymil Thompson - Dorchester County Public Schools, Derek Simmons - Caroline County Public Schools) notified families in January. They stated PowerSchool acknowledged no preventive measures could be taken to prevent the breach.

PowerSchool engaged its cybersecurity response team and is working with a credit reporting agency to provide identity protection services for two years, including complimentary credit monitoring. Two years of identity protection services are also offered for adult students and educators affected by the breach.

title: Dorchester BOE recognizes student contest winners
content:
The Dorchester County Board of Education meeting on January 22, 2025, recognized four student contest winners of the Superintendent's Holiday Card Contest for 2024: 

Vienna Elementary second grader Adalynn Haugh 
Hurlock Elementary third grader Kali Johnson
North Dorchester Middle eighth grader Elisabeth Claggett
North Dorchester High 10th grader Adrien Sinkeldam (could not attend)

The contest, held annually, showcases students' artistic talents and was judged by the district's central office staff. Supervisor of English language learners, library media, and fine arts Theresa Connors noted that each year more submissions are received due to difficulty in selecting the best. The winners received certificates and their designs, including snowmen, Christmas trees, and snow globes, were commended by Superintendent Jymil Thompson and Board members Sheri Hubbard and others.

title: Critchlow Adkins cuts ribbon on new offices in downtown Easton
content:
Critchlow Adkins Children's Centers held a ribbon-cutting ceremony for its new central office building in downtown Easton on January 24, 2025. The nonprofit offers preschool, before- and after-school care, and summer camp programs across five centers in the county.

Executive Director Cristy Morrell stated that the central building will be a hub for community outreach, grant work, and behind-the-scenes operations. The new office is located at 15 S. Hanson St. and serves as Critchlow Adkins' main center.

In August, town approval of a 33-unit townhome development led Critchlow Adkins to look for a new home. Morrell said the organization found an amazing building, purchased it, and made minor changes.

More than 50 community members and leaders participated in the ribbon-cutting ceremony, including Easton Mayor Megan Cook and Town Council President Frank Gunsallus.

title: Dorchester County Public Schools faces budget deficit
content:
Dorchester County Public Schools faces a $10.19 million budget deficit due to $86 million in expected revenues and $97.5 million in estimated expenses for fiscal year 2026. Superintendent Jymil Thompson attributes the deficit to fixed costs and unfunded mandates from the Blueprint for Maryland's Future (2021). The district has taken actions to reduce the deficit, including reducing positions, email campaigns, and eliminating a position.

Thompson is waiting on exact numbers from the state and county before reassessing the deficit. Possible cost-cutting options include revisiting vehicle allocations, auditing programs, revising overtime policies, sharing resources with the county, and reducing staff. The district will host additional budget work sessions on Feb 13 and March, seeking public input to prioritize areas.

Key individuals involved: Jymil Thompson (Superintendent), Jodi Colman (assistant superintendent), Brandy Dawson Cumberland (Board Member), Talibah Chikwendu (Vice President), Sheri Hubbard (President), Chris Wheedleton (Board Member).

Dates: Fiscal year 2026 budget submission due in June, upcoming budget work sessions on Feb 13 and March.

Places: Dorchester County Public Schools, Cambridge.

title: TCPS superintendent addresses immigration enforcement concerns in letter to families
content:
Talbot County Public Schools Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi addressed immigration enforcement concerns in a letter to staff and families on January 30, 2025. She emphasized schools as "safe places" with a priority of ensuring every student can learn without fear. The letter included resources from the American Civil Liberties Union and Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center.

The Trump administration's recent directive reversed a policy that protected areas like schools, churches, and shelters from immigration enforcement. Pepukayi stated that school administrators and staff are prepared to support students and will track policy changes, sharing updates if necessary.

Pepukayi wrote: "The strength of our community lies in our unity and compassion for one another... Together, we can ensure that our schools are safe places for all students, staff, and families to feel supported and valued."

title: After 116 years, 'Junior Naval Academy' closes its doors
content:
Leonard Hall Junior Naval Academy closed its doors after 116 years, leaving eight students to attend other schools. The school's board of trustees president, Amie Milan, announced the closure due to challenges finding a facility that supports both academic and military programs, resulting in limited financial and staffing/volunteer resources.

The school was close to signing a lease at another location but it fell through. In January 2024, St. Mary's County commissioners decided not to ratify the school's lease, citing a failing business plan and consistently low enrollment. An assessment in early 2023 revealed $575,000 in needed repairs and maintenance.

In December 2023, the school submitted 10- and 15-year financial plans that were largely dependent on a grant. However, a social media post in late January 2024 stated the school would remain open. Former student Olivia Flynn, who graduated as a top student leader, said the academy helped her deal with conflict and build relationships.

The school was established in 1909 and became a military academy in 1941.

title: Eastern Shore legislators discuss education funding and county burdens
content:
Eastern Shore legislators discussed education funding and county burdens with Hiram Burch, local government research and analysis manager for the Department of Legislative Services. Local governments will assume $144 million in fiscal year 2026 budget gaps, including $700,000 in Caroline and Talbot counties, $830,000 in Dorchester County, and $970,000 in Queen Anne's County. Del. Steven Arentz questioned whether record education funding was due to Governor Wes Moore or the state's Blueprint for Maryland's Future plan.

Del. Sheree Sample-Hughes expressed concerns over special education funding amid proposed cuts to the Developmental Disabilities Administration. Hiram Burch stated that these reductions would not affect special education funding, which remains unchanged under the governor's proposal.

Del. Chris Adams said the state is willing to pass unfunded mandates down to counties, leading to increased property tax rates and assessments. He noted that this is how Eastern Shore citizens will be funding Maryland.

title: Caroline schools closed, Talbot and Dorchester remote Wednesday
content: On February 11, 2025, Talbot and Dorchester county school campuses will be closed on Wednesday, Feb. 12 due to inclement weather, with students attending virtual classes. Caroline County schools will also be closed, without a virtual learning day for students.

title: Caroline County Public Schools could face major state budget cuts
content:
Caroline County Public Schools may face $41 million in state budget cuts over eight years due to a near $3 billion deficit. Superintendent Derek Simmons stated that while funding will be reduced in 2026, the district will still be "OK." Proposed cuts include:

* Foundation funding per pupil: $868,273 decrease
* Compensatory education funding: $513,912 decrease
* Multilingual learners funding: $91,425 decrease

Total projected reductions over eight years:
- Foundation funding: $25.6 million
- Compensatory education: $13.5 million
- Multilingual learners: $2.5 million

title: Talbot school leaders discuss immediate, long-term effects of Blueprint cuts
content:
Talbot County Public Schools face potential budget cuts of $1.7 million due to Governor Wes Moore's Excellence in Maryland Public Schools Act, which could reduce funding by 30 million over eight years if passed.
Chief Financial Officer Sarah Jones reported a projected gap of 494 words due to state budget deficit.

The bill proposes drastic cuts to education funding amid a nearly $3 billion state budget deficit. Talbot County's funding would be reduced by $685,000 in fiscal year 2026.
District Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi and Board members expressed concerns about the impact on compensatory education and multilingual learners funding.
Superintendents across the state are advocating against the proposals, with some districts expected to seek additional funding from counties.

Cumulative reductions in funding would include:
- $20 million stripped from per-student funding (2026-2033)
- $9 million slashed in compensatory education aid over eight years
- $2.9 million reduced in multilingual learner aid over eight years

Board President Emily Jackson suggested board members begin their own advocacy, while Board Vice President Amy Dodson urged community members to speak up against the proposed cuts.
Dates:
- February 13, 2025: Meeting where the discussion took place
- Fiscal year 2026: Proposed reduction in Talbot County's funding due to the Excellence in Maryland Public Schools Act

- Maryland

title: Talbot Board of Education approves FY2026 budget
content:
Talbot County Board of Education approved its FY2026 unrestricted budget on February 14, 2025, at $86 million, an $8.9 million increase from the previous year. The budget includes:

* $2 million for 33 new positions
* $1.3 million for increased health insurance costs due to inflation
* A total of $95.9 million in funding, up only $3.6 million from last year

The district will present its capital funding request of approximately $18.4 million to the Talbot County Council next month, including:

* $18.1 million for Chapel District Elementary School renovations
* $260,000 for new stadium lights at St. Michaels Middle High School

Key figures include:

* Sarah Jones, Chief Financial Officer: "So it is not, in total, a significant increase... There has been a significant shift from federal to local funding."
* Emily Jackson, Board of Education President: "I will vote yes on the budget when it comes to that, because I feel like this is a very sound budget based in fact of what we do know."
* Cynthia Jurrius, Board Member: "We do know we have some potential things down the road that may change the budget as far as what state funding we get... But for what we know now, I think this is a good budget and a sound plan."

Important dates:

* February 14, 2025: Budget approval
* May: Public budget hearing

title: Talbot Board of Ed discusses dress code, school uniforms
content:
Talbot County Board of Education discussed dress code updates and school uniforms in a virtual meeting on February 14, 2025. Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi shared revised administrative regulations removing language singling out specific clothing items, citing discrepancies in student enforcement.

Board members expressed concerns about policing tiny infractions, with some advocating for standards promoting dignity and value over individual item restrictions. Board Member Ann O'Connor suggested implementing school uniforms to "put everyone on the same playing field" and solve problems, but others expressed hesitation.

The board's attorney, Rochelle Eisenberg, stated that requiring school uniforms is feasible as long as families can afford them. Vice President Amy Dodson supported uniforms, citing her personal experience. The discussion will continue with community input, according to Pepukayi, who plans to consult administrators and advisory committees to gather historical context and formulate questions.

Key figures: 
- Sharon Pepukayi (Superintendent)
- Ann O'Connor (Board Member)
- Emily Jackson (Board President)
- Deborah Bridges (Board Member)
- Rochelle Eisenberg (Attorney)
- Amy Dodson (Board Vice President)

- Talbot County Board of Education
- Easton, MD

February 14, 2025
2022

title: Open Doors Partners in Education continues support of literacy
content:
Open Doors Partners in Education continues to provide free and low-cost tutoring and literacy support to over 100 individuals from pre-k through adult since its opening in fall 2020. The organization hosts an open house at its Chestertown center, attracting over 50 attendees who engaged with tutors and board members. Executive Director Ashley Singer expressed gratitude for the organization's support.

Open Doors utilizes the Orton-Gillingham approach to teach connections between letters and sounds. With 57 students currently enrolled, the number consistently grows annually. The organization has received recognition as a leading nonprofit in the community, winning Organization of the Year by Kent County Chamber of Commerce in 2023 and the Dr. Paul Titsworth annual Community Service Award from The Chestertown Rotary Club in 2023.

The organization was founded since opening its center in fall 2020 and is located at Chestertown. For more information on Open Doors visit opendoorsed.org, a nonprofit organization that provides literacy support to individuals of all ages.

title: Chesapeake Culinary Center offers education everyone
content:
The Chesapeake Culinary Center, a nonprofit organization in Denton, Maryland, offers cooking and budgeting education to people of all ages. Operations manager David Murray, also head chef, started his culinary career in Caroline County and now teaches at the center that serves the community he grew up in.

Murray's first restaurant job was at The Emerson House Restaurant in Denton, where he learned the skills that inform his teaching. The center offers free classes on healthy eating and shopping, as well as workshops and a mini-series for all ages. Attendees save money after learning how to shop in bulk and prepare meals.

The center aims to expand outside of Caroline County into other Eastern Shore areas, offering bartending and serving courses, including classes in English, Spanish, and Haitian Creole. Its main focus is on promoting healthy eating habits, teaching cooking skills, budget management, and utilizing kitchen time for family bonding.

Classes are led by Murray, Perez (Programming and Events Manager), and other instructors. The center has received positive feedback from senior centers, young parents, and new parents who have benefited from its programs.

title: Open house, open doors, open minds and hearts
content:
Open Doors Partners in Education opened in fall 2020, providing tutoring and literacy support to over 100 individuals in Kent County and surrounding areas. Executive Director Ashley Singer hosted an open house at their center on February 1, 2025, attended by over 50 people.

The organization utilizes the Orton-Gillingham approach, a multi-sensory method for struggling readers, and has 57 enrolled students, with 55 receiving free or low-cost instruction in 2022. Open Doors aims to increase literacy rates by offering tutoring, educational enrichment opportunities, and community awareness.

Since its creation, Open Doors has been recognized as a leading nonprofit organization in the community, winning Organization of the Year in 2023 and the Dr. Paul Titsworth annual Community Service Award in 2023. Singer expressed gratitude for board members and public support during the open house event.

title: Dorchester County Public Schools credits test improvement to student accountability
content:
Dorchester County Public Schools credits a significant increase in reading proficiency among its eighth-grade students to student accountability and taking a reading diagnostic seriously. 

- A 20.8% jump in reading proficiency at Mace's Lane Middle School was attributed to supervisors impressing upon students the importance of assessments, particularly college and career readiness.
- The test's national vendor was confused about the major increase, with students growing by 4.5 percentage points instead of 2%.
- Supervisors believe students didn't show "what they're actually made of" on the beginning of the year assessment, resulting in a more accurate picture of student abilities.
- Reading and Language Arts Supervisor Laura Aberg stated that students must feel the importance of showing what they know to demonstrate true growth.
- Board Members Christine LaMonica and Sheri Hubbard emphasized the need for intrinsic motivation, stating that tests are just one aspect, and that teachers must work together with students to build a love for learning.

title: Thousands of Maryland students are chronically absent each year
content:
Maryland students face high rates of chronic absenteeism, with nearly 27% of students chronically absent in the 2023-2024 school year. Chronic absenteeism has surged since the COVID-19 pandemic and is particularly prevalent among Hispanic (45%) and Black students (40%). Factors contributing to chronic absenteeism include school climate, family circumstances, personal health issues, and lack of transportation.

School leaders prioritize attendance, with Baltimore City Principal Yetunde Reeves implementing a campaign to encourage strong attendance. Effective strategies include putting students on attendance contracts, scheduling parent conferences, and providing incentives such as gift cards or snow tubing trips.

Teachers play a significant role in improving student attendance, with engaging lessons and relationships helping to reduce absences. However, some schools face challenges, including alternative high schools or serving students with special needs, which can lead to higher chronic absenteeism rates.

Statewide efforts aim to address chronic absenteeism, including the introduction of a chronic absenteeism task force and bills requiring counties to identify root causes. The Maryland State Department of Education aims to reduce the chronic absenteeism rate to 15% by next school year.

title: Bringing history alive: 9th annual GES Wax Museum honors leaders in African American history
content: On February 21, 2025, Grasonville Elementary School's fourth-graders honored influential African American leaders with the ninth annual Living Wax Museum. Seventy-five students researched prominent figures and presented as living wax figures, including Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and Serena Williams. The event was part of a school project to study African American history throughout February.

title: St. Michaels students advocate for new illuminated sign
content:
St. Michaels Middle High School students Phoebe Cole and Kyle Murphy advocated for a new illuminated sign outside the school, citing increased attention to events and announcements. The current sign is deemed unnoticeable by students, with some information often not being read.

The town's Commissioners introduced an ordinance allowing the school to have an illuminated sign, but proposed changes, including the ability to announce non-school events and changing the ordinance name from "educational facilities" to "public schools." This would allow the town to control more signage.

Students support increased exposure for the school and town, potentially attracting community members to athletic games and plays. The town's government will hold a public hearing on the revised ordinance at their second meeting in March.

title: 2025 senior scholarship application open
content:
The Peoples Bank, Fleetwood Insurance Group, and BGV Insurance offer a $6,000 scholarship fund for graduating seniors in Kent, Queen Anne's, and Talbot Counties. The program recognizes youth education and encourages self-improvement. Key considerations include educational success, community service, extracurricular activities, goals, financial need, and essay response.

Applications (https://pbkc.com/2025-scholarship.html) must be submitted by May 1 to mlivie@pbkc.com or mailed to The Peoples Bank's Human Resources Department. Call 410-778-3500 ext. 1102 for questions.

title: Easton, Kent Island High National Honor Society groups hosting talent show for charity
content:
Easton High School and Kent Island High School's National Honor Society chapters are hosting a charity talent show on March 12, 2025, to raise money for For All Seasons' rape crisis center. The event is organized by Kent Island NHS chapter president Myiah Barnard and Easton NHS chapter president Gabriella Streaker, who collaborated to create the first-time initiative.

The talent show will feature bands, dance performers, color guard groups, and other acts, with admission costing $5. Door prizes will be awarded from businesses sponsoring the event, with all proceeds going towards For All Seasons. The organization helps students, staff, and community members affected by mental health issues, physical abuse, or rape.

For All Seasons does a "really good job" at helping those in need, according to Streaker, and Barnard believes that 50 sets of hands are more influential than one set.

title: Post Labor Day start slated for Caroline 2025-26 school year
content:
Caroline County Board of Education voted on the 2025-26 school year calendar, adopting a post-Labor Day start date. The decision was made despite survey results showing pre-Labor Day start preference among staff and parents, as well as concerns about teachers' summer breaks.

Key dates: 
First day of school: Tuesday, Sept. 2
Teachers return to planning on Aug. 25
Graduations: Colonel Richardson (May 27, 2026), North Caroline (May 28, 2026)
Last day of school for students: June 17
Incorporating three inclement weather days.

Board members discussed factors influencing the decision, including longer teacher breaks and family preferences. Superintendent Derek Simmons noted flexibility in building snow days, which were used to its full capacity in the previous year's calendar.

title: Mid-Shore program aims to teach kids about health care careers
content: Three Mid-Shore women - Dr. Judith Gieske, retired doctor; Ruth Ann Jones, retired nurse; and Cynthia Watson, semi-retired nurse and educator - have developed a program called Introduction to Careers in Healthcare (ITCH) to introduce Eastern Shore students to the healthcare industry, starting with an Easton location.

title: Easton High School takes home ACE Mentor Program gold cup
content:
Easton High School won the gold cup in the ACE Mentor Program of Maryland's Eastern Shore with its multimodal transportation station project in Annapolis, featuring trains, buses, ferries, cars, trails, and bike paths. The program connects high school students with professionals in design and construction industry.

The awards ceremony on March 12 included projects from Saints Peter and Paul High School and St. Michaels Middle High School. Projects judges included Aaron Goller, Jason Loar, and Jay Yerkes. 

Easton High's engineering teacher Nicholas Werner received the ACE Community Award, calling it "wonderful" for opportunities to support students.

The program helps students understand architecture, construction, and engineering, with projects focusing on designing buildings and sites. Rachael Whiting, Eastern Shore affiliate's vice chair, said the program is important for guidance while allowing students to figure out designs.

title: Dorchester County Blueprint costs higher than 2022 projections
content: Dorchester County's projected education expenses for fiscal year 2026 exceed 2022 estimates by $2.4 million, with a total of $26.3 million expected to be owed to Dorchester County Public Schools. This is less than the original estimate of $26.8 million in fiscal year 2030 and $29.4 million in fiscal year 2034. Council President Lenny Pfeffer stated that the county's issue lies with unfunded mandates from the state plan, which he attributed to the Blueprint for Maryland's Future adopted by the Accountability and Implementation Board in 2022.

title: Caroline County discuss Chesapeake College at first FY26 budget workshop
content:
Caroline County Commissioners discussed funding for Chesapeake College's proposed building project at their first FY26 budget workshop on March 19, 2025. The college plans to rebuild Queen Anne's Tech building in three years and needs contributions from all five counties on the Mid-Shore. Clifford Coppersmith, Chesapeake College President, stated that the state will likely fund most of the cost (75%) with local counties sharing the remaining 25%. Caroline County's share would be $2.7 million over three years, with $180,000 in the first year and a larger portion to come in FY2027-28.

County Commission President Travis Breeding expressed concern about capital funds for the next two years and proposed funding the project now to avoid worrying about it later. County Commission Vice President Larry Porter suggested tabling the discussion until the final budget process.

Chesapeake College aims to replace a dated 1976 building, which is the last on campus to be renovated. The state has already shown interest in funding part of the project, with Coppersmith stating that "it's huge" and expecting the state to cover most costs.

title: Community school leaders in Talbot County aim to make a difference
content:
In Talbot County, community school leaders aim to make a difference through removing barriers for students in need and becoming a resource for the community. Katie Fox, manager of Easton Elementary's community school program, focuses on increasing availability of healthy foods, providing mental health resources, raising enrichment by 15%, and adding 100 students to the Choptank Community Health partnership.

Easton Middle School, led by facilitator Shelby Parks, is in its first year and focuses on areas such as mental health, food insecurity, and transportation. Fox noted that transportation to grocery stores is a challenge due to limited walking distance options.

The state's initiative to fund education, The Blueprint for Maryland's Future, introduced community schools in 2019. Over 600 schools are now community schools, including two in Talbot County: Easton Elementary and Easton Middle.

Talbot County Public Schools aim to move forward with community school funding despite Gov. Wes Moore's proposed budget freezing funding at next year's levels. Last week, the House of Delegates amended some of Moore's education cuts, sending a refined Blueprint education bill to the Senate chamber.

The district is watching closely for any impact on community school funding and will "move forward" due to the clear need in the community. Easton High, White Marsh Elementary, and Tilghman Elementary are next in line to become community schools. Fox and Parks emphasize that the goal is not just to help designated schools but to better the entire district.

The concept of working together applies not only within Talbot County schools but for every student across all schools. Fox stated, "You create something for one, it always ends up helping all."

title: Dorchester County Council, Board of Education discuss budget concerns
content:
Dorchester County Council and Board of Education met on March 18 to discuss budget concerns. The county and school district face budget deficits for fiscal year 2026, with DCPS estimating a deficit of $5.59 million (down from $10.19 million in January). State mandates regarding the Blueprint for Maryland's Future are affecting budgets.

DCPS Superintendent Jymil Thompson presented the district's draft budget for fiscal year 2026, citing the need to reduce the deficit further. Board of Education member Chris Wheedleton said the district would present more changes at a March 20 work session.

County Council Vice President Mike Detmer asked how athletic programs and school plays affect the deficit, while Board of Education Vice President Talibah Chikwendu countered that removing extracurriculars would harm student achievement and culture. 

Detmer expressed frustration with the one-size-fits-not-us solution of the Blueprint, stating he'd prefer a tailored plan for Dorchester County.

County Council President Lenny Pfeffer directed county staff to look into options to solve the deficit, including obtaining a special dispensation.

title: CTE students house at Chesapeake College
content: Queen Anne's County High School (QACHS) Career and Technical Education (CTE) students collaborated with Chesapeake College to build a mock house within the Tech Building from February to March 2025. Instructors Ron Frederick and Betsy Ricketts led the project, which provided hands-on experience in carpentry, masonry, electricity, plumbing, and HVAC. The partnership aims to prepare students for success without debt, with Chesapeake College's support. QACHS CTE students have also assisted local community projects.

title: What it was like ... to be a teacher
content:
Tamara Forte was a first-grade teacher in her 15th year when COVID-19 led to unprecedented changes in the educational system. In March 2020, teachers were told to pack up their classrooms for an unknown duration and began sending learning packets home. Forte struggled to balance teaching responsibilities with keeping her family safe.

Teachers adapted to new circumstances, conducting virtual lessons, troubleshooting tech issues, and creating engaging content. Forte's sister helped create a classroom in her basement, and she used laptops and projectors to facilitate online instruction. Teachers organized school parades, created grade-level photo collages, and distributed computers and hot spots to families in need.

When schools reopened with 6-foot distance markings, teachers simultaneously instructed in-person and at-home students. Students struggled without tech-savvy family members, while others required help logging in and out for virtual lessons. Forte's sons had to log in and out at specific times for whole group and small group instruction.

As the pandemic progressed, Forte reflected on its impact, appreciating every smile, hug, and learning moment that occurred during this time. She cherishes the memories, but acknowledges she never wants to go back to this experience.

title: Schools struggle to bridge learning gaps, adapt to a new normal
content:
Maryland school districts continue to address post-pandemic challenges five years after COVID-19 upended classrooms. While academic performance is improving, learning gaps persist, particularly in student engagement, virtual learning access, and social-emotional development. Chronic absenteeism remains high, with rates above 25% in some counties.

Queen Anne's County Public Schools Superintendent Patricia Saelens emphasizes the need for tutoring, academic intervention, and social-emotional strategies to close learning gaps. The district has expanded tutoring services and implemented additional programs in reading and math.

Statewide, schools have seen improvements in attendance and ratings, with 91 schools earning five-star ratings in the 2023-24 school year. However, chronic absenteeism persists across Mid-Shore counties, including Queen Anne's (22.9%), Kent (26%), Caroline (28%), Talbot (28.5%), and Dorchester (38.3%).

Virtual learning remains a challenge due to technology disparities and connectivity limitations. Despite this, educators report successes in adapting to the new normal, with students excelling academically and professionally.

Federal funding has enabled innovation, such as student support coaches, which provide targeted academic support and aid in social-emotional development. Educators emphasize resilience and adaptation, highlighting that disruptions did not define students' futures.

Important figures include:

- Patricia Saelens (Queen Anne's County Public Schools Superintendent)
- Mary Boswell-McComas (Kent County Public Schools Superintendent)
- Matt Evans (Supervisor of Student Services in Queen Anne's County)

Key dates and statistics:

- 2020: Peak home instruction numbers
- 2021-2022: Chronic absenteeism peaked during the school year
- 2023-24: 91 schools earned five-star ratings, with 41% receiving four- or five-star ratings

Important locations and organizations include:

- Queen Anne's County Public Schools
- Kent County Public Schools
- Maryland Department of Education
- Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia)

title: Easton Middle administrators: New cell phone restrictions are working
content:
Easton Middle School administrators reported positive results from implementing new cell phone use restrictions piloted last December. The restrictions, acquired from company Yondr, require students to place their phones in locked pouches at the start of the day and unlock them when leaving. 

Principal Kelly Murdoch stated there's a positive impact on safety, wellness, student engagement, and academic performance. Assistant principals Ashley Quicke and Todd Stoker echoed this sentiment, noting that face-to-face conversations have increased.

The school has a four-step disciplinary process for non-compliance, with parents being called to pick up the student's phone after two offenses. Since December, bullying has decreased, including cyberbullying.

Board members praised Easton Middle administrators, calling them "guinea pigs" and thanking them for participating. President Emily Jackson asked if the policy should be expanded to other schools in the district, with Murdoch saying it's something to consider.

The restrictions' effectiveness was attributed to research showing that cell phone use negatively impacts mental health starting at upper elementary through high school.

title: DCPS looks to staff reductions to balance budget
content:
DCPS faces a $5.59 million deficit for FY 2026 and considers staff reductions to balance budget. Superintendent Jymil Thompson announced plans to reduce 12-24 positions, which could save $900,000-$1.8 million.

Thompson emphasized the need to minimize impact on teaching and learning, stating that retaining teachers is crucial due to a state rating of 23 students per class. He reviewed attrition rate trends and believes this may offset some staff reductions.

Negotiations with staff representatives, including Dorchester Educators, Education Support Professionals, and Administrators and Supervisors Association, are set to address step increases and cost-of-living adjustments, potentially saving $3.5 million.

Key dates: March 22, 2025; FY 2026; FY 2026

Places:

- Cambridge
- Dorchester County Public Schools

Organizations:

- DCPS (Dorchester County Public Schools)
- Star Democrat
- Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia)

People:

- Jymil Thompson, DCPS Superintendent

title: Teacher for a Day brings community into the classroom
content:
On March 3-13, 2025, the Education Foundation of Cecil County Public Schools organized a "Teacher for a Day" event where community members visited elementary schools, middle schools, and high schools across the county. 

Business leaders and community members, including Josh Hayhurst (Superdojo Martial Arts), Darius Humphries (Chesapeake Care Resources), and Nick LaBrant (Utilitrain), participated in the event.

Hayhurst spent time with each elementary grade at Rising Sun and North East elementary schools to experience different teaching styles. He facilitated a gym class and brought fun activities, such as pom poms with googly eyes for reading, making a positive impact on students and faculty.

Humphries sat in on a math class at Elkton Middle School where the teacher pushed students to think critically and strategize. He plans to volunteer more with public schools.

LaBrant taught a Cherry Hill Middle School social studies class about the history of power lines, using an informative presentation and props.

The event aimed to show community members what goes on in local schools every day, highlighting the amazing things that happen and the kids' learning achievements.

School officials said they wanted their community to see the daily activities and the efforts made by teachers.

title: Caroline County Public Schools announce finalists for Teacher, Support Employee of the Year
content:
Caroline County Public Schools announced finalists for Teacher of the Year and Support Employee of the Year. The winners will be announced on April 10 at Cow Barn Events in Ridgely.

Support Employee of the Year Finalists:
- Jenn Claytor (Pre-K instructional assistant), Preston Elementary School
- Chadney Ennals (Multilingual learner instructional assistant)
- Donna Fazenbaker (Instructional assistant), Denton Elementary School
- Desiray Korell (Tech support specialist), North Caroline High School
