Teacher of the Year Finalists:
- Lisa Dayton, Federalsburg Elementary School
- Andrew Buffenmyer, social studies teacher at North Caroline High School
- Tom Cheezum, band and chorus teacher at Colonel Richardson Middle School and High School
- Kimberly Mielke, North Caroline High School
- John Moyer III, North Caroline High School

Superintendent Derek Simmons stated that the school district wants to celebrate teachers who serve as an inspiration for others and advocate for students and the teaching profession.

title: Plan to require school uniforms doesn't gain traction with Talbot Board of Ed
content:
Talbot County Public Schools proposed instituting school uniforms at a Board of Education meeting, but failed to advance due to lack of seconded motions. A community survey conducted by Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi showed nearly 1,900 responses with 74% from parents, 15% from staff and students, and 49% in favor, while 45% were opposed. 

Board member Ann O'Connor suggested a school shop for "hand-me-down" uniforms after one year of implementation, but Vice President Amy Dodson disagreed, citing the significant expense for families on minimum wage. Other board members, including Dyshekia Strawberry and Emily Jackson, expressed concerns about the cost and lack of an overwhelming response to the proposal.

The superintendent stated she was surprised by the high survey response rate and "closeness" of percentages across grade levels. Her team discussed cost factors, but not specifics, due to questions on which families the district helps and how that's determined. Pepukayi does not expect the topic to come up again anytime soon, but leaves room for potential revisitation next school year.

Key statistics:

- 1,900 responses in the community survey
- 74% from parents
- 15% from staff and students combined
- 49% in favor of school uniforms
- 45% opposed

title: Elks National chief spotlights community impact in regional meet
content:
The Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks hosted its Maryland, Delaware, and DC regional conference on Kent Island from March 21-23, drawing 211 attendees to Kent Island Elks Lodge 2576. National leader Douglas A. Schiefer, the Grand Exalted Ruler from Bucyrus, Ohio, was a keynote speaker with a focus on "Elkdom's HEART for America." Key goals include community service, supporting veterans and underprivileged populations, and expanding youth programs.

Local Lodge 2576 has donated over $100,000 annually to charities such as the National Cancer Society, Boys & Girls Scouting programs, and local school sports initiatives. The lodge has sponsored the "Children's Arts Showcase" for 17 years and supports educational scholarships through youth athletic competitions.

Angela Meyer, president of the Maryland, Delaware and DC area, expressed pride in hosting the conference, while Malcolm McPherson, a past Grand Exalted Ruler from New Jersey, attended as regional sponsor. The Elks organization has over 1 million members nationwide and emphasizes its motto: "Elks Care, Elks Share."

title: Amid budget woes, Dorchester cancels summer school, appeals to students to 'get the work done'
content:
Dorchester County Public Schools will not offer summer school in 2025 due to budget restraints. The decision affects elementary and middle school summer sessions as well as the high school credit recovery program. 

The district is facing a $5.59 million deficit for fiscal year 2026, down from $10.19 million since January. Superintendent Jymil Thompson plans to reduce staff by 12-24 positions.

Parents are advised to reach out to schools if their child is failing a course and determine what can be done to help pass the course before the end of the school year. Sheri Hubbard, Board of Education President, emphasized that there is still time for students to improve grades and avoid repetition.

Hubbard recalled her experience as a teacher, where she often found ways to help students bring up their grades when they asked sincerely. She urged parents and students to work together to get the work done before summer break.

title: Education workers empty their offices after recent layoffs
content:
On April 1, 2025, federal education workers in Washington, D.C. packed up their desks and offices after recent layoffs, sparking a demonstration of solidarity outside the Department of Education's headquarters. The layoffs, part of a round of reductions aimed at cutting 50% of the workforce from 4,200 employees, left approximately 1,300 remaining staff members subject to "reduction in force" notices.

Former employee Nikki Churchwell reported that the administration altered procedures for competitive areas, bypassing seniority and performance-based rankings. Veronica Greene, a nearly retired worker, was forced into early retirement after 34 years of service, citing a "culture of fear" and "irrational, cruel" layoffs. Kelisa Wing, another former employee, was escorted out with just 30 minutes to pack up her belongings amidst Homeland Security monitoring.

Advocates, including Kaitlyn Vitez, rallied in support of federal employees, emphasizing the importance of public education as the "great equalizer." Supporters held signs and demonstrated outside the Department of Education headquarters. Retired worker Tony Sarmiento documented the event, expressing concerns that mass layoffs could jeopardize funding programs for students.

Jackie Murray approached her firing with a positive outlook, citing support systems like girlfriends, music, and scripture to cope with the transition. In the coming days, debates will ensue about the department's future and program implementation, with advocates pushing for more resources and support for schools and students.

title: Committee made for potential new Lockerman Middle School
content:
A committee called the Education Specifications Committee was formed on April 1, 2025, to discuss renovating or replacing Lockerman Middle School in Caroline County, MD. 

The committee, consisting of school officials and community members, will provide input on a modern middle school facility design for education in 2025-2026. The architect will use the committee's documents to design the school.

County Administrator Katheleen Freeman said the committee will consider multiple scenarios and specifications, including square footage, traffic flow, and parental drop-off/pick-up logistics. 

The committee includes representatives from Lockerman Middle School, central office officials, parents, and state administrators. 

State funding for the project is estimated to be $76 million (89% of a total estimated $86 million), with the county covering 11%. Caroline County Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Derek Simmons emphasized the need for a responsible use of funds and a community that can be proud of the final result.

Consultant David Lever began the process in summer 2024, working closely with the committee to develop specifications for the middle school facility.

The formation of the committee marks the first step in a long process to bring the middle school together, as Simmons likened it to a "marathon."

title: Talbot County wrestles with schools funding request, long-term Blueprint concerns
content:
Talbot County Council opts not to include $5.7 million in funding for Talbot County Public Schools in the draft fiscal year 2026 budget, citing concerns over property tax increases and potential vulnerability of vulnerable populations. The county's education funding will still meet state mandates under The Blueprint for Maryland's Future, which requires around $55 million.

Council members Keasha Haythe and Pete Lesher disagreed on the issue, with Lesher arguing that delaying education funding could endanger recent investments in new positions due to state pressure to meet $60,000 teacher salary minimums. 

TCPS Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi warned of having to prioritize and make tough decisions if the county only provides minimum required funding.

The county is expected to contribute $90 million to schools in fiscal year 2034 under The Blueprint's forecasts, a significant increase from current projections. Joint strategic planning and time are needed to address this uncertainty, with officials acknowledging that the state doesn't always provide financial solutions for counties.

A budget proposal will be officially introduced on April 15, with the option to amend the funding request in the coming weeks.

title: Lauren Rose named TCPS Teacher of the Year. Giovanni Wynn is Support Staff of the Year
content:
Lauren Rose was named Talbot County Public Schools' Teacher of the Year in 2025-26, while Giovanni Wynn received the Support Staff of the Year award. The awards were announced at the district's annual Talbot Stars celebration on April 3, 2025.

Lauren Rose is band director at Easton High School and was praised by her colleagues for creating a welcoming environment for students. Her nomination read that she transformed the band room into a safe space where students feel supported and encouraged to grow.

Giovanni Wynn is family service coordinator at St. Michaels Judy Center, a family learning hub for children up to 5 years old. St. Michaels Elementary School principal Indra Bullock spoke of Wynn's passion and dedication, saying she understands each family's unique challenges and builds strong relationships with parents and staff.

The finalists for Support Staff of the Year included Stacie Rice, Jane Tillman, and Christina Titz. Lauren Rose was one of four finalists for Teacher of the Year, alongside Rebecca Phillips, Kathy Regan, and Holly Sump.

Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi called Rose and Wynn's names during the ceremony. Easton High School principal Sherry Spurry read aloud a student's nomination of Rose, praising her ability to transform the band room into a welcoming environment.

The Talbot Stars celebration took place at the Easton Elks Lodge, where attendees showered Rose and Wynn with hugs and applause. Board of Education President Emily Jackson thanked the teachers for their hard work and dedication, saying they are life changers, motivators, and inspirations.

title: QA Teacher of the Year is Marcie Mamas
content:
Marcie Mamas, a business teacher at Kent Island High School in Queen Anne's County Public Schools, is the 2025-2026 Teacher of the Year. Mamas is entering her 29th year in education and aims to help students discover their passions and develop real-world skills. Principal Dan Harding praises Mamas for her dedication, compassion, and legacy.

Mamas expressed gratitude to her department, colleagues, administrators, and the selection panel for recognizing her work. She thanked several students who have achieved success in their fields for guiding current students and the program. Mamas said she was seen and heard during the interview process, which strengthened her belief that she is exactly where she is meant to be.

Mamas will represent Queen Anne's County Public Schools as Teacher of the Year and begin her journey on April 3, 2025.

title: University of Delaware asks state for $43.5 million to build Biden Hall, renovate labs
content:
The University of Delaware is requesting $43.5 million from the state legislature for capital projects, including building Biden Hall and renovating aging laboratories. 

Biden Hall will be an interdisciplinary social sciences building named after UD's most famous alumnus, Joseph R. Biden Jr. The university is asking for $20 million to build the hall, with Gov. Matt Meyer's budget recommending the same amount. Construction plans have been in progress since 2018.

The school of public policy and administration, also located within Biden Hall, aims to cultivate academic growth, research collaborations, and civil discourse. 

Additionally, UD is requesting $20 million for deferred laboratory maintenance and another $3.5 million for lab and classroom space renovations in Georgetown and Lewes. The university has struggled with a $1.2 billion backlog of needed repairs and upgrades.

UD President Dennis Assanis expressed the need for state funding to maintain modern facilities, which he said is crucial for preserving the university's stature as a top-tier research institution.

title: Maryland wrestles with blow to the state schools budget
content:
Maryland lawmakers are scrambling to address a $418 million blow to the state schools budget after learning that funds from a pandemic-era fund may not be reimbursed as planned. The federal government's decision affects funding for public schools to cover expenses such as reading materials, after-school programming, and repairs.

The state had already spent approximately $300 million of the money allocated to school districts when they received the news. Mid-Shore school districts are still uncertain about the impact on their budgets.

Senate President Bill Ferguson says the state had allocated the remaining funds to school districts around the state. Senate Democrats had proposed cuts to the state's education plan, known as the Blueprint for Maryland's Future.

However, Republicans say it's even more important to make significant trims. Senator Mary Beth Carozza (R-Somerset, Wicomico, Worcester) introduced an amendment to pause implementation of the Blueprint for the next two years.

President Donald Trump's education department may not reimburse states as previously planned due to a letter from U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon stating that extensions of the pandemic-era fund were "well past the period of performance" and "not justified."

The state is facing a structural deficit, and Senate Republicans are pushing for cuts to balance the budget. Senator Justin Ready (R- Carroll, Frederick) argued that increased spending in education over the last 25 years has not led to improved test scores.

Some Senate Democrats disagree with Republican proposals, citing the need to protect health care, public safety, transportation, and education funding. State Democrats pushed to preserve funding for low-income students and English Language learners.

As of April 4, 2025, Maryland lawmakers are in a stalemate over the education budget.

title: Chapel District Elementary renovations nearing 30% completion mark
content:
Chapel District Elementary School renovations are nearing a 30% completion mark, with around $11.28 million spent to date. The total cost of the project is estimated at $38.26 million, led by Whiting-Turner Contracting Company and funded by Talbot County Public Schools ($27 million) and state funds from Maryland's Interagency Commission on School Construction. Construction began in summer 2024, but started 34 days late due to septic system issues and permitting delays.

Director of operations Kevin Shafer attributed the delay to Bill Stagg, project manager appointed by the Talbot County Council, who prevented a significant delay. The renovation includes adding 16,000 square feet, relocating the media center, and renovating the playground.

The first phase is expected to be completed in June, with school operations continuing in the existing building during this time. Phase two of renovations will begin this summer after school ends. Construction is expected to take a couple years to complete and will continue until August when school resumes.

title: Freedom of speech under assault on campuses
content:
Here is a condensed version of the article:

Robert Koehler writes that freedom of speech on campuses is under assault, citing Columbia University's decision to expel and suspend students accused of peaceful protest due to pro-Palestinian and critical Israel statements. This move is seen as a result of the Trump administration's pressure.

Koehler reflects on his own college days in the 1960s during the Vietnam War, noting that students played a significant role in opposing it through protests. He believes that free speech was crucial in ending the war.

The author notes that the US has been at war ever since, and that controlling public relations is key to maintaining support for these initiatives. However, if peaceful protests continue due to human suffering, such as the Gaza genocide, this could be problematic.

Appellant attorney Joseph Pace comments that the administration's approach is misguided, as they cannot directly muzzle students and faculty without facing First Amendment lawsuits. Instead, they aim to squeeze college cash flow and force private colleges to ban protests and expel protesters.

Pace quotes Christopher Rufo, who described a plan to put schools in "existential terror" unless they target protesters. This approach is seen as flipping reality, similar to how public relations are used in war-related situations.

A UN report notes that Israel's ceasefire violations resulted in hundreds of deaths, with repeated requests for aid being systematically rejected. Criticizing this is considered antisemitic by the Trump administration and its supporters.

The protests continue, keeping human sanity alive as Koehler concludes.

title: Four months in, Easton Middle staff, parents weigh in on cell phone pouches
content:
Easton Middle School's cell phone pouch policy, introduced in December 2024, has seen mixed results four months into its implementation. According to Principal Kelly Murdoch, students are less distracted during instruction and conflicts have decreased, improving restorative management. However, some parents remain concerned about the safety aspect.

Carla Beavers, an EMS parent, initially worried but was alleviated when she learned emergency services professionals recommend students not use their phones during emergencies. Her son left his phone at home, improving focus on school instruction, and making a call from the office was seamless.

Nicole Crosby's son also followed Beavers' approach, seeing improved grades after leaving his phone at home due to the pouches being "ineffective." She believes community investment is necessary for the policy to succeed.

The district acquired Yondr pouches with magnets that can unlock them during emergencies. Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi notes mixed opinions from student advisory board members, with some feeling that relinquishing independence in high school could be beneficial.

Easton High's Gabriella Streaker sees potential benefits for younger students, but acknowledges it wouldn't be popular among older students who rely heavily on their phones. Teachers and administrators appreciate the policy, as it frees them up to focus on instruction.

As of now, the policy is open to expansion to other schools in the district for the next school year at earliest.

title: Schools face shortage of social workers
content:
Here is a condensed version of the article:

A shortage of social workers in schools affects D.C. and nationwide. Project PRESS, launched in 2023 with a $2.6 million grant, aims to address this need by placing Howard University master's students in schools.

The program, which started with 22 second-year students, provides intensive training and places them at one of 11 participating schools for a year. Students receive a $10,000 stipend and are motivated to work in schools where they can provide "big brother love" to their students.

Social workers focus on creating treatment or action plans for specific students, providing mental health support, and connecting people to resources. The program addresses systemic issues and trauma, teaching culturally responsive training and trauma-informed practices.

Project PRESS focuses on underserved areas Wards 7 and 8 in D.C., historically Black and low-income communities. Jaden Smith, a second-year master's student, works at Bard High School Early College DC and aims to follow his mother's footsteps as a school social worker.

The program aims to increase the diversity of school social workers and has already had an impact on students' lives, with Kyaus Washington noting that seeing a Black social worker can be a source of relief for young Black students.

title: Speakers ask to keep St. Mary's elementary music and arts intact
content:
St. Mary's County school board meeting discusses scaling back music and arts programs. On March 26, special area teachers were told about a three-year plan to transition from a 10-day rotation cycle to a four-day cohort model for elementary music and art.

The proposed change aims to enhance instruction quality by minimizing disruptions caused by students participating in band, orchestra, and chorus practices. However, the new model would limit access for some vulnerable learners and potentially lead to meltdowns among students transitioning from elementary to secondary school.

School officials acknowledge inequity in current models, stating that a different approach is needed. The proposed schedule would replace general music classes with participation in one ensemble during special area time, replacing band, orchestra, or chorus.

Superintendent Scott Smith stated that even if the budget was fully funded, he'd want to discuss how instruction is delivered due to inequity issues. The plan aims to reduce disruptions and minimize referrals, suspensions, and ISI (In-School Suspension).

Thirty-six speakers voiced their concerns during the nearly 3½ hour meeting, citing lack of access for vulnerable learners and potential negative effects on students' academic performance. Parents, educators, students, and parents expressed support for maintaining current music education offerings.

The proposed change is part of a broader effort to adopt the cohort model, which has been used by Green Holly Elementary for 10 years and Park Hall is piloting this year. Data shows that reducing transitions in band, orchestra, and chorus classes has helped reduce referrals and suspensions.

Opponents argue against scaling back programs, stating that music education creates a well-rounded curriculum and encourages students to attend school regularly. The board meeting concluded with no clear decision on the proposal.

title: Caroline County Board of Ed declares last day of school, discuss virtual instruction
content:
The Caroline County Board of Education declared June 17 as the last day of school due to inclement weather closures exceeding the four allotted days. The extended school year had a half-day for students and a full day for teachers. Virtual instruction on inclement weather days is unlikely due to challenges in providing internet connectivity, hotspots, and translation services.

 Superintendent Derek Simmons said the district cannot meet virtual learning requirements, citing difficulties in ensuring every student has a hotspot or wifi, as well as maintaining hands-on teacher engagement and preparation for students with disabilities, homeless learners, and multilingual learners.

Robert Wielgosz, supervisor of technology, highlighted concerns over Kajeet hotspots, which were overloaded when used for personal purposes during the pandemic. The estimated cost to provide 700 devices over five years would be $736,000 for students and $35,000 for teachers.

Additionally, Google Meet Breakout Rooms require a premium subscription, costing between $30,000 to $50,000 per year. District officials emphasized the need for equitable access to services for these groups, citing challenges in providing necessary technologies and translation services during virtual instruction.

Teacher and staff negotiations also pose difficulties, with some employees working on inclement weather days and receiving paid time off, while others may receive extra compensation for additional work. The district is responsible for determining how lost work will be made up and negotiating with the teachers' union for proper pay.

title: Rescinded federal reimbursements cause $1.4 million impact on TCPS health center
content:
TCPS health center construction delayed due to rescinded federal reimbursements from US Department of Education. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon's March 28 letter announced non-honoring extension requests for pandemic-era funds, including $1.4 million in funding for Marathon Health Center.

* Total project cost: around $1.4 million
* Remaining costs after $127,000 paid to Marathon: approximately $1.2 million
* State Superintendent Carey Wright stated over $400 million of Maryland schools' pandemic-era funding is at risk.
* About $305 million already spent and awaiting reimbursement; about $112 million not yet paid out by state.
* TCPS Chief Financial Officer Sarah Jones said district contacted Marathon, company quit work on project; district unable to spend remaining costs without authorization.
* Multiple funding options available, including tapping into fund balance.
* Both Caroline County Public Schools and Dorchester County Public Schools have been fully reimbursed for ESSER-related spending.
* TCPS Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi submitted an extension request to US Department of Education.

title: Maryland will slow – not stop – its investment in schools
content:
Maryland lawmakers passed a bill revising Governor Wes Moore's education reform plan, Blueprint for Maryland's Future, on April 10, 2025. The bill:

- Includes marginal cuts instead of dramatic rollbacks proposed earlier.
- Freezes annual funding increases for students in poverty, special education, and English language learners.
- Targets the collaborative time initiative, allowing schools to deviate from previously established teacher planning thresholds for three years (2026-2028).
- Pauses funding increases for fiscal years 2027 and 2028.

Key figures:

- Governor Wes Moore: Introduced the bill in January, proposing significant reforms under Blueprint for Maryland's Future.
- Sen. Jim Rosapepe (D): Sided with Democrats, saying the bill makes "relatively modest changes."
- Sen. Jack Bailey (R): Voted against the bill due to financial concerns it might place on counties.

Organizations:

- Governor's office: Introduced the bill.
- Maryland General Assembly: Passed the revised bill.

Places:

- Annapolis

Dates:

- April 10, 2025 (bill passage)
- January 2025 (initial bill introduction)

Numbers:

- $418 million (federal education spending cut)
- Three years (duration of reduced teacher planning thresholds)

title: Buffenmyer, Marshall named Caroline Teacher, Support Staff of the Year
content:
Andrew Buffenmyer, a social studies teacher at North Caroline High School since 2009, was named Teacher of the Year by Caroline County Public Schools. Buffenmyer's main focus is his students and hopes to continue seeing them succeed. He will represent Caroline County in the state's Teacher of the Year contest. Superintendent Derek Simmons praised Buffenmyer as an excellent representative of the district.

Nick Marshall, head custodian at Greensboro Elementary School since 2022, was named Support Staff of the Year. Marshall credited his colleagues and students for making it enjoyable to come to work, saying it's a pleasure seeing the kids every day. He plans to continue putting in his all for the students regardless of winning the award.

title: Cell phone pouches coming to St. Michaels Middle next year
content:
The Talbot County Board of Education unanimously voted to introduce cell phone pouches at St. Michaels Middle School for the 2025-2026 school year, with a cost estimated at $9,000. The district has piloted a similar program at Easton Middle School since December, citing improved student engagement and decreased bullying.

Board members debated introducing pouches in high schools, with President Emily Jackson requesting more data on effectiveness and Board member Ann O'Connor arguing for its implementation. Chief Financial Officer Sarah Jones estimated an additional $38,000 would be needed for high school students. 

Board Vice President Amy Dodson expressed reluctance to discontinue the program, while Board members Karla Wieland-Cherry and Deborah Bridges voted against introducing pouches in high schools initially. However, O'Connor motioned to extend the program to high schools, with some members voting yes. The decision was made for St. Michaels Middle School only, with plans to reassess high school implementation for future years.

title: 'We can turn lightbulbs on'
content:
A program called Introduction to Careers in Healthcare (ITCH) aims to spark interest in healthcare careers among middle and high school students in Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's, and Talbot counties through a team of retired health care professionals led by Dr. Judy Gieske. The initiative supports local students and builds a skilled, homegrown workforce, with the ultimate goal of reconnecting the hospital and community.

Construction on a modern inpatient medical facility next to the Talbot Community Center began in 2025, expected to open in 2028. However, even an advanced hospital requires skilled staff rooted in the community. The ITCH program's long-term goals are to introduce healthcare careers early, support local students, and build a homegrown workforce.

Memorial Hospital, currently relying on traveling doctors and nurses, once drove local economic growth by providing quality care that attracted retirees, professionals, and families to the area. The hospital's closure had a significant impact on the community's well-being.

Dr. Judy Gieske and her team emphasize the importance of supporting ITCH through mentorship, donations, or spreading awareness, as every effort matters in bringing the hospital back to the community and the community back to the hospital.

title: Maryland State of Reading Report: 'time for a comeback after a decade of decline'
content:
Maryland's schools show progress in reading achievement but still face a deep crisis. The Maryland READS "State of Reading in Maryland 2025" report reveals:

- 67% of fourth-grade students and 66.7% of eighth-grade students cannot read at a proficient level.
- A decade-long decline in literacy, with the exception of Queen Anne's County, where 58.5% of students meet proficiency standards.
- Rising education spending (37%) since 2013, yet significant gaps remain.
- Trish Brennan-Gac, executive director of Maryland READS, calls for a comprehensive approach to literacy, including teacher training, literacy coaching programs, and creating reading ecosystems that address excessive screen time.
- State leaders have taken steps toward solutions but face criticism for inadequate funding for literacy coaches.
- The report emphasizes the importance of strong reading skills for academic success, career readiness, and reducing chronic absenteeism.
- Brennan-Gac stresses that a community-driven effort is necessary to reverse the crisis.

title: High school graduation rate reaches seven-year high
content:
Maryland's high school graduation rate reached 88% in 2024, its highest point since 2017, according to the Maryland State Department of Education. The increase is attributed to targeted supports for student groups that faced barriers to graduation, including a 7-point gain among Hispanic students and a 10-point increase among multilingual learners.

Theresa Timmons Parrott, an MSDE official, credited the gains to sustained efforts on multilingual education and college readiness pathways. However, regional disparities persist, with some districts reporting graduation rates above 90% while others, particularly in rural counties, have rates below 80%.

The Blueprint for Maryland's Future, a landmark education reform law, has driven recent gains. Despite this progress, the Excellence in Maryland Public Schools Act includes a three-year delay in implementing teacher collaborative time and provisions to freeze funding increases if state revenues decline.

State Superintendent of Schools Carey Wright said the data suggests Maryland is on the path to recovery, but long-term commitment to equity, funding, and student support services will be necessary to maintain progress. Key statistics include:

* 95% graduation rate in Talbot County
* Female students graduating at higher rates than male students
* White and Asian students graduating at higher rates than Black and Hispanic peers
* Students with disabilities graduating at a rate of 69%
* Economically disadvantaged students' graduation rate increasing to 82%

Dates mentioned include:

* April 18, 2025 (article publication date)
* 2017 (previous high school graduation rate)
* 2023 (previous year's graduation rate for economically disadvantaged students)

Organizations involved include:

* Maryland State Department of Education
* Blueprint for Maryland's Future
* Excellence in Maryland Public Schools Act

Key people mentioned are:

* Theresa Timmons Parrott, MSDE official focused on multilingual education
* Carey Wright, State Superintendent of Schools

title: College built as an economic engine for Shore
content:
Chesapeake College, established in December 1965, is a regional hub fueling progress on Maryland's Shore. Gov. Wes Moore reinforced its role as an economic engine and innovation center during his cabinet meeting at the Health Professions and Athletics Center.

The college has maintained its focus on connecting Marylanders to jobs, ensuring student success, and creating an equitable economy. Lt. Gov. Aruna Miller and Secretary Sanjay Rai toured skilled trades labs and met with students, highlighting Chesapeake's response to local economic needs.

With five support counties, Chesapeake is the only community college in Maryland covering nearly one-fifth of the state's landmass. The institution has endured for 60 years through partnerships with county leaders, local school systems, donors, and friends.

Chesapeake faculty and staff have supported students with higher graduation and transfer rates, ranking second among community colleges in the state. Ambitious plans include developing cutting-edge workforce training facilities to promote trades jobs and keep Eastern Shore talent local.

The college fosters personal growth through critical thinking, intellectual, and interpersonal connections, preparing students for a rapidly changing world. A celebration of its 60th birthday will take place on April 24 with events, including the dedication of its new mobile welding lab at 1:30 pm on Wye Mills campus.

title: Church Hill Park welcomes StoryWalk
content:
Queen Anne's County Library introduced a new StoryWalk at Church Hill Park on April 22, 2025. The program combines reading with outdoor activities, allowing readers of all ages to explore local parks and libraries. Queen Anne's County Library marketing outreach manager Allison Wood stated that trail books are regularly switched out, with locations also available at Route 18 Park in Centreville and Sudlersville Park.

The StoryWalk was made possible through funding from United Way of Queen Anne's County and Friends of the Library. To learn more about Queen Anne's County Library programs and events, visit qaclibrary.org.

title: Tilghman Island celebrates opening of Judy Center
content:
Tilghman Island's Tilghman Elementary School Judy Center opened in January 2025 and is serving 40 families. The center's coordinator, Lori Julian, emphasized its importance as a transition tool for young children and families to become comfortable in a school environment. Funded by the state through Maryland's Blueprint initiative, the center offers workshops, family support services, enrichment activities, and more for children up to five years old.

Talbot County Public Schools Judy Center Supervisor Amy Walstrum noted that "learning begins at birth" and that families are crucial teachers during these early years. Julian has 25 years of experience as a Judy Center coordinator in Maryland and highlighted the need for local resources, citing the limited availability of community services on Tilghman Island.

The new center aims to address the gap in resources and accessibility faced by local families. The grant was awarded last October, following funding loss due to previous limitations, resulting in the disconnection of half the family's service needs.

title: 'Open up worlds': Donor gifts $1 million to BAAM girls program
content: Dr. Eileen Amy Ryan, a 75-year-old transgender woman from Rochester, NY, donated $1 million to BAAM's girls program, expanding it to include middle-school level students. The gift is the largest one-time donation in recent history and will allow BAAM to invest some funds towards the program while others will last beyond immediate use. Ryan was inspired by her mentors during her gender transition and wants to provide a similar experience for young girls. BAAM Executive Director Dina Daly, who Ryan praised as "an incredible, active listener," will oversee the distribution of funds, ensuring their impact endures.

title: ‘Catastrophic’: Could Trump 'defund" Head Start preschools program?
content:
Here is a highly condensed version of the article:

Head Start preschool program faces potential defunding under Trump administration. Executive directors of Wisconsin and Montana Head Start associations express concern over funding cuts, which could lead to program closures and exacerbate "child care deserts" in rural and poorer communities.

The program serves approximately 800,000 lower-income children nationwide and has a budget of $12.1 billion. Current funding under Trump's austerity efforts is at risk, with Sen. Patty Murray stating that the administration has slowed $943 million in existing Head Start funding.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin says Trump is "defunding Head Start," citing delays in approved disbursements in Wisconsin and a spending freeze implemented after Trump took office. The program employs over 250,000 staff nationwide, including 1,300 workers in Montana.

Head Start advocates warn that cuts would have economic tolls, affecting working-class parents and grandparents' ability to afford childcare and secure jobs. The Trump administration's Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) has also targeted the program for elimination, citing allegations of scandal and abuse.

The Biden administration had raised Head Start teacher pay by $10,000 last year, but the Trump administration has not taken action on the rule. The program offers essential services like hearing and vision screenings, meal and nutrition programs, and childcare options in areas with limited affordability.

title: Maryland graduation rates hit 88% in '24 a seven-year high
content: Maryland's high school graduation rate reached 88% in 2024, a seven-year high since 2017. The state saw significant gains among student groups historically facing barriers to graduation, including Hispanic students (+7%) and multilingual learners (+10%). Anne Arundel County Public Schools reported a 89% graduation rate, with North County High School increasing its rate by 7%. Theresa Timmons Parrott attributes progress to targeted supports for multilingual education. The state's Blueprint for Maryland's Future aims to expand early childhood education, increase college and career readiness, and close equity gaps.

title: Not all heroes wear capes: Character Counts celebrates a community of classroom coaches
content:
Character Counts of Queen Anne's County honored over 100 classroom coaches for their dedication to building students' character skills and shaping a positive school culture through the Six Pillars of Character: trustworthiness, respect, responsibility, fairness, caring, and good citizenship.

The partnership between Character Coaches and Queen Anne's County Public Schools (QACPS) marked its 25th year in the 2024-2025 school year. Over 100 volunteers, including Kimberly Kight and Fred Sheriff, worked with students of all ages, resulting in more than 4,200 young citizens receiving character experiences.

The School Ambassador program put elementary students at the forefront of sharing the Character Counts message throughout the community for the second consecutive year. The annual volunteer appreciation dinner recognized coaches' commitment to coaching and mentoring local children.

Key events include:

- April 24: Volunteer Appreciation Dinner at Hyatt Place Kent Narrows
- February 2024-2025 school year: Partnership between Character Coaches and QACPS began, incorporating life lessons in kindergarten through fifth-grade classrooms

Notable figures include:

- Melinda Ray (Coordinator)
- Kimberly Kight (Classroom Coach)
- Fred Sheriff (Classroom Coach)

Organizations mentioned:

- Queen Anne's County Public Schools (QACPS)
- Character Counts of Queen Anne's County
- Beyond Words Tutoring Home School Co-op

title: PoliTalks transitions leadership as new era begins at Washington College
content:
Washington College's PoliTalks transitions leadership as new era begins under co-presidents Charlotte Schurman and Grace Walsh, who are committed to continuing the club's tradition of providing a safe, respectful forum for political education and conversation. The founders, Stephen Hook and Zach Affeldt, step down after graduation.

Renowned speaker Heather Mizeur, former Maryland state delegate and CEO of WeAreOne Alliance, delivers the lecture "Disagreement is Democratic" on April 24 at Hynson Lounge, introducing her mnemonic device **RESPECTFUL**. She focuses on sovereignty as a key concept, defining it as the ability to stand in one's own agency.

Mizeur emphasizes the importance of maintaining self-control and integrity while responding to political disagreements. She encourages practices like journaling, speaking with friends, and engaging in joyful activities to help individuals maintain sovereignty.

The discussion is attended by guests of all ages, including Chestertown government officials, who find the event eye-opening and meaningful. PoliTalks plans to hold monthly meetings under new leadership, inviting experts on various topics, such as environmental justice.

Key figures include:
- Charlotte Schurman and Grace Walsh (co-presidents)
- Stephen Hook and Zach Affeldt (founders)
- Heather Mizeur
- Serena C. McIlwain (Maryland secretary of the environment)

Important dates and events:
- April 24, 2025: PoliTalks' spring lecture with Heather Mizeur at Hynson Lounge
- October 17, 2024: Mizeur's previous lecture at the Toll Science Center

Organizations involved:
- Washington College
- WeAreOne Alliance
- PoliTalks

title: Assanis to step down as University of Delaware president
content:
Dennis Assanis will step down as University of Delaware president at the end of the school year due to increasing criticism over his handling of finances. He cited making meaningful contributions and advancing the university's mission, but also expressed a desire for a leadership transition with the institution's best interests in mind.

Assanis will work through June 30, followed by an interim president while the board of trustees searches for a new permanent leader. Board President Terri Kelly praised Assanis' inspiring leadership and service, but acknowledged that he left a complicated legacy regarding town-gown relations.

Assanis' tenure saw record campus growth, including the construction of the STAR Campus and various buildings on the main campus. However, he also faced criticism over financial difficulties, including a $250 million deficit during COVID-19 and ongoing budget deficits.

A 2024 study by the faculty union questioned Assanis' handling of finances, citing excessive building spending as a contributor to the problems. Faculty members also expressed dissatisfaction with transparency about university finances and perceived prioritization of construction projects over academics.

Assanis was one of the highest-paid public university presidents in 2023, with a total compensation of over $1.5 million. His departure follows recent high-profile departures, including executive vice president John Long's retirement and senior vice president Mary Remmler's resignation.

title: A dream come true: Italian exchange student spending a year in Maryland
content:
Here is a condensed version of the article:

Emma Agazzani, 17, an Italian exchange student from Mantua, Italy, has been living in Calvert County, Maryland for a year through the American Scandinavian Student Exchange (A.S.S.E.). She applied in February 2022 and was accepted to Huntingtown High School. 

Agazzani's parents were hosts Danielle Higginbotham and her family opened their home to Agazzani. The exchange program aims to foster international understanding through educational and cross-cultural programs.

At Huntingtown, Agazzani has participated in cheerleading, a sport not common in Italy or Europe, and lacrosse. She is taking Advanced Placement English, A.P. Government, pre-calculus, biology, photography, and theater classes. 

Agazzani plans to study science in college and become a neurologist. In her free time, she has traveled with the Higginbothams to several locations, including Disney World, New York City, Atlanta, Philadelphia, Florida, Washington, D.C., and met President Donald Trump.

Comparing her hometown of Mantua to Huntingtown, Agazzani said it's "very different" due to its urbanized character versus the bucolic landscape. The Higginbotham family has created a strong bond with Agazzani, who will graduate in June and return to Italy after her exchange program ends.

title: KCHS students explore STEM careers with local businesses
content: Kent County High School students participated in a STEM job shadowing program where eight local businesses welcomed students to explore careers in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics. The program, supported by Zane Carter for 13 years, allows employers to outline educational requirements and provide real-world demands for students planning their futures. Participating businesses included Chesapeake CNC, DMS & Associates, Eastman Specialty Corp., Modern Stone Age Food Lab, Sunrise Solar, University of Maryland Shore Medical Center, Washington College GIP Program, and the University of Maryland Extension, which partnered with Red Acres Hydroponics to demonstrate agricultural technologies. The program benefits students, parents, and teachers who appreciate businesses' contributions, providing a timely resource for secondary education planning.

title: Talbot council mulling $1.1 million request from school district
content:
Talbot County Council considers $1.1 million request from school district for fiscal year 2026. The request includes:

- $600,000 to fill nine new positions
- $500,000 for teacher and staff salary increases

The request is "scaled-back" from the original $5.7 million ask by Talbot County Public Schools (TCPS).

Council members are left to decide whether to grant the full request or a partial one.

Potential tax supplements:

- Teachers' pensions only: 0.0045 per $100 of assessed value
- Teachers' pensions and salary increases: 0.0096 per $100 of assessed value
- Teachers' pensions and new positions: 0.0106 per $100 of assessed value

District leaders say they're trying to balance funding the school system with preventing tax increases for residents on fixed income.

TCPS Chief Financial Officer Sarah Jones said staff will present a budget amendment package in June, which will adjust the $86 million unrestricted budget.

County Manager Clay Stamp agreed that state mandates and formulas are creating the fiscal situation.

The council's final decision is expected at the May 27 meeting.

title: 100 years and counting: Talbot County Free Library endures as community linchpin
content:
Talbot County Free Library (TCFL) is a community hub that has adapted to societal changes over the past 100 years. The library's executive director, Dana Newman, believes it will continue to serve the community's needs as the world changes.

Founded in 1925 by Caroline Burnite Walker, TCFL started with an 800-book collection and focused on children's services. Today, it has a physical collection of over 130,000 books, computer and technology access, and hundreds of free programs.

TCFL is serving residents across Talbot County, offering early literacy programs, partnerships with local schools, and the Chesapeake Children's Book Festival. The library also provides book clubs, community meeting rooms, tax assistance aid, social services programs, digital literacy classes, and internet access.

In response to the pandemic, TCFL has focused on digital literacy and computer access, demonstrating its ability to adapt to changing needs. The organization is planning renovations for its branch site in St. Michaels, including an expansion of children's spaces.

The library has over 20,000 residents with a library card, with 7,000 being children. Many consider the library a safe space, and unhoused individuals often rely on it. TCFL aims to secure funding for its Bookmobile service, which was discontinued in the 1990s due to lack of funding.

Key dates:

- October 15, 1925: TCFL opens with an 800-book collection
- Present day: Over 130,000 books and a wide range of programs

title: Caroline County schools celebrate teachers
content:
Caroline County Public Schools celebrated Teacher Appreciation Week from May 6-13, 2025, with free coffee and visits from district employees to every school. President Michele Wayman emphasized the importance of recognizing teachers and support staff for their dedication and hard work.

Caroline County Public Schools Educators Association President Amy Bauman said highlighting teachers is crucial in a time when educators face challenges, as they inspire, support, and shape students' futures.

Danielle Dennis, 2024-25 Teacher of the Year, teaches math at Colonel Richardson High School. She became a teacher to make a difference in her community and hopes to have the same influence on students as she had from her own teachers.

Bauman, who has been teaching for 23 years at Denton Elementary School, finds joy in forming bonds with students, not just teaching lessons. Wayman noted that teachers are "very appreciative" of the celebration and recognize the hard work they do to make the school day beautiful for students.

Caroline County Public Schools features:

title: Removal of Safe Space stickers draws criticism
content:
Calvert County School Board member Melissa Goshorn requested removal of "Safe Space" stickers from school buildings in April, citing concerns raised at a National School Boards Association conference. The stickers are used to indicate LGBTQ students won't face discrimination in that space. 

Goshorn's comment was prophetic as 19 of 20 speakers expressed opposition during the May 8 meeting, with most opposing removal and some criticizing "manufactured outrage." President Jana Post defended removing stickers as not violating First Amendment rights. 

Board member Paul Harrison proposed discussing a flag policy at a future meeting to set parameters for displays in school buildings. The board unanimously approved Marc Watson's appointment as supervisor of health, physical education, and athletics. Watson is an Indiana University graduate with previous experience as teacher, coach, and principal in Calvert County and Virginia.

title: A better life: Local kids on why America is beautiful
content:
In May 2025, Galena Elementary School third grader Helena Sanchez won first place in the American Legion Post 246's annual Americanism Essay Contest with her essay on "What does 'America the Beautiful' mean to me (regarding veterans and our military)." The contest, open to students from grades three to 12 nationwide, had a theme of patriotism this year. Other winners included Chloe Cummings (second in third grade), Annistyn Clayton (third in third grade), Liam Miller (first in fifth grade), Amelia Rigby (second in fifth grade), and Samantha Carroll (third in fifth grade).

The contest's winner received $50 and a $50 donation to the Children of Warriors National Presidents' Scholarship fund. The Betterton Auxiliary, led by President Patti Bone, has been hosting the essay contest for over 15 years.

Bone announced plans for a Community Day on Flag Day, June 14, featuring free family-focused entertainment, including a bouncy house, petting zoo, and activities. Winners and their families were treated to a ceremony with refreshments, cookies, and patriotic items.

title: Robbins YMCA opening reading hub to tackle childhood illiteracy
content:
The Robbins YMCA is partnering with the John and Janice Wyatt Foundation to create a reading hub in Dorchester County, Maryland, addressing childhood illiteracy. The initiative aims to improve third-grade literacy and overall English Language Arts proficiency, which ranks 21st out of 24 school districts in the state.

Dorchester County Public Schools faced significant budget cuts, resulting in lost after-school and summer programming. The county has a $10 million deficit, with the Y's contribution helping to fund the new reading hub.

The campaign targets childhood illiteracy from birth to age 5, focusing on prenatal, toddler, and mommy-and-me groups. Partners include Superintendent Jymil Thompson, Dorchester County Public Library, United Way of the Lower Eastern Shore, Operation Pathways, and volunteers from the community.

Key figures involved are:

* Matthew Peterson, executive director of the John and Janice Wyatt Foundation
* Tynice DeShields, director of mental health at the YMCA of Chesapeake
* Bryant Wittington, director of the Dorchester County Campaign for Grade Level Reading

The reading hub will be open to the public and YMCA members, featuring a resource center, community meetings, parental education sessions, and more.

Dates mentioned:

* May 16, 2025 (article publication date)
* 2025 (year referenced in article)

title: Girl Scout project receives two paws up
content:
Girl Scout Troop 10069's Pet Friendly Patios in Our Community project has earned a Bronze Award. The 4-member troop, led by Jaime Larson and Marie Isom, produced maps and decals highlighting pet-friendly patios at 17 Leonardtown eateries and cafes. Decals are now displayed at T&Js Cove, The Front Porch, Dairy Queen, and Noli's, while the map is available online.

The project was conceived by Sarah Mack (11) as a way to make restaurants more welcoming to pets, following her animal shelter volunteering experience. Greta Isom designed a decal featuring a hollow heart with "pet-friendly patio" text, which was chosen over an initial idea of just a heart or paw print.

Troop members spent 3 months working on the project, which required 20 hours each and cost $125. The troop attended a Jan. 13 Leonardtown Town Council meeting to request permission for their project, where they presented their decal idea as a way to show pet-friendly restaurants were "open" to pets.

The Girl Scout Bronze Award consists of seven steps, including building a team, exploring the community, and spreading the word. The troop met the requirements, with each member contributing at least 20 hours to the project's sustainability.

title: It's time to pause state's education blueprint
content:
The state of Maryland's education blueprint, known as the Blueprint for Maryland's Future (Kirwan), has faced intense debate and funding issues. The plan aims to expand pre-kindergarten programs, increase teacher pay, and create career pathways for high school students.

Goals include:

* 80% of all 4-year-olds and 3-year-olds enrolled in pre-kindergarten programs by 2025
* Use a "mixed delivery system" combining public and private providers

Achieving these goals has been elusive. According to the National Institute for Early Education Research at Rutgers University, Maryland lags behind 17 states enrolling kids in public pre-kindergarten programs, despite spending more per child.

In the last school year:

* 38% of 4-year-olds were enrolled in state-funded pre-K programs
* 7% of 3-year-olds were enrolled

Private childcare providers reported low interest in participating in the expanded pre-K program (12.9%), with nearly 40% saying they would not participate.

The General Assembly's nonpartisan legislative budget analysts project a $1 billion structural budget deficit by next year, growing to $3 billion in fiscal 2027.

Moody's downgraded Maryland's fiscal outlook to "negative," citing looming structural deficits driven by state funding needed for Kirwan. The leadership needs to engage in bipartisan dialogue and deliberations on revisions to Kirwan.

In previous negotiations, the General Assembly agreed to delay a Kirwan mandate for local school districts, but more revisions are needed. Governor Moore must call for a special legislative session as soon as possible, with the sole focus being next steps for Kirwan.

The best outcome of this special session should be:

* Bipartisan approval to pause all state funding for Kirwan until a future date
* Bipartisan approval to pause new mandates for local school boards until a future date

Maryland citizens and taxpayers deserve nothing less.

title: TCPS cuts back on summer school; board displeased with how decision was made
content: Talbot County Public Schools (TCPS) reduced summer school programs for elementary and middle school students due to pandemic-era grant cuts, saving $350,000. Superintendant Sharon Pepukayi made the decision without board input, citing a need to "reset" and consult with families, staff, and nearby districts. The district will continue 5 programs: Middle school transition, credit recovery, band camps, Summer Career Enrichment Program (multi-county), and Extended School Year for special education students. Board members expressed disappointment, concern, and dismay over the decision, questioning communication with families and the impact on students who relied on summer school due to COVID gaps.

title: Chesapeake College honors Class of 2025
content:
Chesapeake College honored its Class of 2025 on May 21 with 260 graduates. President Clifford Coppersmith welcomed the class, emphasizing the importance of hard work and connections. Former U.S. Sen. Ben Cardin received the Community Service Award for his advocacy on higher education, human rights, and environmental protection.

Cardin urged graduates to "embrace hope" and recognize history as a guide for action. Cherie Patchett, instructor of psychology, was awarded the Adjunct Innovative Teaching Award for her applied learning methods. Cianni A. Phillips, 2025 graduate, received the John T. Harrison Award for leadership and empathy.

Phillips, member of Phi Theta Kappa Honor Society with a 3.8 GPA, emphasized building support networks and giving back to the community. The commencement ceremony marked the beginning of a new chapter in graduates' lives, with opportunity and hope awaiting them.

title: Students share what America means to them
content:
American Legion Auxiliaries celebrated winners of the Americanism essay contest on May 8 in Queenstown. The contest, held annually nationwide, recognizes students' individual perspectives on what America means to them. Winners included:

- Post 296: Kaleb Brewer, Cash McQuay, Mason Dillehunt, Lily Kennedy, Josie Hall, and Piper Waldman (district winner)
- Post 18: Elsa Taylor, Grace McIntire, Tucker Crandell, Jax Forte, Maya Selby, Stella Leaman, and Aiden Gates (district winner)
- Post 278: Sydney Kreis, Quin DiRusso, Cruze Holtman, Ian Flounlacker, Jocelynn Rose Johnson, Lucy Parks, and Cole Euler (district winners)

Auxiliary heads praised hardworking students, their supportive parents, and teachers who incorporated the national auxiliary program into their curriculum. The contest has been held for 15 years by Post 296 President Nola Willis, who expressed excitement to see children accept their awards amidst a collaborative effort between local auxiliaries.

title: 2 TCPS seniors win Service Star awards
content:
May 25, 2025: Easton High School senior Kirn Khan and St. Michaels High School senior Alexandria Rockwell were recognized as Talbot County Public Schools Senior Service Stars for exceptional community service. 

Khan accumulated over 450 hours of service learning, including volunteering at the YMCA in seventh grade, Interact Club, MY Tech Clinic, Teen Court, and local STEAM camps. She plans to attend the University of Maryland on a full Banneker/Key Honors College Scholarship.

Rockwell earned over 380 hours of service learning, volunteering at the St. Michaels Community Center, National Art Honor Society, Talbot County STEM Camp, and raising funds for the STEM camp as finance and budget chair. She is the first female from St. Michaels High to receive a Naval Academy appointment and will attend the U.S. Naval Academy in the fall.

title: Community rallies around retired teacher after tornado
content:
In May 2025, an EF-1 tornado severely damaged Dan Hortert's home in Galestown, Delaware, where he and his family had lived for 50 years. The community rallied around him after a Facebook post was shared to help with cleanup efforts. Over 100 people showed up, including former students, teachers, parents, and baseball team members, bringing tractors, cranes, food, and support.

Hortert, a retired science teacher and baseball coach at North Dorchester High School, was praised for his kindness and willingness to help others. The tornado damaged two trees in the front yard, one of which snapped through the roof and destroyed a shed, while another tree uprooted itself, destroying a backyard structure. Hortert's family and their cat escaped unharmed, with their kittens also surviving the storm.

Community members expressed admiration for Hortert, who had spent 50 years teaching at North Dorchester High School. He said that his experience showed him how good kids are at heart, and that the public schools in general were getting a bad rap.

title: Maryland school district delves into AI, conduct codes, cheating
content:
Here is a highly condensed version of the article:

Maryland's Calvert County public school system has introduced significant changes to its code of conduct, including guidelines for the use of artificial intelligence (AI). The proposed updates cover educational use, academic integrity, ethical use, supervision and monitoring, and prohibited conduct. Key additions include:

* Definition of "academic dishonesty/cheating" to include unauthorized use of digital or AI-generated materials
* Utilizing AI-generated content to harass, intimidate, or bully members of the school community is also included in the definition of bullying, harassment, and intimidation
* Mandatory inclusion of avoiding plagiarism and AI misuse in a new section titled "responsible use of technology"

The revised code was presented by Cecelia Lewis, director of student services, during the May 22 work session. Other proposed changes include adding Safe Schools Maryland contact information to report concerns.

Board members Melissa Goshorn and Jana Post expressed support for the revisions, which were developed with input from stakeholders and focus on creating a "safe, welcoming environment." The revised code will be posted online until late June for public review and comments.

Additionally, the Patuxent High School Harlequins received recognition from the school board for their superior performance at the 2025 Maryland Thespians Festival.

title: Rocketeers explode onto the scene at nearby farm

May 28, 2025 | Star Democrat

CENTREVILLE — On May 17, hobbyists from The Maryland Delaware Rocketry Association Inc. launched H-130 rockets at Central Sod Farm, following safety guidelines set by the FCC and Tripoli Rocket Association.

The launching activity, organized by association Secretary David Kemp, allowed students in Science Technology Engineering Mathematics (STEM) to learn about rocketry. Association President Fred Wallace encouraged attendees to participate, offering free launch opportunities for those 18 and under.

Club members from the Yorktown Aerospace Club, including Gavin La Rue and Austin Humes, witnessed their rockets' descent through a telescope. Other participants included Rich Custer, Erin Dawson, and married couple Glenn and Adrienne Ramey, who showcased unique rocket designs made from fenceposts and ceiling fan blades.

One landing was rough, with the chute not deploying, but overall conditions were favorable despite windy weather. The association encourages newcomers to try their hand at rocketry, offering rockets for those starting out.

title: Saints Peter and Paul seniors become alumni
content: Sts. Peter and Paul High School held its graduation ceremony on May 28, 2025. Associate Pastor Michael Angeloni gave the opening prayer and remarks, passing along a message from Pastor James Nash who is on pilgrimage. Senior Class President Francesca Villano shared memories of late-night study sessions and early morning practices with her classmates, saying they "grew through" high school. Bishop William Koenig handed out awards to 49 graduates, who were also awarded pens by the Sts. Peter and Paul School Board to sign their book of alumni.

title: Mt. Aviat alumnae gather for first reunion in 40 years
content:
Mt. Aviat alumnae gathered at Schaefer's Canal House in Chesapeake City for their first reunion in 40 years on May 30, 2025. The school was a girls-only boarding and day school from 1960 to 1972. Founded by Swiss nuns led by Sister Francis Marguerite, it had only nine graduating classes during its time.

Notable alumnae include Barbara Ashton Johnson, Eileen Stubbs Viars, Elizabeth "Betsy" Patterson Patterson, Judy Schamme Hart, and Alva Eldridge Dopp. The school was known for its strict rules, including uniform requirements that included clunky black shoes and long dark skirts below the knee.

Alumnae shared memories of their time at Mount Aviat, including a classmate who planned an escape with sheets, and the school's transition from boarding to day school in 1972. They emphasized the importance of camaraderie and relationships formed during their time together.

Key events mentioned include:

* Sister Francis Marguerite's experience being shot by Germans during World War II
* Father Naulty's role as Glee Club director
* The classmate who planned an escape with sheets

Organizations mentioned include:

* Mount Aviat Academy
* Swiss nuns
* Oblates
* Immaculate Conception Church in Elkton

Places mentioned include:

* The Swiss Inn in Elkton (now Mick's Crab House)
* Childs area of Elkton
* Germany and Italy

title: Dorchester graduates go off to write their own stories
content: Dorchester County graduated 177 seniors from North Dorchester High School and 214 from Cambridge-South Dorchester High School on Wednesday and Thursday respectively. Valedictorian Isabelle Hughs said "This moment doesn't just belong to me, it belongs to all of us." Salutatorian Elaina Jones spoke about the journey ahead, while salutatorian Julieanne Tobat and valedictorian Madison Tobat, twins, expressed gratitude for their built-in best friend. Commissioner Sputty Cephas addressed the graduates, saying "Whether you're headed to college, the workforce, the military, a gap year or still trying to figure it all out, you are not behind."

title: Easton, St. Michaels high schools celebrate graduates
content:
Easton High School and St. Michaels High School graduated their seniors in 2025. At Easton High, 291 students graduated with valedictorian Mia Mazzeo emphasizing human connection in an AI-driven world. Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi highlighted connections among students and faculty, stressing their importance.

At St. Michaels High, 60 seniors graduated with valedictorian Alexandria Rockwell, who described her class as having "incredible purpose." School principal Theresa Vener bid farewell to the graduating class after seven years, stating it was an "absolute privilege" to witness their growth into confident young adults.

Vener retired this year after 32 years in the district and received an honorary diploma. Pepukayi emphasized human connection's importance for Generation Z, while Mazzeo advised her classmates to question how the world works to change it.

title: A day for children at the library
content:
When the author was 3, they proposed a name "Coco Bang-bang" for a new sibling, but their parents considered alternatives like Catherine or Robert. A picture book about a child excitedly waiting for a new baby arrived at home from the hospital influenced the author's thinking and helped ease them into sharing attention with the new addition.

Fast forward to June 7, 2025: the 10th annual Chesapeake Children's Book Festival will be held at the Easton branch of the Talbot County Free Library. The festival features 22 children's book authors and illustrators, offering a range of works including Danielle Joseph's "Shrinking Violet," Colleen Kosinski's "A Home Again," Trinka Hakes Noble's "The Day Jimmy's Boa Ate the Wash," Jennifer O'Connell's picture books, and Timothy Young's middle-grade novel.

Traditionally, the festival is a library-sized carnival with activities like the Maryland State Opera Bears, Daughters of the American Revolution crafts, Judy Center's Make-A-Book table, Master Gardeners, Raising a Reader story walk, and more. Sponsors include the Friends of the Library, Maryland Public Television, Easton Utilities, Talbot County Government, Talbot Arts, and the Maryland State Arts Council.

At the festival, children who sign up for the library's Summer Reading Program will receive a free cookie with the crab logo and a voucher for a free book from an author of their choice. The event is open to all children, regardless of age, and promises a fun day of activities and books.

title: 'Green School' programs in Caroline County bring joy to students
content:
Caroline County's Denton Elementary and Greensboro Elementary schools became certified as Green Schools by Maryland Association for Environmental and Outdoor Education (MAEOE) in 2025, completing a two-year application process. Directors attribute the success to community support, stating "you have to work together" and receiving help from various stakeholders.

The certification comes with curriculum requirements, including outdoor environmental instruction per grade level, and projects such as composting, energy-saving, and gardening. Examples include collecting breakfast bags in classrooms (Denton Elementary) and planting gardens, native plants, and strawberries (Greensboro Elementary).

Program directors praise community partners like Pickering Creek Audubon Center, Chesapeake Bay Foundation, and Tuckahoe State Park, citing their support as "wonderful things." Both schools have secured grants for future projects.

Both Julie Strange (Denton Elementary) and Zellie Kneller Kidigarden (Greensboro Elementary) believe every school should be Green School certified, emphasizing the importance of sustainability practices for a healthy planet.

title: Colonel Richardson
content:
Colonel Richardson High School held its annual spring festival, "Festival of Stars," on June 1-2, 2025. The school featured a student-run event with over 150 participants from various clubs and organizations. Students showcased their talents in singing, dancing, playing musical instruments, and performing magic tricks. The festival also included food vendors, games, and activities such as photo booths and face painting.

Colonel Richardson High School's student government, led by student council president Ashley Murphy, organized the event. Over 100 students participated in music performances, including duos and groups.

Notable performers included students from various clubs, such as the school's choir, band, and orchestra. Other notable participants included members of the school's dance teams, cheer squads, and magic club.

The festival was attended by over 500 people, making it a successful event for Colonel Richardson High School.

title: Lockerman Middle School Committee heard and addressed concerns at second meeting
content:
Here is a highly condensed version of the article:

Lockerman Middle School Committee met on June 3, 2025, to address concerns and present options for a new school building. Architect Robyn Toth confirmed that renovating the current building was not feasible due to state assessment results. The county will proceed with a new building.

In May, the committee discussed two potential locations: behind North Caroline High School and on Double Hills Road in Denton. After public feedback, three building layout options were presented for each location.

North Carolina High School design options included two plans for a two-story building with wings separated by grade level, one with relocated baseball and softball fields, and another with a three-story building design. Double Hills Road designs featured the same options but with different entrance, building, and parking locations.

Superintendent Derek Simmons stated that the flexibility of the options allowed for better visualization of the school layout. The public has until June 9 to respond to an online survey, and the top-ranked designs will be presented to the Caroline County Board of Education in July. A decision on a location is expected by August to maintain construction timeline.

Key people involved: Robyn Toth (architect), Derek Simmons (Superintendent).

title: Caroline County graduations highlight memories and futures
content:
Here is a highly condensed version of the article:

Caroline County held graduations on May 28 and 29 at two high schools: Colonel Richardson High School and North Caroline High School.

Colonel Richardson:
