- Keynote speaker Danielle Dennis, teacher of the year for 2024-25, praised the class's special bond.
- DyAsia Thompson, senior class president, reflected on shared memories and formed lasting bonds with classmates.
- Wilson Clough was valedictorian and recognized his guidance counselor, Ms. Reed, on her birthday.

North Caroline High School:
- 274 seniors graduated
- Keynote speaker Marnie Stockman, CEO of multiple businesses, advised graduates to take charge of their lives like a business.
- Three valedictorians: Issabelle Greeno, Elizabeth Knott, and Nadelyn Porter.
- Ten sets of twins were among the graduates.
- Six North Caroline graduates plan to join the military.

Both schools honored graduates who joined the military this year.

title: Trump wiped out 75 years of science leadership
content:
The US higher education system faces a significant threat from the Trump administration's policies, which may drive away foreign students and researchers estimated to contribute $38 billion annually. In 2023-2024, 1.1 million foreign students were studying in the US, with 378,000 supporting academic jobs.

Two cases of Palestinian students (Mahmoud Khalil and Rumeysa Ozturk) were revoked of their student visas for peaceful protesting against the war in Gaza, and around 300 students were listed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio to be expelled.

Foreign students have played a crucial role in successful startups in Silicon Valley, and their presence has contributed significantly to US leadership in medical science research. In the past, Germany's brain drain was reversed after World War II when scientists like Wernher von Braun were invited to the US.

The US has won 72 Nobel Prizes in science since 2000, with around 30% won by immigrants. The Trump administration's policies threaten the academic freedom and funding of top universities, including Harvard University.

The National Science Foundation (established in 1950) and National Institutes of Health (established earlier) are also facing withdrawal of funds, with 75% of respondents to a science publication considering moving their research elsewhere due to government harassment.

title: Stroke of pen loses 75 years of science leadership
content:
The US higher educational system risks losing $38 billion annually due to foreign student exodus. In 2023-2024, 1.1 million foreign students studied in the US, supporting 378,000 academic jobs. On April 19, CNN reported thousands of international students' visas were revoked; 1,400 were later restored by the Trump administration.

Secretary Marco Rubio had a list of about 300 students to expel. The National Immigration Project is challenging the visa cancellations in court. Foreign students contributed to numerous successful startups in Silicon Valley and drove US leadership in medical science research.

US researchers in advanced cancer treatments, Alzheimer's drugs, sudden crib deaths, and CRISPR gene editing will be affected by federal funding cuts. In 2020, US inventors of CRISPR won the Nobel Prize in chemistry. The US once lagged behind Germany (30%) and Great Britain (20%) in science Nobel Prizes; this changed with US universities attracting top scientists.

The Trump administration threatens to withdraw funds from Harvard University ($2 billion) and other world-renowned research facilities, including National Institutes of Health and National Science Foundation. 75% of respondents to a science publication said they would consider moving their research elsewhere due to government harassment. 

US states California, Texas, Illinois, Massachusetts, New York, and Maryland will be economically impacted by the loss of foreign students.

title: Suicide of a superpower
content: The US is experiencing a "suicide of a superpower" due to Trump's cost-cutting measures, particularly targeting universities and government-funded research programs. This move threatens America's scientific ability, which was instrumental in developing the atomic bomb, satellite radio, smartphones, internet, missile shields, drones, and other smart weapons. Key institutions like Princeton, University of Chicago, Columbia, and Berkeley played crucial roles in these advancements. Future conflicts will be fought with high-tech systems, making it essential to maintain research programs and universities, which are globally envied. The author, Ralph Meyer, urges Eastern Shore leaders, including Andy Harris, to push back against Trump's decision.

title: North Caroline grad celebrating more than a high school diploma
content:
Sa'Mauria Ennals, a North Carolina High School graduate, celebrated multiple achievements: 
- Graduating from high school
- Earning an advanced transfer certificate and becoming a certified nursing assistant through Chesapeake College's nursing program
- Maintaining GPAs between 3.6 and 3.7 at both high school and college

Ennals plans to attend Towson University, majoring in nursing starting in the fall.

Her love for health care began in freshman year, solidifying her desire to be a neonatal ICU nurse by sophomore year. Ennals' motivation came from researching and gathering data on various branches of healthcare.

The dual enrollment program at Chesapeake College is not new to Ennals; her two older sisters participated in the program, earning college credits for nursing pursuits.

Ennals faced challenges getting enrolled due to discouragement from guidance counselors. She worked with Maria Bowser, her mother, and professionals like Gabrilla Moreland and Mark Berry to secure a plan allowing her to take four college classes during junior year of high school.

This "prove them wrong" approach fueled Ennals' motivation to succeed in the challenging coursework, solidifying her determination to become a nurse.

title: Massive lunch debt pressures school district
content:
Charles public school system's projected lunch debt is $640,000, straining its budget. A $5.7 million transfer was made to cover emergency repairs and unpaid meal balances. The school district faces a significant increase from pre-pandemic levels of $18,000-$20,000 per year.

Lunch debt likely stems from families choosing not to pay or failing to submit annual free/reduced lunch forms. Board members emphasized the importance of filling out forms to qualify for reimbursement.

The board is considering stronger actions, including sending unpaid debts to collections. Families have until June 30 to pay their outstanding balance.

A $20-$22.50 per hour wage increase was approved for substitute bus drivers, with an estimated cost of $20,000 extra.

title: Book festival gets kids reading
content: The North East Branch Library's annual Children's Book Festival drew over 1,000 attendees on June 20, 2025, despite rain and air quality concerns, moving from outdoors tents to indoors due to Cecil County Public Library organizers' efforts. The event featured local author Annette Whipple, who said enthusiasm remained high despite the venue change. Attendees enjoyed activities like magic shows, facepainting, and musical performances, as well as selecting free books upon arrival. Members of the Dolly Parton Imagination Library praised the festival for its success in promoting early reading among county families. The event's attendance approached last year's 1,200 attendees, with Manager Jennifer Carter stating it was "the best thing we do all year."

title: MidShore Meals til Monday launches summer meals program for kids
content:
MidShore Meals til Monday launches summer meal program for kids in Dorchester County. Founded in 2017, the initiative aims to target child hunger and provides breakfast, lunch, dinner, and snacks for children who may not receive them otherwise. The summer program began last year and will run from June 23 to Aug. 21.

In 2024, 95% of students in Dorchester County qualified for free or reduced-price meals due to the Community Eligibility Provision meal program. However, this program is only available during school hours and not during the summer.

To address this gap, MidShore Meals til Monday's summer program offers one meal box per household, containing seven complete breakfasts and lunches. The program was partially funded by No Kid Hungry and Preston Automotive, with a $5.59 million deficit faced by Dorchester County Board of Education in fiscal year 2026.

The program is available to approximately 5,000 students in Dorchester County and can be registered for online through the DCPS website or at one of the 10 pickup sites during June 23-Aug. 21.

title: Foundation of HOPE's new building to expand middle school girls program
content:
The Foundation of HOPE, a nonprofit in Easton, MD, is building a new $2.2 million, 5,200-square-foot facility to expand its middle school girls' program. The project, approved by the Easton Planning Commission, will provide a dedicated space for programming on economic development, entrepreneurship, and self-confidence. Founded in 2017, the nonprofit has grown from an after-school program to scholarships for high school students. Keasha Haythe, founder and president, remembers comments from first girls eight years ago asking for their own space. Construction could begin as soon as September.

The new building will feature office space, a reading room, fun area, cooking lessons, and more for sixth-grade girls. The program has grown to include 10 students at St. Michaels Middle School, with plans to expand to private homeschooled students. The nonprofit has already raised over $1.8 million towards the project.

Concerns about safety were raised due to the South Washington and South streets vehicular intersection, but town officials acknowledged the need for improved pedestrian and bicycle infrastructure. Permits still need to be obtained before construction can begin.

Haythe envisions a space that will break up lengthy after-school sessions, providing a more engaging experience for students.

title: Olde School Builders welcomes student apprentice
content: Olde School Builders, a local home construction company, welcomed its first apprentice, Kimberly Escalante-Garcia, a 17-year-old rising senior at North Caroline High School, on June 16, 2025. The apprenticeship was facilitated by career readiness coordinator Eric Cook and Olde School Builders President Craig Postlewait. Escalante-Garcia will be involved in all aspects of the company, including construction labor and business operations. She expressed interest in owning her own business one day. This marks a step for Olde School Builders to empower girls and young women in the construction industry, with recent partnerships including Easton Middle School's Girls Who Build club.

title: Shoe drive will start Greensboro Elementary students off on the right foot
content: St. Paul's United Methodist Church is partnering with Greensboro Elementary and the Town of Greensboro to start a shoe drive for students. Rev. Bonnie Shively came up with the idea as a way to serve the community after discussing school supplies with fellow church members. The goal is to provide new shoes for students, as many struggle to get them at the beginning of the year. The church is accepting donations of new shoes in sizes 7 toddler to size 6 adults, excluding flip flops. Residents can drop off donations at Greensboro Town Hall from August 1 to August 29.

title: Ed Spec Committee recommends North Caroline site for new Lockerman Middle
content: The Caroline County Board of Education is considering two locations for a new Lockerman Middle School: North Caroline High School site ($10 million development cost) and Double Hills Road site ($10.5 million development cost). The Ed Specs Committee recommends the North Caroline High site due to its infrastructure, educational alignment, and shared space capabilities. Proponents cite indoor/outdoor activities, event sharing, and lower costs ($500,000 cheaper). However, concerns include a solar array on the property and potential traffic on Central Avenue. The Board of Education will decide in August after considering community input and feedback.

title: Dorchester schools prepare for more cuts
content:
Dorchester County Public Schools project $642,000 federal funding loss after Trump Administration's $6.8 billion education cut. US Department of Education cited states' and localities' budgeting as reason. Programs including teacher training, internal student experiences, and English Language Learner programs impacted.

DCPS struggles financially with January budget deficit of $10.19 million, reduced to $5.59 million in March. The district eliminated after-school and summer programs. Superintendent Jymil Thompson wants to keep class sizes small and retain teachers. Board of Education aims to improve DCPS' state education ranking from 23rd out of 24.

DCPS communications specialist Casey O'Bier stated that federal funding cuts will require reallocating existing funds or eliminating programs, a "worst-case scenario." The district plans to reallocate pre-existing funds to support impacted federally funded programs.

title: Dorchester school board adjusts spending in wake of federal budget cuts
content:
Here is a condensed version of the article:

The Dorchester County Board of Education met on July 11, 2025, to discuss federal budget cuts affecting their funding. The US Department of Education will not provide the $360 million allocated to Maryland, with Dorchester's share being approximately $642,000.

Dorchester County Public Schools are already struggling financially with a $10.19 million deficit. However, the board made several approvals, including:

* A 5-year contract for writing instruction and assessments ($50,000)
* A 5-year IXL learning contract for grades 3-12 ($23,000)
* Math Curriculum Consumables (paid from this year's textbook budget)
* Annual contract with the Dorchester County Health Department
* Facilities Master Plan Update

The board did not renew or approve Lexia, a computer-based literacy program due to concerns over its effectiveness and cost.

Upcoming meetings include August discussions on digital devices, AI, and dress codes.

title: Moving to the music
content:
On June 27, 2025, ten students from Ashton Mooday's modern band camp at Chestertown recorded a song in a professional studio under Ken Schweitzer's grant for small independent artists. The students chose "Best Day of My Life" by American Authors and were assisted by audio engineer students Stevie Lyles and Mariana Kilman, guitar teacher Matt Wirtz, and drum set instructor Emily Holden. Mooday, a 28-year-old singer/songwriter and music teacher, said the experience was beneficial for her students to see the hard work behind music production.

The recording process took two hours, and the finished track was delivered to Mooday in time for a final performance at her Music LLC studio that afternoon. The students performed two songs, including their recorded track and "OK Not To Be OK" by Marshmello. On September 11, 2025, Mooday's sixth year teaching music changed her life and allowed her to share it with others. She owns Mooday's Music LLC, which will expand to add more space for private lessons, kid classes, and homeschoolers.

title: Dorchester County Board of Education discusses student devices
content: The Dorchester County Board of Education will revisit its student device policy due to ineffective pouches implemented at three middle schools in October last year. The pupils outsmarted the pouches, prompting Superintendent Jymil Thompson's comment that they are "crafty young people." To address this issue, the board aims to adopt a new policy by August 21. Instead of pouches, it is likely to lock devices in lockers or backpacks; a motion has been made for first read with revisions to be implemented before final approval at the next meeting.

title: Washington College receives $4.5 million gift
content:
Richard and Tara Wood, Washington College alumni and parents of a recent graduate, have made a $4.5 million multi-year gift to fund endowed chairs in leadership and international business, as well as improvements to tennis and sailing initiatives. The gift will support:

* Creation of the Wood Director of Leadership role ($2.5M), attracting top-tier leaders for special programs
* Establishment of the Wood Family Chair within Business Management Department for International Business ($750,000)
* Indoor tennis facility construction challenge grant ($1 million)
* Washington College Sailing Program support ($250,000)

Washington College President Mike Sosulski said: "This new role will allow us to expand co-curricular offerings and provide dynamic leadership development experiences." The Woods committed: "We are deeply committed to Washington College's enduring mission of cultivating well-rounded citizen leaders."

 Date: July 18, 2025

title: 'Closing gaps': TCPS data shows some literacy, math improvements
content:
Test score data from Talbot County Public Schools (TCPS) shows improvements in math and English literacy for some students, particularly Black and Hispanic students. In 2024-2025:

* 68% of kindergarten students scored at or above the 50th percentile in math.
* Percentage of students meeting or exceeding the 50th percentile mark increased across grades.
* Black and Hispanic third graders saw a 31% year-to-year jump in math, while ELA scores improved by 21%.
* DIBELS scores showed increases in rising first and third graders, but decreased for second graders.
* Fifth-grade ELA performance declined, with drops of 6.6% overall and up to 15.5% among specific subgroups.
* The incoming sixth-grade class performed 4.1% worse in ELA than they did in fourth grade.

TCPS Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi attributes the improvements to improved curriculum and teacher dedication. She plans to focus on addressing trends at the elementary-to-middle transition, including filling open reading and math coach positions.

title: Hip-Hop meets High Street
content:
A two-week summer course called Hip Hop Time Capsule merged local history with creativity in Chestertown, MD. Washington College's Starr Center for the Study of the American Experience and Chesapeake Heartland: An African American Humanities Project partnered with Minary's Dream Alliance to offer students from Cecil, Queen Anne's, and Kent counties, along with Washington College student interns, a hip-hop infused learning experience.

The program focused on local history, particularly that of African American music in Kent County. Students worked with musicians, professors, and museum professionals to research, document, and interpret the rich history of the genre. Pat Nugent led the innovative class for five years, while Darius Johnson oversaw the project's logistics.

Students learned about hip hop, local art, and historic uptown areas before selecting a track (music, murals, metalwork, or screen printing) and spending two hours in workshops with instructors. They accessed 5,600 digitized materials of Black history, including audio clips to build beats and write original songs.

Organizers pared down the initial pool of 60 students to 39, who received $1,200 each and $1,422 for the college interns. The program concluded on July 25 with a special event attended by nearly 100 children from Horizons of Kent and Queen Anne's programs. The art on the building is temporary, intended as a way for interns to express creativity and passion while engaging in community outreach.

The Hip Hop Time Capsule program aims to become a vibrant crossroads for both campus and community, with organizers believing that innovation requires relationships and responsiveness to community interests.

title: Talbot, Kent see rise in student homelessness
content:
Kent and Talbot counties in Maryland saw the largest year-to-year increase in student homelessness, with Kent County's rate rising by 55% to 102 students and Talbot County's increasing by 39% to 324 students. The counts are attributed to improved training for school staff to identify homeless students under the McKinney-Vento Act, as well as economic challenges following the COVID-19 pandemic.

Kent County Public Schools spokesperson Dan Divilio notes that "homelessness in Kent County looks different from the common perception" and that partnerships with local organizations have helped address the issue. Talbot County Public Schools officials attribute the increase to economic challenges faced by families after the pandemic.

Nonprofit leaders, including Julie Lowe of Talbot Interfaith Shelter and Stefanie Johnson of His Hope Ministries, report seeing an increase in calls for assistance from Kent County and other Eastern Shore districts. Shelters are moving to assist homeless youth, but face unique obstacles in helping 13- to 18-year-olds without guardianship or family presence.

The state numbers show that Kent County has 6% of its students experiencing homelessness, while Talbot County has 7%. Other districts on the Eastern Shore have lower rates, but still need assistance. The McKinney-Vento data for 2024-2025 has not yet been released, but shelters are preparing to address the issue.

Easton-based Talbot Interfaith housed 31 children last school year, with a "steady increase" since then. His Hope Ministries faces challenges in helping single parents and families transition from shelter to independent living due to affordability issues.

title: Washington College opens up pub on campus
content: Washington College has opened The Golden Goose pub on campus, located in Hynson Lounge, with a liquor license approved by Kent County Commissioners. The license allows students 21+ to drink, with measures in place to prevent underage entry, including signs and ID checks. Commissioner Bonnie Pearsall will regularly enforce laws, and students are allowed two guests. The pub is not open to the public, and governing bodies decided on it through a discussion that involved Kent County Attorney Tom Yeager and college officials.

title: Lockerman High School celebrates 95th anniversary
content:
Lockerman High School celebrated its 95th anniversary on July 29, 2025. The event featured a theme of "Capturing our history, preserving our legacy and advancing our future." Chairperson Willie Woods described the celebration as "gratifying" to see different generations come together.

The school was founded in 1930 by Isaac Thomas and named after Joseph H. Lockerman, a Black educator born in 1862 near Denton. It remained closed as a Black high school from 1966 until its name was restored in 1993 at a Lockerman Middle School pre-dedication ceremony.

The Lockerman Schools Association Inc., established in 1993, is a nonprofit organization that engages in educational and charitable activities for students with ties to the Lockerman Schools. The association presented awards and certificates to classes 1935, 1945, 1955, and 1965 members who could not attend.

The event also included the presentation of 13 scholarships to Caroline County students pursuing higher education and attendance by Caroline County and Board of Education officials.

title: Green thumbs: Kids, teens learn to grow plants nature's way
content:
Kids in a summer program at Kent County Parks and Recreation are learning to grow plants naturally without pesticides. Former U.S. Rep. Wayne Gilchrest is working with Parks and Recreation to teach kids about horticulture using natural methods. The program uses 40-gallon water drums, compost piles of hay, cedar chips, cow manure, and food scraps.

Gilchrest teaches kids about copying natural conditions in the garden, including attracting wolf spiders that help control insect pests. The program also covers photosynthesis, soil health, and the importance of a vital ecosystem for all living things.

Expert growers like Beth Hill, Eric Fitch, and Master Gardeners from the University of Maryland Extension are involved in the program. Kids learn to identify beneficial and harmful insects, including dogbane beetles, butterflies, and dragonflies.

The program aims to expand, possibly adding a solar-powered well 100 feet deep, with plans to donate plants, hay, and cow manure to support the initiative. The second-year program has received positive feedback from kids and counselors, with hopes for future growth and expansion.

title: Board of Ed selects North Caroline site for new Lockerman Middle
content:
Caroline County Board of Education unanimously voted to select the North Caroline High site for the new Lockerman Middle School on August 5, 2025. The site will allow for 15.52 acres of space and is adjacent to North Caroline High School, allowing for shared events and facilities. Architect Robyn Toth cited infrastructure readiness, educational alignment, and shared event spaces as reasons for the recommended site.

Board director Bill Mengel expressed concern over a solar array on the property, currently being discussed with Tesla for purchase at an estimated $180,000 (excluding relocation costs).

The decision marks an early step in the planning process before the new school's construction.

title: 'Meeting of the hearts': Women to Watch panelists share advice on mindfulness
content:
60 women from the Mid-Shore attended the third annual Women to Watch Summer Speaker Series hosted by APG Chesapeake in Easton on August 7, 2025. Moderator Cassandra Vanhooser emphasized the importance of mindfulness. Four panelists shared their advice:

- Anne Altvater (Campbell's Lane Farm) recommended being present and letting go of judgment, with animals serving as examples.
- Morgan Foster (The Pivot Process) encouraged embracing emotions and recognizing them, saying "sit in it."
- Shania Gregory (Easton YMCA) advised slowing down and finding time to think, using donkeys as a metaphor for mindfulness.
- Amber McGinnis (Chesapeake College) noted the importance of being okay with boredom and avoiding screens during stressful moments.

The panelists discussed ways to remain mindful in a world full of technology. Key takeaways include:

* Being present in the moment
* Embracing emotions and recognizing them
* Finding time to think without screens
* Slowing down and practicing mindfulness

Upcoming events include August 14's Summer Speaker Series at White Oak Manor, featuring Megan McRay moderating a panel of four speakers. This year's panelists will select their successors for the 2026 Summer Speaker Series.

title: New learning center in southern Maryland provides resources for children with autism
content:
A new learning center in Waldorf, Maryland, offers resources for children with autism through SPARKS ABA. The center provides personalized therapy treatments and serves 30 Charles County families. Genevieve Marshall, senior regional director, said the location offers a space for families to stay during sessions. Leah Jones, behavioral analyst, described the learning center as an open space for play, arts, and crafts.

SPARKS ABA uses applied behavioral analysis (ABA) with three components: "applied," focusing on solutions; "behavior," measuring social interactions and skills; and "analysis," evaluating data to ensure goal changes. The organization plans a Halloween-themed open house on October 25.

Every child is assigned a technician for one-to-one support, and they offer multi-learning instruction, including peer-based learning opportunities. SPARKS ABA aims to change the trajectory of a child's learning, with treatment measured in six-month increments. The goal is to integrate therapy into everyday life.

title: 'Horses are my happy place': Horse rescue welcomes student readers
content:
Here is a highly condensed version of the article:

Morgan Chambers, a 9-year-old student at Calvert Elementary, says "horses are my happy place." She participated in the "Read to the Animals" program with her class at Freedom Hill Horse Rescue in Owings, where she read to retired equines. The program, available for kindergarten to fifth-grade students, aims to foster reading fluency and service-learning while promoting animal interaction.

Calvert County Public Schools' coordinator Marcy Gruver launched the initiative, similar to one in Baltimore County. The program has been fully booked every time held at Freedom Hill, with 10 retired horses participating. School officials also explored partnering with local shelters but declined due to staffing constraints.

The program's success has inspired hope that participants will consider volunteering at Freedom Hill when older. Founded 21 years ago, the nonprofit rescue organization partners with public schools, homeschool groups, Scouts, and more, hosting about two programs a month.

title: Caroline County Public Schools welcomes 40 new teachers
content: Caroline County Public Schools welcomed 40 new teachers at a breakfast and orientation. Superintendent Derek Simmons stated, "Our motto, One Family — One Vision, truly defines us." title: How will Talbot County schools regulate AI this year?
content:
Talbot County schools have outlined new guidelines for artificial intelligence use in the 2025-26 school year. Director of Teaching and Learning Robin Werner presented guidelines at a Board of Education meeting, emphasizing responsible AI tool use by staff. Key points include:

* Staff should not rely solely on AI tools for lesson planning or classroom decisions
* Safe procedures for students will be established
* Prohibited uses of AI will be outlined
* A rubric to pilot this school year will be implemented

The guidelines will take effect as the district prepares for back-to-school.

title: Talbot school officials discuss AI guidelines for students, teachers
content:
Here is a highly condensed version of the article:

Talbot County school officials discussed AI guidelines for students and teachers. Director of teaching and learning Robin Werner presented an AI guidelines document to be observed this school year, encouraging transparency and human oversight. The document outlines how staff and students should use AI responsibly.

A committee of teachers and administrators developed the guidelines in response to the district's need to regulate AI use. Werner said the state is lagging behind other states in creating AI rules, but recommended waiting for state updates before revising Talbot County Public Schools' policies.

Board members discussed adopting an AI policy or administrative regulation, with some recommending a clear set of standards. The guidelines highlight specific rules, including prohibitions on using AI to plagiarize or bully, and provide a rubric (0-4) for students to use AI responsibly.

The district will pilot the rubric this year and encourage "teachable moments" instead of automatic discipline. Members of Talbot's AI committee will visit elementary schools to stay on top of the issue and provide guidance.

Key points:

* Robin Werner presented an AI guidelines document to be observed this school year.
* The guidelines emphasize transparency, human oversight, and responsible AI use.
* State rules for AI are lagging behind other states, but Talbot County Public Schools will wait for updates before revising policies.
* Board members discussed adopting an AI policy or administrative regulation, with some recommending clear standards.
* Specific rules include prohibitions on using AI to plagiarize or bully, and a rubric (0-4) for students to use AI responsibly.

title: As students return, Chapel District Elementary begins next phase of renovations
content:
Chapel District Elementary School in Cordova, MD is undergoing a $27 million renovation, part of a multimillion-dollar effort to fully renovate the existing building, adding 16,000 square feet. Construction led by Whiting-Turner Contracting Company began in phases with completion expected in 2026.

Renovations completed so far include the school cafeteria and some classrooms; the Critchlow Adkins Children's Center site was redone in phase one. Teacher and staff returned to the school earlier this week, with Principal Kari Clow noting a smooth transition.

Due to construction, the gym won't be ready on the first day of school (expected by September), and PE classes will be held outside or in select classrooms. Some hallway flooring remains unfloored, but it is deemed safe in the meantime.

Furniture for phases one and two arrived on time, while phase three furniture was ordered at the same time as tariffs took effect; some furniture is being kept in warehouses by the supplier at no cost to the district.

Construction includes renovations to administrative offices, classrooms, and a new media center. Drivers passing the school will see significant construction work obstructing the front of the building. The temporary front office is located at the back of the building.

Talbot County Public Schools Director of Operations Kevin Shafer acknowledged some concessions were made to complete the project on time; Talbot County Public Schools Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi praised the school administrators, teachers, and staff for their efforts despite the construction noise and disruption.

content:

content:

title: Dorchester schools restricting cell phone usage
content:
Dorchester County Board of Education passed a new student policy banning the use of personal electronic devices during school hours, effective September 2. The policy, harsher than previous years', prohibits students from using devices for internet safety and portable communication, with consequences including confiscation and discipline for recording or sharing inappropriate content.

Board President Sheri Hubbard recognized the learning curve for students and parents, citing a presentation by a high school student that showed improved class discussions without phones. Board member Peter Singleton, who has worked 53 years in Dorchester schools, advocated for the stricter policy, citing negative effects of phone usage during classes or hallways.

The board received 115 public comments, with 38 in favor, 59 offering suggestions, and seven opposing the policy. Board members acknowledged the responses and addressed concerns regarding the policy's language. Assistant Superintendent Michael Collins stated that the new policy aims to improve face-to-face communication among students.

Key dates: August 21 (board meeting), September 2 (school year begins).

Key people: Sheri Hubbard (Board President), Peter Singleton (long-time Dorchester schools employee), Chris Wheedleton (Board member), Michael Collins (Dorchester Assistant Superintendent).

title: If we want reading success, we need to invest
content:
Maryland is on track to release its 2025 MCAP test scores, reflecting investments since 2013 and ongoing policies under state Superintendent Carey Wright. Despite progress in establishing a pre-K-3 Literacy Policy, revising standards, and launching coaching models, the state's commitment remains time-limited and unsustainable.

Wright has secured $40 million over five years from the US Department of Education, $6.8 million from the IBIS Group, and over $3 million in private funding for literacy coaching programs. However, these investments are insufficient to address the reading crisis and will not lead to dramatic improvement without sustained state commitment.

In contrast, Mississippi's Literacy-Based Promotion Act dedicated $15 million annually to literacy coaching and support under Wright's leadership, resulting in significant gains. Maryland's Excellence in Schools Act authorized a school leadership training program but allocated zero dollars for implementation, leaving only the expiring Targeted Support and Improvement program as direct support for reading.

To achieve results similar to Mississippi, Maryland must invest real, sustained resources in literacy, rather than relying on federal and philanthropic grants or external funding. The state legislature must step up to fund a comprehensive reading agenda worthy of its children's potential.

title: State test scores: Mid-Shore school districts see mixed results
content:

The Mid-Shore's five counties - Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's, and Talbot - showed mixed results:

- Dorchester County outpaced all other counties in year-to-year gains in English, increasing by 7.6% to a 41.3% proficiency rate (19th in the state).
- Queen Anne's remains the Mid-Shore county most proficient in math at 31.6%, with a 2.9% hike.
- Kent County saw a decrease in English and math proficiency, ranking 20th in English and 21st in math.
- Talbot County Public Schools experienced significant decreases in both subjects: -1.9% for English (16th) and 0.6% for math (18th).

title: Cellphone pouches are back in Caroline County middle schools
content:
Caroline County Public Schools will reintroduce cellphone pouches in middle schools for a second year, starting from the 2025-26 school year. The program aims to keep students off their phones during the school day. Each student has a locked pouch with their phone inside, which is unlocked at the end of the day using a magnetic device.

Cellphone pouches were introduced in the 2024-25 school year as a pilot program and saw a success rate, according to Superintendent Derek Simmons. Statistics showed:

* 30.6% fewer referrals
* 130 fewer attacks, threats or fights
* 200 fewer instances of disrespect and disruptions

Simmons stated that students and parents have been receptive to the pouches, with minimal resistance. The program was created by Yondr and tested in both middle schools last year.

After another school year at the middle school level, CCPS will revisit the topic and potentially incorporate cellphone pouches into the high school level.

title: Constitution Bowl contest is coming to Easton
content:
The Mid-Shore Constitution Alliance hosts the inaugural U.S. Constitution Scholastic Competition on Sept 20, 9 a.m.-12:30 p.m. at the Talbot County Free Library, in partnership with the Colonel Tench Tilghman Chapter of the Sons of the American Revolution. Six schools (Cambridge-South Dorchester High School, Easton High School, The Gunston School, North Caroline High School, St. Michael's High School, Saints Peter and Paul High School) compete in teams of three students plus alternates, earning community recognition and prizes for top performers.

The event is part of the Constitution Alliance's events during Constitution Week (Sept 14-20), including a Sept 17 celebration at the Academy Art Museum featuring Frederick Douglass and Thomas Jefferson reenactors. The competition follows federal requirements that schools recognizing Constitution Day during this timeframe must provide an engaging educational experience.

title: Dorchester schools climb in state rankings after first year of ambitious reform plan
content:
Dorchester County Public Schools Superintendent Jymil Thompson implemented a three-year reform plan to move from ranking 23rd out of 24 in Maryland Comprehensive Assessment Program evaluations to 15th. One year into the initiative, testing data shows progress: moving up two spots overall and improving English Learning Arts proficiency from 19th to 17th.

Key strategies include setting a clear vision, quarterly walkthroughs, instruction focus, teacher support, differentiated learning, simplified processes, and system structures. The district's "Believe in Us" strategic plan guides these efforts with core values of joy, prioritizing children, and accountability.

Thompson emphasizes community involvement for successful implementation: "Education is a community issue." He aims to act as a catalyst for countywide transformation through incremental progress and innovation.

Recruiting certified teachers and administrators to improve the district's attractiveness to parents is underway. Early results are promising, but Thompson acknowledges challenges ahead. He remains committed, stating, "There's no challenge we can't overcome" if the community works together creatively.

Challenges will not deter Thompson, who wants community members to be active participants in the process and happy with progress rather than just innocent bystanders.

title: Federalsburg Judy Center celebrates 25 years
content:
The Federalsburg Judy Center Hub in Caroline County, Maryland celebrated its 25th anniversary. The center, operated by Caroline County Public Schools, aims to promote school readiness through community partnerships and provides early intervention services for children ages 5 and younger.

Heather Harding, coordinator, explained the center's approach: "We offer play groups, family engagements, parent training, and service that meets family needs." Elizabeth Saylor, supervisor of instruction, said the celebration focused on families, featuring a big family event and inviting previous employees to return as "work families."

Staff praised the impact of their work, with Harding stating, "The best reward is seeing the difference made in children's lives." Ms. Tearesa French, former supervisor, had led Early Head Start for 22 years.

title: Country Cooking: Welcome back to school and school lunches
content:
Country Cooking author Marie Savage reflects on school lunches from her childhood to the present day in Easton, Maryland. She shares memories of her young elementary school days, waiting for the bus with new clothes and packed lunch boxes containing staples like oatmeal, scrambled eggs, and peanut butter sandwiches.

Savage notes that many counties now offer free school lunches, a long-overdue change. However, she acknowledges that some children still prefer to pack their own lunches, which can be expensive.

As Savage explores school lunch options from the 1950s to the present day, she highlights the evolution of food choices and packaging. She shares recipes for classic dishes like BBQ chicken cups, PB&J apples, pickle roll-ups, turkey club roll-ups, grilled cheese roll-ups, and Nutella banana sushi.

Savage also mentions changes in school cafeterias, including the introduction of new menu items, staff growth, and increased allergen awareness due to rising peanut, gluten, and dairy restrictions. She expresses appreciation for the food staff's efforts to provide enjoyable lunches for students nationwide.

The article concludes with Savage sharing her own pre-packaged snacks and lunch ideas, such as a "lunchbox basket" filled with trail mix, whole grain crackers, and fruit leather, as well as a community park built on the site of a former school.

content:

title: Gen Z’s lessons on Sept. 11: A generation raised in its shadow calls for deeper lessons
content:
Addison Nogar, a junior at Kent Island High School, reflects on September 11 and its impact on her generation. Growing up in the shadow of the tragedy, she never fully grasped its enormity until visiting the 9/11 Memorial in 2023.

The author recalls learning about Welles Crowther, a 24-year-old volunteer firefighter who died on 9/11 while saving over 18 lives. He wore a red bandana under his helmet, which became a symbol of courage and selflessness.

Nogar's fifth-grade teacher introduced her to Crowther's story, sparking her interest in the tragedy. In 2013, she watched the movie "World Trade Center," which left a lasting impression on her.

In April 2023, Nogar visited the National September 11 Memorial and Museum, where she took a 90-minute tour that explored the history of the site and highlighted the stories of those affected by the attacks. She was particularly moved by the Survivor Tree, a Callery pear tree that survived the attacks and now stands as a living reminder of resilience.

Nogar believes that September 11 deserves deep respect and appreciation, and that teachers should dedicate time to discuss its impact. With her generation being old enough to grasp the tragedy more fully, it's fitting for them to share narratives from that day and honor the moment of silence it has earned.

* 2010: Survivor Tree returns to the memorial after recovery

* 2023: Author becomes old enough to grasp the tragedy more fully

title: Girls' STEM gains are slipping
content:
On September 17, 2025, a Star Democrat article reported that girls' gains in math and science subjects are declining at a faster rate than boys nationwide since the pandemic. Local Mid-Shore school districts showed this trend. After reaching out to district representatives for explanations and responses, only one district responded.

To gather more information, reporter Lily Tierney contacted a statewide youth STEM programming group, which rounded out her story. The article provided insights into this growing issue affecting girls in STEM education.

title: Girls lose gains in math and science post-pandemic
content:
Girls lost gains in math and science post-pandemic, with a national trend showing girls declining at a faster rate than boys. In Maryland, girls fell behind by an average of 49% of a grade level more than boys between 2019 and 2024.

Maryland experienced one of the largest drops in girls' math scores compared to boys. Talbot County followed this trend, with Caroline and Dorchester counties also showing declines. However, some districts stood out more than others, such as Dorchester County's "23 no more" initiative, which aimed to improve achievement across the board.

Dorchester County saw the worst decline in girls' math scores, dropping 1.05 points, while boys dropped 0.85 points. The district is working to address learning gaps with initiatives such as teacher training, small-group math support, and expanded STEM opportunities.

Girls were initially outperforming boys in math and science on average, but this trend reversed in 2023. Boys outperformed girls in nine out of every 10 school districts, including Talbot County. However, girls still outperformed boys in two Mid-Shore districts, Caroline and Dorchester counties.

No Maryland district has fully recovered their pre-2019 math levels. The Stanford Education Data Archive found that both boys and girls are roughly 2 to 2½ grade levels behind in math compared to the state average.

title: Queen Anne's denies charter school application
content:
Queen Anne's County Public Schools Board of Education voted 3-2 to deny the Queen Anne's County Classical Charter School application due to significant deficiencies in academic planning, operational capacity, and demonstrated need.

The committee recommended denial citing gaps in evidence for financial readiness, staffing, facility acquisition planning, and serving students with disabilities. However, the group acknowledged the charter school's enthusiasm for the classical model, timely communication, and commitment to school choice.

The application lacked evidence of innovation, governance readiness, and failed to articulate how it would meet diverse student needs. The committee noted major gaps despite multiple opportunities to address deficiencies.

The Queen Anne's County Classical Charter School group presented a final report and answer questions before the Board's decision. If approved, the charter school would continually seek collaboration with QACPS in establishing a charter agreement.

The group claimed interest from the community, including letters of support from the county commissioners and partners like the Giving the Edge Foundation. However, the Board questioned student sustainability and demonstration of need.

A broad petition collected over 200 signatures from county residents and outside supporters. The committee planned to perform more surveys and ensure future marketing to target families with elementary-age children.

The QACPS Board of Education will next meet on Oct. 1 at 6 p.m. The charter school applicant retains the right to appeal to the Maryland State Board of Education or resubmit during the next application window.

title: Early Head Start funding discussion expected at County Commissioners meeting on Tuesday
content: The Caroline County Commissioners meeting on September 23, 2025, will discuss Early Head Start funding. Charles Huester, executive director of the Maryland Rural Development Cooperation (MRDC), is expected to attend to discuss the program's ending due to lack of Office of Head Start funding. The MRDC announced that the program would end effective September 2, 2025, and staff will remain available until September 30, 2025. title: Caroline County officials learn about Early Head Start cut
content:
Caroline County officials learned about the Early Head Start program cut by Charles Huester, executive director of Maryland Rural Development Cooperation. On August 27, MRDC announced the program's end due to a funding decision by Office of Head Start. The organization applied for $3 million but as a direct recipient instead of a subrecipient, losing its funding. 

MRDC reached out to Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md., 1st), who sent a letter to the Office of Head Start without a response. Huester discussed exploring options, including introducing a Patty Center model and fee structure with Greensboro and Federalsburg spaces. Existing Head Start spots will be converted, and a collaboration with Maryland State Department of Education for classroom models is being considered.

September 2 marked the effective date of the program's end. The free program supported pregnant women and young children's learning and development, with over $1 million in funding initially secured by MRDC.

title: Talbot school board dives into test score trends
content:
Talbot school officials analyzed 2024-2025 Maryland Comprehensive Assessment Program scores, showing upward trends in math and English for some grades but dips in others. 

Helga Einhorn presented breakdowns of state test scores by grade and student group to the Talbot Board of Education on Sept. 15. Proficiency rates increased statewide, but Talbot County students saw mixed results.

English proficiency dropped to 45.4%, with significant year-to-year decreases for fifth (5.6%) and tenth (10%) grades, while fourth-grade proficiency rose to 50%. 

Math proficiency increased in some grades, such as fourth (32%), sixth (18.9%), and seventh (17%). However, Algebra II proficiency plummeted from 32.8% to 7.1%.

The district's results kept board member Deborah Bridges up at night, and she wondered about missing solutions. Board members emphasized finding solutions rather than blaming teachers or staff.

Board President Emily Jackson expressed concerns over the gap in math proficiency for Black students, with only 4% proficient in 2024-2025. The district plans to address this through community partnerships and new math standards going into effect next school year.

title: Test data shows areas for growth in Talbot schools
content: Talbot County school officials analyzed student test data and identified key areas for improvement, despite some gains in scores. The county fell behind other counties last year. Board members discussed findings from a workshop and regular meeting, with one admitting the results kept them up at night.

title: Maryland Supreme Court coming to Easton for first time since 1851
content:
The Maryland Supreme Court is holding a special oral arguments hearing at Easton High School on October 3, 2025. Two cases - one civil and one criminal - will be heard starting at 9:30 a.m., open to the public. The court's Justice Brynja Booth said this event aims to increase public confidence in the judiciary, as trust has eroded lately.

Booth believes off-site hearings, happening in Prince George's, Baltimore, Montgomery, and St. Mary's County, will encourage students to explore law on the Eastern Shore. She hopes to attract more attorneys to the area, calling it a "wonderful place to practice law and raise a family."

The court, consisting of Chief Justice Matthew Fader and seven justices, including Booth, has not sat in Easton since 1851. The special hearing is a historic event for the Maryland Supreme Court, which usually operates from its Annapolis building.

Two cases will be heard: one involving whether courts can require unlicensed landlords to pay rent, and another about police stopping drivers for suspected mobile phone use. Students from local high schools and Chesapeake College are expected to attend, including those from Talbot County Public Schools, where Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi and Assistant Superintendent Helga Einhorn coordinated the event.

title: Maryland Supreme Court makes 'unprecedented' trip to Easton
content: The Maryland Supreme Court visited Easton High School on October 3, 2025, for oral arguments in two cases, marking an unprecedented event as it had been 174 years since the court last held a session there in 1851. Hundreds of students and public members attended the event, which is part of the Maryland Judiciary's off-site trip initiative. Easton High junior Lorelai Yacks asked justices about their experiences, while Talbot County Public Schools Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi praised the real-world experience for her students.

title: A day to remember at the library
content:
The Talbot County Free Library celebrated its 100th anniversary on October 16, 2025. The library was a community undertaking in 1922, led by Caroline Burnite Walker and 40 women who raised $4,149 to establish it. The first librarian was hired for $900/year, and the library opened with an 800-book collection.

In 1925, Josephine Baker's La Revue Nègre premiered in Paris, Howard Carter discovered Tutankhamun's burial chamber, and a War of the Stray Dog broke out between Greece and Bulgaria. The library will host a gala soirée inspired by the roaring '20s on October 16.

Upcoming events include:

* A talk by Carole Boston Weatherford and Jeffrey Boston Weatherford about "Kin: Rooted in Hope" on October 7
* A talk by professor Richard Bell about Tench Tilghman on October 25
* The official launch of "Adventures in Shelving, Vol. 2" on December 1

The library will feature music by Darrell Parsons' Julie Parsons Project Jazz Duo and upscale hors d'oeuvres prepared by Royal Oak Catering. Tickets are available at tcfl.org/CentennialTicketsSponsorships/.

title: 'Priceless': Students watch Maryland Supreme Court hearings at Easton High
content:
On October 3, 2025, the Maryland Supreme Court held hearings at Easton High School, a rare event that marked the first time the court had sat in the school since 1851. Seven justices, led by Justice Brynja Booth, heard oral arguments for two cases: one civil and one criminal, involving whether police officers have reasonable suspicion to pull over drivers for touching or manipulating a cell phone while driving and whether a court can require tenants to pay rent when asked by an unlicensed landlord.

The court also participated in a question-and-answer session with hundreds of students from local high schools, including Easton High School, St. Michaels High, The Gunston School, and Chesapeake College. Students asked the justices about their experiences, how they check for personal biases, and what cases have stood out to them.

Notable remarks included Justice Stephen Gould stating that he prefers cases with excellent lawyers and Justice Angela Eaves emphasizing that the court resolves cases based on factual records and law, rather than personal feelings. Chief Justice Matthew Fader advised students studying law to keep their learning broad and emphasized that law is a field that encompasses many areas of life.

The event aimed to expose students to the law field and allow them to interact with the justices through a lunch session, with Talbot County Public Schools Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi praising the experience as "priceless" for its real-world examples and experiences.

title: 'Bring people together': Radio station honoring Harriet Tubman launches in Mid-Shore
content:
A new radio station, WFHW 90.3 FM, will launch in Mid-Shore Maryland on October 10, 2025, honoring Harriet Tubman's legacy. The station is a joint effort between WHCP 91.7 FM and the Harriet Tubman Museum and Educational Center. Amanda Tilghman, WHCP station manager, and Linda Harris, museum director, spearheaded the project over two years.

The call letters "Find Harriet Within" reflect the station's goal of educating residents about Tubman's life as an abolitionist who escaped slavery and helped others using the Underground Railroad. Harris hopes to read books on Tubman on-air and tape interviews with participants in the museum's walking tours.

WFHW aims to unite people by hosting a five-day-a-week, hour-long talk show interviewing local figures and sharing their journeys. The station will also expand Radio Chesapeake's reach, making it more accessible to residents on the western side of the Eastern Shore. A partnership with Building African American Minds (BAAM) nonprofit will allow kids in BAAM programs to host their own shows.

Programming on WFHW includes WHCP's lead news programs and nationally syndicated shows. Harris plans to convey a message of love, community, compassion, and empathy over the airwaves, stating "we need that now more than ever."

title: Banned books once again increasing
content:
The American Library Association's Banned Book Week began its 43rd year on October 5-11, 2025. PEN America reported a surge in book bans during the 2024-25 school year: 6,870 titles challenged across 23 states and 87 public school districts. Targeted books include works by authors of color, LGBTQ+ authors, women, and those addressing racism, sexuality, gender, and history.

Public library collections saw a 92% increase in challenged titles in 2023, driven by organized groups and politicians. Libraries provide vital access to information, and censorship denies citizens' fundamental right to free speech, setting a precedent for further abuses of power.

Banned Books Week's theme "Censorship is So 1984" reflects the increasingly Orwellian world. The week aims to raise awareness about censorship and take action against it in democratic societies.

title: Talbot Board of Ed digs into student discipline trends
content:
Talbot County Public Schools officials reviewed student discipline trends during a Board of Education work session on October 14, 2025. Director of Student Services Darlene Spurrier explained that expelling a student requires an "imminent threat" indication, which is a difficult standard to meet. In the last three full school years and this year, there have been no expulsions.

Suspensions range from one to 44 days, with out-of-school suspensions steady at 46 so far this year. Arrests are on school grounds or result in action off-school grounds, while reportable offenses occur off-school grounds. Compared to neighboring counties, TCPS has a relatively low rate of suspended or expelled students.

Bullying reports have hovered around 72-73 per year. Board members discussed encouraging families to fill out bullying reports, with President Emily Jackson saying that even increased numbers are better than discouraging them.

Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi noted the state tracks disproportionate disciplinary practices for Black students and students with disabilities. Director Spurrier acknowledged the district's need to ensure equity in discipline.

title: Students experience Farm to School eating
content:
In October 2025, St. Mary's public school system hosted Farm to School events for National Farm to School Month, marking 16 years of such initiatives. 

Kaitlin Fraer, a school nutrition specialist, led three elementary schools in organizing events with various stations dedicated to farm animals, fruits, and vegetables. Three stations were visited by students: 

1. An American Dairy Association station taught students about cows and fresh milk, led by youth nutritionist specialist Beth Palumbo.
2. A University of Maryland Extension station showed kids where their fruits and vegetables come from, led by Christine Allred and Deon Littles.
3. A Beagle Hill Farm station introduced students to tractors, sweet potatoes, and farm animals like horses, pigs, goats, and bunnies.

Farmers from Beagle Hill Farm, including Adrian Hill and Greg Butterfield, taught students about agriculture while farmers from other farms provided meat for the school lunches. 

Students participated in planting sweet potatoes, using a planter to plant seeds, and met farm animals. They also received plastic toy fruits or vegetables to throw into a "fruit salad" parachute.

The events aimed to educate students about healthy eating, local produce, and agriculture. According to Butterfield, the events aim to make the next generation of farmers as the connection to food sources is getting less frequent among younger generations.

title: Talbot Board of Ed OKs contracts for EHS auditorium, Chapel Elementary windows
content: The Talbot Board of Education approved contracts for two projects: auditorium lights at Easton High School ($1.1 million) and window glazing at Chapel District Elementary School ($132,000) through a Maryland Center for School Safety grant. The work will be completed in the summer of 2026 and includes security film "prevents easy access" to the school building. Director of Operations Kevin Shafer said preliminary work will start this spring with no impact on events like concerts or plays. Board President Emily Jackson expressed slight concerns about privacy, suggesting future hearing about potential safety grants for screening students' activities.

title: 'This place impacts lives': Talbot County Free Library celebrates 100th birthday
content:
The Talbot County Free Library celebrated its 100th birthday on October 17, 2025, with community leaders and residents in attendance. State Senator Johnny Mautz returned two children's books that had been missing for 50 years, "The Ugly Duckling" (1975) and "The Steadfast Tin Soldier" (1975). Mautz called the library an "anchor" of the community and thanked staff and volunteers for their dedication.

Board of Trustees President Susan Sherman blew out candles on a 100th birthday cake. Director Dana Newman credited Caroline Burnite Walker, the library's founder in 1925, for its success. The library has grown from a small space with $15 monthly rent to a full-fledged community hub with books, computers, and research rooms.

Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher spoke about the library's impact on his life, saying it made him a better person and citing over 200 cardholders. Local authors, including Tim Young and Carole Boston Weatherford, reflected on how the library helped their journeys.

The St. Michaels branch is currently undergoing renovations to expand and add children's spaces, with completion expected in early 2026. State officials praised the library, saying it's critical for job applications, tax returns, and community services.

Comptroller Brooke Lierman said libraries like Talbot County Free Library are essential for people seeking education, resources, and community support. Governor Wes Moore's mother, Joy Moore, read a citation to the library aloud during the gala. Maryland State Librarian Morgan Miller acknowledged Talbot as an inspiration for rural libraries on the Eastern Shore.

Key dates include:

- 1925: Caroline Burnite Walker founded the Talbot County Free Library.
- 1975: "The Ugly Duckling" and "The Steadfast Tin Soldier" were last checked out.
- 2023: Carole Boston Weatherford used the library's Maryland Room for research on her book "Kin: Rooted in Hope".
- Early 2026: The St. Michaels branch expansion project will be completed.

title: Empowerment Center offers after-school education
content:
Here's a highly condensed version of the article:

The Cambridge Empowerment Center is a non-profit on historic Pine Street offering after-school education, summer learning, pre-K programs, food drives, and senior health initiatives. Director Tammy Washington oversees programs for children aged 5-13, with available slots for pre-K (free, 9 am - noon). After-school programming runs 3-6 pm with themed days like math, art, and IXL. The summer program costs $125 for six weeks, offering breakfast, lunch, field trips, education, and tennis.

The center opened in 2003, initially operating on donations and volunteers. Post-pandemic, it shifted to grant funding and now employs paid staff. Board member Julia Barker said they "had to reinvent" themselves after the pandemic. An open house is scheduled for November 9. Key figures include:

- Tammy Washington (Director of Children's Programs)
- Julia Barker (Board Member)

title: Rotarian from Uganda talks about life
content: Robin Kibuka, a Ugandan Rotarian, spoke to the Rotary Club of Cambridge about his life growing up in Uganda and its impact on his education at Yale University, Harvard University (Ph.D. in economics), and career at the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Upon retirement, he focused on giving back, sharing his legacy through books like "Build Legacy Not Inheritance" and serving on professional boards globally. He stressed the importance of listening, citing it as a key to better leadership and empathy. As a member of Muyenga Rotary Club in Kampala, Uganda, Kibuka participates in Rotary's service work, including presenting a banner from his club to the Cambridge club's president, Angie Hengst.
